title: OXO
description: OXO (1952) is noughts and crosses on Cambridge's EDSAC computer, written by A. S. Douglas for a thesis on human-computer interaction — one of the first video games.
longDescription: OXO played noughts and crosses against a human on the EDSAC, a room-sized computer at the University of Cambridge's Mathematical Laboratory and one of the first stored-program computers. Players chose one of the nine squares with a rotary telephone dial, and the board appeared on one of the EDSAC's three 35×16 dot-matrix cathode-ray tubes, normally used to show the state of its memory, which Douglas repurposed as a display. The screen updated only when the game state changed: the player's move, then the computer's. The computer could play a perfect game. Douglas wrote it in 1952 to illustrate research into how people interact with machines, and it could only be played at Cambridge's Mathematical Laboratory with special permission.
trivia: The name OXO was not Douglas's: it comes from the file name in historian Martin Campbell-Kelly's EDSAC simulator, which recreated the game.
Christopher Strachey's draughts program ran at about the same time, and it is unclear which was first to show visuals on a screen.
Under some definitions OXO is a contender for the first video game; under others it is excluded.
Its input device was a rotary telephone dial.
Some definitions exclude it because its graphics neither move nor update continuously.
devStory: Alexander "Sandy" Douglas, a doctoral candidate in mathematics at Cambridge, programmed OXO in 1952 as part of a thesis on human-computer interaction, calling it nothing more than noughts and crosses. The EDSAC had run its first program on 6 May 1949 and stayed in use until 11 July 1958. The game was discarded once it had served its purpose and later reconstructed for an EDSAC simulator.

title: Tennis for Two
description: Tennis for Two (1958) is William Higinbotham's tennis game for an oscilloscope, built for a Brookhaven National Laboratory open day and one of the earliest electronic games.
longDescription: The game showed a side view of a tennis court on an oscilloscope: a horizontal line for the court, a short vertical line for the net and a point of light for the ball. Each player had an aluminium controller with a knob to set the angle of a shot and a button to hit the ball, and a shot without enough arc hit the net. The computer reversed the ball's path when it bounced and simulated air resistance. Higinbotham considered a second knob for speed but dropped it as too complicated. Hundreds of visitors queued to play it at the 1958 exhibition, and Higinbotham said high school students liked it best. An improved 1959 version had a larger screen and let players choose the gravity of the Moon or Jupiter.
trivia: Higinbotham felt the game was not worth patenting.
In the late 1970s and early 1980s he testified for the defendants when Magnavox sued over Ralph Baer's video game patents.
A Brookhaven team rebuilt it in 1997.
A placard at the 1959 exhibition called it "Computer Tennis".
Creative Computing editor David Ahl, who played it in 1958, called Higinbotham the "Grandfather of Video Games".
devStory: Higinbotham, head of the instrumentation division at Brookhaven National Laboratory in Upton, New York, read in the manual for a Donner Model 30 analog computer that it could calculate a bouncing ball with wind resistance, and designed the game in a few hours; technician Robert V. Dvorak helped build it over about three weeks. Most of the circuitry used vacuum tubes and relays, with transistors for the graphics, and the display was a 5-inch oscilloscope. It debuted at the laboratory's public exhibition on 18 October 1958. After the 1959 exhibition it was taken apart so its parts could be reused. During the war he had headed the Manhattan Project's electronics division, and he preferred to be remembered for his work against nuclear proliferation.

title: Spacewar!
description: Spacewar! (1962) is the MIT game in which two players fly the needle and the wedge around a star's gravity well, firing torpedoes — one of the most influential early computer games.
longDescription: Two ships duel around a central star whose gravity pulls them in, and a hyperspace button sends a ship to a random spot as a last resort. Steve Russell, Martin Graetz and Wayne Wiitanen conceived it, with Russell as the main programmer. Dan Edwards wrote the gravity well, Graetz added hyperspace, and Peter Samson's "Expensive Planetarium" drew the background from real star charts.
trivia: Only 53 PDP-1s were ever sold, and the game spread to many of those few dozen installations.
Stewart Brand wrote about it in Rolling Stone in December 1972, in "Spacewar: Fantastic Life and Symbolic Death Among the Computer Bums".
In 2007 it was named among the ten most important video games in history, the start of a game canon for the Library of Congress.
Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney based the first coin-operated video game, Computer Space, on it.
devStory: It was written for the DEC PDP-1 at MIT by a group connected with the Tech Model Railroad Club. Features were added by different members over time, and the code was shared freely between installations.

title: The Sumerian Game
description: One of the first strategy games ever made: a text simulation of running an ancient Sumerian city-state, written for an IBM mainframe as an experiment in teaching schoolchildren with computers.
longDescription:
The Sumerian Game grew out of a 1964–1966 research project by IBM and the Board of Cooperative Educational Services of Westchester County, New York, which wanted to know whether computer simulations could work as classroom tools. Mabel Addis, a fourth-grade teacher, designed it, and William McKay programmed it for the IBM 7090, a time-shared mainframe.

Players ruled a Sumerian city, deciding each season how much grain to plant, store and feed to the population as land and resources changed. A group of 30 sixth-graders played the first version in 1964. A revised edition, with a sharper focus, more story and added audiovisual material, was tested on a second group of students in 1966. Its turn-based resource management makes it an ancestor of the city-building and strategy games that followed.
trivia: It was programmed in Fortran and played on an IBM 1050 teleprinter, with slide-projector images alongside the printed text.
Commentators have called it the first video game with a narrative and the first edutainment game, and Addis the first female video game designer.
Doug Dyment's 1968 King of Sumeria was based on it, and David Ahl's later version became Hamurabi.
devStory: The Sumerian Game was created in 1964 by Mabel Addis, a school teacher, and William McKay, an IBM programmer, as an educational tool for sixth-grade students in Westchester County, New York. It is one of the earliest known educational computer games and one of the first games designed for children. Addis wrote the narrative and game design; McKay implemented it on an IBM 7090 mainframe. The project was funded by the Board of Cooperative Educational Services.

title: Hamurabi
description: Hamurabi (1968) is a turn-based game of ruling Sumeria for ten years — buying land, feeding the people and planting grain — first written by Doug Dyment as King of Sumeria and spread in David Ahl's BASIC books.
longDescription: The player is the Babylonian king Hammurabi, managing three resources: people, acres of land and bushels of grain. Each of the ten rounds is a year. The player decides how much land to buy or sell, at a random price of 17 to 26 bushels an acre, how much grain to feed the people and how much to plant, since each person can farm only so much land. Yields are random, rats eat random amounts of grain, new people arrive each year, and a plague can halve the population. The reign ends after ten years, or earlier if everyone dies or at least 45% starve in a single year. A verdict then judges the reign, comparing a bad ruler to Nero and Ivan IV.
trivia: The missing "m" in the name began with an eight-character file name limit.
It is described as an ancestor of the city-building genre, and influenced M.U.L.E. and Anacreon.
Richard Merrill is sometimes wrongly credited as its creator.
Jerry Pournelle wrote in 1989 that "half the people I know wrote a Hammurabi program back in the 1970s."
Its descendants include Kingdom, Dukedom and Santa Paravia en Fiumaccio.
devStory: It descends from The Sumerian Game, written in 1964 by teacher Mabel Addis and programmed by IBM's William McKay for a Westchester County education project. Doug Dyment, a DEC employee who had heard about it after a talk at the University of Alberta, wrote King of Sumeria in 1968 in the FOCAL language for a PDP-8; its ruler's name changed from Luduga to Hamurabi to fit a 4K machine. David Ahl ported it to BASIC around 1971, renamed it Hamurabi and published it in DEC's newsletter Edu, adding the end-of-reign appraisal, then republished it in 101 BASIC Computer Games in 1973. The 1975 edition, BASIC Computer Games, sold over a million copies.

title: Lunar Lander (1969)
description: Lunar Lander (1969) is Jim Storer's text game about landing on the Moon, written at Lexington High School, which grew into a whole genre.
longDescription: Each turn stands for ten seconds of descent. The player reads the lander's vertical speed and remaining fuel and types how much thrust to burn, trying to touch down gently before the fuel runs out. There are no graphics: the game reports its numbers as text. Later text versions added more: Eric Peters's BASIC Rocket showed the distance to the surface, and William Labaree II's LEM added horizontal speed and angled thrust.
trivia: David H. Ahl converted it to BASIC for his 1973 book 101 BASIC Computer Games, and called it "by far and away the single most popular computer game" of its time.
In 1973 DEC commissioned Jack Burness's graphical Moonlander, controlled with a light pen.
Atari's 1979 arcade Lunar Lander let players insert more coins to buy extra fuel.
Burness wrote Moonlander in ten days, using real lander specifications from MIT.
About 300 Asteroids games were sold in Lunar Lander arcade cabinets.
devStory:
Jim Storer wrote it in the autumn of 1969, as a student at Lexington High School, in FOCAL for a DEC PDP-8, and uploaded it to the system library as Rocket after the Christmas break. His computer teacher sent it to DEC's users' newsletter as FOCAL Lunar Landing Simulation (APOLLO), and DEC's 1970 FOCAL-8 program book included it as Lunar Module. David Ahl converted it to BASIC, and his 1973 book 101 BASIC Computer Games included three versions.

The name "Lunar Lander" first appeared for this kind of game in the 1975 book What to Do After You Hit Return, and by the end of the 1970s such games were collectively called "lunar lander" games. In 1973 DEC commissioned Jack Burness's graphical Moonlander, which is thought to contain the first video game easter egg, a McDonald's the player can crash into.

title: Star Trek (BASIC)
description: Star Trek (1971) is Mike Mayfield's text strategy game, in which the Enterprise hunts Klingons across an 8×8 galaxy before time runs out.
longDescription:
The Enterprise hunts an invading Klingon fleet across a galaxy of 8×8 quadrants, each split into 8×8 sectors, before a random time limit runs out. A short-range scan prints a text map of the current quadrant with the ship as "-E-", and a long-range scan counts the stars, Klingons and starbases in neighbouring quadrants. Warp drive moves the ship, taking time in proportion to distance, and movement, combat and shields all drain energy, restored at starbases.

Combat is turn-based. Phasers need no aiming but weaken with distance, with the player choosing the power of each shot, while photon torpedoes keep their strength and destroy a Klingon in one hit but must be aimed by angle. Klingons fire back on their turn. The game ends when the Enterprise is destroyed, every Klingon is gone or time runs out, and a rating weighs energy used, damage and time left.
trivia: David Ahl included a version in 101 BASIC Computer Games (1973).
Bob Leedom's expanded Super Star Trek appeared in BASIC Computer Games (1978), the first computer book to sell a million copies.
Mayfield credited the HP version to Centerline Engineering, a company he was thinking of founding.
Star Raiders (1980) began as a real-time 3D take on it.
A C port, BSD Trek, is still in Debian's bsdgames package.
devStory:
Mike Mayfield wrote it in BASIC in 1971, in his last year of high school, on an SDS Sigma 7 at the University of California, Irvine, to which he had illicit access; it had only a Teletype printer, so he aimed for a Spacewar!-style game that would work on paper, saving to punched tape each day. When a local Hewlett-Packard office offered him an HP 2000C, he rewrote it from scratch, finishing on 20 October 1972, and it entered HP's public-domain library in 1973 as STTR1.

David Ahl and Mary Cole ported it to DEC BASIC that summer, and in 1974 Bob Leedom expanded it into Super Star Trek, with three-letter commands, moving Klingons and named quadrants. By 1978 Ahl said it was hard to find a computer installation without a version.

title: Colossal Cave Adventure
description: Will Crowther's 1976 cave-exploring game, expanded by Don Woods in 1977 — the first well-known text adventure, and the game that gave the adventure genre its name.
longDescription:
Will Crowther wrote Colossal Cave Adventure in 1976 for the PDP-10 mainframe, and Don Woods expanded it substantially in 1977. The player explores a cave system said to be full of treasure and gold, travelling between dozens of locations and interacting with objects by typing short one- or two-word commands, which the game interprets.

The program responds as a narrator, describing each place and the result of every action. Colossal Cave was the first widely known work of interactive fiction and the first well-known adventure game; the genre takes its name from it, and its influence runs directly into Zork and the text adventures that followed.
trivia: Much of its cave matches the Bedquilt section of Kentucky's Mammoth Cave, which Crowther had explored and mapped.
"You are in a maze of twisty little passages, all alike" became famous in hacker culture.
Don Woods got the source code by emailing "crowther" at every domain on ARPANET.
devStory: Will Crowther, a programmer at Bolt Beranek and Newman who worked on ARPANET, wrote it in 1975–76 on a PDP-10, after his divorce, partly because he missed his two daughters and wanted something they could play. Don Woods found it on a PDP-10 at Stanford Medical School and, from March to May 1977, expanded it with fantasy elements such as a dragon and ten more treasures.

title: Computer Space
description: The first arcade video game and the first video game sold commercially: Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney's 1971 cabinet, adapted from the earlier computer game Spacewar!
longDescription:
Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney built Computer Space in 1971 while working together as Syzygy Engineering, the partnership that soon became Atari. It took its idea from Spacewar!, the 1962 computer game that had spread between university installations, and turned it into a coin-operated machine — making it both the first arcade video game and the first commercially available video game of any kind.

The player steers a rocket through a starfield, trading missiles with two flying saucers controlled by the hardware. The aim is to score more hits than the saucers before time runs out; doing so earns a free round. Its controls and rules were demanding for a public that had never played a video game, and its modest sales led Bushnell and Dabney towards a simpler idea for their next machine: Pong.
trivia: It was housed in a futuristic fibreglass cabinet designed by Bushnell.
A white cabinet appeared in the 1973 film Soylent Green, the first appearance of a video game in a movie.
Bushnell said it sold between 1,300 and 1,500 units; its complex controls are blamed for the modest sales.
devStory: Bushnell and Dabney built it in 1971 as Syzygy Engineering, and Nutting Associates manufactured it. Bushnell had played Spacewar! against Jim Stein at Stanford's AI Project. Its modest sales led them towards a simpler game, Pong, and they founded Atari soon after.

title: Galaxy Game
description: Galaxy Game (1971) is Bill Pitts and Hugh Tuck's coin-operated Spacewar! machine at Stanford, believed to be the second video game to charge money to play, after Computer Space.
longDescription:
Galaxy Game was built in 1971 by Bill Pitts and Hugh Tuck, who took the 1962 computer game Spacewar! — one of the earliest games to spread between computer installations — and expanded it into a coin-operated machine driven by a PDP-11 minicomputer.

Two players each fly a ship, "the needle" or "the wedge", and fight a dogfight while the gravity of a central star pulls them both in. Unlike the mass-produced Computer Space of the same year, Galaxy Game was a hand-built installation, and it remains a key exhibit in the earliest history of arcade games.
trivia: The PDP-11 at its heart cost about $14,000, and the first prototype about $20,000 in all.
The second version ran up to four games on four monitors, and crowds gathered ten deep to watch.
It moved to the Computer History Museum in 2000 and later returned there as a playable exhibit.
devStory: Pitts, a Stanford student, and Tuck, a Cal Poly student, installed the first prototype in Stanford's Tresidder student union in November 1971. A second version replaced it in June 1972 and stayed until May 1979. It was never manufactured commercially.

title: Pong
description: Pong (1972) is Atari's table tennis game, designed by Allan Alcorn as a training exercise, and the first commercially successful arcade video game.
longDescription: Two players each move a paddle up and down one side of the screen, bouncing a ball between them like table tennis; a player scores whenever the other fails to return it, and the first to eleven points wins. Each paddle is divided into eight segments: the centre ones return the ball straight, and the outer ones at sharper angles. The ball speeds up the longer a rally lasts and resets when someone misses. A circuit defect stops the paddles from reaching the top of the screen, which Alcorn chose not to fix, and the sound effects are tones taken from the sync generator. A test machine at Andy Capp's Tavern in Sunnyvale stopped working within days of growing popular because its coin mechanism had overflowed with quarters.
trivia: Magnavox sued in 1974, saying it copied the Odyssey's tennis game; Atari settled in 1976 for $1.5 million and became a licensee.
Home Pong, sold through Sears, sold about 150,000 units in the 1975 holiday season.
Atari had sold more than 8,000 arcade machines by the end of 1974, and numerous clones followed.
It was Atari's first game.
It was inducted into the World Video Game Hall of Fame in 2015 and is in the Smithsonian's permanent collection.
devStory: Nolan Bushnell gave Allan Alcorn, who had no video game experience, the project as a training exercise; Alcorn has said it responded to Bushnell seeing the Magnavox Odyssey's tennis game in May 1972. The prototype, a $75 Hitachi black-and-white television in a four-foot wooden cabinet, went into Andy Capp's Tavern in August 1972. Banks declined to fund production, but Wells Fargo gave Atari a line of credit, and Atari announced Pong on 29 November 1972, building about ten machines a day at first. Each earned about four times as much as other coin-operated machines, and Atari sold them for about three times what they cost to make.

title: Space Race
description: Space Race (1973) is Atari's second arcade game after Pong, a two-player race to fly a rocket up the screen through a stream of asteroids — the first arcade racing game.
longDescription: Each player steers a ship straight up from the bottom of the screen, moving only up or down, while dashes representing asteroids drift across from left to right over a starfield. A ship that is hit vanishes for a few seconds and reappears at the bottom, and reaching the top scores a point. A line at the bottom centre of the screen shortens as time runs out, and the higher score wins. A game cost a quarter, and operators could set one or two rounds of 45 seconds to three minutes. It was built from discrete electronic components rather than a computer, with the ship drawn by a diode array shaped like half a ship and mirrored on screen.
trivia: Atari made it to fulfil a contract with Midway, which sold it as Asteroid; Atari's near-identical Space Race led to a settlement in which Atari gave up its royalty.
Only about 50 of the tall fibreglass cabinets were built, the first Atari machines to carry the Atari logo.
The fibreglass cabinet stood nearly five feet tall and weighed over 200 pounds.
Namco released it in Japan in 1974.
Taito's Astro Race (1973) was a clone.
devStory: Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney conceived it while making Computer Space, and Bushnell spent a few days on it as Asteroid in 1972 before setting it aside to run Atari. Work resumed in spring 1973, after Pong, as a racing game to fulfil a contract with Midway, which had turned down Pong; Dabney claimed the final design, and Allan Alcorn did the engineering. Atari released it on 16 July 1973 as its second game, but it sold poorly next to Pong; Ralph Baer estimated about 1,500 units. It was the first arcade racing game and the first whose goal was to cross the screen while avoiding obstacles, the idea behind Frogger and Freeway.

title: Gotcha
description: Gotcha (1973) is Atari's two-player maze game designed by Allan Alcorn, in which one player chases the other through a maze that keeps changing.
longDescription: One player, the Pursuer, a square, tries to catch the other, the Pursued, a plus sign, inside a maze built from a repeating pattern. Two invisible lines, half a screen apart, scan down the maze and redraw it, so it keeps changing as the players run. An electronic beep speeds up as the Pursuer closes in. A catch scores a point for the Pursuer, the maze briefly vanishes, and the Pursuer reappears at a random spot on the right; the Pursued never scores. A game cost a quarter, and rounds ran from 30 seconds to two minutes. Gotcha was the first arcade maze video game.
trivia: It was not a commercial success, and later accounts describe it as arousing little more than controversy.
George Faraco designed the cabinet.
Its colour version is believed to be the first colour arcade game.
Its maze came from a Pong testing glitch.
Namco distributed it in Japan from 1974.
devStory:
Allan Alcorn, who had designed Pong, began it in July 1973 as Atari's fourth game, after Pong, Space Race and Pong Doubles, taking the idea from a Pong test defect that scattered fragments of numbers across the screen; Steve Mayer of Cyan Engineering built a prototype. George Faraco designed the cabinet, over five feet tall, whose joysticks were first set in pink domes; standard joysticks replaced them early in the production run, before Atari released the game on 11 October 1973. A colour version, shown that November and made in 20 to 100 units, is believed to be the first colour arcade game.

It was not a commercial success; Ralph Baer estimated about 3,000 units sold.

title: Gran Trak 10
description: Gran Trak 10 (1974) is Atari's overhead racing game with a steering wheel, gear stick and pedals, called the first arcade car racing video game and believed to be the first arcade game to use integrated-circuit ROM.
longDescription: The player races against the clock around a single track seen from above, its edges marked by white dots standing for pylons; hitting one stops the car and spins it, and a black oil slick stops it from turning. The controls are a steering wheel, accelerator and brake pedals and a gear stick with reverse and three forward gears. The pedals are digital, so pressing harder does not change the speed, the wheel turns the car only while it is being turned and does not centre itself, and turning while braking causes a skid. One counter shows the time left and the other the checkpoints passed, and a placard on the front rates scores from "License Revoked", for 10 points or fewer, to "Real Pro", for over 40. A game lasts 105 seconds by default. It is called the first arcade car racing game and the first video game with a steering wheel.
trivia: Atari sold it to distributors for $995 when it cost $1,095 to make, a $100 loss on each unit until the price was corrected.
It contributed to a $500,000 loss in Atari's 1974 fiscal year.
A two-player version, Gran Trak 20, followed in August 1974.
An early design included a small printer for high scores.
Tomohiro Nishikado disliked its twisting track and complex controls, but it still inspired his Speed Race (1974).
devStory: Atari revisited the idea of a driving game in late 1973, and Cyan Engineering, its semi-independent research subsidiary, created the design. Larry Emmons designed the circuits for the car's braking, acceleration and movement, and stored the track graphics in mask ROM rather than the diode arrays earlier games used, believed to be a first for an arcade game. With Allan Alcorn on leave and the project behind schedule, a short production run in March 1974 revealed design problems; Alcorn returned and redesigned it with standard parts, and Atari announced full production in May 1974, with Namco releasing it in Japan that September. Each unit cost $1,095 to make but sold to distributors for $995, and Atari's $500,000 loss for fiscal 1974 led it to be called "the game that nearly put Atari out of business".

title: Tank
description: Tank (1974) is Kee Games' two-player arcade game, in which tanks duel in a maze dotted with mines — one of the first games to store its graphics in mask ROM.
longDescription: Two players, one with a white tank and one with a black tank, try to shoot each other in a maze seen from above, made of blocks set at right angles around an empty central square, with land mines, marked as Xs, in the middle. A shell or a mine destroys a tank, and the opponent scores a point; after a brief explosion, during which it cannot shoot, the destroyed tank reappears where it was, but destroyed mines do not return. Each tank has two joysticks: pushing both moves it forward, pulling both back stops it, and moving them differently turns it, with a fire button on the right stick. A quarter bought 60 seconds by default, and the higher score at the end wins. It was one of the first games to store its graphics in mask ROM.
trivia: Kee Games was a secret Atari subsidiary, set up in 1973 to sell Atari clones and get around distributors' exclusive deals.
The Atari 2600's Combat includes variations of Tank.
It sold over 10,000 units in 1974, and Ralph Baer counted 5,000 more in 1975.
The joysticks for a cancelled Tank II console became the Atari 2600's standard controllers.
Ed Rotberg's Battlezone (1980) was primarily inspired by it.
devStory: Atari set up Kee Games in 1973 to sell clones of its games as a separate competitor, getting around distributors' exclusive deals, and Tank was one of its few original titles. Steve Bristow, Kee's only engineer, who had worked on Computer Space, wanted to replace that game's rocket ships with tanks and make it two-player; he built a prototype himself, then handed it to new hire Lyle Rains, who added the maze and minefield, developed the final hardware and created the controls. Peter Takaichi designed the cabinet. Kee merged into Atari in September 1974, and Tank came out that November, helping Atari's finances at a critical time.

title: Gun Fight
description: Gun Fight (1975) is Midway's Wild West duel, remade from Taito's Western Gun by Dave Nutting as the first arcade game to run on a microprocessor.
longDescription: Two cowboys duel across a single screen, each with one joystick to move and another to aim; shot characters fall to the ground with a message above the body. Cacti, and in later rounds a moving stagecoach, block shots, which can also ricochet off the top and bottom of the playfield, and each player has six bullets per round. Taito's Western Gun, designed by Tomohiro Nishikado on discrete logic and based on Sega's 1969 electro-mechanical Gun Fight, let both players roam the whole screen; Midway's version confined each to their own half, enlarged the characters and added indestructible trees, rounds and the stagecoach. Western Gun was the first video game to depict human-against-human combat, and possibly the first twin-stick shooter.
trivia: It sold 8,600 units in the United States.
Ports followed on the Bally Astrocade in 1977 and Atari 8-bit computers in 1984.
Its hardware, including the barrel shifter, was reused in Sea Wolf and closely resembles Space Invaders'.
David Crane's Atari 2600 game Outlaw (1978) was based on it.
The Guardian ranked it 11th among the greatest video games of the 1970s.
devStory: Taito released Western Gun in Japan in September 1975, but Midway disliked its graphics, and Dave Nutting Associates rebuilt it around an Intel 8080 for Midway, with Jeffery Fredriksen designing the hardware, including a cost-effective framebuffer and barrel shifter, and Tom McHugh as principal programmer, writing in assembly. Gun Fight reached North America that November and sold 8,600 cabinets in the US. Nishikado felt his original was more fun but admired Gun Fight's smoother animation, and the experience inspired Space Invaders, whose hardware is very similar. Boot Hill followed in 1977.

title: Sea Wolf
description: Sea Wolf (1976) is Midway's submarine game, played by looking through a periscope and timing torpedoes to hit passing ships. It sold 10,000 cabinets.
longDescription:
The player looks through a large periscope on the cabinet, swivelling it to aim at destroyers and a fast PT boat crossing the top of the screen, while floating mines get in the way. Torpedoes are fired with a thumb button on the right handle and travel up the screen, so each shot has to be led. Back-lit panels show the torpedoes left, a red "RELOAD" light comes on after five, and a light reflected into the scope marks each hit. A blue overlay colours the sea, and the sounds include a sonar ping, the whoosh of torpedoes and the PT boat's klaxon.

Play is against the clock, and reaching an operator-set score earns extra time. It was one of the first video games to keep a high score, held until the machine was switched off.
trivia: It ran on the same Intel 8080 hardware first used for Gun Fight.
A colour sequel, Sea Wolf II, followed in 1978 and sold about 4,000 more units.
It was Japan's fifth-highest-grossing arcade game of 1976 in Game Machine's first arcade chart.
Commodore released it on cartridge for the VIC-20 and Commodore 64 in 1982.
Alan Radue set the world record of 11,300 points in 2011.
devStory:
Dave Nutting and programmer Tom McHugh of Dave Nutting Associates developed it, reusing the Intel 8080 hardware Jeffery Frederiksen had built for their Gun Fight (1975). The distributor Joe Robbins suggested a video upgrade of the electromechanical Periscope. When McHugh fell ill near the end, Jamie Fenton put together the final stages.

Midway released it in North America in April 1976, and Taito in Japan that July. It sold about 10,000 cabinets and was the top-grossing US arcade game of 1976 and 1977.

title: Night Driver
description: Night Driver (1976) is Atari's first-person night racing game, which draws the road as rows of roadside pylons — one of the earliest first-person racing games.
longDescription: The player drives at night, steering between the reflectors that mark the road's edges, drawn as scaled rectangles, or "pylons", rushing out of the dark; the night setting explained the minimal graphics, since most of the scenery would be invisible anyway. The car itself is not drawn at all: its bonnet is printed on a plastic insert in front of the monitor. An accelerator pedal, steering wheel and four-position gear lever control it, and the road grows narrower and more winding as play goes on, with sharper and more frequent turns on the pro and expert tracks. Operators set games of 50 to 125 seconds, and reaching 300 points earns bonus time; expert difficulty scores more, making it the easiest way to earn extra time.
trivia: Its concept came from a German game later identified as Nürburgring 1, released earlier in 1976.
The Atari 2600 version, programmed by Rob Fulop, sold over 1.9 million copies by 1983.
The upright cabinet has a blacklight that lights up the bezel.
The score wraps back to zero at 1,000.
Midway's Midnight Racer, later renamed Datsun 280 ZZZAP, followed it in November 1976.
devStory: Dave Shepperd led development at Atari, assigned to make a first-person driving game from a drawing of a cabinet he remembered as possibly German; the inspiration was later identified as Nürburgring 1, shown in Germany in spring 1976. Atari reused leftover cabinets from its 1975 racer Hi-way, and production began in October 1976, with Namco releasing it in Japan in April 1977. Play Meter ranked it the sixth-highest-earning US arcade game of 1977. Rob Fulop's Atari 2600 version of 1980, which added colour, other cars, houses and trees, sold 161,352 copies that year and over 1.9 million by 1983.

title: Sprint 2
description: Sprint 2 (1976) is Kee Games' overhead racing game for two, with computer-driven cars that steer themselves round the track — one of Atari's first mass-produced microprocessor games.
longDescription: Two players race around an overhead track against each other and computer-driven cars, which steer themselves without following a set course and adjust to how well the player is doing; Lyle Rains created a vector map that tells each computer car which way to drive, so their paths never repeat. Atari's earlier racers, Gran Trak 10, Gran Trak 20, Indy 800 and LeMans, had all made money, and Sprint 2 updated them: reverse driving from Gran Trak 20 was dropped, as was the brake pedal, since lifting off the accelerator slows the car. The race still runs against a timer rather than laps. It was one of Atari's first mass-produced games built around a microprocessor, the 6502, which Rains said made it faster and more exciting than earlier racers.
trivia: It was the second-highest-earning US arcade game of both 1977 and 1978.
Sprint 4 and Sprint 8 followed in 1977, and a one-player Sprint 1 in 1978.
It was one of the first Atari games to use the "Atari arcade font".
Its line continued through Super Sprint and Championship Sprint (1986) to NeoSprint (2024).
There is no brake pedal: lifting off the accelerator slows the car.
devStory: Dennis Koble and Lyle Rains designed it at Kee Games, with Wendi Allen and Dan Van Elderen on the team; Koble had to learn 6502 programming to make it and drew the graphics himself, since Atari's staff artists then only did cabinet artwork. Kee released it in North America on 2 November 1976, and Namco in Japan in June 1977. It was the second-highest-earning US arcade game of 1977, behind Sea Wolf, and of 1978, behind Space Wars, and the seventh-highest-earning game of 1977 in Japan.

title: Blockade
developer: Lane Hauck & Ago Kiss / Gremlin Industries
description: Blockade (1976) is Gremlin's two-player arcade game in which each player steers a line that leaves a wall behind it — the forerunner of the snake genre.
longDescription: Each player steers an arrow that keeps moving and leaves a solid trail of blocks behind it; whoever crashes into the screen's outer barrier, their own trail or the opponent's sets off an explosion and gives the other player a point. Operators set how many crashes ended a game, from three to six. It is described as the progenitor of the snake genre, which runs through Atari's 2600 Surround to Nokia's Snake.
trivia: Gremlin reportedly took 3,000 orders at the 1976 MOA show but sold only a fraction once it shipped, leaving a large stock.
Rival versions included Atari's Dominos, Ramtek's Barricade and Bally's Checkmate, and counterfeits were common.
Taito released it in Japan as Barricade II.
Play Meter called it "probably the most played game at the show".
Hauck also made a four-player version, CoMotion.
devStory: Lane Hauck, a physics and engineering graduate who had taught himself assembly language on a PDP-8, made it at Gremlin in San Diego, where nobody else understood microprocessors; Ago Kiss also programmed it. A random-walk experiment Hauck called "Drunk and the Lamppost" led to the idea of trails that could not be crossed, and then to a two-player game, which was tested on a miniature golf course. Gremlin took 3,000 orders at the 1976 Music Operators of America show and released it that November, but counterfeits spread and demand faded faster than expected, leaving the company with a large stock. Gremlin, which had no major hit after it, was bought by Sega in 1978.

title: Breakout
description: Breakout (1976) is Atari's single-player take on Pong, in which a paddle bounces a ball to knock out a wall of bricks — the prototype built by Steve Wozniak.
longDescription: Eight rows of bricks, two each of yellow, green, orange and red from the bottom up, sit above the player's paddle, worth 1, 3, 5 and 7 points. The player has one ball and three turns to clear two screens of bricks, losing a turn whenever the ball gets past the paddle. The ball speeds up after four hits, after twelve, and when it reaches the orange and red rows, and once it breaks through the red row and hits the top wall the paddle shrinks to half size, so the later stages are much harder. The maximum score for one player is 896, 448 per screen. The monochrome screen is tinted by coloured cellophane strips, and the cabinet art frames the game as a prison escape. Nolan Bushnell and Steve Bristow designed it, wanting a single-player Pong.
trivia: Wozniak's breadboard used 44 chips; Atari's production version used about 100.
Jobs kept a $5,000 chip-reduction bonus secret from Wozniak, who said he received $350.
Wozniak said many features of the Apple II came from having designed Breakout.
Ruth Bader Ginsburg, then an appeals judge, ruled that it could be copyrighted as an audiovisual work.
Tomohiro Nishikado cited it as an inspiration for Space Invaders, and it later inspired Taito's Arkanoid.
devStory: Bushnell assigned Steve Jobs to build a prototype for $750, plus $100 for each chip under 50, and Jobs promised it in four days. He asked Steve Wozniak, then an engineer at Hewlett-Packard, to help, and Wozniak worked four nights in a row at Atari from verbal descriptions, with Jobs as breadboarder and tester; the breadboard used 44 chips. Atari's production version, released in May 1976, used about 100, though Wozniak said its gameplay matched his. Atari made 11,000 cabinets, and it was among the top five arcade games of 1976 in the US and Japan. Brad Stewart's Atari 2600 version of 1978 sold 1,650,336 cartridges by 1983.

title: Death Race
description: Death Race (1976) is Exidy's driving game in which players run down fleeing gremlins that leave crosses behind — one of the first video games to cause a public outcry over violence.
longDescription: One or two players each drive a car, with a steering wheel and an accelerator pedal, and try to run down "gremlins" fleeing across the screen. A hit gremlin screams or squeals and is replaced by a tombstone, and the tombstones clutter the field and have to be avoided. Curbs at the left and right let the gremlins hide and stall any car that tries to cross them, while the top and bottom edges wrap around, as in Atari's Space Race. The cabinet is mostly black, with white art of a muscle car racing through a cemetery and a vulture in a tree. From July 1976 newspapers and civic groups attacked the game for depicting violence, and since the gremlins look much like people from above, it drew coverage from 60 Minutes and The New York Times.
trivia: Many sources linked it to the film Death Race 2000, but Exidy denied it was an adaptation; the name reflected the undead monsters on the cabinet.
An early working title was "Death Race 98".
By the end of 1977 it had dropped out of the headlines.
Working machines are on show at Funspot and the Musée Mécanique in San Francisco.
Play Meter ranked it the seventh-highest-grossing arcade game of 1977.
devStory: Exidy had licensed its 1975 game Destruction Derby to Chicago Coin, which ran into financial trouble in 1976, leaving Exidy unable to profit from it, so it needed an interim product. Howell Ivy, recently arrived from Ramtek, modified Destruction Derby, turning the targets from cars into walking figures, and artist Michael Cooper-Hart drew undead monsters for the cabinet. It shipped in April 1976, meant only to tide Exidy over until Car Polo. An AP article by Wendy Walker, written after she played it in Seattle, spread the controversy, and many at Exidy credit the attention with a large jump in sales. RePlay ranked it the eighth-highest-grossing US arcade game of 1976.

title: Circus
description: Circus (1977) is Exidy's Breakout variant: bounce clowns off a seesaw to pop rows of balloons. Atari licensed it for the 2600 as Circus Atari.
longDescription: Three rows of balloons — yellow, green and blue — drift along the top of the screen. The player slides a seesaw along the bottom to catch a clown launched from a jumping board; the clown on the other end is then flung upwards to burst balloons, passing through several if moving fast enough, though a clown that does not land squarely may not reach them. Yellow balloons score 20, green 50 and blue 100; clearing a whole row scores ten times as much and instantly replaces it, and clearing the blue row earns an extra clown. A missed clown dies to two bars of Chopin's funeral march. Coloured cellophane on the screen gave the balloons their colours.
trivia: Howell Ivy said it was Exidy's most profitable game, and it was among Japan's top arcade games of 1977 under Taito.
Imitations included Midway's Clowns and Sega's Seesaw Jump; Atari released Circus Atari for its VCS in 1980.
Exidy thought it might appeal to female players.
Midway's version added "Oof" and "Pow" sounds when a clown hits the ground.
Taito's Plump Pop (1987) is a remake with a trampoline in place of the seesaw.
devStory: Howell Ivy developed it at Exidy from his earlier Ramtek game Clean Sweep, wanting something cute; adding a teeter-totter led to the balloons. It was Exidy's second game to run entirely on a microprocessor, coded on a 6502 using a teletype, and Ivy remembered hearing the fireworks while working on it on 4 July 1977. Exidy released it in 1977 and supplied boards for licensed versions by Sega, Midway and Taito; it was Japan's fourth-highest-earning arcade game of 1977, and Ivy said it was Exidy's most profitable game.

title: Atari Football
description: Atari Football (1978) is Atari's overhead American football game played with a trackball — the game that popularised the trackball in arcades, and the first non-racing game to scroll vertically.
longDescription: Two teams, shown as X's and O's, play American football on an overhead field that scrolls vertically to follow the action, making it the first non-racing game to scroll vertically. Players control their team with a trackball, for one or two players, and a four-player version followed. It was not the first trackball game — Sega's soccer game World Cup came seven months earlier, in March 1978 — but it popularised the trackball in arcades.
trivia: It was the second-highest-earning US arcade game of 1979, behind Space Invaders.
Dave Theurer, who programmed the 1979 four-player version, later created Missile Command and Tempest.
Its players are drawn as X's and O's, like a coach's diagram.
Its trackball was copied from a Japanese soccer cabinet the team brought into the lab.
It was the first non-racing video game to scroll vertically.
devStory: Steve Bristow designed it, Michael Albaugh programmed it and Dave Stubben engineered the hardware. The trackball was inspired by an earlier Japanese soccer game: Bristow's team brought a cabinet into their lab and imitated its controls, though Stubben and Albaugh later remembered the maker differently. Atari released it in October 1978, with Namco distributing it in Japan, and an Atari 2600 version followed in March 1979. It was the second-highest-earning US arcade game of 1979, behind Space Invaders.

title: Space Wars
description: Space Wars (1977) is Cinematronics' two-player vector duel, Larry Rosenthal's commercial version of the MIT classic Spacewar!, drawn in crisp vector lines.
longDescription: Two ships fight around a central star in Cinematronics' arcade version of MIT's 1962 Spacewar!, drawn in black-and-white vector lines. Buttons rotate each ship left and right, fire thrust, shoot and jump into hyperspace, which makes the ship vanish and reappear somewhere at random. Operators could switch on a central star that pulls ships towards it or pushes them away, wraparound screen edges and bouncing shots. A ship could survive a glancing hit, losing fragments and then turning and accelerating more slowly. Two human players were needed: there was no computer opponent. A quarter bought a minute and a half, and a $10 roll of quarters kept two players going for an hour.
trivia: It sold 10,000 cabinets in 1978 and was the top-earning US arcade game that year.
Its hardware became the basis for Cinematronics' later vector games, including Tail Gunner and Star Castle.
A damaged ship visibly loses pieces and handles more sluggishly.
It could not be played alone.
It was the sixth-highest-earning US arcade game of 1979.
devStory: Larry Rosenthal, an MIT graduate, built his own hardware and software so he could play Spacewar!, and Cinematronics worked with him to turn it into Space Wars, released in November 1977; Taito brought it to Japan in 1978. It sold about 10,000 cabinets in 1978, the highest-earning US arcade game of the year, and its hardware became the platform for most of Cinematronics' later vector games, including Star Castle and Tail Gunner. A Vectrex version followed in 1982.

title: Zork
developer: Tim Anderson, Marc Blank, Bruce Daniels, Dave Lebling
description: The definitive text adventure: four MIT programmers' 1977 game of treasure-hunting in the Great Underground Empire, later split into the Zork trilogy and the foundation of Infocom.
longDescription:
Tim Anderson, Marc Blank, Bruce Daniels and Dave Lebling wrote Zork in 1977 on a PDP-10 mainframe. The player explores the ruins of the Great Underground Empire in search of treasure, moving through hundreds of locations and handling objects by typing commands in ordinary English. The game answers as a narrator, describing where the player is and what happens after each instruction.

The original was too big for the home computers of the time, so its creators — now working as the company Infocom — divided it into three games: Zork I: The Great Underground Empire, Zork II: The Wizard of Frobozz and Zork III: The Dungeon Master, released for a wide range of personal computers from 1980. Its parser, wit and atmosphere made Zork the most famous work of interactive fiction and set the template for Infocom's later games.
trivia: The team chose "zork", one of several nonsense words used in the lab, as a file name for a program still in development.
"It is pitch black. You are likely to be eaten by a grue" warns players to carry a light in dark places.
A 1978 Fortran port was called Dungeon, until TSR claimed the name infringed its trademark.
Activision bought Infocom in 1986, after its business database Cornerstone sold poorly.
devStory: Tim Anderson, Marc Blank, Bruce Daniels and Dave Lebling began it in May 1977 at MIT's Dynamic Modelling Group on a PDP-10, inspired by Colossal Cave Adventure and using the MDL language. They ran out of the megabyte of memory allotted to it, and as Infocom they split it into Zork I (1980), II (1981) and III (1982) for home computers.

title: Fire Truck
description: Fire Truck (1978) is Atari's co-operative driving game: one player drives the tractor of an articulated fire engine while another steers its ladder trailer.
longDescription: Two players work together to drive a fire truck through traffic as far as they can without crashing, avoiding parked cars and oil slicks. The front player sits and works the tractor's gas and brakes, while the rear player stands and steers the tiller that swings the trailer, so getting round corners takes coordination. Flashing arrows mark the correct turns at intersections, a fuel gauge shows the play time left, and there is a choice of an easy or a hard course. In one-player mode the computer takes either the front or the rear role. At the end each crew gets a score and a driving rating, from Sorry and So-So to Good and Ace.
trivia: Smokey Joe, a one-player cabinet released the same year, is internally identical.
It was not the first co-operative arcade game — players had teamed up as early as Pong Doubles (1973).
Its bells and horns make noise but do nothing in the game.
The rear player stands while the front player sits.
It is included in the 2022 compilation Atari 50.
devStory: Wendi Allen, who joined Atari in 1976, programmed and developed it, building on the technology of Super Bug (1977), which Allen had designed, and adding a separate motion object for the ladder end, more sounds and a second steering wheel; Allen said tuning the computer-controlled player "took a lot of tweaking". John Ray, who joined Atari in 1977, engineered the hardware on his first video game project, designing the analogue circuits for the siren and horn. Atari released it in North America in June 1978, and Namco distributed it in Japan. Operators felt the two-player cabinet took up too much floor space for its takings, which led to Smokey Joe; RePlay ranked Smokey Joe ninth and Fire Truck twelfth among US arcade games of 1978.

title: Space Invaders
description: Space Invaders (1978) is Tomohiro Nishikado's Taito shooter, in which a laser cannon picks off rows of descending aliens — a worldwide hit that made video games a mass medium.
longDescription: Five rows of eleven aliens march back and forth, edging lower, while the player shoots up from behind crumbling shields. The fewer aliens remain, the faster they move — a side effect of the hardware drawing fewer sprites, which Nishikado kept as a feature — and a four-note bass line speeds up with them. Its 1980 Atari 2600 version was the first official home version of an arcade game and quadrupled the console's sales.
trivia: Nishikado felt that shooting human characters was immoral, which pushed him towards aliens.
Many publications credit it with the first saved high score, but Sea Wolf (1976) did it first.
It was reported to have grossed $2 billion by 1982, the highest-grossing entertainment product of its time.
devStory: Nishikado spent about a year designing the game and the custom hardware and tools it needed. His influences included Breakout, Star Wars and The War of the Worlds.

title: Asteroids
description: Asteroids (1979) is Atari's vector-graphics shooter in which a small ship blasts boulders that split into smaller pieces — Atari's best-selling arcade game.
longDescription: The triangular ship rotates, thrusts and fires, keeping its momentum and drifting slowly to a stop when not thrusting, while large asteroids break into smaller, faster ones that are harder to hit and worth more points. Hyperspace jumps the ship to a random spot, at the risk of exploding or landing on a rock. Two saucers appear from time to time: the big one fires at random, and the small one aims at the ship, with only the small one appearing after 40,000 points and its aim growing more accurate as the score rises. Objects leaving one edge of the screen reappear on the other. Players start with three to five lives and gain one every 10,000 points, the score turns over at 99,990, and a heartbeat soundtrack quickens as each wave goes on.
trivia: Some players "lurked" near the edge opposite a saucer and shot across the screen boundary to farm saucers while leaving a rock or two in play.
Some operators had to install larger boxes to hold all the coins.
It was the top-grossing US arcade game of 1980, ending Space Invaders' run, and the 2600 version sold over three million copies.
John McAllister set a record of 41,838,740 points in 2010 during a 58-hour livestream.
The Museum of Modern Art added it to its collection.
devStory: Lyle Rains conceived it and Ed Logg programmed it, building on an unfinished Atari game called Cosmos, with an indestructible asteroid, and discussed in April 1979. Logg chose a vector monitor over Rains' raster graphics for precise aiming, and modelled the ship, controls and physics on Spacewar!; the board has no sound chip, and its 13 sound effects were built by hand. Its vector hardware, designed by Wendi Allen, had been used for Lunar Lander. After tests in Sacramento arcades it came out in North America in November 1979. Atari sold over 70,000 cabinets, earning an estimated $150 million, though it was a commercial failure in Japan.

title: Galaxian
description: Galaxian (1979) is Namco's answer to Space Invaders, whose aliens break formation to dive at the player — one of the first games with RGB colour graphics.
longDescription: The player's ship, the Galaxip, faces aliens that gather in formation at the top of the screen and peel off in diving attacks, firing as they come. Only one shot can be in flight at a time, so a miss leaves the player waiting. Destroying a Flagship diving with its two red escorts earns a bonus, more if the Flagship is hit last, and enemies move and fire faster as the rounds, shown as flags, go by. The team followed a "simple is best" approach, with two enemy types and an endlessly looping design, enemies that watched the player's movement and attacked accordingly, and a constant number of enemies on screen while difficulty rose. Its tile-based hardware, with multicoloured sprites and a scrolling starfield, made it one of the first games in full RGB colour.
trivia: Namco's president asked for the best "post-Invaders" game the team could make.
Its sequel, Galaga (1981), became even more popular.
Its hardware sprites over a scrolling background influenced Nintendo's Radar Scope, Donkey Kong and the Famicom.
The Galaxian Flagship is the sixth bonus fruit in Pac-Man.
The Guardian ranked it the greatest video game of the 1970s in 2021.
devStory: Namco president Masaya Nakamura asked for the best "post-Invaders" game the team could make, and Kazunori Sawano, who had worked on Namco's electro-mechanical shooting galleries, designed it with Shigeichi Ishimura over six months; its enemies were first drawn to resemble Star Wars TIE fighters, and it was Namco's first arcade game with music composed on a synthesiser. Namco released it in Japan on 15 September 1979, and Midway, which had lost its Taito licence, brought it to North America in February 1980. It was the second-highest-grossing arcade game of 1979 in Japan and of 1980 in the US, and sold about 50,000 US units by 1982.

title: Lunar Lander
description: Lunar Lander (1979) is Atari's vector-graphics landing simulator: manage fuel, thrust and rotation to set a module down gently on the Moon.
longDescription: Seen from the side in black-and-white vector graphics, the module stays centred while jagged terrain, with only a few flat landing areas, scrolls beneath it; near the surface the view zooms in. Two buttons rotate the module, a large handle controls the thrust, and an abort button sets it upright and fires the thruster at the cost of a lot of fuel. The lander keeps its momentum, so the player has to arrive slowly and upright on a flat area: a crash comes from landing too fast, too far from vertical or on uneven ground. Smaller landing areas flash with higher bonus multipliers, and good landings award a little fuel. There is no time limit; the game ends when the module crashes after the fuel runs out, and coins buy more fuel. Four difficulty levels, changeable during play, alter the landing areas and controls, and on the hardest the module keeps rotating until the player counters it.
trivia: Operators could set how much fuel a coin bought, from 450 to 900 units.
It sold 4,830 cabinets.
The first 300 Asteroids units shipped in Lunar Lander cabinets.
With Asteroids, it was one of the first two games registered with the US Copyright Office, in 1980.
A crater showing previous crashes and a McDonald's easter egg were cut.
devStory: The Lunar Lander concept began as a text game in 1969, and DEC's graphical Moonlander followed in 1973. Atari began a vector engine after Cinematronics' Space Wars, and Wendi Allen developed Cyan Engineering's initial hardware into an engine for designers. Development began in fall 1978, with Allen on hardware and Rich Moore, at Atari only a few months, programming; Moore drew graphics on graph paper, and code was written on paper and typed in. Realistic movement proved nearly unplayable, so the team settled on four difficulty levels, and Allen chose a large handle with ten thrust levels over a joystick. Atari released it in August 1979, its first vector game; it sold 4,830 cabinets before Asteroids, on the same engine, overtook it.

title: Monaco GP
description: Monaco GP (1979) is Sega's top-down racing game on a scrolling road that narrows, ices over and passes through tunnels and over bridges.
longDescription: Seen from above, the player races to finish the course before time runs out, weaving between rival cars and scoring points through five areas. As play goes on the rivals speed up, the road narrows and the surface turns to ice and gravel, with puddles, narrow bridges and tunnels where the player can only see as far as the headlights. The timer runs until 2,000 points, after which the game switches to a limited number of lives, and rival cars speed up again at 6,000 and 8,000. The deluxe cockpit cabinet has a padded steering wheel, accelerator pedal and gear stick, and scores are shown on LEDs.
trivia: It ran on discrete TTL logic rather than a microprocessor, with over 100 chips on two boards.
It was Japan's third-highest-grossing arcade game of 1979, and Cash Box called it the most popular US arcade driving game of 1981.
It appeared on RePlay's monthly charts for seven years, a record.
Super Monaco GP designer Hisao Oguchi had played it before joining Sega.
A Sega Ages remake came to the PlayStation 2 in 2003.
devStory: One of Sega's last games built on discrete TTL logic rather than a microprocessor, it used over 100 chips across two boards, with custom ROMs for the sprites and analogue circuitry for its engine, siren and tyre sounds; the timer was reportedly Sega president Hayao Nakayama's idea. First shown at a Tokyo trade show, it was released in November 1979 and was Japan's third-highest-grossing arcade game of the year. It stayed on RePlay's monthly US earnings charts from April 1980 to April 1987, a record, and RePlay's Eddie Adlum called it the "most evergreen" hit of 1979. Pro Monaco GP, harder and with battery-saved high scores, followed in 1980.

title: Tail Gunner
description: Tail Gunner (1979) puts the player in the rear turret of a spacecraft, shooting down wireframe fighters drawn in vector graphics.
longDescription: The player is the tail gunner of a large spaceship, aiming crosshairs at enemy fighters that attack in groups of three and shooting them before they get past the ship's cannons. Because of the rearward view, the stars stream towards the left and centre of the screen rather than flying outward. A shield, usable only a limited number of times, can block ships from getting past, and the game ends when ten have slipped by. The monochrome vector graphics give the attackers a wireframe, three-dimensional look. The controls are a single metal joystick with the fire button built into its tip.
trivia: It was also sold as Tail Gunner II in a sit-down cabinet.
Its stars stream inwards, because the player is looking backwards.
The game ends once ten enemy ships have got past.
Its fire button sits in the tip of the joystick.
Its joystick input runs through the monitor's DAC, so the cabinet cannot simply host other games.
devStory: Dan Sunday and Larry Rosenthal designed it at Vectorbeam, on Vectorbeam's own hardware, and Cinematronics published it in November 1979. Its sound card was more complex than any earlier Cinematronics or Vectorbeam game, and because the cabinet used the monitor's DAC to read the joystick, other games could not necessarily be installed in a Tail Gunner cabinet.

title: Adventure
description: Adventure (1980) is Warren Robinett's Atari 2600 action-adventure — a graphical take on Colossal Cave Adventure, and home of one of the earliest known video game Easter eggs.
longDescription: Adventure turned the text game Colossal Cave Adventure into pictures: players guide a square hero through 30 one-screen rooms — the Golden, White and Black castles, mazes, some of them invisible, and catacombs — to return an enchanted chalice to the Golden Castle. The hero carries one object at a time: castle keys, a sword that slays dragons, a magnet and a magic bridge. Three dragons — yellow Yorgle, green Grundle and red Rhindle — can eat the hero, and a roaming bat carries off objects and even dragons, swapping them around. An eaten hero can be revived at the Golden Castle, but the dragons revive too. Level 1 is a simplified layout, Level 2 the full game and Level 3 the full game with objects placed at random. Because Atari did not credit its programmers, Robinett hid a room reading "Created by Warren Robinett", reached by bringing a hidden dot and other objects to a corridor wall below the Golden Castle.
trivia: Atari stopped crediting developers so competitors could not recruit them and they had less leverage in negotiations.
Adam Clayton, a 15-year-old from Salt Lake City, found the secret room and wrote to Atari; by then Robinett had left the company.
It sold more than a million copies, among the 2600's best sellers.
Robinett said Atari paid him about $22,000 a year, with no royalties.
Its Easter egg is a plot element in Ready Player One.
devStory: Robinett began designing it around mid-1978, with a 2600 that had 4 KB of cartridge ROM and 128 bytes of RAM; his supervisor, George Simcock, first said it could not be done. A first prototype took about a month, and a second, in late 1978, had about eight rooms, one dragon and two objects. He worked out the plot with Steve Harding, submitted the code in June 1979 and then left Atari, which released it in March 1980. Removing the Easter egg would have needed a new ROM mask costing about $10,000, so Atari left it in and adopted the term "Easter eggs".

title: Temple of Apshai
developer: Jim Connelley, Jon Freeman & Jeff Johnson
description: Temple of Apshai (1979) is Automated Simulations' graphical dungeon crawler, whose room descriptions were printed in the manual for players to read as they explored.
longDescription: The game comes as two programs: the Innkeeper, which creates or loads a character with six base values taken from Dungeons & Dragons and sells weapons and armour at negotiable prices, and the Dunjonmaster, which runs the exploration. A single adventurer explores four dungeons of rising difficulty, with over 200 rooms and 30 kinds of monster, shown from above alongside a status summary, and hunts for traps, treasure and secret doors. Each room has a number, which players look up in the manual to read its description. Combat mixes turns with real time: a turn can move up to nine steps, attack or try to talk a monster out of fighting, but enemies keep acting if the player waits. Actions tire the character according to their stats and the weight they carry, and a defeated character may be rescued by non-player characters who take part of the inventory as payment. There is no fixed goal beyond fighting, treasure and experience.
trivia: It sold 30,000 copies by mid-1982 and about 400,000 by 1986.
It began the Dunjonquest series, which grew to ten titles including the sequel Hellfire Warrior.
The 1985 Temple of Apshai Trilogy bundled it with two expansions.
It won the first Origins Award for Best Computer Game, for 1980.
Early tape versions could not save; later floppy versions saved the character to disk.
devStory: Jim Connelley programmed the original in BASIC for the TRS-80 and Commodore PET, with Jon Freeman designing the Dunjonquest role-playing system and Jeff Johnson the dungeon levels; its documentation explained how to import pen-and-paper characters. Automated Simulations, later renamed Epyx, released it in August 1979, at $24.95 on cassette and $29.95 on disk, and an Apple II version followed in 1980. It won the Origins Award for Best Computer Game of 1980, the first in that category, and remained a best-seller for at least four years.

title: Missile Command
description: Missile Command (1980) is Dave Theurer's Atari arcade game about defending six cities from nuclear attack, a battle that always ends with "The End".
longDescription:
With a trackball and three missile bases, the player defends six cities against waves of incoming warheads, moving a crosshair and pressing one of three buttons to fire from the left, centre or right battery. Each counter-missile explodes at the crosshair and leaves a fireball that lingers for a few seconds, destroying any warhead or aircraft that flies into it, so the skill lies in leading targets rather than hitting them directly.

Each battery starts a wave with ten missiles, and the centre battery's are much faster, the only ones that can reliably catch a smart bomb at a distance. Later waves bring warheads that split in flight, smart bombs that dodge badly aimed shots, and bombers and satellites that cross the screen launching missiles of their own. At most three cities can fall in a single wave, and bonuses are paid for every missile and city left at the end of it.

A score multiplier rises every second wave up to 6x, and bonus cities earned at set scores are held in reserve to replace lost ones. There is no way to win: the attacks keep getting faster and denser until the last city falls, and the game closes with "The End" rather than "Game Over".
trivia: Theurer suffered nightmares of being destroyed in a nuclear blast.
Atari had a rule that a programmer's first game was not released; Missile Command was a noted exception.
Rob Fulop hid his initials in the 2600 version: they appear on wave 13 if the player runs out of missiles without scoring.
A two-player sequel, Missile Command 2, was field-tested in late 1980 but never released.
In 1981 Jody Bowles played for 30 hours on one quarter in Pensacola, Florida, scoring 41,399,845 on marathon settings.
Tony Temple set a tournament-settings record of 1,967,830 points in 2006.
John Connor plays it in an arcade in Terminator 2: Judgment Day.
devStory:
Gene Lipkin, president of Atari's coin-op division, asked department head Steve Calfee for a game based on a radar-screen image he had seen in a magazine, and the job went to Dave Theurer, a junior programmer who had just finished Atari Soccer. Because the project was high-profile, Rich Adam was assigned to help him. Early versions defended six named California cities, from Eureka to San Diego; Theurer insisted that no countries be named, that the game be purely defensive and that the player could never retaliate. He chose a trackball over a joystick for speed, and it became Atari's first colour game. A panel of indicator lights on the prototype cabinet was removed after field tests found it distracting.

It came out in North America in June 1980 and in Japan that July, where it was among the year's ten highest-grossing arcade games. It sold nearly 20,000 cabinets. Rob Fulop's Atari 2600 version followed in April 1981, with versions for the Atari 8-bit computers, the 5200, the Atari ST and, from 1992, the Game Boy.

title: Battlezone
description: Battlezone (1980) is Atari's first-person tank game, built in 3D vector graphics and viewed through a periscope — one of the first true 3D video games.
longDescription: The player commands a tank on a flat wireframe battlefield under a green-and-red colour overlay, with mountains on the horizon, an erupting volcano and a crescent moon. Two joysticks drive the left and right treads, like a real tank, and the fire button sits on top of the right stick. Indestructible pyramids and blocks block movement and shots and can be used as cover. Enemies can come from any direction, including behind, so the radar is essential: slow tanks at first, then faster missiles, then aggressive supertanks, with saucers that appear on no radar, never attack and are worth bonus points. The game is housed in an upright cabinet with a periscope viewfinder, while spectators watch from the sides.
trivia: The US Army commissioned a version for training Bradley gunners; Rotberg agreed to work on it only after being promised he would never be asked to do military work again.
Owen Rubin came up with the volcano's eruption animation.
About 15,000 cabinets were sold, and a later cabinet dropped the periscope.
One of the two Army trainers was found by a collector near a dumpster at Midway Games.
Its 3D hardware was reused for Red Baron (1981).
devStory: The idea for a tank game came out of a brainstorming session on new uses for Atari's vector hardware, built on the 3D "Math Box" developed by Jed Margolin and Mike Albaugh. Ed Rotberg led the design, inspired by Atari's Tank, and Owen Rubin, who shared his office, proposed and animated the volcano. Atari released it in November 1980, and about 15,000 cabinets were sold. A Bradley Fighting Vehicle trainer for the US Army followed, which some Atari staff refused to work on; Rotberg joined only after being promised he would never be asked to do military work again. Historians call it the first true 3D arcade game with a first-person view.

title: Rally-X
description: Namco's 1980 maze game behind the wheel: steer a race car around a scrolling maze, collecting flags while red cars give chase and a smoke screen buys a few seconds of escape.
longDescription:
Namco released Rally-X in Japanese arcades on 3 October 1980. Midway Manufacturing distributed it in North America from February 1981, and Karateco brought it to Europe the same year.

The player drives a blue Formula One-style car through a maze that scrolls in every direction, hunting for yellow flags. Boulders block some routes, red enemy cars chase the player and end the run on contact, and fuel steadily drains. The car can release a smoke screen that stuns pursuers, but each puff costs fuel — a simple trade-off that gives the game its tension. Rally-X was one of the first games with a scrolling playfield and a radar map of the whole maze.
trivia: It is credited as one of the first games with continuous background music.
A much-repeated story says Rally-X outshone Pac-Man at the 1980 AMOA show; Play Meter reported that both got only mild attention.
A Special Flag doubles the value of every flag collected after it.
devStory: Hirohito Ito designed it, with Kazuo Kurosu programming and Kouichi Tashiro developing the hardware. Namco released it in Japan in October 1980 and Midway in North America in February 1981. Pac-Man went on to overshadow it.

title: Crazy Climber
description: Crazy Climber (1980) is Nichibutsu's skyscraper-climbing game, played with two joysticks at once — one for each side of the climber's body.
longDescription: The player scales the faces of four skyscrapers, working each side of the climber with its own joystick to haul him up from window to window. Windows open and close, and objects fall from above, so their patterns have to be learned. The game ends when the climber misses a handhold and falls.
trivia: It is described as the first climbing game, predating Donkey Kong (1981).
An Easter egg that changes "JORDAN.LTD" to "JORDAN" gives two extra credits.
Crazy Climber '85 was finished but shelved in favour of Terra Cresta.
Sequels include Crazy Climber 2 (1988), Hyper Crazy Climber (1996) and the 3D Crazy Climber 2000.
It was the debut title of Hamster's Arcade Archives line on PlayStation 4 in 2014.
devStory:
Shigeki Fujiwara designed it at Nichibutsu, and later created the Bomberman series at Hudson Soft. He wanted the climber to be chased by a wall of fire, but Nichibutsu rejected the idea. Toshikazu Sato and Kyoji Oda of Jorudan programmed it over five months, working from storyboards. Nichibutsu released it in Japan in October 1980, and Taito brought it to North America that December.

It was the third-highest-grossing arcade game in Japan in 1980, behind Pac-Man and Galaxian, and the eighth in 1981; in North America it reached the top ten in summer 1982. Ports followed for the Atari 2600, the Famicom (1986), the X68000 and the WonderSwan, which added four stages.

title: Berzerk
description: Berzerk (1980) is Stern's maze shooter: blast robots room by room, and keep moving before the unkillable Evil Otto bounces in.
longDescription: The player's Humanoid Intruder enters each maze-like room at the middle of one edge and has to shoot the robots and escape through an opening on another side. Robots move slowly and sometimes fire, in eight directions, and the player can also fire in eight directions with the joystick, but cannot move while firing. A robot or its shot, a wall or Evil Otto costs a life. Evil Otto, an indestructible smiley face, eventually bounces in from the side the player entered, passing through walls in pursuit, and was added to push players out of rooms they had cleared. Clearing every robot in a room earns a bonus. Digitised speech taunts the player during play and in attract mode, made with a chip that produced hisses and tones through custom hardware.
trivia: Evil Otto was named after Dave Otto, an office manager at Dave Nutting Associates.
Peter Burkowski died of a heart attack after playing it in 1982; McNeil denied rumours of other deaths.
Stern sold around 15,000 units, a sizable hit for the company.
Early large joysticks were replaced with standard Wico sticks because players pulled hard enough to tip the cabinet.
Eugene Jarvis noticed that holding fire stopped movement but still allowed aiming, which inspired Robotron: 2084's second joystick.
devStory: Alan McNeil designed and programmed it, and also did its art, graphics and debugging. He had worked at Dave Nutting Associates on Boot Hill and Sea Wolf II, and rejoined Stern in 1979, building the first prototype on a Tektronix development system; it was influenced by an earlier game called Chase, and its title came from Fred Saberhagen's Berserker novels. The robots at first moved too fast, so McNeil slowed them and changed how many shots they fired per room, and colour was added in the last month of production. Stern revealed it at the AMOA show in Chicago from 31 October to 2 November 1980, where crowds reportedly lined up daily, began shipping that November and sold about 15,000 units.

title: Space Panic
description: Space Panic (1980) is Universal's arcade game of ladders and floors, the first to have characters climb ladders between platforms: dig holes to trap aliens, then knock them through.
longDescription: Seen from the side, the hero cannot jump. Instead he runs along layered platforms, climbs ladders between them and digs holes for the pursuing aliens to fall into, then knocks them through with his shovel and off the screen. In later levels stronger aliens need two or more holes lined up vertically to fall through. A dwindling supply of oxygen acts as the timer. It was the first game built around climbing ladders between walkable platforms, before Donkey Kong, in what were first called "climbing games" and later platform games.
trivia: It did well in Japan but was an obscure, unsuccessful release in North America.
Apple Panic (1981), an unauthorised clone, outsold the original in North America, and Lode Runner (1983) took inspiration from its digging.
Chuckie Egg's creator, Nigel Alderton, cited it as an inspiration, down to its colour scheme.
Over a dozen clones appeared, many with "panic" in the title.
Michael Thomasson called it the foundation of platformers.
devStory: Universal developed it, with Kazutoshi Ueda, later designer of Lady Bug and Mr. Do!, on the team, taking the digging and trapping of Heiankyo Alien (1979) and turning it side-on with platforms and ladders. It came out in November 1980 and did well in Japan, where it tied as the 14th-highest-grossing arcade game of 1981, but flopped in North America; Electronic Games blamed the novelty of the idea and reported an average play time of 30 seconds. Casio and Coleco published home versions in 1983, after an unauthorised clone, Apple Panic, had already become an Apple II best seller.

title: Pac-Man
description: Pac-Man (1980) is Namco's maze game in which a yellow disc eats dots while four ghosts give chase — designed by Toru Iwatani to draw women and couples into arcades, and the best-selling arcade game of all time.
longDescription: Pac-Man eats the dots in a maze while the ghosts Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde hunt him; power pellets briefly turn the tables so he can eat them. Blinky chases him directly, Pinky and Inky try to get ahead and corner him, and Clyde switches between chasing and fleeing. Within a year more than 100,000 cabinets had sold, taking over $1 billion in quarters.
trivia: Iwatani often said a pizza with a slice missing inspired the shape; in 1986 he said that was only partly true, and that he also rounded off the Japanese character for "mouth".
The ghosts' Japanese names mean chaser, ambusher, fickle and playing dumb.
An integer overflow garbles level 256, making it impossible to finish.
Billy Mitchell scored a perfect 3,333,360 in 1999; Guinness reinstated the record in 2020.
devStory: Iwatani's team began in early 1979 and took one year and five months, then the longest development of any video game. Namco released it in Japan in May 1980, and Midway in North America later that year. It led to a Hanna-Barbera cartoon and the No. 9 hit "Pac-Man Fever".

title: Centipede
description: Centipede (1981) is Atari's trackball shooter, designed by Ed Logg and Dona Bailey, in which a centipede winds down through a mushroom field — one of the first arcade games with a large female audience.
longDescription: The player's Bug Blaster, moved with a trackball along the bottom of the screen, fires darts at a centipede that enters at the top and drops a row and reverses each time it touches a mushroom or the edge. Each segment hit becomes another mushroom, and shooting a middle segment splits the centipede in two, the rear piece growing a new head. Mushrooms take four shots to clear, and a crowded field brings the centipede down faster. Once it reaches the bottom, extra heads keep arriving from the sides. Fleas drop straight down leaving mushrooms, spiders zig-zag across eating mushrooms and score more the closer they are shot, and scorpions poison the mushrooms they touch, sending any centipede that hits one diving straight at the player. Each new centipede is one segment shorter, with a faster detached head.
trivia: One estimate put half its players as women.
The Atari 2600 version sold 1,475,240 cartridges in 1982–83.
Its sequel, Millipede, followed in 1982.
It was used in the final round of the 1981 Atari World Championships.
Jim Schneider's 1984 score of 16,389,547 is the arcade record.
