The Supershot was a charged projectile that could clear entire rooms — holding the fire button for a few seconds was a skill in itself.
devStory: Gauntlet II was designed by Ed Logg at Atari Games in 1986. It expanded on the original with new enemy types including ghosts that could only be damaged briefly, IT enemies that transferred their status on touch, and the Supershot — a charge-up weapon. The game retained the four-player simultaneous format and the health-draining over time mechanic that made the original a revenue powerhouse.

title: Rygar
description: Rygar (1986) is Tecmo's side-scrolling action game in which a warrior fights with the diskarmor, a spiked shield on a chain.
longDescription: Rygar, a legendary warrior, battles through a mythic land with the diskarmor — a spinning, spiked shield flung out on a chain. The arcade game is a fast, straight-ahead side-scroller with power-ups that extend its reach and strength. The NES version that followed was a very different game, reworking the idea into a non-linear adventure with RPG-style growth and abilities that open new areas.
trivia: The arcade and NES versions of Rygar are essentially different games — the NES version added open-world exploration and RPG progression the arcade never had.
The diskarmor weapon — a spinning shield on a chain — was one of gaming's more exotic weapons, functioning as both attack and grapple.
Rygar on NES had no save system — the game had to be completed in a single session or abandoned.
The game's non-linear world and ability-gated areas make it a direct ancestor of the Metroidvania genre, despite predating the term.
devStory: Rygar was developed by Tecmo in 1986. The arcade version was a straightforward side-scrolling action game, while the NES version transformed it into an open-world adventure with RPG elements. The NES Rygar is considered one of the earliest "Metroidvania" style games — a largely non-linear world where new abilities unlocked previously inaccessible areas.

title: Ghosts 'n Goblins (NES)
description: The NES Ghosts 'n Goblins (1986) is Micronics' conversion of Capcom's arcade game, the first Famicom game on a 128 KB cartridge, which sold 1.64 million copies.
longDescription: Sir Arthur sets out to rescue Princess Prin-Prin, kidnapped by Astaroth, king of the Demon World, fighting zombies, giants, demons, cyclopes and dragons on the way. He can pick up new weapons, bonuses and extra suits of armour. The first hit strips his armour and the second kills him, sending him back to the start of the level or the last checkpoint, and he also dies if a level is not finished in time. Some bosses are immune to certain weapons. Beating Astaroth is not the end: the whole game must be played again on a higher difficulty to reach the true ending.
trivia: It was the first Famicom game to use a 128 KB cartridge.
Famitsu gave it its Best Port award for 1986.
Computer Gaming World called it "an excellent example of what the [NES] can do".
Nintendo Power ranked it 129th in its Top 200 Games.
A version on Nintendo's classics service gives immediate access to the final level.
devStory:
Tokuro Fujiwara directed the arcade original at Capcom, with music by Ayako Mori. Micronics programmed the Famicom conversion, which Capcom published in Japan on 13 June 1986, the first Famicom game on a 128 KB cartridge, and it reached the NES in North America that November. A hidden credits screen confirms Mori as composer.

The Famicom version won Best Port at the 1986 Famitsu Best Hit Game Awards, and Computer Gaming World praised the NES version. It sold 1.64 million copies. Later critics were harder on it: GameRankings lists it at 55%, and Game Rant ranked it among the hardest games ever made.

title: Image Fight
description: Image Fight (1988) is Irem's demanding vertical shooter: a combat simulation where poor performance sends the pilot through penalty stages.
longDescription: Image Fight frames its vertical-scrolling missions as a training simulation. Players collect pods that attach to the ship and fire in different directions, and can switch the ship's speed. Five simulation stages test accuracy, and failing to destroy enough enemies sends the pilot to a punishing penalty stage before the real battle. From the studio behind R-Type, it is aimed at players who want a severe challenge.
trivia: Failing to achieve a minimum score in regular stages triggered mandatory penalty stages — a shame mechanic built into the game design.
Image Fight's difficulty was extreme even by Irem's standards — the studio that made R-Type made this game for players who wanted more punishment.
The game was set in a military near-future, with a training simulation framing that explained the penalty stage mechanic in-fiction.
Pod attachments mirrored R-Type's Force concept — Irem was developing a house style for shooter mechanics.
devStory: Image Fight was developed by Irem in 1988. The vertical-scrolling shooter was notable for its extreme difficulty and an unusual penalty system — playing poorly in the main stages forced players through "penalty stages" designed to be even harder. The game was designed for players who found other shooters too easy.

title: Twin Cobra
description: Twin Cobra (1987) is Toaplan's vertically scrolling helicopter shooter, the sequel to Tiger-Heli, with four colour-coded weapons, screen-clearing bombs and two-player co-op.
longDescription: The player flies a gunship helicopter through ten stages over land and sea, each ending in a boss. Carriers drop icons that change colour between red, blue, green and yellow, switching between four weapon types, while "S" icons strengthen the current weapon — until a hit drops it back to its starting level. "B" icons add bombs, gold star medals are worth 3,000 points, and 1-ups appear too. Depending on the region, a lost life returns the player to a checkpoint or respawns them on the spot. After the last stage the game loops with harder enemies and denser bullets. Two players can play at once.
trivia: Its Japanese title, Kyūkyoku Tiger, reportedly comes from Yes's album Going for the One.
A Seibu Kaihatsu artist claimed Raiden borrowed ideas from it.
Its sequel, Twin Cobra II, was finished by Takumi Corporation and released in 1995.
It was Toaplan's second game to use FM synthesis.
Bitwave Games brought it to Steam in 2023.
devStory:
A team of about five at Toaplan, three of them designers, made it in six months, among the studio's early users of written design documents. Its structure came from Slap Fight, and the bomb idea from the development of Tiger-Heli. Kōetsu Iwabuchi drew the art, mostly from hand sketches, and Masahiro Yuge and Tatsuya Uemura composed the music and also programmed; two-player play was added after the single-player game was finished, partly for the American market. It ran on a Motorola 68000 board shared with Flying Shark.

Taito released it in Japan in October 1987 and Romstar in North America that November, and it was reportedly Japan's highest-grossing arcade conversion kit of 1988. Conversions followed for the PC Engine, NES, Genesis, X68000 and FM Towns.

title: Truxton
description: Truxton (1988), Tatsujin in Japan, is Toaplan's vertical shooter, created by Masahiro Yuge, with three switchable weapons and screen-clearing bombs.
longDescription: The player pilots Tatsuo in the Super Fighter through five vertically scrolling stages, each ending with a boss, against the Gidans, who have invaded the planet Borogo aboard five asteroids. The main gun reaches the full height of the screen, and three bombs destroy enemies within their blast radius. Destroying carriers releases three weapons: red, a wide shot; blue, a homing laser; and green, a straight beam. Collecting a colour switches to that weapon, and consecutive "P" icons build up its power, alongside 1UPs and speed increases. Being hit costs a life and resets firepower, and a single player restarts from the last checkpoint. Hidden bonuses reward meeting certain requirements, and after the last stage the game loops back to the first, harder the second time.
trivia: Tatsujin means "master" or "expert" in Japanese.
Game Machine listed it as the most successful table arcade unit of November 1988.
Yuge said it sold well in Japan but less so in the West.
Truxton II followed in arcades in 1992.
The company Yuge founded in 2017, which owns the Toaplan rights, is named Tatsujin after it.
devStory: Masahiro Yuge, who had worked on Tiger-Heli, Slap Fight and Twin Cobra, created it as his first original project as producer and composer, starting it privately during Twin Cobra's production and developing it alongside Hellfire; Naoki Ogiwara, Sanae Nitō and Yuko Tataka designed it. Its memorisation and secrets came from Slap Fight, and the blue homing laser from a dream Yuge had. Taito released it in Japan in October 1988 as Tatsujin, and Midway and Taito released it in the West in February 1989. It was Toaplan's first game to show its logo on the title screen. The original staff made the Mega Drive version in-house, released in Japan in December 1989.

title: Mercs
description: Mercs (1989) is Capcom's three-player overhead run-and-gun, a follow-up to Commando, sending mercenaries to rescue a kidnapped president.
longDescription: Mercs sends a team of up to three mercenaries into a war zone to rescue a kidnapped former US president, fighting through jungles, rivers and bases in eight stages. Weapons can be upgraded, vehicles such as jeeps and boats can be commandeered, and a limited mega crash bomb clears the screen. It was released as Senjō no Ōkami II in Japan, the sequel to Commando, and was one of Capcom's last major overhead military shooters.
trivia: Mercs brought back Super Joe from Commando — one of gaming's earlier examples of sequel narrative continuity for a non-major character.
Three-player simultaneous play was supported in the arcade version, one of the earlier three-player overhead action games.
The shop system between missions let players purchase new weapons and equipment, adding RPG-lite progression.
Mercs was the last entry in Capcom's overhead military shooter lineage — the studio moved to Final Fight and Street Fighter II.
devStory: Mercs was developed by Capcom in 1989 as a sequel to Commando. Super Joe returned as the lead character, now heading a mercenary team. The overhead military shooter added a third player slot, varied missions, and a shop system for purchasing equipment between stages. It was one of Capcom's last major overhead run-and-gun games before the genre was largely replaced by beat-em-ups.

title: WrestleFest
description: WrestleFest (1991) is Technos Japan's WWF arcade wrestling game, with tag-team matches and a Royal Rumble for up to four players.
longDescription: Up to four players can join in, and extra credits buy more energy. Saturday Night's Main Event pairs two wrestlers as a tag team through a series of matches ending in a title bout against the Legion of Doom, Hawk and Animal, with many double-team moves. The new Royal Rumble mode takes a single wrestler through a Rumble match. The ten selectable wrestlers are Hulk Hogan, the Ultimate Warrior, Ted DiBiase and Big Boss Man, back from WWF Superstars, plus Jake Roberts, Earthquake, Mr. Perfect, Sgt. Slaughter and Demolition's Smash and Crush, each with signature moves. Ring announcer Mike McGuirk provides commentary and introductions, and Gene Okerlund's voiced cutscenes return.
trivia: Sinclair User named it Best Beat 'Em Up of 1991, jointly with Konami's Vendetta.
It was the highest-grossing arcade conversion kit of 1992 in the US.
THQ released a remake, WWE WrestleFest, for iOS in 2012.
RetroMania Wrestling (2021) was promoted as its successor.
The Legion of Doom appear only as the champions to beat.
devStory: Technōs Japan made it as the sequel to WWF Superstars, with Yoshihisa Kishimoto and Shinichi Saito directing and Kunio Taki producing, adding more wrestlers, better graphics and sound and more voice samples. It came out in North America in June 1991, and later in Japan and Europe, where Tecmo distributed it. RePlay ranked it the second most popular arcade game in North America that October, and the AMOA named it the highest-grossing arcade conversion kit of 1992 in the US. Sinclair User gave it 88%, praising its variety of characters and replay value.

title: Galaxy Force II
description: Galaxy Force II (1988) is Sega's 3D space shooter, flying through planets and fortresses on Super Scaler hardware, some cabinets rotating the player.
longDescription: Galaxy Force II flies a starfighter into the screen across planet surfaces and into enemy fortresses, locking on to multiple targets and firing homing missiles while managing a draining energy supply. Sega's sprite-scaling hardware pushed large numbers of scaled objects to create a convincing sense of 3D speed. It was offered in a motion cabinet that could turn the seated player, one of the most elaborate machines of its time — and correspondingly rare in arcades.
trivia: The Galaxy Force II cabinet could rotate completely — full 360-degree motion in sync with the on-screen action.
The scaling hardware processed more sprites per frame than almost any other 1988 arcade game.
The game's cost and mechanical complexity made it rare in arcades — a paradox where the most impressive games were seen by the fewest players.
devStory: Galaxy Force II was developed by Sega in 1988. The third-person rail shooter used Sega's most advanced scaling hardware to render a vast three-dimensional tunnel at high speed. The motion-simulator cabinet version rotated 360 degrees. It was one of the most technically impressive arcade games of 1988, though its difficulty and the cabinet's mechanical complexity limited its commercial reach.

title: Thunder Blade
description: Thunder Blade (1987) is Sega's helicopter gunship shooter, alternating between overhead stages and behind-the-craft 3D flight.
longDescription: Thunder Blade pilots an attack helicopter against tanks, gunships and fortresses. Each stage begins viewed from above and then switches to a third-person view behind the helicopter as it weaves between skyscrapers and canyons. It used Sega's sprite-scaling hardware for its 3D sections, and a deluxe cabinet moved the seat with the flight stick. It was part of Sega's run of high-end arcade spectacles in the late 1980s.
trivia: Thunder Blade switched between overhead and third-person perspectives within the same game — a technical achievement in 1987.
The hydraulic joystick — rather than a full motion cabinet — was Sega's cost-reduced approach to simulated flight.
Both aircraft and ground enemies required different attack approaches, forcing players to switch mental models between phases.
Sega's Super Scaler hardware family — used across Space Harrier, Out Run, After Burner, and Thunder Blade — was the most capable sprite-scaling system of the era.
devStory: Thunder Blade was developed by Sega in 1987. The helicopter combat game alternated between overhead and third-person behind-the-craft perspectives, using Sega's Super Scaler hardware for smooth sprite scaling. The hydraulic cabinet tilted the joystick platform rather than the entire seat. Thunder Blade was part of Sega's late-1980s push to dominate the high-end arcade market.

title: Super Mario Bros. 2
description: Super Mario Bros. 2 (1988) is Nintendo's Western NES sequel, rebuilt from Doki Doki Panic: pluck vegetables and throw enemies as Mario, Luigi, Toad or Peach.
longDescription: Rather than release Japan's punishing Super Mario Bros. 2 abroad, Nintendo reworked Doki Doki Panic into a new Mario game set in the dream world of Subcon. Before each level players pick one of four heroes — Luigi jumps highest, Peach can float, Toad digs and carries fastest, Mario is balanced — and defeat enemies by pulling up vegetables and throwing them, or by lifting enemies themselves. The villain is Wart, and the ending reveals it was all Mario's dream. It was later released in Japan as Super Mario USA.
trivia: Super Mario Bros. 2 was originally a different game — Doki Doki Panic — with the characters reskinned as Mario, Luigi, Toad, and Peach.
The four playable characters each moved differently: Luigi jumped highest, Peach could float, Toad ran fastest, Mario was balanced.
Enemies were defeated by picking up and throwing objects rather than jumping on them — a complete departure from the Mario formula.
The "it was all a dream" ending, where Mario wakes up and the adventure is revealed as a dream, became a beloved gaming cliché.
The real Japanese sequel (Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels) was eventually released in the West as part of Super Mario All-Stars.
devStory: Super Mario Bros. 2 (Western version) was developed by Nintendo EAD in 1988. The Japanese Super Mario Bros. 2 was considered too difficult for Western markets, so Nintendo reworked Doki Doki Panic — a licensed Fuji TV game — with Mario characters. The result was a game structurally unlike any other Mario game: four distinct characters with different abilities, no Koopa Troopas, and a dream-world framing device.

title: Zelda II
description: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link (1987) is Nintendo's side-scrolling action RPG sequel, with experience levels, spells and swordplay built on high and low attacks.
longDescription: Zelda II travels across an overhead map of Hyrule, but its towns, palaces and battles take place in side-scrolling scenes. Link gains experience to level up his attack, magic and life, learns spells such as Shield, Jump and Fairy from townspeople, and fights with a sword and shield that block and strike high or low. His quest is to restore six crystals to six palaces and wake the sleeping Princess Zelda. It is the most different game in the series and among the hardest.
trivia: Zelda II is the only mainline Zelda game to use experience points and traditional RPG levelling — a design that was never repeated.
The side-scrolling combat required holding the shield button to defend, then switching to attack — a timing-based system unusual for 1987 Nintendo.
The game's extreme difficulty — particularly the final dungeon and Ganon's revival threat — made it polarising among Zelda fans.
Link could learn new spells by visiting towns and meeting specific characters, adding an exploration reward system to the RPG elements.
devStory: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link was designed by Tadashi Sugiyama and Shigeru Miyamoto at Nintendo in 1987. It was a radical departure from the original — a side-scrolling action RPG rather than a top-down adventure. Link gained experience points, levelled up stats, and fought in real-time combat with a specific offensive and defensive stance system. The game's difficulty was notoriously high.

sources.title: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link

title: Kirby's Adventure
description: Kirby's Adventure (1993) is HAL Laboratory's late-era NES platformer that introduced Kirby's Copy Ability: swallow enemies to take their powers.
longDescription: King Dedede has broken the Star Rod and handed out its pieces, and Kirby sets out across Dream Land to retrieve them. Inhaling certain enemies lets him copy their abilities — fire, ice, sword, beam, spark and many more — which open secret paths and change how each level plays. Kirby can also float over most hazards, making it welcoming to newer players. Arriving near the end of the NES's life, its graphics and effects pushed the hardware remarkably far.
trivia: Masahiro Sakurai was 22 years old when he designed Kirby's Adventure — he later created Super Smash Bros., another game about absorbing others' abilities.
Released in 1993, Kirby's Adventure pushed NES hardware beyond what developers thought possible — one of the most technically impressive NES games ever made.
The copy ability system, where Kirby absorbed enemies to steal their powers, had over 20 distinct abilities — more variety than most action games of the era.
Kirby's pink colour was finalised only after Miyamoto and Sakurai debated whether he should be pink or yellow.
The game's final boss, Nightmare, was one of the most dramatic in NES gaming — a cosmic entity fought across two phases in open space.
devStory: Kirby's Adventure was designed by Masahiro Sakurai at HAL Laboratory in 1993. Sakurai was 22 years old during development and created Kirby's copy ability — absorbing enemies to gain their powers — as the central mechanic. The game used the NES hardware at a level of technical sophistication that shocked contemporary developers; it was released near the end of the NES life cycle but looked more advanced than many Super Nintendo games.

title: Final Fantasy
description: Final Fantasy (1987) is Square's Famicom role-playing game, directed by Hironobu Sakaguchi and scored by Nobuo Uematsu, in which four Light Warriors restore the darkened crystals.
longDescription:
Four youths, the Warriors of Light, each carry one of four elemental crystals that have been darkened by the Four Fiends: Lich of Earth, Kary of Fire, Kraken of Water and Tiamat of Wind. The quest begins with the defeat of Garland, an evil knight, and ends 2,000 years in the past, where it emerges that Garland sent the Fiends into the future and created a time loop; he returns as the archdemon Chaos.

The player picks a party of four at the start from six classes — Fighter, Thief, Black Belt, Red Mage, White Mage and Black Mage — and cannot change it, though later in the game each class is upgraded, gaining a more mature portrait and new weapons or magic. White magic heals and protects, black magic harms, and spells come in eight levels of four each, of which a character can learn three per level. Battles are turn-based and menu-driven, with random encounters, and travel opens up by ship, canoe and finally airship.
trivia: Its working title was Fighting Fantasy, changed because of the gamebook series of that name.
Uematsu linked the word "final" to Square's troubles, but Sakaguchi said "any word that starts with an 'F' would have been fine".
Its "Prelude", "Opening Theme" and "Victory Fanfare" have recurred through the series.
It had no PAL release until Final Fantasy Origins in 2003.
Nasir Gebelli also programmed a sliding-puzzle minigame.
devStory:
Hironobu Sakaguchi wanted to make an RPG, but Square refused, expecting poor sales, until Dragon Quest's success in Japan changed its mind; the game drew on Ultima and Wizardry. Sakaguchi directed a core team of seven. Akitoshi Kawazu designed the battle system, based on Dungeons & Dragons and Wizardry, Kenji Terada wrote the scenario from Sakaguchi's story, Koichi Ishii came up with the crystals, Yoshitaka Amano designed the characters, Nasir Gebelli programmed it and Nobuo Uematsu composed the music, his sixteenth game score.

The first shipment of 200,000 was raised to 400,000, and the Famicom version shipped 520,000 copies in Japan after its release in December 1987. Nintendo of America published it in North America in 1990. It was praised for its graphics but criticised for grinding and slow pacing; Famitsu scored it 34 out of 40.

title: Missile Command (Atari)
description: Missile Command (1981) for the Atari 2600 is Rob Fulop's home version of the arcade classic, trading the trackball for a joystick-guided cursor.
longDescription: The 2600 Missile Command keeps the arcade game's premise — defend six cities from waves of falling warheads — while fitting it to a single joystick and button on Atari's home console. The cursor sweeps across the sky rather than following a trackball, which changes how players line up their shots, and the game offers many variations of speed and difficulty. Converted by Rob Fulop, it was one of the best-selling cartridges on the system.
trivia: Rob Fulop ported Missile Command to the 2600 in eight weeks, adapting the trackball gameplay to joystick controls.
The joystick version required different targeting strategies from the arcade — players swept across the screen rather than pinpointing with a cursor.
Missile Command 2600 was one of the best-selling Atari cartridges, demonstrating that faithful-enough ports could drive console sales.
Fulop later created Demon Attack, one of the best-selling original 2600 games, showing his talent extended beyond porting.
devStory: The Atari 2600 version of Missile Command was ported in 1981 by Rob Fulop. The trackball of the arcade was replaced by a joystick, significantly changing how the game felt. Fulop achieved a faithful adaptation despite the hardware constraints. The home version sold millions of copies and was one of the most popular 2600 games.

title: Pitfall II
description: Pitfall II: Lost Caverns (1984) is David Crane's Activision sequel: guide Pitfall Harry through vast Peruvian caverns, with music from a custom chip.
longDescription: Pitfall Harry descends into huge caverns in Peru to find his niece Rhonda, his cat Quickclaw, a rat and the Raj diamond. The world scrolls vertically as well as horizontally, with rivers to swim, balloons to ride and condors, bats and eels to avoid. There are no lives: touching a hazard costs points and sends Harry back to the last checkpoint. David Crane designed a special chip inside the cartridge that let the 2600 play a full musical score and draw more on screen.
trivia: Pitfall II featured a continuous musical soundtrack on the Atari 2600 — technically unprecedented and achieved through a custom chip Crane added to the cartridge.
The balloon respawn system replaced the lives mechanic — death docked points rather than ending the game, reducing frustration.
Crane added a custom chip (called the "Pitfall II chip") to the cartridge PCB to enable the music — essentially upgrading the hardware through the cartridge.
The game's underground cavern world was larger and more complex than the original's jungle, with multiple interconnected paths.
devStory: Pitfall II: Lost Caverns was designed by David Crane at Activision in 1983. The sequel moved from the original's jungle to underground caverns and replaced the time-limit pressure with a balloon respawn system — dying sent Pitfall Harry back to the nearest balloon, losing points rather than lives. The game was a technological marvel for the Atari 2600, featuring smooth vertical scrolling and a complete musical soundtrack.

title: Knight Lore
description: Ultimate Play the Game's 1984 isometric adventure, in which the werewolf-cursed Sabreman has forty days to brew a cure — the game that made isometric 3D a genre of its own.
longDescription:
Knight Lore was developed and published in 1984 by Ultimate Play the Game and written by the company's founders, Chris and Tim Stamper. The player character, Sabreman, has been cursed to become a werewolf at night and has forty days to find the ingredients for a cure hidden around a castle.

Each room of the castle appears on a single screen in monochrome, drawn in isometric perspective, and is filled with blocks to climb, hazards to avoid and puzzles to solve. Its convincing three-dimensional rooms impressed players and developers alike, and Knight Lore is credited with popularising isometric graphics in games.
trivia: Ultimate held back Knight Lore for six months to not overshadow Sabre Wulf — the game was so ahead of its time they worried it would make their other work look primitive.
The isometric "filmation" engine (as Ultimate called it) was the Stampers' proprietary technology — a genuine competitive advantage.
Knight Lore's isometric perspective created genuine three-dimensional puzzle design on hardware with no actual 3D capability.
Tim and Chris Stamper, Knight Lore's creators, went on to found Rare — the studio behind Donkey Kong Country, Goldeneye, and Banjo-Kazooie.
devStory: Knight Lore was created by Tim and Chris Stamper at Ultimate Play the Game in 1984. The isometric 3D perspective was so advanced that Ultimate held the game back for six months so that it would not make their current release, Sabre Wulf, look dated. Knight Lore established isometric gaming as a genre, directly inspiring dozens of games including Head Over Heels and Batman. The Stampers later founded Rare.

title: Sabre Wulf
description: Ultimate Play the Game's 1984 Spectrum jungle maze, where Sabreman hunts for amulet pieces across 256 screens with no instructions at all — the start of his adventures.
longDescription:
Sabre Wulf was released by the British developer Ultimate Play the Game for the ZX Spectrum in 1984. The player guides Sabreman, in his pith helmet, through a two-dimensional jungle maze, collecting the four pieces of an amulet needed to get past the guardian at the exit.

The maze covers 256 connected screens, and Sabreman moves from one to the next by walking off the edge. Each screen is crowded with colourful plants, randomly appearing creatures and occasional items. In keeping with Ultimate's mystique, the game gives no explicit instructions, leaving players to work out what to do by trial and error.
trivia: Sabre Wulf launched at £9.95, well above the usual Spectrum price, in a large box — a bet on Ultimate's reputation that paid off.
Sabreman, the protagonist, appeared in multiple Ultimate games: Sabre Wulf, Underwurlde, Knight Lore, and Gunfright.
The jungle maze was one of the largest game worlds on the ZX Spectrum, with hundreds of screens and a procedurally respawning enemy.
devStory: Sabre Wulf was created by Tim and Chris Stamper at Ultimate Play the Game in 1984, released a few months before Knight Lore. The jungle maze adventure starred Sabreman, who became the studio's recurring protagonist. Ultimate Play the Game was the most prestigious ZX Spectrum developer of its era, able to sell its games on reputation alone.

title: Phantasy Star
description: Phantasy Star (1987) is Sega's Master System role-playing game: Alis Landale travels across three planets to avenge her brother, through first-person 3D dungeons.
longDescription: Phantasy Star follows Alis Landale, whose brother is killed on the orders of the tyrant King Lassic, as she gathers companions — the cat Myau, the warrior Odin and the wizard Noah — and travels between the planets Palma, Motavia and Dezoris. Its dungeons are explored in smoothly animated first-person 3D, and its setting mixes swords and sorcery with spaceships and robots. Its female lead, animated monsters and science-fantasy world made it one of the most ambitious 8-bit RPGs.
trivia: Alis Landale was one of the earliest female leads in a console RPG — nine years before Tomb Raider's Lara Croft.
The 3D first-person dungeons were technically demanding — programming them for the Master System required significant engineering effort.
Yuji Naka, later famous for creating Sonic the Hedgehog, programmed Phantasy Star's game engine.
The game's science fiction setting — spaceships, robots, and technology alongside swords and magic — was a blend no other RPG of 1987 attempted.
Phantasy Star is still considered one of the greatest RPGs ever made for 8-bit hardware, and its storyline spanned multiple sequels on the Mega Drive.
devStory: Phantasy Star was developed by Sega and released for the Master System in 1987. The team was led by Yuji Naka (who later created Sonic) and Rieko Kodama, with art direction by Kotaro Hayashida. Kodama designed the protagonist Alis as a female lead — radical for a JRPG in 1987. The game featured first-person 3D dungeons (rare for its era), a science fiction setting (unusual among fantasy-dominated RPGs), and an epic story spanning three planets.

title: Hang-On
description: Sega's 1985 motorbike racer, designed with Yu Suzuki: one of the first 16-bit arcade games, and in its deluxe form a full-size bike you leaned into the corners.
longDescription:
Hang-On was developed and published by Sega for arcades in 1985. The player races a motorcycle against the clock and against computer-controlled riders.

It was one of the first arcade games to use 16-bit graphics, and it ran on Sega's Super Scaler technology — built with design input from Yu Suzuki — which scaled sprites to give a convincing impression of 3D speed. The deluxe cabinet was a large motorbike that the player sat on and leaned to steer, so body movement controlled the rider on screen: one of the first motion-controlled arcade cabinets, and the start of a run of Sega "taikan" (body-sensation) games.
trivia: The full-size motorcycle cabinet was tilted physically by the player to steer — one of the most immersive arcade controls ever built.
Hang-On ran at 60 frames per second using Sega's new Super Scaler hardware — smoothness that console ports couldn't replicate for years.
Yu Suzuki designed Hang-On, OutRun, Space Harrier, and After Burner across just three years — an unmatched creative run in arcade history.
A sit-down cabinet version with a more conventional steering mechanism was produced for operators who couldn't accommodate the motorcycle cabinet.
devStory: Hang-On was designed by Yu Suzuki at Sega in 1985. The motorcycle racing game was built around a full-size motorcycle cabinet that players physically leaned to steer — tilting the bike controlled direction. Suzuki's Super Scaler hardware ran at 60 frames per second, creating a sensation of speed that home technology couldn't match for a decade.

title: Star Wars (Arcade)
description: Star Wars (1983) is Atari's 3D colour vector arcade game, in which the player flies an X-wing through a dogfight, over the Death Star and down the trench to fire the fatal torpedo.
longDescription: The player is Luke Skywalker, Red Five, flying an X-wing with a yoke that has four fire buttons, one for each wingtip laser. Each wave has three phases: a dogfight with Darth Vader and TIE fighters near the Death Star, a flight over its surface against bunkers and, from the third wave, laser towers, and the trench run, ending with a proton torpedo into the exhaust port. The player does not have to destroy everything, only survive. The X-wing starts with six shields, losing one to each collision or shot, and enemy fire comes as fireballs that can be shot down. A direct hit on the port destroys the Death Star and restores a shield, and a "using the Force" bonus rewards firing only at the port. Speech synthesis imitates the film's actors.
trivia: It began in 1981 as a project called Warp Speed before Atari licensed Star Wars.
A conversion kit turned the cabinet into its 1985 sequel, The Empire Strikes Back.
On odd waves the Death Star's grid lines spell "May the force be with you"; on even waves, developers' names.
In 1985 three players took turns for over five days on one credit, scoring more than a billion points for charity.
The arcade game was included in Star Wars Rogue Squadron III: Rebel Strike.
devStory:
It began in 1981 as Warp Speed under Ed Rotberg, who had worked on Battlezone, using a controller designed for Army Battlezone, a training simulator for the US Army. After Rotberg left that October, Atari licensed Star Wars from Lucasfilm and finished the game, with Mike Hally designing, Greg Rivera and Norm Avellar programming and Earl Vickers on sound. Released on 5 May 1983 in upright and cockpit cabinets, it was Atari's best-selling arcade game of the year, with 12,695 built, and topped Play Meter's street-location chart that October.

Parker Brothers released home versions in 1983 and 1984, and Domark and Broderbund published Vektor Grafix's computer conversions from 1987. Next Generation later called it "probably the best licensed game ever".

title: City Connection
description: Jaleco's 1985 arcade game in which Clarice drives her Honda City across elevated highways, painting the road as police cars give chase — released in North America as Cruisin'.
longDescription:
City Connection was developed and published by Jaleco for arcades in 1985, and released in North America by Kitkorp under the title Cruisin'.

The player controls Clarice in her Honda City hatchback, driving and hopping across layers of elevated road; every stretch she drives over is painted, and the stage ends when all of it has been covered. Police cars pursue her, and she can stun them by throwing oil cans. The idea of covering a whole level while avoiding pursuers came from maze chase games such as Pac-Man (1980) and Make Trax (1981).
trivia: City Connection's objective — painting every road tile while evading police — was entirely unique in 1985 arcade gaming.
The car could bounce off the sides of the screen, wrapping around horizontally — useful for evading police but disorienting for new players.
Oil cans produced cats when hit, which instantly killed the player on contact — a whimsical hazard in an already unusual game.
The world tour locations — each with a distinct backdrop — gave players a sense of international travel unusual in arcade games.
devStory: City Connection was developed by Jaleco in 1985. Players drove a car around the world, covering road tiles with paint while avoiding police and cats that appeared from oil cans. The game's mechanic of covering every road tile gave it a completion-based objective unusual in arcade games. The world tour setting — from New York to London to Paris — gave it an aspirational travel theme.

title: Terra Cresta
description: Nihon Bussan's 1985 vertical shooter, sequel to Moon Cresta, in which collected ship parts dock with your craft to add new weapons — and can combine into a giant phoenix.
longDescription:
Terra Cresta was developed and published by Nihon Bussan for arcades in 1985. It is the sequel to Moon Cresta (1980), the company's first big arcade hit, and the second game in its Cresta series.

The player flies a craft defending humanity against the Mandler army. The central idea is modular: shooting certain targets releases extra ship parts, and each part that joins the player's craft adds its own weapon, such as a wave gun or double shot. With enough parts assembled, the ship can temporarily transform into a powerful phoenix formation.
trivia: Terra Cresta's five ship sections could combine in different formations for different attack patterns — strategic assembly was part of the game.
The full combined ship could execute a screen-clearing Phoenix attack, but splitting the ship was sometimes more useful for navigating tight spaces.
Moon Cresta, Terra Cresta's predecessor, was one of the most cloned games of the early 1980s — Nichibutsu's formation concept was highly influential.
The game's European distribution was stronger than its Japanese commercial performance — Nichibutsu found a significant audience in British arcades.
devStory: Terra Cresta was developed by Nihon Bussan (Nichibutsu) in 1985 as a sequel to Moon Cresta. Players collected sections of a combined spacecraft, assembling a larger vessel with more firepower. The formation system — five sections that combined into a powerful combined form — was the game's central mechanic. Nichibutsu was a smaller Japanese arcade developer whose games were popular in Europe.

title: Gradius II
description: Konami's 1988 sequel to Gradius — Vulcan Venture in North American arcades — refining the series' power-up bar into one of the most admired horizontal shooters of its era.
longDescription:
Gradius II was developed and published by Konami in 1988 as the sequel to Gradius, and it was followed by Gradius III. In North American arcades it was titled Vulcan Venture.

It keeps the series' distinctive weapon system, in which collected power-ups advance a selection bar that the player spends on speed, missiles, lasers and options, and adds a choice of weapon configurations at the start of the game. After its arcade release it was ported in Japan to the Family Computer, the PC Engine Super CD-ROM² and the Sharp X68000, and the arcade version was later included in Gradius Deluxe Pack for PlayStation and Saturn and in Gradius Collection for the PlayStation Portable.
trivia: Gradius II offered four weapon configuration choices before the game began — players could customise their loadout from the start.
The Bacterion Empire's bosses were larger and more complex than the original, requiring multi-stage strategies to defeat.
The PC Engine (TurboGrafx-16) port was considered technically astonishing — a near-perfect home version of a demanding arcade game.
devStory: Gradius II was developed by Konami in 1988, and was considered a significant advancement over the original. The game offered four selectable weapon configurations at the start, each changing the power-up bar layout and available weapons. New power-ups including Twin Missiles and Photon Torpedo added variety. The PC Engine port was considered one of the finest home conversions of any arcade game.

title: Darius
description: Darius (1987) is Taito's horizontal shooter on a three-screen cabinet, in which the Silver Hawk takes a branching path through zones full of fish-shaped bosses.
longDescription:
Fleeing a polluted, exhausted Earth, colonists settled a planet they named Darius, until the Belser Army attacks it with an armada of sea-creature-shaped craft, and pilots Proco and Tiat are chosen to defend it in Silver Hawk fighters. The screen is three times wider than normal, spread across three monitors joined by mirrors so they look seamless. The Silver Hawk has forward missiles, aerial bombs and a force field, each upgraded by coloured orbs that specially coloured enemies drop.

Each zone ends with a boss, and after each one the path branches so the player picks the next zone: there are 28 in all, but only seven are played in a run. Enemies are fish, crabs and other sea creatures, and the bosses are screen-filling battleships, where most shooters of the day used machines or insects.
trivia: The cabinet had a headphone jack and a "body sonic" speaker under the seat.
Hisayoshi Ogura, founder of Taito's band Zuntata, composed the music.
Its first-zone theme, "Captain Neo", began as a placeholder theme for Metal Soldier Isaac II at trade shows.
Darius Plus is the only commercial HuCard with enhanced SuperGrafx support.
Only about 2,000 copies of the 2020 Mega Drive version, Darius Extra Version, were made.
devStory:
Junji Yarita designed it, Akira Fujita planned it and Toru Sugawara programmed it. Fujita wanted a huge battleship boss at the end of every stage and themed them on sea creatures; Yarita drew 26 battleship designs, but time allowed only 11, each taking about ten days. Enemy names came from medicines and from staff names spelled backwards. Natsuki Hirosawa designed the cabinet, whose headphone jack and seat speaker, which Taito called "body sonic", had first been planned for Laser Grand Prix in 1983 but dropped as too expensive. Taito's house band Zuntata, founded by Hisayoshi Ogura, made the music.

It debuted at the ATEI show in London in January 1987 and reached Japan in February, where Game Machine listed it as the most popular upright arcade unit that April; it was the third highest-grossing large arcade game of 1987 in Japan.

title: Contra (arcade)
description: Contra (1987) is Konami's arcade run-and-gun for two players, mixing side-scrolling stages with into-the-screen base assaults.
longDescription: Commandos Bill Rizer and Lance Bean fight through jungle, alien-infested bases and waterfall stages to stop the Red Falcon organisation. Falcon-shaped power-ups swap in new guns, such as the famous spread shot, and one hit costs a life. The base stages switch to a view behind the players, shooting into the screen at wall-mounted defences. The arcade game led to the widely admired NES version, and was released in Europe as Gryzor.
trivia: The arcade Contra preceded the NES version by months — the home version refined and improved upon the original structure.
The base stages switch to a view behind the players, shooting into the screen at wall-mounted defences.
The two-player simultaneous mode was the primary attraction — very few games in 1987 offered this in a run-and-gun format.
The NES version added the Konami Code in the attract screen — transforming a debug tool into gaming's most famous cheat.
devStory: The original arcade version of Contra was developed by Konami in 1987. The game ran on hardware capable of displaying detailed sprite-scaled backgrounds for the 3D stages. The arcade version had a more linear structure than the NES port, which is generally considered the definitive version due to its more refined level design. The arcade served as the proof of concept that Konami polished into one of the greatest NES games ever made.

title: Super Mario World
description: Super Mario World launched alongside the Super Famicom in Japan in 1990 and the SNES in North America in 1991, bundled with the system. The game introduced Yoshi — a rideable dinosaur who could eat enemies — and expanded Mario's moveset with the Cape Feather. 96 exits across 72 levels made it the largest Mario game to date.
longDescription: Super Mario World was the last Mario game produced primarily under Shigeru Miyamoto's direct design control. The game's overworld map — a branching network of paths through Dinosaur Land — allowed players to choose their route and skip levels through the Star World shortcuts. Yoshi's design emerged from a concept Miyamoto had wanted to include since the original Donkey Kong; the NES hardware hadn't been capable of supporting the sprite. The SNES version sold 20 million copies, making it one of the best-selling SNES games and one of the best-selling games ever made.
trivia: Super Mario World was the first Mario game to allow players to save their progress — previous games started over completely each session.
Miyamoto had wanted Mario to ride a dinosaur since the original Super Mario Bros., but the NES could not handle it — Yoshi finally arrived on the SNES.
The game contains 96 exits, far more than any previous Mario title — finding all of them requires discovering multiple secret routes and hidden levels.
devStory: Super Mario World was developed by Nintendo EAD under Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka as the SNES launch title. Development was compressed to approximately 1.5 years to ship alongside the console hardware in 1990. Miyamoto has described the game as the fullest realisation of the design ideas established in Super Mario Bros. 3.

title: F-Zero
description: F-Zero was a SNES launch title in Japan that demonstrated the console's Mode 7 scaling capability. Set in the year 2560, players raced hovercrafts around futuristic tracks at high speeds with no weapons — pure racing against time and aggressive AI. The game established a franchise and a visual vocabulary for futuristic racing.
longDescription: F-Zero's tracks were rendered using the SNES's Mode 7 hardware, which applied an affine transformation to a background layer to simulate perspective. By changing the transformation parameters on each horizontal scanline, Nintendo's programmers created the illusion of a ground plane receding toward the horizon. The technique was the primary demonstration of SNES capability over the NES in Nintendo's early marketing. The game featured four playable craft with different weight and handling characteristics, and a Grand Prix mode across multiple cups.
trivia: F-Zero used Mode 7 hardware scaling to simulate 3D perspective — the track surface was actually a flat 2D image transformed mathematically each frame.
The game has no weapons or items — the only way to attack opponents is to ram them off the track, which also damages your own energy meter.
Captain Falcon, F-Zero's most iconic character, was a bounty hunter whose backstory was developed primarily through Nintendo Power magazine.
A proper F-Zero sequel wasn't produced until F-Zero X on the N64 in 1998, which ran 30 cars simultaneously at a locked 60 frames per second.
devStory: F-Zero was directed by Kazunobu Shimizu, with Shigefumi Hino among its designers, as a technical demonstration of the SNES Mode 7 graphics mode. The game was developed in approximately one year and launched with the Super Famicom in Japan in November 1990.

title: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past
description: A Link to the Past returned the Zelda series to a top-down perspective after Zelda II's side-scrolling departure. The game introduced the Dark World — a parallel dimension mirroring the Light World — and remains the template that most subsequent 2D Zelda games follow. Its overworld, dungeon design, and item progression set a standard for the action-adventure genre.
longDescription: A Link to the Past was directed by Yoshiaki Koizumi and produced by Shigeru Miyamoto. The game's dual-world structure — players switch between the Light World and the Dark World through specific locations — was used to create puzzles that required reasoning about both worlds simultaneously. The game's 12 dungeons introduced themed environments, items specific to each dungeon that were required to defeat the boss, and a boss fight format that subsequent Zelda games codified. A Link to the Past sold over 4 million copies on SNES and is routinely cited in lists of the greatest games ever made.
trivia: A Link to the Past was the first Zelda game to introduce the Master Sword as the definitive weapon — previous games used unspecified swords.
The game's map design process involved Miyamoto personally testing every screen for navigational clarity and enemy placement balance.
A Link to the Past introduced the now-standard Zelda convention of collecting three MacGuffin items before accessing the final dungeon.
devStory: A Link to the Past was developed by Nintendo EAD under producer Shigeru Miyamoto and director Takashi Tezuka. The game was designed in response to criticism that Zelda II had strayed too far from the original's formula. Development took approximately two years and the game launched in Japan in November 1991.

sources.title: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past

title: Super Mario Kart
description: Super Mario Kart invented the kart racing genre. Eight playable characters from the Mario universe raced around tracks rendered in Mode 7 perspective, collecting items to attack opponents or gain speed advantages. The formula proved durable enough to sustain a franchise that continued selling tens of millions of units per entry decades later.
longDescription: Super Mario Kart was designed by Hideki Konno and produced by Shigeru Miyamoto. The game's item system — random power-ups collected from boxes on the track, ranging from banana peels to red-homing shells to the invincibility star — created a race dynamic where skilled players could be set back and less skilled players could catch up. The Mario Kart item system became the defining feature of the franchise and the template for every kart racing game that followed. The game sold 8.76 million copies on SNES.
trivia: Super Mario Kart was developed partly because Nintendo engineers were experimenting with split-screen racing using Mode 7 and decided the concept was strong enough to build a game around.
Computer-controlled racers use 'rubber-band' behaviour, speeding up or slowing down to stay near the player — a feature players have argued about ever since.
Lakitu, the referee who holds the starting light and retrieves players who fall off the track, debuted in Super Mario Bros. as an enemy.
Battle Mode pits two players against each other in closed arenas, popping each other's balloons — a mode many players loved as much as the racing.
devStory: Super Mario Kart was developed by a small team led by Hideki Konno who was experimenting with split-screen Mode 7 racing. When Miyamoto played the prototype he recognised the design potential and production expanded to a full game. The game launched in Japan in August 1992.

title: Mega Man X
description: Mega Man X was a harder, faster reimagining of the Mega Man formula on the SNES. The new protagonist X could dash and wall-jump from the start — movements the original Mega Man couldn't perform. Defeating bosses gave their abilities, but the game's real depth was in finding hidden armour upgrades that expanded X's capabilities beyond the base game.
longDescription: Mega Man X was directed by Keiji Inafune as an intentional reset of the franchise for the 16-bit era. The game's movement system — the wall jump specifically — was designed to give players freedom to navigate the stages in ways the level design hadn't fully anticipated, rewarding creative play. The hidden capsules containing Dr. Light's armour upgrades required exploration beyond the designed path. The darker tone — X searches for Mavericks who have turned against humans — distinguished the series from the more cartoonish original Mega Man.
trivia: Mega Man X's opening stage is specifically designed to teach the game's new mechanics without a tutorial: the dash, wall jump, and charged shot are all discoverable through natural exploration.
The Hadouken is a secret: with every upgrade collected, a hidden capsule in Armored Armadillo's stage grants Street Fighter's fireball, which destroys almost anything in one hit.
Keiji Inafune has said that Mega Man X was his attempt to show what Mega Man would look like if the series had been designed for the 16-bit era from the beginning.
The game's soundtrack by Setsuo Yamamoto is considered one of the finest on the SNES, making heavy use of the console's SPC700 sample playback.
devStory: Mega Man X was produced by Keiji Inafune and directed by Yoshinori Takenaka at Capcom. Inafune wanted to create a harder, more action-oriented version of Mega Man that would appeal to the older audience the SNES attracted. The game launched in Japan in December 1993.

title: Star Fox
description: Star Fox was the first SNES game to use the Super FX chip — a custom coprocessor inside the cartridge that handled 3D polygon rendering. The result was a rail shooter in which the player piloted an Arwing fighter through three-dimensional environments that no SNES game had previously produced. The Super FX chip made Star Fox technically impossible on any other hardware of its era.
longDescription: Star Fox was developed in collaboration with Argonaut Software, a British company that had demonstrated 3D polygon rendering to Nintendo. The Super FX chip was designed by Argonaut's Ben Cheese and Peter Warnes specifically for the Star Fox project. The chip rendered approximately 15 polygon-based objects per frame at 15-20 frames per second — crude by modern standards but a genuine visual breakthrough in 1993. The game's multiple routes — different difficulty paths through the solar system — gave it replay value beyond its relatively short linear playtime.
trivia: The Super FX chip inside the cartridge made Star Fox more expensive to produce than a standard SNES game.
Argonaut Software approached Nintendo with a 3D Game Boy demo; Nintendo redirected their expertise to the SNES, resulting in both Star Fox and the Super FX chip.
The game's characters — Fox McCloud, Falco Lombardi, Peppy Hare, and Slippy Toad — were designed to be recognisable in 3D with minimal polygon counts.
Tapping a shoulder button twice sends the Arwing into a spinning roll that deflects enemy fire — the move Star Fox 64 later made famous as the 'barrel roll'.
devStory: Star Fox was developed jointly by Nintendo EAD and Argonaut Software, a British company specialising in 3D graphics. Argonaut's Jez San had pitched Nintendo on 3D gaming possibilities, leading to the development of the Super FX chip and the game simultaneously. The project took approximately two years.

title: Super Metroid
description: Super Metroid is the refinement of the original Metroid's connected-world exploration to a point of near perfection. Samus returns to Zebes to retrieve the last Metroid larva from Ridley. The game's atmosphere — conveyed through environmental detail, ambient sound, and minimal text — created a template for environmental storytelling that influenced game design for decades.
longDescription: Super Metroid was directed by Yoshio Sakamoto and produced by Gunpei Yokoi at Nintendo R&D1. The game's opening hours were designed to introduce Samus's abilities gradually, teaching the player how to use them through environmental design rather than instruction. The game's map — displayed on a sub-screen with optional overlay — communicated explored and unexplored areas without obscuring the navigation challenge. Super Metroid's influence on the Metroidvania genre is definitive: the connected world structure, ability-gated exploration, and environmental storytelling approach it established became the genre's template.
trivia: Super Metroid's opening narration — 'The last Metroid is in captivity. The galaxy is at peace.' — was spoken in English even in the Japanese version.
The game teaches the wall jump and Mockball techniques through environmental design without ever explicitly telling the player these abilities exist.
The final boss sequence contains one of the most emotionally resonant moments in 16-bit gaming, achieved entirely through game mechanics rather than cutscene.
Super Metroid sold only modestly on release but became a critical reference point over the following decades, its reputation growing as the Metroidvania genre it defined became recognised.
devStory: Super Metroid was produced by Makoto Kano and directed by Yoshio Sakamoto at Nintendo R&D1. The team wanted to create a game with a strong cinematic atmosphere while maintaining the exploration depth of the original Metroid. Development took approximately two years and the game launched in Japan in March 1994.

title: Donkey Kong Country
description: Donkey Kong Country revived the Donkey Kong franchise with pre-rendered 3D graphics that made the SNES appear capable of visuals beyond its hardware specification. Rare rendered the characters and environments on Silicon Graphics workstations and converted the output to 2D sprites, producing a visual quality no other SNES game matched. The game sold 9 million copies.
longDescription: Donkey Kong Country was developed by Rare using Alias/Wavefront modelling software on Silicon Graphics INDY workstations. Each animation frame was rendered in 3D and converted to a 2D sprite, giving the game a visual depth that was not achievable through conventional 2D sprite art. Nintendo's marketing made the pre-rendered visuals a central selling point, positioning the game as a technical leap that competitors couldn't match. The game's music, composed by David Wise, became one of the most celebrated SNES soundtracks.
trivia: Donkey Kong Country's development time was approximately 18 months — unusually fast for a game of its visual ambition, achieved through Silicon Graphics workstations that cost hundreds of thousands of dollars.

The 'silhouette' levels — in which the characters appear only as shadows against brightly lit backgrounds — were designed specifically to reduce sprite memory requirements while creating a distinctive visual style.
Donkey Kong Country's development was kept secret until its reveal at the 1994 CES, where the visual quality caused genuine shock among attendees who had assumed the SNES was at its limits.
devStory: Donkey Kong Country was developed by Rare in Twycross, England, under producers Tim and Chris Stamper. Nintendo licensed the Donkey Kong name to Rare after seeing their pre-rendered graphics demonstration. The game launched in November 1994 and was Nintendo's Christmas title for that year.

title: EarthBound
description: EarthBound was an RPG set in a contemporary American suburbia rather than a medieval fantasy world. Players controlled Ness, a boy with psychic powers, battling enemies including New Age Retro Hippies, Rowdy Mice, and a cosmic evil named Giygas. The game's self-aware humour, emotional depth, and unconventional setting made it a cult classic despite initially modest sales.
longDescription: EarthBound was designed by Shigesato Itoi — a celebrity copywriter and media personality rather than a game designer — and developed with technical support from HAL Laboratory, where a young Satoru Iwata contributed significantly to the game's programming. The North American release in 1995 was marketed with a deliberately unusual campaign: 'This game stinks' ads that included a scratch-and-sniff card. The campaign was ineffective and EarthBound sold poorly at launch. Its reputation grew through emulation and online communities in the late 1990s and 2000s.
trivia: EarthBound's final boss — Giygas — is one of the most disturbing in RPG history, designed to represent an unknowable, formless evil that cannot be comprehended.
The game's 'rolling HP meter' — your character's health decreasing gradually rather than instantly — means you can survive a killing blow if you act fast enough.
EarthBound was never released in Europe in its original SNES form — European players had to wait for the Wii U Virtual Console in 2013.
When development stalled, HAL's Satoru Iwata reviewed the project and proposed a way to finish it in months rather than years — a turning point for the game.
devStory: EarthBound was designed by Shigesato Itoi, who had no game design background but convinced Nintendo to back his concept for a contemporary RPG. HAL Laboratory provided technical development under Satoru Iwata. The game launched in Japan in August 1994.

title: Final Fantasy VI
description: Final Fantasy VI — released as Final Fantasy III in North America — is widely considered the pinnacle of the 16-bit RPG. An ensemble cast of 14 playable characters, an opera sequence, and a villain (Kefka) who actually succeeds in destroying the world mid-game made it unlike anything players had encountered. Its ambition as a narrative work exceeded any comparable console game of its era.
longDescription: Final Fantasy VI was directed by Yoshinori Kitase and Hiroyuki Ito, with character design by Yoshitaka Amano and music by Nobuo Uematsu. The game's narrative structure — an ensemble cast rather than a single hero, with individual character backstories woven into the main plot — allowed emotional investment across the entire cast. The opera sequence, in which the character Celes performs on stage with music playing from the SNES's SPC700 chip, was the most ambitious set piece in console RPG history at its release. The second half of the game — in which the villain wins and the world is transformed — broke RPG narrative conventions in ways that players had not anticipated.
trivia: The famous opera sequence required Nobuo Uematsu to write music specifically calibrated to the SNES sound chip's limitations, producing one of the most memorable pieces of game music ever written.
Kefka Palazzo — the game's antagonist — is the only Final Fantasy villain to actually succeed in his plan to destroy the world, making him arguably the most successful villain in the franchise.
Final Fantasy VI has 14 playable characters, more than any other SNES RPG, and the game's second half allows players to form their own teams from the available survivors.
devStory: Final Fantasy VI was produced by Hironobu Sakaguchi and directed by Yoshinori Kitase and Hiroyuki Ito at Square. It was the largest production in Square's history to that point, with a development team of approximately 50 people and a development time of around 18 months. The game launched in Japan in April 1994.

title: Chrono Trigger
description: Chrono Trigger was the product of the 'Dream Team' collaboration between Final Fantasy creator Hironobu Sakaguchi, Dragon Quest creator Yuji Horii, and Dragon Ball artist Akira Toriyama. A time-travel RPG spanning prehistoric times to the apocalyptic future, it featured a battle system with no random encounters, dual and triple character combo attacks, and 13 different endings.
longDescription: Chrono Trigger's development brought together three of Japan's most prominent creators in separate domains: Sakaguchi from Final Fantasy, Horii from Dragon Quest, and Toriyama from Dragon Ball. The resulting game synthesised their approaches. The battle system — in which enemies were visible on screen before combat began, eliminating random encounters — and the tech system — allowing character pairs and triples to combine abilities — were innovations the genre had not previously seen.
trivia: The game has 13 distinct endings, each accessible from different points in the story, encouraging players to approach the final boss at various stages of the game.
The 'New Game+' feature — starting the game again with all equipment and abilities from the previous playthrough — was invented in Chrono Trigger and subsequently adopted widely across the industry.
Nobuo Uematsu composed the score alongside Yasunori Mitsuda, who had demanded Sakaguchi let him compose for a major project or he would resign from Square.
devStory: Chrono Trigger was developed by Square's 'Dream Team' — Hironobu Sakaguchi, Yuji Horii, and Akira Toriyama — in approximately two years. The game's exceptionally high production budget came from Square's strong financial position following Final Fantasy VI's success. It launched in Japan in March 1995.

title: Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island
description: Yoshi's Island was a radical visual and mechanical departure from the main Mario series. The crayon-and-watercolour art style combined with a gameplay system in which Yoshi carries Baby Mario, temporarily losing him when hit rather than dying, created a game of distinctive identity. It is the SNES game most admired for visual design.
longDescription: Yoshi's Island was directed by Takashi Tezuka at Nintendo EAD and used the Super FX 2 chip to achieve its hand-drawn visual aesthetic. The chip handled the sprite scaling and rotation required to display the game's animated enemies and environments with the organic irregularity of hand-drawn art. The gameplay design — in which Yoshi, not Mario, was the player character — inverted the usual relationship: Yoshi protected Mario rather than Mario being the agent.
trivia: Yoshi's Island was developed in response to concerns that Donkey Kong Country's pre-rendered 3D graphics would make SNES games look outdated — Nintendo responded with a deliberately hand-drawn aesthetic.
The crying that plays when Baby Mario is separated from Yoshi was specifically designed to be annoying enough to motivate players to rescue him quickly.
The game's final boss sequence was designed as a demonstration of the Super FX 2 chip's sprite scaling capability.
Yoshi's Island introduced the Flutter Jump — holding the jump button to extend airtime — that became a staple of Yoshi's subsequent games.
devStory: Yoshi's Island was developed by Nintendo EAD under director Takashi Tezuka as both a technical showcase for the Super FX 2 chip and an artistic response to Rare's Donkey Kong Country. The game took approximately two years to develop and launched in Japan in August 1995.

title: Sonic the Hedgehog
description: Sonic the Hedgehog was Sega's answer to Super Mario Bros. — a platform game defined by speed rather than precision. Sonic accelerated through curving levels using a momentum physics system designed by Yuji Naka, building speed downhill and carrying it through loops. The game made the Genesis competitive with the SNES and established one of gaming's most recognisable characters.
longDescription: Sonic the Hedgehog was developed by Sonic Team — Yuji Naka on programming, Naoto Ohshima on character and world design, Hirokazu Yasuhara on level design. The character emerged from a design brief requiring a mascot that communicated attitude and speed. Naka's momentum physics engine — in which Sonic's speed built and carried through curved surfaces using trigonometric angle tracking — was the technical achievement that made the game's feel unique. The game was bundled with the Genesis from 1991, replacing Altered Beast as the pack-in, and sold over 15 million copies.
trivia: Sonic's speed was designed to showcase the Genesis's hardware scrolling capability — the fast horizontal scrolling was a deliberate competitive demonstration against the SNES.
Yuji Naka wrote the Sonic engine in 68000 assembly language and optimised it to run at a locked 60 frames per second.
The iconic Green Hill Zone music was composed by Masato Nakamura, bassist for Japanese pop group Dreams Come True.
Early Sonic designs included a human girlfriend character and a band; Naoto Ohshima's final hedgehog design was chosen after multiple character concepts were rejected.
devStory: Sonic the Hedgehog was developed by a team of approximately fifteen people at Sega over approximately ten months. Yuji Naka led programming, Naoto Ohshima led character and art design, and Hirokazu Yasuhara designed the levels. The game launched in Japan in July 1991 and became the Genesis's defining title.

title: Streets of Rage
description: Streets of Rage was Sega's beat 'em up for the Genesis — three playable characters, responsive combat, and a celebrated Yuzo Koshiro soundtrack that applied house and techno music to a video game for the first time. The game established a franchise and demonstrated what Genesis hardware could produce in the genre.
longDescription: Streets of Rage was developed internally at Sega as a response to Capcom's Final Fight, which had arrived on SNES but not Genesis. The game's music — composed by Yuzo Koshiro using FM synthesis to produce house and techno tracks — was technically remarkable for 1991 game music and remains one of the most distinctive soundtracks of the era. The three characters — Axel, Blaze, and Adam — had different speed and power characteristics that made character selection a meaningful choice.
trivia: Streets of Rage's soundtrack by Yuzo Koshiro applied house and techno music production techniques to FM synthesis, producing music that contemporary DJs played in clubs without knowing it was from a video game.
The game includes a special police attack — calling in a police car that fires a rocket at all enemies on screen — that could be used once per level.
Streets of Rage was released on Genesis because Sega couldn't port Final Fight, which had launched as a SNES exclusive.
Yuzo Koshiro composed the Streets of Rage soundtrack using a custom music sequencer he had written himself.
devStory: Streets of Rage was developed by Sega's internal development team as a direct competitor to Capcom's Final Fight. The game launched in Japan in August 1991. Yuzo Koshiro's music became the game's most celebrated element.

title: Sonic the Hedgehog 2
description: Sonic the Hedgehog 2 introduced Tails — a two-tailed fox who followed Sonic and could be controlled by a second player — and the spin dash, a move that allowed Sonic to accelerate from a standstill. The game outsold its predecessor and introduced the Emerald Hill Zone aesthetic that remained the franchise's visual identity for years.
longDescription: Sonic the Hedgehog 2 was co-developed between Sonic Team in Japan and Sega Technical Institute in San Francisco. The spin dash — spinning in place to build speed before launching — addressed a design problem in the first game: the need to run to build speed before slopes. The game introduced the two-player competitive mode and the Super Sonic transformation achieved by collecting all seven Chaos Emeralds.
trivia: 'Sonic 2sday' — the November 24, 1992 simultaneous worldwide release — was one of the first coordinated global game launches.
Several levels were cut from Sonic 2 during development, including Hidden Palace Zone, which was restored in the 2013 remaster based on remnant code found in the original cartridge.
Tails was designed by an artist who won an internal Sega design competition — the character's full name, Miles 'Tails' Prower, is a pun on 'miles per hour.'
Sonic 2 introduced the Super Sonic transformation as a reference to Dragon Ball Z's Super Saiyan form, complete with golden palette swap and invincibility.
devStory: Sonic the Hedgehog 2 was developed jointly by Sonic Team in Japan and Sega Technical Institute in the United States under significant deadline pressure. The collaborative arrangement was contentious but produced a game that outsold the original.

title: Streets of Rage 2
description: Streets of Rage 2 (1992) is Ancient's Mega Drive beat 'em up, in which Axel, Blaze, Max and Skate fight through Wood Oak City to rescue Adam from Mr. X, scored by Yuzo Koshiro.
longDescription: A year after the first game, Mr. X and the Syndicate return for revenge. Skate comes home to find his house wrecked and his brother Adam missing, with a photo of Adam chained at Mr. X's feet, and Axel and Blaze set out to rescue him, joined by Skate and the wrestler Max, as crime spreads through Wood Oak City. One or two players fight waves of enemies and pick up weapons and items. Max is slow but powerful, and Skate, Adam's younger brother, gets around on rollerblades. Standard attacks were expanded from the first game, each character has a Blitz Attack performed by double-tapping a direction, and Special Attacks, which cost health but hit enemies on all sides, replace the first game's police car. A Duel mode lets two players fight each other. The trail ends on Mr. X's island, against him and his bodyguard Shiva.
trivia: In Japan it is Bare Knuckle II, and Skate is called Sammy.
Sega Force said it was the first 2 MB cartridge on the Mega Drive.
Yuzo Koshiro was invited to DJ its music in nightclubs.
Mr. X's cigar was removed outside Japan.
M2's 3D Streets of Rage 2 for the 3DS added a Rage Relay mode and stereoscopic 3D.
devStory:
Ayano Koshiro was the lead graphic designer, designing the graphics, characters and combat, and Yuzo Koshiro wrote most of the music, with three tracks by Motohiro Kawashima; the team was inspired by Street Fighter II, which had a cabinet in Ancient's office. Yuzo composed on a PC-8801 in his own music language, drawing on house, techno and breakbeat, and critics called the soundtrack "revolutionary". Sega released it in North America in 1992 and in Japan in January 1993 as Bare Knuckle II.

It was the top-selling Mega Drive game in Japan in January 1993 and entered the UK chart at number one. Computer and Video Games called it the finest scrolling arcade beat 'em up on any format, and GamePro the "side-scrolling street fighter to beat".

title: Gunstar Heroes
description: Gunstar Heroes was the debut game from Treasure — a studio founded by ex-Konami developers — and demonstrated technical ambitions the Genesis had not previously been pushed to achieve. A run-and-gun with combinable weapon types, enormous bosses, and combat that filled the screen with projectiles and enemies, it established Treasure's reputation for hardware-pushing action design.
longDescription: Gunstar Heroes was developed by Treasure, founded in 1992 by developers who had left Konami. The game pushed the Genesis hardware to display more simultaneous objects and projectiles than previous Genesis games had managed. The weapon combination system — four base weapons that could be combined into ten distinct weapon types — created varied play styles. The game's bosses, some occupying most of the screen, required different strategies for each encounter.
trivia: Treasure was founded by developers who had worked on Contra and other Konami games and wanted to create more technically ambitious action games than Konami's production process allowed.
Gunstar Heroes uses techniques Sega had marketed as a Genesis advantage — Treasure's game is one of the few that genuinely exploited them.
The dice game boss — a board game in which landing on certain squares triggers different bosses — was a self-contained game within the game.
Gunstar Heroes sold modestly on release but became a collector's item, with original cartridges selling for high prices decades later.
devStory: Gunstar Heroes was developed by Treasure in approximately one year as the studio's debut title. The small team of approximately ten developers, all ex-Konami, designed the game to showcase Genesis hardware capabilities they felt hadn't been fully exploited. Sega published the game in Japan in September 1993.

title: Shinobi III: Return of the Master Ninja
description: Shinobi III (1993) is Sega's Mega Drive ninja platformer, delayed a year so its gameplay and graphics could be reworked, and one of the system's most praised action games.
longDescription: Two years after its defeat, the crime syndicate Neo Zeed rises again under the Shadow Master. Joe Musashi senses its return and leaves his mountain home in Japan to face his old enemy. It is a hack-and-slash platformer that reviewers found faster than its predecessor and, Power Unlimited said, a little easier; MegaTech singled out its new attacks and moves. Mega thought it far too easy apart from its tricky bosses, while Complex called the last level "freaking impossible".
trivia: Previews showed levels and moves that never made the final game; a beta later leaked as a ROM.
In Japan it was called The Super Shinobi II.
Sega producer Yosuke Okunari called it the most refined 2D Shinobi game when M2 chose it for the Sega 3D Classics series.
Lizardcube said Shinobi: Art of Vengeance (2025) was directly inspired by it and The Revenge of Shinobi.
Retro Gamer included it in its top ten Mega Drive games.
devStory:
Tomoyuki Ito and Takeshi Matsuhashi directed it, Naohisa Nakazawa designed it, and Hirofumi Murasaki, Morihiko Akiyama and Masayuki Nagao composed the music. It was set for 1992, and previews in GamePro, Mean Machines and Computer and Video Games showed levels, enemies and moves that never made the final game; Sega delayed it to 1993 to improve the gameplay and visuals, cutting many features and adding new ones. It came out in Japan as The Super Shinobi II on 23 July 1993 and in the West that September.

MegaTech gave it 93% and a Hyper Game award, IGN's Levi Buchanan called it "a legit Genesis great", and Complex later ranked it the third-best Genesis game.

sources.title: Shinobi III: Return of the Ninja Master

title: Comix Zone
description: Comix Zone (1995) is Sega Technical Institute's Mega Drive beat 'em up set inside the panels of a comic book, in which artist Sketch Turner is trapped in his own creation by the villain Mortus.
longDescription: While Sketch Turner works on his comic during a thunderstorm, lightning strikes the page and frees its villain, the mutant Mortus, who sends Sketch into the comic, meaning to kill him and take his body. Inside a post-apocalyptic world of ruined New York, the Himalayas and the atolls of Zealand, Sketch joins General Alissa Cyan against Mortus. Every screen is a comic panel with speech balloons. Six pages in three episodes hold enemies or simple puzzles, sometimes with branching panels, and Sketch can use the art itself, tearing a page into a paper plane to attack. He carries up to three items, his pet rat Roadkill peels back parts of the page to reveal them, and iced tea is the only thing that restores health. Losing all health or falling into a pit ends the game unless a continue has been earned.
trivia: The game is notoriously hard: health items are rare, and punching through scenery to find a path drains Sketch's own health.
Sega of Japan reportedly called it a symbol of American culture's flaws; the team took it as a compliment.
It and The Ooze were the only games to carry the S.T.I. logo.
Morawiec later regretted following the testers' advice to make it harder.
A film adaptation was announced in 2022.
devStory:
Peter Morawiec conceived it after a trip to a comic shop in Palo Alto with Sega Technical Institute colleagues, taking the story from a-ha's "Take On Me" video, and pitched a demo, "Joe Pencil Trapped in the Comix Zone", in December 1992. It was delayed for Sonic Spinball, and work began in late 1993 with Morawiec, Adrian Stephens and Dean Lester.
