Natives can be dealt with peacefully, conquered, or, with the right choices and some luck, converted, turning the village into a mission, but a few accidental killings are tolerated and too many turn them hostile; the language barrier can sour things too, and ambushes between towns are common. There are no set goals and no score. The King comments on the player's conduct but does not step in if natives are slaughtered, and hidden lost cities, often far from other land, can be plundered for tribute.
trivia: The title refers to Quivira and Cíbola, legendary cities said to lie in the American Southwest.
Bunten said the King's complaints about mistreating natives, while still taking the gold, reflected a historical double standard.
In 1996 Computer Gaming World ranked it the 61st best game of all time, noting that its treatment of indigenous tribes offended some.
Rolling Stone called Sid Meier's Pirates! probably the second open-world game, after this one.
A 1993 Commemorative Edition won the Origins Award for Best Military or Strategy Computer Game.
devStory:
Danielle Bunten Berry, credited as Dan Bunten, created it at Ozark Softscape with Bill Bunten, Jim Rushing and Alan Watson, and Electronic Arts published it in 1984 for the Atari 8-bit, Apple II and Commodore 64. The team wanted a large, detailed New World without long load times, and built a streaming system to load map data during play. Besides a world modelled on the real one, down to the Florida Keys and the best-known rivers, a world generator lets players create new continents and save them to disk. Bunten considered the Atari version the only full one, the others being ports made with limited resources, and said the peaceful approach worked best.

It sold over 100,000 copies by the time Computer Gaming World's readers voted it Strategy Game of the Year for 1985, and is considered one of the earliest open-world games.

sources.title: The Seven Cities of Gold (video game)

title: Rescue on Fractalus!
description: Rescue on Fractalus! (1985) is Lucasfilm Games' first-person flight game, in which a Valkyrie fighter rescues downed pilots from a planet of fractal-generated mountains, some of whom are aliens in disguise.
longDescription:
The player flies a Valkyrie fighter, adapted for search and rescue, low over the jagged mountains of Fractalus, generated with fractals, which give the planet and game their name. A direction finder points to downed Ethercorps pilots whose beacons are often hidden behind ridges, while anti-aircraft guns in the mountains must be dodged or destroyed, and on later levels Jaggi pilots fly kamikaze saucers. Missions move into the boundary between day and night, where only the altimeter helps.

After landing beside a pilot, the player shuts down the engine, since starting it too soon incinerates him, and lowers the shields to let him in; the acidic atmosphere kills anyone outside within a minute, and the pilot knocks on the door to be let in. Some "pilots" are disguised Jaggi aliens, a twist George Lucas suggested and kept out of the manual, who leap up at the windscreen unless the shields are restored. Early Jaggi have green heads, but later ones wear the same helmets as humans.
trivia: Fox said the disguised Jaggi made it "the first computer game to really scare people".
The squiggles on the Jaggi suit are the team's initials turned sideways, since Atari did not allow developer credits.
Its working title was Behind Jaggi Lines!
An abandoned sequel, Return to Fractalus, was eventually turned into Star Wars: Rogue Squadron.
Zzap!64 gave it 91%.
devStory:
It and Ballblazer were the first two games from the games group Lucasfilm founded in 1982 with $1 million from Atari. David Fox led and designed it, Charlie Kellner wrote most of the music, and its working title was Behind Jaggi Lines!, a pun on the aliens and on jagged "jaggies". The team wanted a Star Wars setting, but Lucas refused. Ready by March 1984, it was caught up when Warner sold Atari's consumer division that July, and Epyx published the Atari 8-bit version by May 1985 and the Commodore 64 version that August.

Computer Gaming World said it set "a new standard for arcade-style games", and in 1996 ranked it the 82nd best game ever.

title: Ballblazer
description: Ballblazer (1984) is Lucasfilm Games' futuristic one-on-one ball game, played on a split screen in first person, whose theme music was generated by algorithm.
longDescription:
Two hovering craft called rotofoils, each flown by a human or by a computer "droid" with ten difficulty levels, compete to fire or carry a floating ball into the other's goal. The field is a flat checkerboard, and each player's half of the screen shows their own first-person view. Running into the ball takes possession and holds it in a force field ahead of the craft; the other player can knock it loose with the fire button. Without the ball a rotofoil turns automatically to face it, and with the ball it turns towards the opponent's goal, whose posts slide from side to side and close in as goals are scored.

Pushing the ball through the goal scores one point, a close-range shot two, and a long shot from where the posts cannot be seen three. The combined score is capped at ten, so points beyond the cap come off the opponent's total. The game ends when a player reaches ten or time runs out, and a draw goes to sudden death.
trivia: Its theme, "Song of the Grid", is generated by Peter Langston's "riffology" technique, which assembles a lead melody at random from 32 eight-note riffs.
Some pirated copies carry its development title, "Ballblaster".
An IBM PC version announced in 1984 was never released.
LucasArts and Rainbow Arts released a follow-up, Masterblazer, in 1990.
A remake, Ballblazer Champions, came out on the PlayStation in 1997.
devStory:
Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus! were the first two games from the games group Lucasfilm founded in 1982 with $1 million from Atari, which got first refusal as publisher. David Levine was its principal creator and programmer, with Peter Langston, David Riordan and Garry Hare also credited, and it was called "Ballblaster" during development. It was ready by March 1984 and shown on 8 May, but when Warner sold Atari's consumer division to Jack Tramiel that July the deal fell through, and Epyx took it on at the January 1985 CES.

Epyx published the Atari 8-bit version by May 1985 and the Commodore 64 version by September, Activision published other versions in Europe, and Atari Corporation later released 5200 and 7800 cartridges. Zzap!64 gave the C64 version 98% and a Gold Medal, faulting only its sound effects, and Computer and Video Games gave the 7800 version 97% in 1989.

title: California Games
description: California Games on the Lynx was a technical demonstration disguised as a sports anthology — the BMX and skateboarding events used the Lynx's hardware sprite scaling in ways that no Game Boy port could replicate.
longDescription: Epyx's California Games was one of the Lynx launch titles and demonstrated the hardware's capabilities immediately. The Lynx's custom blitter chip could scale and rotate sprites in hardware; the BMX event's perspective shifts used these capabilities for smooth animation the Game Boy couldn't produce.
trivia: California Games was bundled with the Lynx in some markets, establishing it as the system's flagship technical showcase.
The Game Boy version had notably inferior animation, illustrating the hardware capability gap between the two systems.
devStory: California Games was developed by Epyx — the same company that designed the Lynx hardware — and was one of the system's launch titles.

title: Chip's Challenge
description: Chip's Challenge (1989) is Chuck Sommerville's tile-based puzzle game for the Atari Lynx, in which Chip collects computer chips across 148 levels to join the Bit Busters Club.
longDescription:
Chip McCallahan, a high-school student, meets Melinda the Mental Marvel in the school science lab, and to join her Bit Busters Club he must complete the puzzles of her "Clubhouse". Each of the 148 levels needs enough computer chips collected to open the chip socket before Chip reaches the exit, among buttons, locked doors, water and lethal monsters. Some levels lean towards action and others towards puzzles: there are block-pushing levels like Sokoban, levels about dodging enemies, and mazes, and most are timed.

Four-letter passwords let players skip to levels, and the game offers to skip one after repeated failures. Each level scores more for finishing quickly and in fewer attempts, and the total score is the sum of them all.
trivia: The Windows version has 149 levels, one more than the Lynx original.
In the Windows version, the password "TONY" opens a level crediting its test team.
Players shared home-made level editors and unofficial level sets on bulletin boards and early internet forums.
Sommerville made Chip's Challenge 2 in 1999, but it was held up over the trademark until its release on Steam in 2015.
Tile World is an open-source clone of the game.
devStory:
Chuck Sommerville led an Epyx team for ten weeks in 1989, shortly before the Lynx launched, having first built a prototype on an Apple II to test the logic and show Epyx it was fun. He designed about a third of the levels, Bill Darrah another third and other Epyx staff the rest, and Atari Corporation published it as a Lynx launch title. Images Software made most of the conversions to other computers.

Microsoft licensed it for Windows, where Tony Krueger coded it by reverse-engineering the MS-DOS version and Ed Halley redrew the art. Released in Microsoft Entertainment Pack 4 in 1992 and again in Best of Microsoft Entertainment Pack, that version became very popular. STart's Clayton Walnum praised the consistent quality of its puzzles and predicted it would help sell Lynxes.

title: Todd's Adventures in Slime World
description: Todd's Adventures in Slime World (1990) is Epyx's Atari Lynx exploration game, in which Todd hunts for gems on a slime-covered planet, credited as the first game for eight players.
longDescription:
Todd, a galactic explorer in the Andromeda sector, finds a starship whose log describes Slime World, a planet full of disgusting life forms and valuable slime gems. He explores it with a water gun that fires at many angles and kills most creatures in one hit, clinging to and climbing most walls and making high and long jumps, and many rooms are really puzzles about using those abilities. Shields and pools of water wash off slime damage, but shooting red creatures releases red slime that kills instantly even through a shield, and hidden Snappers kill anyone who steps on them. Lives are usually unlimited: dying strips Todd's items and sends him back to the last checkpoint arrow.

Seven modes change the goal. Easy is for learning, Exploration offers a big map full of secrets, Action the toughest opposition, and Logic, for one player only, disables the gun and resets the world on death. Suspense runs on a clock extended by collecting mushrooms, Arcade disables checkpoints, and Combat pits players against each other with slime guns and room-destroying mega bombs; in multiplayer there is only one single-seat escape capsule, so players fight to reach it first.
trivia: Up to eight Lynx handhelds could be linked with the ComLynx cable, making it the only eight-player Lynx game.
In Arcade mode on the Lynx, the automap's layout spells out a hint to a hidden "zit popping" minigame.
Game Players magazine named it its game of the year.
In Logic mode the water gun does not work at all.
Renovation Products published the Genesis version in North America.
devStory:
Peter Engelbrite programmed it at Epyx, then Atari's programming arm, saying he saw slime in many children's films of the time, and Atari released it for the Lynx in 1990. Linking up to eight machines through ComLynx, it is credited as the first eight-player game and is the only eight-player Lynx game. Computer and Video Games scored it 90, calling it a "superb exploration game", Raze gave it 92%, and STart's Clayton Walnum called it "wonderfully gross". Game Players named it its game of the year.

Matt Householder ported it to the Genesis and PC Engine CD in 1992, reducing multiplayer to two-player split screen; Sega-16 later said that change and the always-visible map removed most of its appeal.

title: Klax
description: Klax (1990) on the Atari Lynx is a close port of Atari's arcade puzzle game: catch coloured tiles from a conveyor and stack them into matches.
longDescription: Klax on the Lynx brings the arcade puzzle game to Atari's handheld, played with the screen turned vertically to match the arcade layout. Tiles tumble down a conveyor to be caught on a paddle and dropped into bins, forming rows, columns and diagonals of matching colours, called Klaxes, across a sequence of waves with different goals. It was widely regarded as one of the best home versions of the game.
trivia: The Lynx Klax was considered the closest to the arcade original of any home version.
devStory: Klax was developed by Atari Games for the arcade and converted to the Lynx as a launch title.

title: Rygar
description: Rygar (1990) on the Atari Lynx is Haehn Software's conversion of Tecmo's arcade game, fought with the Diskarmor, a spinning shield on a chain.
longDescription: Rygar's only weapon is the Diskarmor, thrown and pulled back like a yo-yo. The Lynx version has 23 levels instead of 27, some of them new, an expanded story and a larger, tougher final boss. Throwing the shield upward needs a power-up.
trivia: Tecmo's arcade original came out in Japan in 1986.
devStory: Haehn Software made it and Atari Corporation released it in North America in August 1990.

title: Vampire Killer
description: Vampire Killer (1986) is Konami's MSX2 version of the first Castlevania, with maze-like stages in which Simon Belmont hunts for keys, merchants and treasure chests.
longDescription:
Simon Belmont enters Dracula's castle with the whip inherited from his father to slay the count. The premise, music, characters and locations are shared with the Famicom Castlevania, as is the structure of 18 stages with a boss at the end of every third. But the stages here are labyrinths rather than straight paths: Simon has to find the exit and a skeleton key to unlock it, and because of the MSX2's limits the screen flips from room to room instead of scrolling.

Items and weapons come from breaking candle stands and certain walls, from merchants hidden in the castle, and from treasure chests opened with keys. The whip can be swapped for a chain whip, throwing daggers, a battle axe or a cross, the last two returning like boomerangs. Simon can carry a map, usable three times, holy water, an hourglass that freezes enemies and a shield, and hearts serve both as ammunition and as money. Other items affect his intelligence, which changes merchants' prices, or his speed and jump. After each boss he loses his equipment except his hearts and map, and he has three lives with no way to earn more.
trivia: Its Japanese title, Akumajō Dracula, means "Demon Castle Dracula".
Neither it nor the MSX2 was released in North America.
Plugging in Konami's Game Master cartridge enables continues and stage select.
The Famicom Castlevania debuted a month earlier under the same Japanese title.
Time Extension ranked it near the bottom of the Castlevania series, calling it a historical footnote.
devStory:
Akihiko Nagata produced and designed it at Konami, with music by Kinuyo Yamashita and Satoe Terashima, and it came out in Japan on 30 October 1986 as Akumajō Dracula, a month after the Famicom Disk System game of the same name. Europe got it in 1987 without Castlevania branding; the series took that name abroad only when the NES version reached North America that year, and neither this game nor the MSX2 was released there.

Continues are available only with Konami's Game Master cartridge in the second slot, which also allows choosing the stage and the number of lives. It was re-released through Project EGG in 2014 and on the Japanese Wii U Virtual Console that December.

title: Gradius
description: The MSX Gradius brought Konami's landmark horizontal shooter to the platform with the powerup progression system that defined the series. The Vic Viper's shield, double, laser, and option upgrades were implemented in full.
longDescription: Konami's Gradius had defined the horizontal shooter genre in arcades. The MSX version maintained the core powerup system — collecting consecutive capsules filled a meter, and the player chose which upgrade to activate.
trivia: Gradius's powerup system spawned the entire 'Gradius-type' shooter category.
The famous Konami Code comes from Konami's NES conversion of Gradius, where programmer Kazuhisa Hashimoto added it as a testing aid.
devStory: Gradius was converted from the arcade original by Konami's MSX development team. It was one of the MSX's most commercially successful games.

title: Knightmare
description: Knightmare (1986) is Konami's MSX vertical shooter, in which the warrior Popolon fights through a Greek-inspired fantasy world to rescue Princess Aphrodite.
longDescription:
Popolon must rescue Princess Aphrodite from the evil priest Hudnos across eight stages of a Greek-inspired fantasy world. The screen scrolls constantly until a boss appears, and shooting certain spots reveals hidden bridges over rivers. Popolon starts with a bow and arrows. Flashing crystals change his weapon, and taking the same one twice upgrades it, while black "P" crystals cycle through power-ups as they are shot — boomerangs, three-way shots, swords, speed, invincibility and a shield. Question-mark blocks, some of them hidden, release chess-themed jewels that can help or hinder, and some stages have secret exits that warp ahead.

Being hit, or being trapped by an obstacle and scrolled off the screen, costs a life and resets the weapons. Extra lives come every 100,000 points or from a yellow jewel.
trivia: Its follow-ups changed genre: The Maze of Galious on the MSX and Shalom: Knightmare III on the Famicom, both in 1987.
Compile's Takayuki Hirono cited it as an influence on Zanac, especially its power-up system.
Popolon and Aphrodite later appeared in Parodius (1988).
A planned PC-8801 and X1 sequel with role-playing elements was previewed in magazines but never released.
Fans have remade it for the ZX Spectrum, ColecoVision and Amiga.
devStory:
Konami's MSX division made it under Shigeru Fukutake, with a team of four or five working for four to six months; the staffer who created Popolon became lead designer and writer. Fukutake said it was made hard because MSX shooters were meant to be played at home. Miki Higashino, a part-time composer at Konami, wrote the music with Yoshinori Sasaki, and Masaaki Kukino said the title combines "knight" and "nightmare".

Konami released it in Japan on 29 March 1986 as Majou Densetsu and in Europe later that year. Tilt named it the best MSX action game of 1986, and MSX News called it "an authentic masterpiece", though several reviewers noted how hard it is.

title: SD Snatcher
description: SD Snatcher (1990) is Konami's Japan-only MSX2 role-playing remake of Snatcher, which carries the story past the original's unfinished ending.
longDescription:
It retells Snatcher's story in super-deformed style — that is what "SD" stands for. In Neo Kobe City, an artificial island metropolis in Japan, humanoid robots called Snatchers are killing people and taking their places in society, and the amnesiac Gillian Seed joins the anti-Snatcher task force JUNKER to hunt them. Where the original was a menu-driven adventure, this is a role-playing game: Gillian explores a top-down map, and encounters switch to a first-person battle screen where the player shoots enemies with one of many guns, aiming at different body parts.

The original Snatcher had been cut from five planned acts to two because of memory limits and ended on a cliffhanger. SD Snatcher carries the story further, and its new segment later became the third act of the PC Engine, Sega CD, PlayStation and Saturn versions.
trivia: Its 1993 fan translation by the Dutch group Oasis is one of the earliest known fan translations of a game.
Hideo Kojima and his team joined late in development to help finish it.
"SD" stands for "super deformed".
Its added story became the third act of later Snatcher versions, starting with the PC Engine's Snatcher CD-ROMantic in 1992.
It was released only in Japan.
devStory: Yoshihiko Ota and Hideo Kojima are credited with the design, with Yutaka Haruki producing; Kojima, busy with Metal Gear 2, joined late in development to help finish it. Konami released it on the MSX2 in Japan on 27 April 1990. The original Snatcher, which Kojima wrote and designed, had been released for the PC-8801 and MSX2 in 1988.

title: Road Rash
description: Road Rash (1994) on the 3DO is EA's motorcycle combat racer rebuilt for CD: video scenes and a soundtrack of real bands including Soundgarden.
longDescription: Road Rash on the 3DO keeps the series' formula — races along open roads where riders punch, kick and club each other off their bikes while dodging traffic and police — and dresses it up for CD. Filmed video sequences frame the races, and the soundtrack features licensed tracks from alternative rock bands, including Soundgarden and Therapy?, still a novelty for console games at the time. Races take place across five routes with increasingly powerful bikes.
trivia: Road Rash on 3DO was one of the first games to feature licensed music from real contemporary bands on CD.
The 3DO version's live-action video sequences were produced separately and stored as compressed video on the disc.
devStory: EA developed Road Rash specifically to showcase 3DO capabilities, creating a version that exceeded the 16-bit originals in presentation.

title: The Need for Speed
description: The Need for Speed (1994) is EA Canada's 3DO racer made with Road & Track magazine, with eight licensed sports cars, traffic, police pursuits and video commentary on each car.
longDescription:
Players drive eight licensed sports cars, exotic models and Japanese imports such as the Ferrari 512 TR, on three point-to-point tracks, each split into three stages, with or without a computer opponent. Traffic has to be avoided, and police give chase: a caught driver gets a ticket, and repeated tickets lead to arrest. Electronic Arts worked with Road & Track to make the cars behave like the real ones, down to the sound of the gear levers.

Each car comes with specifications, history, spoken commentary, magazine-style photographs of its interior and exterior and short videos, and a replay mode offers several camera views and playback controls.
trivia: Its full title is Road & Track Presents: The Need for Speed.
In Japan it was released as Road & Track Presents: OverDrivin'.
The Special Edition hides a fictional jet-powered car, the Warrior PTO E/2, and a Lost Vegas track.
It was runner-up for Computer Gaming World's Action Game of the Year for 1995.
A planned Atari Jaguar CD version was never released.
devStory:
EA Canada developed it with Pioneer Productions, drawing on Test Drive, with which it shared staff; Hanno Lemke produced, Brad Gour programmed and Jeff van Dyck and Saki Kaskas wrote the music. Electronic Arts released it for the 3DO in December 1994, and it reached number five in the UK chart. EGM praised its realistic graphics and sound, while Next Generation called it "a pleasant Sunday drive".

MS-DOS, PlayStation and Saturn versions in 1995 and 1996 added closed circuits and extra tracks, and GamePro called the PlayStation one "practically a sequel". It began the Need for Speed series, followed by Need for Speed II in 1997.

title: Shock Wave
description: Shock Wave (1994) is Electronic Arts' 3DO combat flight game, in which an F-177 fighter fends off an alien invasion between full-motion video scenes.
longDescription:
In 2019 aliens attack Earth and wipe out its military, leaving the orbital carrier UNSF Omaha and its squadron of F-177 pilots as humanity's last hope. The player is a rookie, Lt. J. "Wildcard" Adair, flying missions to destroy aliens around the world, rescue a downed ally and fetch oxygen for the Omaha, before a final strike on the brain of the alien mothership. On board, Dr. Lawrence discovers that the aliens are robotic vessels harvesting humans and incubating eggs, and that the real invasion is still to come.

The F-177 resembles the F-117 Nighthawk but can fly in space. It has a rapid-fire laser that uses energy and a limited supply of homing missiles, levels off automatically and hovers over the ground, so it cannot crash. Thrusters burn fuel for a speed boost, and flying under refuelling drones restores fuel, energy and shield. Each of the ten missions opens with a briefing, takes place over terrain based on real regions, such as desert in Egypt and jungle in Peru, and ends with a boss.
trivia: It was packed in with the GoldStar 3DO.
Its 1995 expansion, Operation Jumpgate, needed a save file from the original.
Losing all lives ends the story with Wildcard's death.
A sequel, Shock Wave 2: Beyond the Gate, followed in 1995.
A planned Atari Jaguar CD version was never released.
devStory:
Electronic Arts' Advanced Technology Group made it, with Kelly Pope directing and Michael Becker designing, and EA released it for the 3DO in North America on 27 June 1994; it was the pack-in game with the GoldStar 3DO. EGM praised its texture-mapped graphics and full-motion video but found the controls over-sensitive, while Next Generation called it a no-frills shooter for fans of the genre.

The Operation Jumpgate expansion, set in 2026 around Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, followed in May 1995. Later versions for Windows, Mac, PlayStation and Saturn, retitled Shockwave Assault, combine both and have 15 missions. The Windows version was EA's first game built to use Windows 95 features.

title: Tempest 2000
description: Tempest 2000 (1994) is Jeff Minter's Jaguar remake of Atari's Tempest, with 100 webs, new power-ups and a techno soundtrack, and one of the console's most acclaimed games.
longDescription:
Players shoot their way up the rims of 100 webs, whose colours and variations change every 16 levels, with progress saved every couple of levels. Power-ups appear after destroying enough enemies or bullets: among them the Particle Laser, Jump and the A.I. Droid. The Superzapper clears the screen once, and a second use destroys one random enemy. Three Warp tokens and a cleared level open a bonus stage worth 25,000 points and a five-level skip, and "Outta Here!" destroys everything on screen except spikes and warps ahead.

Clearing all 100 webs unlocks Beastly Mode, with faster, tougher enemies and a slower-firing ship. Traditional Tempest recreates the arcade game, Tempest Plus mixes the two styles, and Tempest Duel is a two-player battle with a Mirror power-up that reflects the rival's shots.
trivia: Atari never released the rotary controller the game supported, a common complaint.
Imagitec Design's soundtrack was also sold on CD, including six tracks that did not fit on the cartridge.
The PlayStation version, Tempest X3, hides the original Tempest 2000 behind a high-score name code.
Its source code was released in 2008 in the Jaguar Source Code Collection.
Minter's test unit used a modified Atari 2600 driving controller.
devStory:
When Atari asked prospective Jaguar developers which arcade games they wanted to convert, Jeff Minter volunteered for Tempest, and Llamasoft made it in Wales; the Jaguar's creator reportedly told Minter it was a weak showcase for the hardware. Imagitec Design's Ian Howe, Alastair Lindsay and Kevin Saville wrote the soundtrack in Amiga MOD format, and Atari sold it on CD. Atari released the game in North America on 13 April 1994.

It sold over 30,000 copies by April 1995, second on the Jaguar only to Alien vs Predator. EGM named it the Best Jaguar Game of 1994, GamePro called its music "the best techno-rave tracks anywhere", and Next Generation said it "did more for Atari's reputation than anything the company's marketing team had managed".

title: Alien vs. Predator
description: Alien vs. Predator (1994) is Rebellion's Atari Jaguar first-person shooter, with three playable species: Alien, Predator or Colonial Marine.
longDescription:
The game is set in a simulation of Golgotha, a Colonial Marines training base overrun by two alien species, spread over five sublevels joined by lifts and air ducts, with the Alien and Predator ships docked alongside. The Alien must rescue its queen from the Predator ship. It fights with claws, jaw and tail, cannot heal, and survives by cocooning Marines, whose embryos grow into eggs that act as extra lives; it cannot use lifts and travels through the ducts. The Predator must kill the queen and claim her skull. It can turn invisible, though not against Aliens, and earns its combistick, smart disc and shoulder cannon by scoring points, which it loses by killing while invisible.

The Marine, Lance J. Lewis, starts on sublevel 3 with no weapons, clearance or motion tracker, gathers guns from fallen Marines and needs a level 10 security card to reach the self-destruct before escaping in a pod. Aliens spray acid when killed up close, facehuggers drain health until shaken off, and enemies respawn when a saved game is resumed.
trivia: Game Informer named it Jaguar Game of the Year for 1994.
It sold more than 85,000 copies, the Jaguar's best seller.
An Alien queen model had to be smuggled into the UK after customs blocked shipments.
In Japan it was packed in with the Jaguar.
Its source code was released in 2008 in the Jaguar Source Code Collection.
devStory:
It began as a Lynx game at Atari's Chicago office before producer James Hampton redirected it towards a first-person shooter. Rebellion, founded by Jason and Chris Kingsley in 1992, won the Jaguar contract in 1993; Mike Beaton and Andrew Whittaker programmed it, Whittaker spending six months on the enemy AI. It overran its contract by about ten months, the programmers missed salaries when the budget ran out, and Sam Tramiel approved more time and a bigger cartridge.

Atari released it in October 1994. Reviewers praised the choice of characters, large environments and tense atmosphere but noted slow stretches and a low frame rate, and GamesMaster's Marcus Hawkins wrote: "Never before has so little had so much impact." Rebellion later made the PC Aliens versus Predator (1999).

title: Doom
description: Doom (1994) on the Atari Jaguar is id Software's own port, with 22 of the PC game's 27 levels plus two new ones, squeezed onto a 2 MB cartridge.
longDescription: The game fills the whole screen above a status bar and runs at a fairly steady frame rate. It drops the Cyberdemon, Spider Mastermind and Spectre, plays no music during levels, and offers two-player deathmatch through the JagLink 2. Weapons are chosen on the controller's number pad.
trivia: Next Generation called it "definitely the best Jaguar title we've seen so far".
Rebecca Heineman built the later 3DO version from the Jaguar port's code.
devStory: id Software developed it and Atari released it in November 1994, stripping the game down to fit the cartridge. Progress saves automatically, and players can restart at any level they have reached.

title: Virtual Boy Wario Land
description: Virtual Boy Wario Land (1995) is Nintendo's platformer for its 3D headset, in which Wario climbs back out of a treasure cave and leaps between foreground and background.
longDescription: On holiday in the Awazon river basin, Wario follows strange creatures behind the Aldegara waterfall into a treasure cave, falls deep underground and must climb back to the surface through 14 floors of non-linear levels, each needing treasure collected and a key found to work the lift to the next. He stuns enemies by jumping on them or charging, then picks them up and throws them, and shoulder-charges or body-slams through blocks. Bull, eagle and dragon hats give strength, flight and fire breath, and the eagle and dragon together make the King Dragon hat with all three. Jump pads send him between the background and foreground, and the bosses every three floors use the stereoscopic display. Each level hides one of ten artifacts, and the ending depends on finding them all, the coins collected and the time taken.
trivia: It was first shown as Wario Cruise and was to be called Wario's Treasure Hunt in North America.
Totaka's Song is hidden in the closing credits.
Polygon called it the best Wario game despite being the least popular.
Renegade Kid's Jools Watsham said he proposed a colour 3DS remake to Nintendo and heard nothing back.
It was added to Nintendo Classics in February 2026.
devStory:
A large team at Nintendo R&D1 made it, with Hiroji Kiyotake and Hirofumi Matsuoka co-directing, Gunpei Yokoi producing and Kazumi Totaka composing, in his last project at R&D1. Shown at E3 1995 as Wario Cruise, it came out in North America in November 1995 and Japan that December. GamePro called it the best Virtual Boy game, and N64 Magazine said it "should have sold the machine by the million", though Next Generation thought its 3D added little.

Retrospective reviews have been warmer still, often naming it among the best Virtual Boy games, and its background-hopping inspired Donkey Kong Country Returns and Mutant Mudds.

title: Teleroboxer
description: Teleroboxer (1995) is Nintendo's first-person robot boxing game for the Virtual Boy, using its 3D display to put opponents in your face.
longDescription: In the 22nd century, telerobotic machines that imitate human movement are built for jobs people cannot do, and Doctor Edward Maki Jr. creates a tournament in which two of them box. Teleroboxing becomes popular around the world and grows into a world championship. The player controls a boxing robot seen from its own viewpoint against a series of computer-controlled opponents, using both of the Virtual Boy controller's d-pads; reviewers found the controls convoluted and the opponents very fast. Like every Virtual Boy game it is drawn in red and black, using parallax to create depth, and progress can be saved.
trivia: It was shown at the 1994 CES under the name Teleroboxing.
Official Nintendo Magazine noted it as the most common Virtual Boy game.
GamesRadar listed it among the five best Virtual Boy games.
It was added to Nintendo Classics in February 2026, and its soundtrack to Nintendo Music that July.
devStory:
Nintendo R&D1 developed it, with Yoshio Sakamoto directing, Gunpei Yokoi producing and Katsuya Yamano composing the music. It was shown as Teleroboxing at the 1994 Consumer Electronics Show, where Steve L. Kent reported that players complained of headaches but that it made the best use of 3D of the Virtual Boy games on show. Nintendo released it in Japan on 21 July 1995 and in North America on 14 August.

Many critics compared it with Punch-Out!!: Next Generation called it a "high-tech" remake of the NES game, and IGN AU a spiritual successor that was "fun and bitterly hard". Wired's Chris Kohler called it "too difficult for its own good", while Nintendo Life found it very easy once learned.

title: Red Alarm
description: Red Alarm (1995) is T&E Soft's wireframe 3D space shooter for the Virtual Boy, inspired by Star Fox, in which the Tech-Wing fights the rogue AI KAOS.
longDescription:
After a 70-year world war, humanity has built a weapon-free utopia, until KAOS, a defence AI that helped end the war, becomes sentient and builds an army to wipe out humanity. The player's Tech-Wing fighter can move in any direction, firing lasers and guided missiles for armoured targets, and since its shields offer limited protection, dodging matters. The six levels each end with a boss, and some have branching corridors and dead ends that force backtracking.

It uses a 3D polygon engine, unlike most Virtual Boy games, but drawn as bare wireframes, like Battlezone, since solid 3D was beyond the hardware. The stereoscopic depth can be adjusted, there are three third-person views and a cockpit view, and each level can be replayed from several angles.
trivia: It is one of the few third-party Virtual Boy games.
Its design takes inspiration from Star Fox.
EGM's Andrew Baran called it "a nifty show-off game".
Wired's Chris Kohler said in 2010 that it "kind of sucked".
It was added to Nintendo Classics in February 2026.
devStory:
T&E Soft, known until then for golf games, was one of the few third-party studios invited to make Virtual Boy games; Gunpei Yokoi said Nintendo kept tight control of third-party releases to keep out poor-quality games. Shown at the Winter 1995 CES and confirmed as a launch game at E3, it came out in Japan on 21 July 1995 and in the US that August.

Reviews split over its wireframes: EGM's four reviewers found them confusing, while GameFan's Nicholas Barres called it "the one and only reason to buy a Virtual Boy". Next Generation gave it 1 out of 5, calling it a wasted opportunity.

title: Stunt Race FX
description: Stunt Race FX (1994) is Nintendo and Argonaut's polygon racing game for the Super NES, the second game to use the Super FX chip, starring cars with eyes for headlights.
longDescription: Its tracks and cars are built from 3D polygons, drawn by the Super FX GSU-1 chip in the cartridge, with road bumps, overpasses and billboards. Three vehicles are available at the start: the Formula One-style F-Type, the Coupe and the 4WD monster truck, with a 2WD to unlock and a Trailer lorry in bonus games, each differing in speed, body and acceleration. The cars, with eyes for headlights, are heavier and clumsier than in most racing games; boosting speeds them up, L and R sharpen turns, and collisions cause damage. There are three racing levels, an obstacle course, test drives, time attack and two-player racing.
trivia: In Japan it is called Wild Trax.
The Japanese manual describes the Coupe as female and the other cars as male; English manuals call them all male.
Kellogg's offered a Hot Wheels F-Type for two Apple Jacks proofs of purchase.
Its working title was FX Trax.
It returned on Nintendo Classics in 2019, its first re-release in over two decades.
devStory:
Nintendo and Argonaut began developing the Super FX chip in 1991, mainly for Star Fox, and experimented with other 3D games along the way. Tentatively titled FX Trax, it was directed by Tatsuya Hishida and produced by Shigeru Miyamoto, who had the designers stress realistic handling: the F-Type's weight sits at the back, so its tail drifts more easily in corners. Giles Goddard and Colin Reed programmed it with Nintendo staff, the cars' eyes were a late addition, and Wataru Yamaguchi made clay models of the cars for the box and manuals.

Nintendo released it in Japan on 4 June 1994 as Wild Trax and in North America that July. Edge called it one of the best racing games on any home system, while EGM found it a disappointment after Star Fox, and PC Zone reported in 1998 that it had sold over a million copies.

title: Virtua Racing
description: Virtua Racing (1994) for the Genesis squeezes Sega's polygon arcade racer onto a cartridge, using the built-in SVP chip to draw its 3D graphics.
longDescription: The Genesis Virtua Racing is a conversion of Sega's pioneering polygon arcade racer. To draw its 3D cars and tracks, the cartridge includes the Sega Virtual Processor, a custom chip that did the heavy lifting for the console. It offers the arcade game's courses, several camera views and a two-player split-screen mode. The extra hardware made it one of the most expensive Genesis cartridges ever sold.
trivia: Virtua Racing on Genesis was the most expensive consumer cartridge ever released at $99 — nearly double typical Genesis game prices.
devStory: The Genesis Virtua Racing was released in 1994 with the Sega Virtua Processor cartridge chip — a significant engineering undertaking.

title: Super Star Wars
description: Super Star Wars (1992) is the SNES action platformer retelling A New Hope, with Luke, Han and Chewbacca playable and landspeeder and X-wing stages.
longDescription: Super Star Wars follows the original film from the deserts of Tatooine to the Death Star trench, mostly as run-and-gun platforming. Instead of buying the droids, Luke has to climb a Jawa sandcrawler, leaping between moving conveyor belts. His blaster can be upgraded several times, and he wields a lightsaber once Obi-Wan gives it to him. Later stages let the player control Han Solo or Chewbacca, others put the player behind the wheel of a landspeeder and in an X-wing, and the ending recreates the trench run, with Darth Vader in his TIE Advanced. Brief cutscenes between levels tell an abbreviated version of the story.
trivia: Two sequels followed: Super The Empire Strikes Back (1993) and Super Return of the Jedi (1994).
One boss is based on the chess piece R2-D2 plays with on the Millennium Falcon.
Flux called it "the second great SNES platform game after Super Mario World".
A prototype of the cancelled Mega Drive version was dumped in 2020.
It was re-released on PS4 and PS Vita in 2015.
devStory:
Sculptured Software developed it with LucasArts, and JVC published it in North America in November 1992. Kalani Streicher directed, produced and designed it, with Peter Ward programming, Jon Knoles designing the characters and Harrison Fong drawing backgrounds. Paul Webb arranged John Williams's scores from his handwritten originals for the Super NES's eight sound channels. A trash compactor level was dropped for lack of cartridge space, and PC and Mega Drive versions were started and cancelled.

EGM gave it 9/10 from all four reviewers and named it Best Action/Adventure Game and Best Movie-to-Game of 1992, and Nintendo Power placed it fourth among the year's SNES games.

title: Samurai Shodown
description: Samurai Shodown was the first major weapon-based fighting game — SNK's feudal Japan fighter where a single sword strike could deal catastrophic damage, creating a fundamentally different fighting game experience.
longDescription: SNK's Samurai Shodown replaced the punch-kick fighting game template with weapon-based combat where single hits were genuinely threatening. The game rewarded careful spacing and timing over aggressive attack.
trivia: Samurai Shodown's weapon-clash mechanic — both players attacking simultaneously creating a struggle — was widely copied in subsequent fighting games.
The game's Japanese historical setting was unusual for 1993 fighting games.
devStory: Samurai Shodown was developed by SNK and released on the Neo Geo MVS arcade and home cartridge simultaneously in 1993. It spawned a long-running franchise.

title: Blazing Star
description: Blazing Star (1998) is Yumekobo's Neo Geo horizontal shooter, a gentler follow-up to Pulstar with a charge shot, remembered for its "You fail it" game over message.
longDescription: Cyborgs who have regained their humanity fight to destroy the AI systems building cybernetic armies. Each selectable ship has its own shot types, power and speed. Tapping the fire button gives a standard shot, tapping it rapidly gives a different one, and holding it charges a focused shot that can burst into smaller bullets, with effects and range varying from ship to ship. Power-ups strengthen the weapons, while collectable items raise the score and count towards a ranking at the end of each stage, some appearing only after particular enemy waves are wiped out. Later stages add hazards such as narrow passages, and every stage ends with a boss worth a bonus if it is beaten within the time limit.
trivia: Its game over message, "You fail it", is cited, by the linguist Ben Zimmer among others, as inspiring the internet interjection "fail".
Zero Hour and The Zenith were considered as titles; the team did not know Blazing Star is also the name of a plant.
Character endings were planned but cut.
A Neo Geo CD version was planned but never released.
It is included on SNK's Neo Geo Mini.
devStory:
It was the first game from Yumekobo, formerly Aicom, which had rebranded to work closely with SNK. It began as a follow-up to Pulstar, and the team treated it as a side story; the company president wanted Pulstar in the title, and it was at one point called Pulstar Blast, but SNK objected because Pulstar had done poorly in the West for being too hard. Pulstar's director wanted a charge shot to make it easier. Sprites were limited to 16 colours each by the Neo Geo hardware, and the sprite limit capped bullet counts and caused some flicker. Leefa was modelled on Yuko Asahina from Tokimeki Memorial, and JB on Jean Reno.

It came out in Japanese arcades on 19 January 1998 and for the home Neo Geo that February. Edge praised its colourful backgrounds and "frenetic, old-school" play, and Edge, Next Level and Video Games all praised the bosses, though Video Games found it too short and too easy.

title: Ys I & II
description: Ys I & II (1989) is the PC Engine CD remake of Nihon Falcom's first two Ys games, one of the first CD-ROM games, with animated voiced cut-scenes and a CD-audio soundtrack.
longDescription:
The red-haired swordsman Adol Christin is shipwrecked on Esteria, an island cut off by a wall of storms, and gathers the six Books of Ys, which tell of an ancient land, a demon invasion and the sealing of the magic metal Cleria, climbing the Tower of Darm to defeat Dark Fact. The books' magic then carries him to a floating island, where he cures a sick girl, Lilia, fights through mines, glaciers and lava and finally destroys the Black Pearl, Darm, revealing the island's captive goddesses to be Feena and Reah, two girls he met along the way. Combat works by walking into enemies slightly off-centre rather than pressing an attack button.

The disc holds 732 MB: 41 music tracks, 24 minutes of voice acting and 20 minutes of animated cut-scenes. Its Red Book soundtrack, arranged by Ryo Yonemitsu from the original music by Yuzo Koshiro, Mieko Ishikawa and Hideya Nagata, was one of the first CD soundtracks in a game.
trivia: It was one of the first video games on CD-ROM.
In North America it was called Ys Book I & II.
EGM gave it Best RPG and Best Music and Sound awards.
RPGFan called it the first RPG on a console CD-ROM.
It was a pack-in game with the TurboDuo in 1992.
devStory: Alfa System developed it, with Masaya Hashimoto directing, and Hudson Soft released it for the PC Engine CD-ROM² in Japan on 21 December 1989; NEC brought it to the TurboGrafx-CD in North America in May 1990 as Ys Book I & II, and it was later packed in with the TurboDuo. Its English version was among the first to use voice dubbing. EGM called it the "most phenomenal RPG ever made", TurboPlay called its soundtrack the best it had heard in a game, and OMNI named it Game of the Year for 1990.

title: Dracula X: Rondo of Blood
description: Rondo of Blood (1993) is Konami's PC Engine CD Castlevania, in which Richter Belmont storms Dracula's castle along branching routes and can rescue Maria Renard as a second playable hero.
longDescription:
In 1792 Dracula's servant Shaft kidnaps Annette, beloved of the 19-year-old vampire hunter Richter Belmont, as bait for a trap, and Richter goes to the castle to rescue her. He fights with the Vampire Killer whip and one of six sub-weapons: axe, dagger, bible, pocket watch, cross or holy water. Item Crash turns a sub-weapon into a super attack, an ability later Castlevania games reused. The nine stages have four alternate routes, and some levels have more than one exit, changing the environments, enemies and bosses that follow.

Along the way Richter can rescue four women, among them Maria Renard, an orphaned 12-year-old relative who then becomes playable. Maria fights with doves and sub-weapons drawn from the Four Symbols of Chinese mythology, such as a white tiger kitten and a baby phoenix; she is faster than Richter, can double jump and hits twice as hard, but takes more damage. The CD format let the music play as Red Book audio alongside the console's sound chip.
trivia: It stayed in Japan for fourteen years, until the PSP's Castlevania: The Dracula X Chronicles included it in 2007.
Maria Renard's sub-weapons are based on the Four Symbols of Chinese mythology.
A hidden minigame, Akumajyo Dracula Peke, plays if the console lacks the required Super System Card.
Netflix's Castlevania: Nocturne is set in 1792 with Richter and Maria as its leads.
IGN gave the Wii Virtual Console release 9/10 and an Editors' Choice award.
devStory:
Toru Hagihara directed it at Konami, with Yoshiaki Yamada producing, and it came out in Japan on 29 October 1993 for the PC Engine Super CD-ROM², the tenth Castlevania. It sold 19,616 copies in its first month, and EGM, which named it the Best Japanese Action Game of 1994, said it "can easily be the best CD title yet", its only drawback being that it never came out in the US.

Its direct sequel, Symphony of the Night, followed worldwide in 1997, reusing many of its monsters. The Super NES Castlevania: Dracula X of 1995 reused much of its graphics with new levels, and the original first reached the West in 2007 as an unlockable in the PSP remake The Dracula X Chronicles, then on the Wii Virtual Console in 2010.

title: Battletoads
description: Battletoads became the canonical example of Nintendo-era difficulty — a beat-em-up with two-player cooperative play where the notorious Turbo Tunnel level failed the majority of players. Its visual creativity and animation quality were exceptional for NES hardware.
longDescription: Rare's Battletoads combined creative enemy design, large sprite animation, and gameplay variety (racing sequences, climbing sections, brawling) with difficulty calibration that bordered on hostile. The Turbo Tunnel's rapid-fire obstacles required memorisation rather than skill.
trivia: The two-player cooperative mode had friendly fire — players could hurt each other, often accidentally, which became its own source of difficulty.
devStory: Battletoads was developed by Rare and published by Tradewest in 1991. Its difficulty became so legendary that it spawned internet-era memes about calling GameStop to ask if they had it in stock.

title: Little Samson
description: Little Samson (1992) is Takeru's NES platformer, in which four heroes — a boy, a dragon, a golem and a mouse — fight the demon king Ta-Keed, now one of the rarest NES cartridges.
longDescription:
The demon king Ta-Keed, sealed inside a mountain long ago, is freed by a lightning strike, and Emperor Hans XIV summons four bell-bearing warriors to defeat him. Little Samson throws bells and climbs walls and ceilings; Kikira the dragon flies briefly, breathes charged fire and grips ice; Gamm the golem is slow but strong, can walk on spikes and strikes in any direction; and K.O. the mouse has the least health but squeezes through narrow passages, climbs and drops bombs.

The first four stages are tutorials for each character and can be played in any order, after which the player can switch between them at any time. Each has a separate life bar but all share one pool of lives, and a fallen hero stays down until the stage ends or a potion revives them, though losing Samson means restarting. A password saves progress after each boss, and only Normal difficulty leads to the true final boss.
trivia: It became one of the rarest and most expensive NES games on the collectors' market.
Its director, Shinichi Yoshimoto, had worked at Capcom on Ghouls 'n Ghosts and Strider.
Limited Run Games announced a re-release for 2026, with the licence obtained through Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs because the rights holder could not be found.
In Japan it was called Seirei Densetsu Lickle.
IGN, USgamer and Paste have listed it among the best NES games.
devStory:
Takeru, which had made Cocoron, developed it, with Shinichi Yoshimoto, a former Capcom designer on Ghouls 'n Ghosts and Strider, directing, producing and writing, and Kiyoshi Utata drawing the art. Taito published it in Japan in June 1992 as Seirei Densetsu Lickle and in North America that November, after showing it at the summer CES. Poor marketing led to weak North American sales.

Contemporary reviews were middling, with Famitsu's scores from 5 to 7, but its reputation has grown: AllGame called it "a tour de force of excellent game design, attractive graphics and pure entertainment value", and Retro Gamer one of the most technically impressive NES games.

title: Out Run
description: Yu Suzuki's Out Run was the first major arcade game to use a hydraulic sit-down cabinet, fake road curvature through sprite scaling, and branching course selection. Its Ferrari Testarossa setting and Magical Sound Shower synthesiser music defined the mid-1980s arcade aesthetic.
longDescription: Out Run innovated in cabinet design (hydraulic motion synchronised to road curves), game structure (branching routes at each fork, multiple endings), and visual spectacle (sprite-scaled curved roads giving the illusion of genuine perspective). The selectable music tracks — three options at the beginning — pioneered in-game music choice.
trivia: The car is unmistakably a Ferrari Testarossa, but Sega did not license it — Ferrari's name appears nowhere in the original arcade game.
The three music tracks — Magical Sound Shower, Passing Breeze, and Splash Wave — became iconic enough to be remixed and released as standalone music.
devStory: Out Run was developed by Yu Suzuki at Sega AM2 and released in arcades in 1986. It became one of the most successful arcade games of its era and spawned numerous ports and sequels.

title: Shinobi
description: Shinobi (1987) is Sega's ninja action game: Joe Musashi rescues kidnapped children from the Zeed organisation with shuriken, blades and ninja magic.
longDescription: The ninja Joe Musashi sets out to stop the criminal organisation Zeed, which is kidnapping the children of his clan, across five missions: three stages in the first and four in each of the rest, each mission ending with a boss. Before each one the player sees the objective, a photo file of the boss and a map of the next stage. An eight-way joystick and three buttons, for attack, jump and ninja magic, control him; jumping with up or down moves between the upper and lower floors of a scene. He has unlimited shurikens, punches and kicks, and freeing certain hostages upgrades the shurikens to a gun and his close-range attacks to a katana slash. Three ninja magic techniques — thunderstorm, tornado and doppelganger — each work once per stage, clearing ordinary enemies or badly damaging a boss. Each stage has a three-minute limit, and a first-person bonus round of throwing shurikens at incoming ninjas awards an extra life.
trivia: Musashi can bump into most enemies harmlessly; only attacks, projectiles and bottomless drops kill him.
Later re-releases altered a character who resembled Spider-Man, reportedly over licensing concerns.
Den of Geek called it arguably the most important and influential ninja game.
Tengen's unlicensed NES version turned its vertical-scrolling stages into horizontal ones.
Its sequels include The Revenge of Shinobi and the arcade game Shadow Dancer, both from 1989.
devStory: Sega R&D 1 developed it on the System 16 arcade hardware, with Yutaka Sugano directing and Yasuhiro Kawakami composing the music. It was released in Japan on 16 November 1987 and in North America in February 1988, topped Game Machine's Japanese table arcade chart for December 1987, and was a blockbuster hit in the United States, where Cash Box named it the highest-grossing conversion kit of 1988. A Master System version in 1988 replaced one-hit deaths with a health gauge, and home computer ports by The Sales Curve followed in 1989.

title: Combat
description: Combat (1977) was the two-player duel packed in with most Atari 2600 consoles for five years: tanks, biplanes and jets trading shots in rounds just over two minutes long.
longDescription: Two players face each other on one screen, each steering a vehicle with a joystick and firing at the other. The cartridge offers three kinds of battle. Tank games are played from above, with variations that add obstacles, shots that bounce off walls and tanks that turn invisible. Biplane fights are seen from the side, and jet battles return to an overhead view. A round lasts two minutes and sixteen seconds, and whoever scores more hits wins. The whole game fits in two kilobytes of ROM, and it grew out of Atari's 1974 arcade game Tank.
trivia: Combat was bundled with most Atari 2600 consoles from 1977 to 1982. Sears' Tele-Games version of the console came with Air-Sea Battle instead, and sold Combat under the name Tank Plus.
A sequel, Combat Two, was announced in 1982 but never released. A prototype surfaced in 1999 and was later included on the Atari Flashback 2 and Atari 50 collections.
devStory: Combat was programmed by Ron Milner, Steve Mayer, Joe Decuir and Larry Wagner, and Mayer was already working on it by late 1975, when Atari bought his consulting firm Cyan Engineering. It shipped as a launch title for the Atari Video Computer System in 1977.

title: Yars' Revenge
description: Yars' Revenge (1982) is Howard Scott Warshaw's Atari 2600 shooter, in which an insect-like Yar chews through a shield to expose the Qotile and blast it with the Zorlon Cannon.
longDescription: The player flies Yar, a fly-like creature, against the Qotile, which hides behind an energy shield on the right of the screen. Yar eats away at the shield, then summons the Zorlon Cannon and fires it across the screen at the exposed Qotile. A shimmering Neutral Zone down the middle hides Yar from the Qotile's homing destroyer missile, but nothing can be fired from inside it. The Qotile can also turn into a Swirl and launch itself at the player. Yar starts with four lives, and the Swirl attacks more often as the score climbs.
trivia: Yars' Revenge came with a comic book, Yars' Revenge: The Qotile Ultimatum, and credited Warshaw as programmer, making him the first Atari programmer publicly credited on a release.
Warshaw hid Yars aliens as a secret in his next two games, Raiders of the Lost Ark and E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial.
devStory: Warshaw was assigned a 2600 port of the arcade game Star Castle. He told his supervisor it could not be done properly on the hardware and proposed a new game that rearranged its ideas instead. First developed as Time Freeze, it took nine months and was released in May 1982 as Warshaw's first game for Atari.

title: Enduro
description: Enduro (1983) is Activision's Atari 2600 endurance race, in which each in-game day brings snow, fog and nightfall and a quota of cars that must be passed to keep going.
longDescription: The player drives in the National Enduro, a race that runs day after day. To stay in it, the driver must pass 200 cars on the first day and 300 on each day after that, and the traffic grows harder to avoid as the days go by. Conditions change with the hours: icy patches make the car hard to control, fog cuts visibility, and at night only the taillights of the cars ahead can be seen. Within the console's tight graphical limits, Larry Miller gave priority to the curving road and the distant mountains.
trivia: Players who lasted five days or more saw an on-screen trophy; mailing a photo of it to Activision earned an 'Activision Roadbuster' patch.
Enduro won Best Sports Videogame at the 5th Arkie Awards, and Retro Gamer later called it arguably the 2600's best racer.
It appears as a hidden game in Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War (2020).
Brett Weiss judged it superior to Pole Position in involvement and atmosphere.
James Software ported it to the ZX Spectrum.
devStory:
Miller, who had made Spider Fighter at Activision, preferred the 2600 for its fast action and wanted a "realistic driving game" drawn from his own driving through California's fog, sun, snow and ice. He wrote it in assembly language on an Apple computer in about three months of 100-hour weeks, fitting it into a four-kilobyte ROM. Released in May 1983, it was the top-selling video game in June, and Activision promoted it with a sweepstakes whose first prize was a Datsun 280ZX pace car.

The Video Game Update called it an "extremely impressive auto racing game", and Games magazine an "outstanding achievement" for the 2600. Its road and traffic code later became the engine of The Great American Cross-Country Road Race (1985).

title: H.E.R.O.
description: H.E.R.O. (1984) is Activision's mine-rescue game: Roderick Hero hovers down flooded, magma-lined shafts with a backpack rotor, a helmet laser and six sticks of dynamite.
longDescription:
The name stands for Helicopter Emergency Rescue Operation. Volcanic activity has trapped miners deep inside Mount Leone, and Roderick Hero flies down to reach them, hovering on a backpack rotor. A microlaser in his helmet deals with spiders, snakes and other creatures and destroys some walls, and he carries six sticks of dynamite per level for others; lit fuses briefly light up dark screens. Glowing magma walls are deadly, lanterns go out if touched and darken the screen, and a power gauge drains from the moment he starts moving.

Points come from completing levels, enemies shot, walls blasted and leftover dynamite and power. Roderick starts with four lives and earns another every 20,000 points, and reaching a million points ends the rescue operation. Higher difficulty settings start at later levels.
trivia: Reviewing the Commodore 64 version for Zzap!64, Julian Rignall wrote that it 'looks awful, sounds terrible but plays absolutely beautifully'.
Retro Gamer ranked it second among the 25 best Atari 2600 games in 2008.
It is hidden as a secret game in Call of Duty: Black Ops II.
The SG-1000 version added music, stalactites, lava geysers and female miners.
Van Ryzin's spiritual successor, Alien Abduction!, came out on the Atari VCS in 2023.
devStory:
John Van Ryzin designed it at Activision under the working title Heli, after his first project, Cosmic Commuter, was judged not fun by playtesters. The idea came from a cave tour and from Superman's heat vision. He programmed it in assembly on a PDP-11 and made the art and sound himself, fitting it on an 8-kilobyte cartridge; co-workers suggested the lanterns that go out, and he also added dynamite, snakes in the walls, a raft and a tentacled monster. It came out for the Atari 2600 on 30 March 1984, followed by ColecoVision, Commodore 64, Atari 5200 and other versions.

Van Ryzin said it was not a big financial success because of the market crash. Jeremy Parish later called it important to the platformer, influencing Bionic Commando and Bangai-O.

title: Solaris
description: Solaris (1986) is Doug Neubauer's late Atari 2600 space epic: a 16-quadrant galaxy of Zylon fleets, minefields and wormholes, searched for the lost planet Solaris.
longDescription: The player pilots a starship across a galaxy of 16 quadrants and 48 sectors, charted on a Galactic Scanner, fighting the alien Zylons while searching for the planet Solaris. Sectors held by the Zylons must be cleared of enemy ships, while others contain star clusters, mine fields and wormholes to other quadrants. On Federation planets the player can refuel at docking stations, and when the Zylons attack one in the current quadrant there are 40 seconds to defend it before it falls and the quadrant turns red on the scanner. On Zylon planets stranded space cadets can be rescued for points, and flying over a key in a guarded corridor destroys the planet.
trivia: Fans have called it the true successor to Neubauer's Star Raiders, but Neubauer said it is not a sequel.
In June 1989, three years after release, Electronic Gaming Monthly reported it as the best-selling 2600 or 7800 game in the US that month.
Its box art reused illustrations from the 2600 Star Raiders.
Neubauer said he preferred Star Raiders' cockpit view to Solaris.
It was included in the Atari 50 compilation in 2022.
devStory:
Doug Neubauer, who had made Star Raiders at Atari in 1980 and then film tie-ins for Fox Video Games, pitched it to Atari in 1984, and the company suggested tying it to the film The Last Starfighter. After Jack Tramiel bought Atari most staff were laid off, and the project stalled until Atari contacted Neubauer again in 1986; his cousin Randy Emberlin, a comic inker, helped with the graphics. It needed a 16K bank-switched cartridge and 256 bytes of RAM, and Neubauer's notes were used almost word for word in the manual.

Shown at the June 1986 CES, it came out in November 1986. The Video Game Update called it the best space game on the system, and Retro Gamer later called it "widely regarded as the console's most technically impressive commercial release".

title: Paradroid
description: Paradroid (1985) is Andrew Braybrook's Commodore 64 classic, in which a weak little droid clears a fleet of rogue robots by shooting them or taking them over through a circuit-board duel.
longDescription:
Robots aboard a fleet of spaceships have turned hostile, and the player controls the Influence Device, droid number 001, sent to neutralise them and save the humans aboard. Every droid carries a three-digit number that marks its strength, across 24 types. Rather than simply shooting them, the player can attempt a takeover: a short subgame played on a circuit diagram of logic gates, where the droid with more power supplies tends to win and a draw is replayed. Losing destroys the droid being used, and losing as the Influence Device ends the game. A captured droid's abilities are the player's, but the higher its number the sooner it burns out.

Each ship has 20 decks and more than 400 screens joined by lifts and doors, only droids in line of sight are visible, and terminals give maps and droid information. The game never truly ends: after the eighth ship, "Itsnotardenuff", play continues on the final ship with tougher droids.
trivia: Braybrook kept a development diary that Zzap!64 published, and the magazine gave the finished game 97% and a Gold Medal.
Braybrook said the droid-swapping idea came from the arcade game Front Line.
Steve Turner's Quazatron (1986) brought similar play to the ZX Spectrum.
Free clones include Freedroid and Paradroid Redux.
Retro Gamer's readers voted it the best C64 game.
devStory:
Andrew Braybrook began it at Graftgold straight after Gribbly's Day Out, reusing some of its code, and Hewson published it in 1985. Its influences included the arcade game Front Line, for the droid-swapping, the cover of the album Technical Ecstasy, the corridors of the film Aliens and Survive, an IBM mainframe game Braybrook had played at Marconi. Zzap!64 printed his development diary every month.

Zzap!64 gave it 97%, a Gold Medal and the verdict "THE classic shoot em up", and in 2002 its readers named it the best Commodore 64 game ever. A faster Competition Edition followed in 1986, Heavy Metal Paradroid in 1987 and Paradroid 90 for the Amiga and Atari ST in 1990.

title: Uridium
description: Uridium (1986) is Andrew Braybrook's Commodore 64 shooter: a Manta fighter skims fifteen giant Dreadnoughts, strafing their defences before landing to destroy each one.
longDescription: Enemy Super-Dreadnoughts orbit fifteen planets, draining their mineral cores, and the player's Manta fighter must destroy each one. Every level is a single huge Dreadnought, named after a metal and ending with the fictional Uridium. The Manta flies at a fixed height over the hull, which scrolls in both directions, and must flip sideways to slip through narrow gaps in later ships. Waves of enemy fighters attack, and flashing ports release homing mines that cannot be shot and eventually burst on their own. Once enough defences are gone, a "Land Now!" signal tells the player to slow down and touch down on the landing strip, after which the reactor self-destructs and the ship crumbles beneath the departing Manta. Players can score more by ignoring the signal to hunt elite fighters.
trivia: The C64 cannot scroll a separate background layer, so the stars are drawn as characters whose pixels shift against the scroll, making them appear to stand still.
It won Best Arcade-style Game of the Year at the 1986 Golden Joystick Awards and reached number one in the British all-formats chart.
A message on the last Dreadnought reads "GOOD ZAPPING... TURKEY.", visible only once the ship is destroyed.
Crash's readers voted it the best shooting game of the year.
Uridium 2 followed on the Amiga.
devStory: Andrew Braybrook designed it at Graftgold, with music by Steve Turner, and Hewson released it for the Commodore 64 on 28 February 1986; Robert Orchard coined the name, saying in the manual, "I really thought it existed". It reached number one in the Commodore 64 and all-formats charts, and Zzap!64 gave it 94%, calling it "visually awesome, sonically sound, technically stunning and a brilliant shoot em up to boot". Dominic Robinson programmed the ZX Spectrum version, and other ports followed for the Amstrad, Atari ST, BBC Micro and PC; in 1990 Mindscape reused it for an NES game licensed from the film The Last Starfighter.

title: The Last Ninja
description: The Last Ninja (1987) is System 3's isometric action-adventure, in which Armakuni crosses the island of Lin-Fen to recover the Koga Scrolls from the shogun Kunitoki.
longDescription: The Fujiwara clan practised Ninjutsu for centuries, and every ten years its ninja gathered on the island of Lin-Fen to honour the White Ninja. The shogun Kunitoki, envious of their art, attacked the gathering to steal the Koga Scrolls and train his own men. Armakuni survived only because he was at the Bunkinkan shrine, and as the last ninja he sets out to reach Kunitoki's palace, kill him and recover the scrolls. The world is seen from an isometric viewpoint with movement in eight directions, and the game mixes exploration, puzzles and combat. Traps and fatal terrain demand precise jumps, kneeling at shrines and fountains reveals the next item, and items hidden in trees and bushes flash briefly as each screen loads. Fights aim blows at the head, body or legs, with a ninjato, nunchaku, staff, shuriken and smoke bombs.
trivia: It was the best-selling Commodore 64 game of its time, with over 750,000 copies sold in Europe; designer Mark Cale has put total sales at about 4 million.
It was runner-up for Game of the Year at the 1988 Golden Joystick Awards and was followed by Last Ninja 2 and Last Ninja 3.
Its fights let players aim at the head, body or legs.
Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum versions were made but never released.
It came to the Wii Virtual Console in 2008.
devStory: Designed by Mark Cale and Tim Best, it was first developed for almost a year by SoftView, a Hungarian team at Novotrade, in a Forth-like language meant to ease porting; when it missed every deadline, the advance was refunded, the team went uncredited, and Cale took the code to London, where John Twiddy rewrote the engine for the Commodore 64. Cale cited the square cursor of Atari's Adventure as an inspiration, Hugh Riley drew the art, and Ben Daglish and Anthony Lees wrote the music. System 3 released it in 1987, and Computer Gaming World said "there is no exaggerating the graphic excellence" of it. Amiga and Atari ST versions followed in 1990 as Last Ninja Remix.

title: Wizball
description: Wizball (1987) is Sensible Software's colour-restoring shooter: a bouncing wizard and his cat collect red, green and blue paint to bring grey Wizworld back to life.
longDescription: The evil Zark has drained the colour from Wizworld, and the wizard Wiz, travelling as a bouncing green ball, sets out with his cat Nifta, as Catellite, to restore it. Each of the eight levels starts in three shades of grey and needs a different colour, mixed from quantities of red, green and blue paint, and portals lead between them; only the first three are open at the start. Wiz bounces at a fixed rate, and the player controls only how fast he spins, which decides how he moves after each landing. He cannot collect paint himself: that is Catellite's job, gathering droplets released by shooting coloured spheres, and holding fire while moving the joystick steers the cat instead of the wizard. Pearls dropped by some enemies buy better control, more firepower and the cat itself. In two-player co-op, the second player controls Catellite.
trivia: Zzap!64 gave it 96%, later rated it 98% as the best C64 shoot 'em up, and in December 1988 named it the best game it had ever reviewed.
Martin Galway composed the music for the Commodore 64 version.
Retro Gamer's readers voted it the second-best C64 game in 2011.
The C64 version sends four or five waves of enemies at once, making it much harder than the Amiga and ST versions.
A sequel, Wizkid, appeared in 1992.
devStory: Jon Hare and Chris Yates, the founders of Sensible Software, made it; Hare said it began as a Nemesis-inspired shooter, with the bouncing ball and its controls coming first and the wizard story last, and work paused while they made Parallax. Martin Galway wrote the Commodore 64 music. Ocean released it for the C64 in 1987, with Spectrum and Amstrad versions that year and Amiga and Atari ST versions in 1988. Zzap!64 gave it 96% and a Sizzler but not a Gold Medal, which its former editor later said it should have had, and in December 1988 named it the best game of all time; Hare blamed Ocean's marketing for disappointing sales.

title: Alex Kidd in Miracle World
description: Alex Kidd in Miracle World (1986) is the Master System's signature platformer, in which Alex punches through 17 stages and plays rock-paper-scissors against Janken the Great's henchmen.
longDescription: Janken the Great has overthrown King Thunder of Radaxian and kidnapped Prince Egle and his fiancée, Princess Lora. Alex, a young martial artist, punches enemies and breaks rocks to open new paths across 17 stages, some scrolling and some single-screen, collecting money to spend in shops on items and vehicles such as a motorbike and a helicopter. Many stages end with a game of rock-paper-scissors against one of Janken's three henchmen, and losing costs a life, just as a single hit does. Alex learns he is King Thunder's lost son, defeats Janken, who is turned to stone, and recovers the crown, and Egle becomes king. There is no save system.
trivia: The game was built into many Master System and Master System II consoles. The built-in version swaps the original's rice-ball map icon for a hamburger and inverts the buttons.
Entering a button code on the Game Over screen continues the game, at a cost of 400 Baums.
It began as a Dragon Ball game before the licence expired.
IGN gave it 9/10 and an Editor's Choice award in 2008.
The 2021 DX remake lets players switch between modern and retro graphics.
devStory: Kotaro Hayashida designed it, with art by Rieko Kodama and music by Tokuhiko Uwabo, and it began in 1984 as a licensed Dragon Ball tie-in; when the licence expired, Sega president Hayao Nakayama had it restarted from scratch. Sega released it in Japan on 1 November 1986 and in North America that December. From 1990 a modified version was built into Master System II consoles in the US, Australia and Europe. Computer and Video Games called it "Sega's answer to Mario", and Power Play named it the best Sega game of 1987. A remake, Alex Kidd in Miracle World DX, followed in 2021.

title: Psycho Fox
description: Psycho Fox (1989) is Vic Tokai's Master System platformer, in which a fox uses a Shinto stick to become a monkey, hippo or tiger on the way to overthrowing the evil deity Madfox Daimyōjin.
longDescription: Fox priests worship Inari Daimyōjin, the fox deity, until Madfox Daimyōjin, an evil fox, rises through the priesthood, seizes the shrine, corrupts the land and fills it with creatures. A young fox, later known as Psycho Fox, is chosen to rid the land of him. Each side-scrolling level runs left to right through crowds of enemies, and AllGame noted that each offers a choice of two routes. A Shinto stick transforms the hero into three other animals: the hippo is slow and jumps low but punches through special blocks, the monkey jumps highest and the tiger runs fastest. The bird ally Bird Fly can act as armour or be thrown like a boomerang, and if the player is hit while carrying it, the bird flies off instead of a life being lost.
trivia: In Brazil, Tec Toy released it as Sapo Xulé: Os Invasores do Brejo, with the fox replaced by a cartoon frog.
Vic Tokai made Kid Kool as an NES counterpart, and Decap Attack on the Mega Drive is regarded as its spiritual successor.
Sega Power and S: The Sega Magazine both scored it 93%.
EGM's four reviewers each gave it 7 out of 10.
Its hero's transformations are triggered by a Shinto stick.
devStory: Toshihisa Hasegawa directed it at Vic Tokai, with Shoji Suzuki programming and music by Fumito Tamayama and Hiroto Kanno, and Sega published it for the Master System in Europe in December 1989 and North America in May 1990. Mean Machines gave it 90%, praising its addictiveness and graphics, and S: The Sega Magazine scored it 93%, calling it "one of the best games for the Master System". AllGame was cooler, calling it "a fun, if largely unoriginal game".

title: Wolfenstein 3D
description: Wolfenstein 3D (1992) is id Software's fast first-person shooter, in which Allied spy B.J. Blazkowicz fights his way out of a Nazi castle — the game that set the template for the genre.
longDescription: B.J. Blazkowicz, a Polish-American Allied spy, is captured while seeking the plans for Operation Eisenfaust and imprisoned in Castle Wolfenstein. Across the first three episodes he escapes, stops a Nazi plan to build undead mutants at Castle Hollehammer, and fights Adolf Hitler in a robotic suit with four chain guns beneath the Reichstag; the second three, The Nocturnal Missions, are a prequel about German chemical warfare. Each level is a flat grid of equal-height walls and doors, drawn in real time with ray casting, while guards, dogs and objects are flat sprites drawn from set angles. Players fight with a knife, pistol, submachine gun and chain gun, reach an elevator or beat a boss to finish each level, and find secret areas behind walls that slide back. Each episode starts with four lives, and points come from kills, treasure and par times.
trivia: Germany banned the game in 1994 over its Nazi symbols; the ban was lifted in 2018 and the game removed from the index in 2019.
For the Super NES version, Nintendo required the Nazi imagery and German voice clips to be cut, the blood removed and the attack dogs replaced with giant rats.
It hides a level modelled on Pac-Man.
It was the first shareware title to win a Codie award.
Carmack's side work on a new engine during its follow-up became the basis for Doom.
devStory:
John Romero proposed remaking Muse Software's 1981 Castle Wolfenstein in 3D, and id began work on 15 December 1991, buying the Wolfenstein trademark for $5,000. John Carmack wrote the ray-casting engine in about a month, Romero and Tom Hall designed it, Adrian Carmack drew the sprites at eight angles and Bobby Prince wrote the music; the graphics moved from 16-colour EGA to 256-colour VGA four months before release. Apogee released the first episode as shareware on 5 May 1992, with Scott Miller persuading id to make six episodes instead of three, and FormGen published Spear of Destiny that September.

The whole game cost about $25,000 in rent and salaries. Apogee's first royalty cheque was $100,000, and it is called the grandfather of 3D shooters.

title: The Lords of Midnight
description: The Lords of Midnight (1984) is Mike Singleton's ZX Spectrum epic: an adventure and a wargame at once, fought across a frozen land seen in first-person panoramas.
