Michel Ancel created the character as a teenager and, after joining Ubi Soft, built a prototype on the Atari ST with Frédéric Houde, which was approved in 1992. Its style drew on Celtic, Chinese and Russian fairy tales and Ancel's childhood, and its animations ran at 60 frames per second. Development moved to a Super NES CD-ROM version, abandoned when Nintendo cancelled that hardware in 1993, then to the Atari Jaguar, the PlayStation and the Saturn. Michel Guillemot allotted 15 million francs, the team grew to 100 people, and Rémi Gazel composed the music.

Ubi Soft released it for the PlayStation in North America on 7 September 1995, as a launch title there and in Europe. It sold 400,000 copies in Europe by the end of 1995, 900,000 by 1997 and over 3 million in all, became the best-selling PlayStation game in the UK and was Ubisoft's first major success, helping the company go public in 1996.

title: Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee
description: Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee (1997) is a cinematic platformer in which Abe, a slave at a meat-packing plant, escapes and frees his fellow Mudokons using speech and possession instead of guns.
longDescription:
Abe, a Mudokon floor-waxer at the RuptureFarms meat-packing plant, discovers that its Glukkon boss Molluck, faced with falling profits since the Meech went extinct, plans to turn the Mudokons themselves into the next product. Abe escapes, falls from a cliff and is found by Big Face, a Mudokon shaman, who sends him through the lands of the Paramites and Scrabs to earn the power of the Shrykull. He returns to free his people and shut the factory down. Rescuing at least 50 of the 99 Mudokons earns the good ending.

Abe carries no firearms: he tiptoes past enemies, runs to clear gaps and rolls under obstacles, and throws meat, rocks and grenades. In safe areas he can chant to possess the armed Sligs and turn them on their own side, unless flying chant suppressors are nearby. With GameSpeak he tells other Mudokons to follow or wait, then chants open bird portals to lead them to freedom. Slogs bark and chase, Scrabs defend their territory and Paramites hunt in packs, and Abe can ride the loyal but easily distracted Elum. The game saves only at checkpoints.
trivia: In Japan it was retitled Abe a GoGo, and the Mudokons' hands were changed from four fingers to three.
A Sega Saturn version was announced but never released.
Just Add Water remade it in 2014 as Oddworld: New 'n' Tasty!
It won Best Director at the 1997 World Animation Festival.
It was planned as the first part of a five-part series.
devStory:
Production began in January 1995 under the title Soul Storm, and GT Interactive took on publishing in 1996. Lorne Lanning directed it at Oddworld Inhabitants, which he co-founded with Sherry McKenna, who pushed the emphasis on communication and rewarding peaceful play; Lanning said GameSpeak was partly inspired by the audio puzzles of Loom. It cost $4 million, and GT spent $10 million marketing it, its biggest campaign to date. The Meeches were cut for lack of disc space and written into the story as extinct.

It came out on 19 September 1997, "Odd Friday", and sold over a million copies by January 1998. Critics praised its originality, art direction, cutscenes and creature AI, while finding it very hard.

title: Tenchu: Stealth Assassins
description: Tenchu: Stealth Assassins (1998) is Acquire's ninja game set in Sengoku-era Japan, which helped define the stealth genre alongside Metal Gear Solid and Thief.
longDescription:
In Sengoku-era Japan, the Azuma clan ninja Rikimaru and Ayame serve Lord Gohda, whose daughter, Princess Kiku, treats Ayame like an older sister. The dark ninja Onikage is stirring up trouble to bring his demonic master, Lord Mei-Oh, into the world, and kidnaps Kiku to use against Gohda. Rikimaru is tougher and slower with one blade; Ayame is weaker and faster with two.

The player picks one of them for eleven sandbox missions, each with a map and three possible layouts chosen at random. Sneaking up undetected allows an instant kill, with a cinematic death animation at close range. The Ki meter shows how alert nearby enemies are, from a question mark to a double exclamation mark, and how far away they stand. Items include health potions, poisoned rice cakes, caltrops, shuriken, smoke bombs and mines, but the grappling hook is the only one kept after death or between missions. Each mission is ranked from "Thug" to "Grand Master" according to kills, detection and whether civilians were harmed.
trivia: The Western release added two levels and alternate mission layouts, and was later released in Japan as Tenchu: Shinobi Gaisen.
It was Acquire's first project.
It remained Acquire's best seller until Octopath Traveler (2018).
The opening theme, "Addua", is sung in Hausa.
A Japanese standalone expansion, Shinobi Hyakusen, offered 100 levels created by players.
devStory:
Takuma Endo founded Acquire with friends in 1994, and after Sony turned him down twice he won a place through a Sony Music Entertainment Japan audition. The first pitch was set in a near-future New York, influenced by Judge Dredd and Batman, before the team moved to feudal Japan under the influence of Akira Kurosawa's films, the early 2D Metal Gear games and Tomb Raider's camera. Endo directed, planned, wrote, edited the sound and tested it; there were no dedicated designers. Night settings helped within the PlayStation's limits, Sho Kosugi provided motion capture for Rikimaru, and Noriyuki Asakura composed the music.

It came out in Japan on 26 February 1998. Sony had no plans for a Western release until Activision bid for it. It scored 87 on Metacritic and helped define the stealth genre alongside Thief and Metal Gear Solid.

title: Syphon Filter
description: Syphon Filter (1999) is Eidetic's third-person stealth-action shooter, in which agents Gabe Logan and Lian Xing hunt a terrorist and his bioweapon.
longDescription:
Agents Gabriel Logan and Lian Xing investigate outbreaks caused by the terrorist group Black Baton, led by Erich Rhoemer, after a fellow agent is found dead in Costa Rica. Rhoemer threatens Washington, D.C. with viral bombs in the subway, on the National Mall and at the Freedom Memorial, and the trail leads to the pharmaceutical firm PharCom, to Kazakhstan — where Lian is apparently killed but turns up alive and infected — and to a stronghold in Ukraine. There Gabe learns that the Agency's director, Thomas Markinson, has been working with Black Baton.

It is a third-person shooter with a freely rotating camera, mixing action with stealth missions and some puzzles. The display shows armour, a "danger meter" and a radar, and some weapons switch to first person for aiming. Dark areas force the use of a flashlight, which makes stealth harder. Levels run from the narrow streets of Washington to the open plains of Kazakhstan, and IGN counted at least thirty weapons and pieces of equipment.
trivia: It scored 90 on Metacritic and sold more than 900,000 copies.
It was followed by Syphon Filter 2 (2000), Syphon Filter 3 (2001) and three more games on the PS2 and PSP.
Edge gave it 6/10, noting what it borrowed from GoldenEye 007 and Metal Gear Solid.
Spike published it in Japan in August 1999.
It was a finalist for Console Action Game of the Year at the 3rd Interactive Achievement Awards.
devStory:
It began as little more than a name and a one-page synopsis from a 989 Studios producer. Lead designer Richard Ham wanted a cinematic action game inspired by John Woo's films; the E3 1997 trailer for Metal Gear Solid discouraged him into aiming for something "radically different", while GoldenEye 007 pushed him towards a "super spy" game. Eidetic's team of thirteen had little third-person experience — its only previous console game was Bubsy 3D — and the project nearly died several times over missed deadlines and rewrites; the original story was a science-fiction tale of kidnapped scientists building a time machine. John Garvin became creative director and rewrote it.

989 Studios released it in North America on 16 February 1999. It scored 90 on Metacritic, with praise for its blend of stealth and action and its AI, though IGN criticised its low resolution and frame rate.

title: Dino Crisis
description: Dino Crisis (1999) is Shinji Mikami's "panic horror" game, in which agent Regina fights dinosaurs on Ibis Island in real-time 3D environments rather than Resident Evil's pre-rendered backgrounds.
longDescription:
In 2009 the special forces unit S.O.R.T. sends four agents — Regina, Gail, Rick and Cooper — to Ibis Island to capture Dr. Edward Kirk, a scientist reported dead three years earlier who is running a secret weapons project. Cooper is eaten by a Tyrannosaurus almost as soon as he lands, and the staff of the facility are dead. Kirk's Third Energy experiment has swapped a pocket of the island with the past, bringing dinosaurs into the present. Choices about whether to follow Gail or Rick change the story and lead to three endings.

Regina can push and climb objects, turn on the spot and use automatic aiming. Items can be combined to make new ones, such as anaesthetic darts. Locked doors need D.D.K. codes and discs, red force fields can be switched on to block pursuers, and colour-coded emergency boxes unlocked with plugs share their contents with others of the same colour. Hemostats stop bleeding, which leaves a trail, and in "DANGER" moments the player must hammer the buttons to survive. Dinosaurs can knock Regina's gun out of her hand.
trivia: Critics often called it "Resident Evil with dinosaurs".
It sold more than 300,000 copies in its first week in Japan.
The PlayStation version sold 2.4 million copies.
The North American version has more dinosaurs than the Japanese one, of the same species.
Two Game Boy Color versions were started and cancelled.
devStory:
Shinji Mikami directed and produced it at Capcom Production Studio 4 as a spiritual successor to Resident Evil without its fantasy elements, influenced by The Lost World: Jurassic Park and Aliens. He described Resident Evil as "horror in the fun house" and Dino Crisis as a roller coaster. Its engine draws the environments in real time rather than over pre-rendered backgrounds, for more cinematic action; the indoor setting built claustrophobia, and a jungle scene was dropped because of hardware limits. The dinosaurs' animation drew on crocodiles and dogs, and their behaviour on lions and tigers.

It came out in Japan on 1 July 1999 and topped the charts in its first week. Critics praised its intensity, real-time graphics and dinosaur AI, but found the dinosaurs too few in kind — IGN said it was "90% Raptors" — and the puzzles tedious.

title: Jumping Flash!
description: Jumping Flash! (1995) is a first-person PlayStation platformer starring Robbit, a mechanical rabbit that can jump three times in mid-air. Guinness World Records lists it as the first platform game in true 3D.
longDescription:
The mad astrophysicist Baron Aloha has been carving up Crater Planet to build private resorts and has hidden the twelve jet pods that propel its worlds. Universal City Hall sends Robbit, a mechanical rabbit, to recover them, with his sidekick Kumagoro offering hints and warnings. Robbit can jump up to three times in mid-air, and on the second and third jumps the camera tilts down to his shadow so the player can judge the landing.

The game is seen in first person, with a laser aimed at the centre of the screen and fireworks — cherry bombs, rockets, Roman candles and spinners — as stronger weapons. Carrots extend health, hourglasses add time, time-outs freeze the level and power pills give brief invincibility. Six worlds of three levels each, the last a boss fight, give 18 main levels, each with four jet pods to find within ten minutes; hidden entrances lead to bonus levels. Cutscenes feature the MuuMuus, small white five-limbed creatures with palm trees on their heads, in a tavern.
trivia: It was developed as a technology demonstration for the PlayStation.
Some critics found it short and easy, but Next Generation ranked it 86th in its 1996 top 100 games.
Guinness World Records lists it as the first platform game in true 3D.
Ultra renamed itself Muu Muu after its release.
1UP.com saw it as a precursor of Mirror's Edge.
devStory:
Exact, which had made games for the X68000, built it on the engine of its earlier Geograph Seal. Sony's Koji Tada paired Exact with Ultra after seeing that game and took over as director; Exact made the engine and gameplay, and Ultra the story, cutscenes and characters, including Robbit. It was first shown in early 1994 as "Spring Man", a PlayStation technology demonstration, and Sony hoped it would launch a platform star to rival Sonic or Mario. Takeo Miratsu composed the music.

Sony released it in Japan on 28 April 1995 and in North America that November. It won PlayStation Game of the Year and 32-Bit Game of the Year at the GameFan Megawards, and averaged 84% on GameRankings, though some critics found it short and easy.

title: Klonoa: Door to Phantomile
description: Klonoa: Door to Phantomile (1997) is Namco's 2.5D platformer, in which Klonoa grabs enemies with a magic ring and throws them or uses them to jump higher, through the dream world of Phantomile.
longDescription:
Ghadius sets out to turn the dream world of Phantomile into a world of nightmares, stealing a moon pendant and kidnapping the singer Lephise. Klonoa can run, jump and hover briefly, and with a ring inhabited by his companion Huepow he grabs enemies, then throws them or uses them as a springboard for a higher jump. The levels scroll from side to side through 3D scenery, a 2.5D approach, and some end in boss fights.

Klonoa and Huepow defeat Ghadius and the beast Nahatomb, after which Huepow reveals he is not from Phantomile, and Klonoa is pulled back to his own world.
trivia: Klonoa won Best Character at the 1997 Japan Game Awards.
GameSpot called it "one of the best side-scrollers in years".
It began as an adaptation of the manga Spriggan.
An animated film was announced in 2016 and cancelled in 2019.
devStory:
Hideo Yoshizawa directed it, his tenth project, and Yoshihiko Arai designed Klonoa. It began as a planned adaptation of Spriggan, and when the licence fell through the team made an original game instead. Namco released it in Japan on 11 December 1997, in North America in March 1998 and in Europe that June.

Reviews were generally positive, praising its level design and visuals, though some found it formulaic or too cute. Klonoa won Best Character at the 1997 Japan Game Awards. Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil followed on the PS2 in 2001, and the original was remade for the Wii in 2008 and again in the Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series in 2022.

title: Harvest Moon
description: Harvest Moon (1996) is Yasuhiro Wada's Super Famicom farming game, in which the player restores a run-down inherited farm. It is considered one of the first farm life sims.
longDescription: A young man inherits a run-down farm from his grandfather and sets about restoring it. Each day is split between clearing land, planting and watering crops, selling the harvest, raising livestock, foraging, going to festivals and getting to know the villagers, with marriage as a central goal. Crops left unwatered stop growing but do not die. Animals must be fed every day: cows also need to be talked to, brushed and milked and can sicken or die if neglected, and chickens left outside can be lost to storms or wild dogs. After dark the only place open in town is the bar.
trivia: The localised versions changed references to alcohol to "juice".
Later games in the series are released under the name Story of Seasons, because of a rights split over localisation.
Wada did not expect it to be released outside Japan.
Its success led to Harvest Moon GB and Harvest Moon 64.
A four-episode Satellaview version was broadcast in Japan in 1996.
devStory:
Yasuhiro Wada conceived it in his early years in Tokyo, drawing on his childhood in the countryside of Miyazaki and on the manga Dr. Slump. The first draft was finished in 1993, and the game took three years with a team of eight to ten. Early versions centred on herding cows and talking to villagers, which proved too complex and dull, so cow-raising was simplified and land-clearing and crops were added. When the parent company went bankrupt late in development, only Wada, programmer Tomomi Yamatate and designer Setsuko Miyakoshi stayed to finish the last six months.

Pack-In-Video released it in Japan on 9 August 1996. It sold only about 20,000 copies at first, but good reviews and word of mouth lifted it past 100,000. Natsume released it in North America in 1997 and Nintendo in Europe in 1998. Engadget later called it "one of the most quietly influential games in the industry".

title: Tales of Phantasia
description: Tales of Phantasia (1995) is the first game in the Tales series, a Super Famicom RPG with real-time battles and a sung opening theme on a 48-megabit cartridge.
longDescription:
In the world of Aselia, the sorcerer king Dhaos was once sealed away with two magic pendants by four heroes. The dark knight Mars destroys the village of the young swordsman Cress Albane, killing his parents and the sister of his friend Chester, and uses the stolen pendants to free Dhaos. Escaping a jail with the healer Mint, Cress is sent a century into the past by one of the original heroes, where he recruits the summoner Claus and the half-elf magician Arche and takes up the Eternal Sword to stop Dhaos moving through time. The tree spirit Martel reveals that Dhaos came from a dying planet whose world tree was drained by magic technology.

Battles use the real-time Linear Motion Battle System, inspired by fighting games, on a 2D plane wider than one screen. The player controls Cress directly while the other party members follow orders to attack, defend or cast, and a menu pauses the action for spells and items.
trivia: It needed a 48-megabit cartridge to hold its voice clips and vocal opening theme.
The story grew from Yoshiharu Gotanda's unpublished novel Tale Phantasia.
Trouble during development led many staff to leave Wolf Team and form tri-Ace.
Fans translated the Super Famicom version into English in 2001.
A four-episode anime adaptation was released from 2004 to 2006.
devStory:
Yoshiharu Gotanda programmed it at Wolf Team and wrote the story, based on his unpublished novel Tale Phantasia, drawing mainly on Norse mythology with names borrowed from Michael Moorcock and H. P. Lovecraft. The team wanted a publisher other than its parent company; Enix turned it down and Namco signed it. Kōsuke Fujishima redrew the character designs, and the music was by Motoi Sakuraba, Shinji Tamura and Ryota Furuya, with a sung opening theme, "Yume wa Owaranai". Eiji Kikuchi directed.

Namco released it in Japan on 15 December 1995, and it sold 212,000 copies there; Famitsu gave it 30 out of 40. Its 1998 PlayStation version added an anime opening and a 3D world map, and the Game Boy Advance version of 2006 was its first official English release.

title: Revelations: Persona
description: Revelations: Persona (1996) is Atlus's first Persona game, in which high-school students in the town of Mikage-cho gain the power to summon Personas after playing a fortune-telling game.
longDescription:
In Mikage-chō in 1996, a group of St. Hermelin High students play a fortune-telling game called "Persona" and are knocked out by the energy of a ghostly girl; afterwards Philemon grants the silent hero the power to summon Personas. Their classmate Maki Sonomura lies in hospital, and Takahisa Kandori, who runs the local SEBEC facility, is behind the Deva System, a machine that alters reality and traps the town inside an idealised version of itself. A second route, the Snow Queen quest, sends the group into three towers to gather shards of a Demon Mirror after a cursed mask possesses their teacher.

Towns are seen from above and dungeons in first person, and a moon-phase icon affects demons' moods. Battles take place on a grid with Attack, Contact, Analyze and Form commands; Contact lets the party talk to demons, and provoking the same emotion three times makes them attack, flee or hand over an item or spell card. Each Persona holds up to eight skills and gains experience with use, and in the Velvet Room Igor fuses new Personas from two spell cards and an item.
trivia: The North American version changed names, hairstyles and ethnicities and cut the Snow Queen route; the 2009 PSP version restored it.
The Velvet Room was inspired by the Black Lodge in Twin Peaks.
Philemon's appearance was based on paintings of Zhuang Zhou.
Its European debut came on the PlayStation Classic in 2018.
Shoji Meguro directed the 2009 PSP remake, his first time directing.
devStory:
Development began in 1994, after the high-school setting of Shin Megami Tensei If... was well received, and the Persona system grew from that game's Guardian system, designed by Katsura Hashino. Kouji Okada produced it, Kazuma Kaneko designed the characters, and new writer Tadashi Satomi spent about a year and twenty drafts on the script; the aim was a Megami Tensei game newcomers could enjoy. Philemon draws on Jung's archetype of the wise old man.

Atlus released it in Japan on 20 September 1996, selling 201,147 copies in its first week — the series' best start until Persona 5 — and 391,556 that year. It reached North America that December and became a cult classic, leading to Persona 2: Innocent Sin in 1999.

title: Puzzle Bobble
description: Puzzle Bobble (1994), known internationally as Bust-a-Move, is Taito's Bubble Bobble spin-off, in which the player fires coloured bubbles to make groups of three before the ceiling comes down.
longDescription:
A spin-off of Bubble Bobble that uses its characters and themes, Puzzle Bobble has the player aim a pointer at the bottom of the screen and fire bubbles upwards. Each bubble's colour is chosen at random from those still on screen, and if the player waits too long the bubble fires itself. Bubbles travel in a straight line, bounce off the side walls and stick where they hit. Groups of three or more of one colour burst, taking any bubbles hanging below them, and the aim is to clear the screen before any bubble crosses the bottom line.

The ceiling drops after every few shots, more often when fewer colours remain, and the music speeds up as the bubbles approach the bottom. The arcade game has 30 levels, plus a two-player mode.
trivia: Its working title was Bubble Buster.
The Neo Geo version was Japan's second-highest-grossing arcade software of 1995, behind Virtua Fighter 2.
It inspired many clones, including Snood, Frozen Bubble and Bubble Shooter.
Next Generation called the SNES version "addictive as hell".
Puzzle Bobble Everybubble! (2023) includes a mode crossing over with Space Invaders.
devStory:
Kazuhiro Kinoshita and Seiichi Nakakuki designed it at Taito, with Yasuo Tsumori programming and music by Kazuko Umino and Yasuko Yamada, on the Taito B System; its working title was Bubble Buster. Taito released it in Japanese arcades in June 1994, and a near-identical Neo Geo MVS version that December added stereo sound and translated text. Conversions for the Super NES, Neo Geo CD and 3DO followed in 1995; in North America it was called Bust-A-Move.

The Neo Geo version was Japan's second most popular arcade game in February 1995, and EGM called the SNES version "a thoroughly enjoyable and incredibly addicting puzzle game". Edge later ranked it 73rd among the best video games.

title: The Lost Vikings
description: The Lost Vikings (1993) is the puzzle-platformer from Silicon & Synapse, later Blizzard, in which the player switches between three Vikings with different abilities to escape an alien zoo.
longDescription:
Tomator, emperor of the alien Croutonians, kidnaps three Vikings for an intergalactic zoo. They escape his ship but are scattered across different periods of time, and must defeat Tomator to get home. The player switches between them: Erik the Swift runs, jumps and smashes some walls and enemies with his helmet; Baleog the Fierce fights with a sword and a bow, which can also hit distant switches; and Olaf the Stout blocks enemies and shots with his shield, glides on it and lets the others stand on it.

Each Viking has three hit points, lost to falls and enemies and restored by food, and if one dies the level cannot be finished, though continues are unlimited. Vikings standing together can swap items such as keys, bombs and food. The game has 37 levels, or 42 on the Mega Drive, whose version also lets two or three players control the Vikings at once.
trivia: It started out inspired by Lemmings, and the planned hundreds of tiny Vikings shrank to five and then three.
The Vikings later became playable heroes in Heroes of the Storm.
Olaf and Baleog appear in Rock n' Roll Racing, where Olaf is an unlockable driver.
StarCraft II's Viking unit is named in its honour.
It was re-released in the Blizzard Arcade Collection in 2021.
devStory:
Ron Millar designed it at Silicon & Synapse, later Blizzard Entertainment, with music by Charles Deenen. It began under the influence of Lemmings, with players managing hundreds of tiny Vikings to beat enemies and take territory, but because it was aimed at consoles the characters were enlarged and the cast cut to five and then three; the artists chose bright colours to stand out on television screens. Interplay released it for the Super NES in April 1993, followed by Amiga and MS-DOS versions the same year.

Computer Gaming World called it "a clever blend of comedy and role playing", and Nintendo Power ranked it the seventh-best SNES game of 1993. The Lost Vikings 2 followed in 1997.

title: Rock n' Roll Racing
description: Rock n' Roll Racing (1993) is Silicon & Synapse's isometric combat racer, set to licensed rock and heavy metal songs and called by announcer "Loudmouth Larry".
longDescription:
Four cars race four laps around isometric tracks, with up to two human players. Rip and Shred appear in every race, joined by a rival unique to each planet. Finishing blows with front or rear weapons earn attack bonuses, a full lap's lead earns a lapping bonus, and wrecked cars respawn within seconds. Tracks are scattered with mines, oil slicks, snowdrifts and lava, along with health and money pickups.

The top three in each race earn money and points, and each planet has two divisions that must be passed to move on. Money buys engines, tyres, shocks and armour, front weapons such as missiles, rear weapons such as mines or slip sauce, and jump jets or nitro boosts, each upgradeable up to seven times; buying a new car loses them. Passwords save progress between seasons. The soundtrack includes "Bad to the Bone", "Highway Star", "Paranoid", "Peter Gunn" and "Born to Be Wild".
trivia: ZZ Top were the first choice for the music, but their fee was too high.
It began as RPMII, a sequel to RPM Racing.
Electronic Gaming Monthly named it the Best Driving Game of 1993.
In two-player mode the game may ask: "Leave your loser friend behind?"
Blizzard released a Definitive Edition in 2021 with four-player split screen.
devStory:
It began at Silicon & Synapse as RPMII, a sequel to RPM Racing, until Interplay's marketing added licensed music and a new name. Alan Pavlish designed it, with Bob Fitch, Patrick Wyatt and Ayman Adham programming, Samwise Didier among the artists and music by Tim and Geoff Follin and Matthew Cannon. Its AI was derived from Racing Destruction Set. Interplay released it for the Super NES on 4 June 1993, and a Genesis version followed in 1994; Silicon & Synapse later became Blizzard Entertainment.

Game Informer called its soundtrack one of the best on the SNES, and EGM named it Best Driving Game of 1993. It averaged about 83% on GameRankings.

title: Bosconian
description: Bosconian (1981) is Namco's multidirectional space shooter, in which the Starfighter fires forwards and backwards at once to destroy enemy bases, guided by radar and voice alerts.
longDescription: After the "Rock War", in which aliens used missile-firing space stations to destroy nearly every city on Earth, humanity builds a single Starfighter to fight back. It flies in eight directions with the screen centred on it, firing forwards and backwards at once. Each round has several green Bosco bases, more each round, and all must be destroyed to advance: each has six cannons around a core, and destroying the core or all six cannons defeats it, the cannons paying more. In later rounds the cores open and close while launching missiles. Asteroids, mines, missiles and ships fill space, bases launch formation attacks whose leader scatters the rest when shot, and a spy ship turns the alert red if it escapes. A radar shows enemy positions, and a digitised voice announces what is coming.
trivia: It inspired Sinistar (1983) and Time Pilot (1982).
It won the 1983 Arcade Award for Best Science Fiction/Fantasy Coin-Op Game, beating Gravitar and Zaxxon.
Its voice was provided by Hideyuki Nakajima, president of Namco America.
Retro Gamer called it "a granddaddy of the multidirectional shooter".
Midway released it in North America in February 1982.
devStory:
Seiichi Sato was asked to create games that could run on swappable ROM boards for Galaxian, Pac-Man and Rally-X, which became Galaga, Dig Dug and Bosconian; he worked on Bosconian and Galaga with Shigeru Yokoyama before each took one. Kazuo Kurosu programmed it and Nobuyuki Ohnogi composed the music, and the voice lines, first recorded by a woman from Namco's sales department, were redone by Hideyuki Nakajima, then president of Namco America.

Namco released it in Japan on 20 November 1981, the seventh highest-grossing arcade game there that year. It was less successful abroad, where many unsold cabinets were converted to Galaga. Electronic Games praised its simultaneous front and rear fire, which it called a first.

title: Marathon
description: Marathon (1994) is Bungie's Macintosh first-person shooter set aboard a colony ship under alien attack, guided by three shipboard AIs. It was one of the earliest shooters with mouse-driven free look.
longDescription:
In 2794 the colony ship UESC Marathon, built from the moon Deimos and bound for Tau Ceti, is attacked by aliens with an electromagnetic pulse that leaves only one of its three AIs, Leela, working. The player, an unnamed security officer, fights back against the Pfhor and the S'pht they force to fight for them, and learns that the AI Durandal had contacted the aliens before the attack and has become "rampant", thinking freely. Destroying the organism the Pfhor use to control the S'pht sets off an S'pht revolt, and Durandal leaves with them.

Texture-mapped levels with dynamic lighting are explored with the mouse aiming the view, one of the earliest uses of free look. Terminals tell the story, set objectives and teleport the player onwards, and some hide designers' jokes. Shields and oxygen are refilled at wall stations rather than by pick-ups, and saving needs a pattern buffer, placed rarely and missing from some levels. Some levels have low gravity, no air or magnetic fields that scramble the motion sensor. Up to eight players can fight over a local network.
trivia: MacUser named it the best action game of 1995, ahead of Doom II.
Time included it in its 2012 list of the 100 best video games.
Bungie released the source code of Marathon 2 in 1999, which became the Aleph One engine.
A Pippin version, Super Marathon, combined it with Marathon 2.
A Marathon reboot, an extraction shooter, came out in 2026.
devStory:
Bungie built it on an engine derived from its 1993 Pathways into Darkness, with Jason Jones programming and designing it with Greg Kirkpatrick, Reginald Dujour and Alex Seropian, who also composed the music. Alain Roy wrote almost all of the multiplayer code, which Jones said delayed the game by about a month. A demo came out on 23 November 1994 and the full game on 21 December.

It sold more than 150,000 copies by October 1995, with demand that Seropian said was ten times that for Pathways, causing shortages. Historians call it the Mac's answer to Doom. Marathon 2: Durandal followed in 1995 and Marathon Infinity in 1996.

title: Magic Carpet
description: Magic Carpet (1994) is Bullfrog's 3D action game, in which a wizard on a flying carpet collects mana and builds a castle to restore balance to each world.
longDescription:
Mana was once a blessing, but the hunt for it left the lands barren and drove corrupt wizards to war, summoning monsters that often turned on them, until one wizard's all-powerful spell shattered the worlds. Only his apprentice survived, and the player, as that apprentice, sets out on a flying carpet to restore each spherical world to "equilibrium" by filling a castle with the required share of its mana.

Mana floats as pearls, found lying free or won by killing monsters and razing rival castles, and hot-air balloons from the player's castle carry it home, ignoring any claimed by an enemy wizard. A bigger castle sends out more balloons and armed guards, and it is also where the player heals and respawns: while any of it stands, the player cannot be killed for good. The carpet moves through three dimensions like a helicopter and climbs automatically over obstacles rather than crashing. Two spells can be ready at once, one in each hand, and stored mana unlocks stronger ones. The box promised 50 worlds, but the game has 45, because five level numbers were skipped.
trivia: It supported anaglyph 3D, autostereogram effects and the VFX1 headset.
The Hidden Worlds expansion added 25 winter-themed levels in 1995.
3D glasses came in the box.
Mike Diskett judged a Jaguar port impossible because of the console's difficulty with texture mapping.
Maximum called the Saturn version "a perfect mix of strategy and mindless blasting".
devStory:
Bullfrog developed it, with Sean Cooper and Mark Huntley among the programmers, a design team that included Jonty Barnes, Sean Masterson, Barry Meade, Daniel Russell and Alex Trowers, and music by Russell Shaw. EA released it for MS-DOS in 1994, followed by the Hidden Worlds expansion and Magic Carpet 2: The Netherworlds in 1995, and Krisalis's PlayStation and Saturn versions in 1996; ports to the Jaguar CD and 3DO were announced but never released.

Computer Gaming World gave it five stars out of five and Edge 9/10, and White Wolf's reviewer called it "highly addictive and worth all the trouble it will bring!" Next Generation singled out its originality.

title: Heretic
description: Heretic (1994) is Raven Software's dark-fantasy shooter on a modified Doom engine, one of the first first-person games with an inventory and the ability to look up and down.
longDescription:
The three Serpent Riders — D'Sparil, Korax and Eidolon — possessed the seven kings of Parthoris, and the Sidhe elves who resisted were declared heretics. In the war that followed the elves destroyed the kings and their armies, but were so weakened that the Riders killed their elders. The surviving elf Corvus sets out for revenge on D'Sparil, the weakest of the three, through the City of the Damned, past the Iron Liches guarding Hell's Maw and the Maulotaurs at the portal to D'Sparil's dome.

Raven added an inventory to the Doom engine, along with looking up and down, flying, and water and wind that push the player around. Health potions can be carried for later, the Tome of Power gives certain weapons a stronger mode, and the Morph Ovum turns enemies into chickens. Doom's famous cheat codes were turned against the player: one strips away every weapon but the quarterstaff, and another kills the player with the message "Trying to cheat, eh? Now you die!"
trivia: John Carmack reportedly told the team to "do it like Doom, and add the fantasy flavor".
Computer Gaming World ranked being turned into a chicken third among the best ways to die in computer games.
Raven released the source code in 1999.
A hidden third episode, Fate's Path, can be reached with a cheat code; its last level has no exit.
A 2025 remaster with Hexen added a new campaign, Faith Renewed.
devStory:
Raven's debut, Black Crypt, had caught id Software's attention, and id had already given Raven a modified Wolfenstein 3D engine for ShadowCaster. Around November 1993 John Romero proposed a medieval game like Doom, and John Carmack told the team to "do it like Doom, and add the fantasy flavor". Brian Raffel directed and wrote it, Ben Gokey led programming, Kevin Schilder composed the music and Gerald Brom painted the cover; flight, added by Chris Rhinehart, was a "happy accident", Raffel said. Work began in March 1994.

The shareware version came out on 29 December 1994 with online play through DWANGO, and the retail Shadow of the Serpent Riders added two episodes in 1996. Computer Gaming World gave it five stars. It sold more than 500,000 copies, and Hexen: Beyond Heretic followed.

title: I.Q.: Intelligent Qube
description: I.Q.: Intelligent Qube (1997) is a PlayStation puzzle game, known as Kurushi in Europe, in which the player clears rows of giant rolling cubes and is graded with an IQ score.
longDescription:
The player runs about on a platform as rows of cubes roll towards them, marking a square and triggering it as a cube rolls onto it to capture it. Grey cubes should be captured; green advantage cubes leave a mark that clears a 3×3 area around it when triggered; black forbidden cubes must be allowed to fall off the edge, and capturing one costs a row of the platform. Normal cubes that fall off also count against the player, and too many cost a row; being flattened by a rolling cube sends every cube in the wave to the tally. Falling off the platform ends the game.

Clearing a wave perfectly adds a row, and bonuses reward taking the ideal number of rolls. Stages grow from sets of three rows four cubes wide to fourteen rows seven wide, and at the end the score is turned into an IQ rating between 0 and 999. Two players can take turns.
trivia: Its designer, Masahiko Sato, was a professor at the Tokyo University of the Arts.
It won an Excellence Award for Interactive Art at the 1997 Japan Media Arts Festival.
Its sequels were I.Q. Final, I.Q. Remix+ on the PS2 and I.Q. Mania on the PSP.
It was one of the 20 games on the PlayStation Classic.
Finishing without continues guarantees an IQ of at least 350.
devStory:
Masahiko Sato, a professor at the Tokyo University of the Arts, designed it, and Kenji Sawaguchi directed it at G-Artists with help from Sony Computer Entertainment Japan. Takayuki Hattori's eerie orchestral score was singled out by reviewers. Sony released it in Japan on 31 January 1997, and it sold about 500,000 copies there by March and nearly 750,000 by the end of the year; it reached Europe as Kurushi that October and North America in November.

Critics praised its balanced challenge and music, but faulted the lack of simultaneous multiplayer and its slowdown. EGM named it runner-up for Puzzle Game of the Year.

title: Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen
description: Ogre Battle (1993) is Yasumi Matsuno's real-time tactical RPG, in which a Liberation Army sends squads across a map to free towns from the Zeteginean Empire. Its 13 endings depend on the army's reputation.
longDescription: Twenty-five years earlier, Endora of the Northern Highlands conquered the continent's other four kingdoms in about a year with the dark magic of the sage Rashidi, who betrayed his friend King Gran of Zenobia, and her rule as empress has turned harsh. The player, whose name and gender are chosen, leads the Liberation Army formed from the Knights of Zenobia; the seer Warren's tarot questions, each tied to one of the 22 Major Arcana, set the leader's abilities and starting troops. Squads of up to five fighters, with dragons and griffons counting as two, are sent across the map in real time to liberate towns and temples, which pay income but can be retaken if left undefended. Day and night alternate, with vampires and werewolves fighting only at night. Battles play out automatically by the chosen tactic — Best, Strong, Weak or Leader — and tarot cards such as The Lovers, which turns enemies to the player's side, can be played. Characters' alignment and the army's reputation decide which of 13 endings the player reaches, from a just new ruler to a regime as evil as Endora's.
trivia: The title comes from two songs by Queen, a band Matsuno liked.
The Japanese print run was doubled from 200,000 to 400,000 copies and still sold out soon after release.
Enix's North American run of about 25,000 sold out and was reordered several times; unboxed cartridges later sold for over $150.
It is the fifth chapter of a planned seven-part Ogre Battle Saga.
Atlus's PlayStation version did well enough to lead to the localisation of Tactics Ogre.
devStory: Yasumi Matsuno began it at Quest in summer 1991, pitching a real-time tactical game, uncommon in Japan then, to compete with Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy; never having played a tactical game, he learned from Nobunaga's Ambition. Akihiko Yoshida and Hiroshi Minagawa handled the graphics, and Hitoshi Sakimoto, in his first orchestral work, composed with Masaharu Iwata and Hayato Matsuo, simulating an orchestra on a Roland SC-55. It came out in Japan on 12 March 1993, and Enix America released it in North America in May 1995. Saturn and PlayStation versions followed in 1996.

sources.title: Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen

title: Grandia
description: Grandia (1997) is Game Arts' Saturn RPG, in which young adventurer Justin searches for Alent, the ancient city of knowledge, with a battle system built around a turn-order bar.
longDescription:
Justin of Parm inherits a Spirit Stone from his missing father, and a hologram of the woman Liete tells him to seek Alent, the ancient city of knowledge, in the east. With his young friend Sue and the adventurer Feena he sails to the New World and climbs the "End of the World" wall, joined along the way by the beast-man knight Gadwin and the salesman Guido. The militaristic Garlyle Forces under General Baal are reviving Gaia, an entity that spreads corruption, aided by his son Colonel Mullen and the young soldier Leen, who turns out to be Feena's lost sister. An epilogue set ten years later shows Justin and Feena with children.

The game puts 2D sprites on 3D maps with a camera the player can rotate. Monsters wander the field, and touching one from behind earns a pre-emptive strike. In battle, a rotating IP bar sets the order of turns, and hitting an enemy while it prepares an attack cancels it. Weapon and magic skills — swords, maces, axes, whips, knives and the elements — improve with use and add permanent stats.
trivia: The game contains 20,000 frames of animation.
It was first planned for the Mega-CD before moving to the Saturn.
It won a CESA Excellence Award in 1997 as runner-up for game of the year.
A Japan-only expansion, Grandia: Digital Museum, followed in 1998.
It was re-released on the Switch and PC in 2019.
devStory:
Game Arts made it over more than two years after Lunar: Eternal Blue, first for the Mega-CD and then for the Saturn once Sega abandoned that system; Takeshi Miyaji and Toshiaki Hontani directed it, with Yoichi Miyaji producing. Its 20,000 frames of animation drew on studios including Gonzo and Production I.G, and Noriyuki Iwadare's score was recorded at Skywalker Sound. It came out in Japan on 18 December 1997, selling 181,219 copies in its first week and 344,554 in all.

The Saturn version never left Japan, but the PlayStation version reached North America in October 1999 and scored 89 on Metacritic. Its battle system carried over to later games in the series.

title: Bushido Blade
description: Bushido Blade (1997) is Lightweight's sword-fighting game with no health bar or time limit, in which most hits are fatal.
longDescription:
The 500-year-old Meikyokan dojo, which teaches Narukagami Shinto, hides the Kage, a society of assassins. Its leader Hanzaki, who seized power from Utsusemi, has found the cursed sword Yugiri and begun to abandon the group's honour, and one member defects. The player, as the escaping assassin, is chased into the ruins of a labyrinthine castle and must kill former comrades one by one; despite the samurai-film styling, the setting is modern, with a helicopter pad in a city.

Fights are one-on-one, with no health bar and no time limit, and most hits are fatal. The Body Damage System means a lesser wound can slow an opponent, disable an arm so two-handed attacks are impossible, or cripple the legs and force them to crawl. There are eight weapons — katana, nodachi, long sword, saber, broadsword, naginata, rapier and sledgehammer — six characters and three stances: high, neutral and low. Fighters can run, jump and climb through connected arenas. In story mode, striking an opponent in the back, throwing dirt or attacking while they bow is dishonourable and ends the playthrough early.
trivia: Its director wanted to capture the tension of a fight that could end with a single blow.
Some critics found the one-hit kills polarising.
Its European weapons are noticeably shorter than their historical counterparts.
Slash mode pits a katana-wielding fighter against 100 enemies in a row.
Bushido Blade 2 followed a year later, and Lightweight later made Kengo: Master of Bushido.
devStory:
It was the first game by Lightweight, then partly owned by Square, directed by Shuhiko Nakata, who wanted to bring the tension of one-hit kills to the fighting game; with hit detection covering the torso, head and limbs, it was called a "swordsmanship simulator". Its honour code stresses survival rather than the "way of dying" of the Hagakure. Shinji Hosoe composed the music with Ayako Saso and Takayuki Aihara. Square released it in Japan on 14 March 1997, and Sony in North America that October, where the yellow flash of a fatal blow became blood.

Critics praised its innovation, graphics, open arenas and limb damage. It sold 387,937 copies in Japan in 1997 and 324,083 in the US by 2003.

title: Space Channel 5
description: Space Channel 5 (1999) is Tetsuya Mizuguchi's Dreamcast rhythm game, in which reporter Ulala out-dances an alien invasion in a 1960s-styled future, with a cameo from Michael Jackson.
longDescription:
In a science-fiction future styled after the 1960s, the reporter Ulala covers an invasion by the dancing alien Morolians for the news network Space Channel 5. Over four stages she copies her opponents' moves and shouts in time to the music, Simon Says-style, using six inputs: four directions and two action buttons, each announced with a "chu". Dance sections raise a Ratings meter, and in combat sections she shoots enemies and rescues hostages, who then dance along behind her. Bosses take away a heart for every mistake, and the game ends if the hearts run out or the ratings fall too low. Ulala never kills anyone.

The invasion turns out to have been staged by her boss, Chief Blank, to boost ratings. Michael Jackson appears as "Space Michael".
trivia: The main theme is "Mexican Flyer", written by Ken Woodman in 1966.
Deee-Lite's singer Kierin Kirby sued Sega in 2003 over Ulala's resemblance to her; she lost and was ordered to pay Sega's legal fees.
Michael Jackson provided his own voice lines and approved his character.
The "chu" began as the word "shoot" during voice recording.
The game fills just over 99% of its GD-ROM.
devStory:
Tetsuya Mizuguchi conceived it when Sega asked him for a Dreamcast game for women and casual players; after interviewing young girls, he found they preferred puzzle games to high-score chasing. Its influences included nightclub culture, Street Parade, Wassily Kandinsky, 1960s music and Peter Gabriel and Michael Jackson videos. The concept dated from 1993, full production began in 1998 at Sega AM9, later United Game Artists, and the team grew from 10 to 27 people, with Takashi Yuda directing. Naofumi Hataya and Kenichi Tokoi wrote a big-band score. Ulala's design drew on Barbarella, and her orange outfit refers to the Dreamcast logo.

Sega released it in Japan on 16 December 1999. Critics praised its music, art direction and style but found it short, and Mizuguchi later said it was not a commercial success.

title: ChuChu Rocket!
description: ChuChu Rocket! (1999) is Sonic Team's four-player puzzle game, in which players lay arrows to steer mice into their rockets and away from cats — the first Dreamcast game with online multiplayer.
longDescription:
Players place arrows on the floor — up to three at a time — to steer ChuChus, mice, into their own rocket while keeping KapuKapus, cats, away from it. The arrows fade over time, and a cat that hits the same arrow twice destroys it. Modes include single-player puzzles with a limited number of arrows, a puzzle editor, a 30-second cooperative challenge and competitive games for up to four players.

It was the first Dreamcast game with online multiplayer, letting players upload and download puzzles and chat by keyboard. Critics praised the multiplayer, the cute retro style and the low price, though network lag and login trouble drew complaints.
trivia: Yuji Naka wanted to test the Dreamcast by moving about 100 sprites at once.
In Europe it was mailed free to Dreamarena subscribers.
Lessons from its online play helped Sonic Team build Phantasy Star Online.
Fans restored its online servers in 2016.
A follow-up, Dee Dee Planet, was cancelled around 2001; a beta leaked in 2021.
devStory: Yuji Naka directed and produced it at Sonic Team, with Takafumi Kaya as designer and music by Tomoya Ohtani. Naka wanted to use the Dreamcast's power to move about 100 sprites at once, and the team used the game to test online play. Announced in September 1999 as Sonic Team's second Dreamcast game after Sonic Adventure, it came out in Japan on 11 November 1999, selling 35,000 copies in its first week and reaching number one, and in North America in March 2000 for $29.99. A planned NAOMI arcade version was dropped.

title: Seaman
description: Seaman (1999) is Yoot Saito's Dreamcast virtual pet, a creature with a human face that the player talks to through a microphone. Leonard Nimoy narrates the English version.
longDescription: The player raises a Seaman, a creature with a human face, talking to it through the Dreamcast's microphone and running the tank's machinery with the controller, in real time: it must be checked on at least once a day or it may die. It begins as a Mushroomer, a parasite that hatches from an egg and eats its way out of a nautilus, then becomes a Gillman, a fish with a human face that at first only repeats what it hears as gibberish but learns to talk; the Gillmen kill each other until two remain. They become Podfish, which mate and die in a tank turned terrarium, and their young, the Tadmen, grow into Frogmen, which the player finally releases into the wild. The Seaman shares trivia, tells the player what happened on their birthday and insults them, growing tamer over time. Leonard Nimoy narrates the English version.
trivia: Saito modelled the Seaman's face on his own.
Testers' long sentences confused the creature, so Saito gave it the reply "You talk too long, I don't understand."
It was the third best-selling Dreamcast game in Japan.
Its fictional backstory follows a French biologist, Jean-Paul Gassé, who studied Seaman in 1930s Egypt.
A sequel, Seaman 2, came out on the PlayStation 2 in 2007.
devStory:
Yoot Saito got the idea from a joke about a tropical fish simulator a colleague was making, and built the prototype on a Macintosh; converting it to the Dreamcast took about a year and a half. The Seaman's face is modelled on his own, and he voiced the adult creature in Japanese after turning down Sega's request for a celebrity, while his daughter voiced the baby. Vivarium released it in Japan on 29 July 1999, and Sega's nine-month English localisation, released in North America in August 2000, toned down dialogue about sex, politics and slang.

It sold 399,342 copies in Japan, won an Excellence Award at the 1999 Japan Media Arts Festival and Edge's Gameplay Innovation award, and Next Generation called it the Dreamcast's "most bizarre title ever".

title: Vib-Ribbon
description: Vib-Ribbon (1999) is Masaya Matsuura's minimalist rhythm game, drawn in white vector lines, which builds its levels from any music CD the player puts in.
longDescription:
Vibri, a rabbit, walks along a line of obstacles timed to the beat of the music: blocks, loops, waves and pits, each matched to a button, with combined obstacles needing two buttons at once. Missing one turns her briefly into a scribble, and repeated misses degrade her into a frog and then an insect; being hit too often in insect form ends the game. Clearing enough obstacles in a row as a rabbit turns her into Super Vibri, boosting the score, and a high score earns a song from her. The game has six songs over bronze, silver and gold courses.

Because the whole game loads into the console's memory, players can swap in their own audio CDs, and the game analyses the music eight seconds ahead to generate a course from its changes, harder for more intense tracks. The soundtrack is by the J-pop band Laugh and Peace.
trivia: It began as an advertisement for the Mercedes-Benz A-Class, until the car failed the moose test and Mercedes dropped the idea.
The Museum of Modern Art acquired it in 2012.
It reached North America only in 2014, after Sony's US chief mentioned it at E3 not realising it had never been released there.
Its two-handed controls came from Matsuura's background as a drummer.
A Vib-Ribbon stage appears in Astro's Playroom on the PS5.
devStory:
It began when Mercedes-Benz asked Sony for a game to promote its A-Class, and NanaOn-Sha's first prototype made the player a living car on levels shaped like sound waves; Mercedes dropped the idea after the car failed the moose test. Work stopped for a year and a half until a programmer found a way to analyse CD audio on the PlayStation. Masaya Matsuura, who designed and produced it with a team of eleven, wanted players to use their own music, and its wireframe look reflected both his love of early computer graphics and the need to fit the game in memory. Vibri's voice was made with a speech synthesiser.

Sony released it in Japan on 9 December 1999, where it sold 100,000 copies in its first week, and in Europe in 2000. Sony of America reportedly found its graphics too simple to release it there.

title: Shin Megami Tensei
description: Shin Megami Tensei (1992) is Atlus's Super Famicom RPG of a demon-overrun Tokyo, in which the player recruits demons by talking to them and fuses them into new ones, and the player's choices push them towards Law or Chaos.
longDescription: In near-future Tokyo, "199X", an unnamed teenage boy who lives with his mother and dog in Kichijōji receives an email containing a program for talking to demons, just as a scientist opens a portal to the demon world. The US and Japanese militaries disagree over how to deal with the demons, and Thorman, the US commander, launches missiles at Tokyo whatever the hero decides; the story resumes thirty years later in the flooded ruins, where the Order of Messiah and the Ring of Gaea fight over a cathedral. Exploration is in first person and battles are turn-based, with swords and guns bought from merchants. Demons can be talked into joining, and since they gain no experience, fusing two or three at the Cathedrals of Shadows is the only way to strengthen them; allied demons also consume magnetite as the player walks. The hero's choices move him along Light–Dark and Law–Chaos axes, changing how demons and factions treat him and leading to Law, Chaos or Neutral endings.
trivia: It was not localised at the time, partly because of its religious content; the first official English release came on iOS in 2014.
Toby Fox cited it as an inspiration for Undertale, especially its dialogue system.
Louis Cyphre takes his name from the character in the 1987 film Angel Heart.
Early drafts set the finale in Israel.
The Chaos Hero's transformation later became the core idea of Digital Devil Saga.
devStory: Atlus saw it as a chance to build its own brand after the first two Megami Tensei games, tie-ins to Aya Nishitani's Digital Devil Story novels, had been published by Namco; when Tokuma Shoten failed to trademark the name, Atlus registered it. Yōsuke Niino directed, Kazuma Kaneko drew the art, Tsukasa Masuko composed and Ryutaro Ito and Kazunari Suzuki wrote it, setting it in Tokyo under the influence of manga such as Devilman and Fist of the North Star. It came out on the Super Famicom on 30 October 1992, and Famitsu gave it four 9s, among its highest scores of the year. Its success helped establish Atlus, and Shin Megami Tensei II followed in 1994.

title: Star Ocean
description: Star Ocean (1996) is tri-Ace's Super Famicom RPG with real-time battles and voice clips packed onto the cartridge with the S-DD1 compression chip. It stayed in Japan until a 2008 remake.
longDescription: In S.D. 346, in the village of Kratus on the planet Roak, Roddick, Millie and Dorne of the village Defence Force look for a cure for a disease spreading from the neighbouring town that turns people to stone. On Mt. Metorx they meet Ronyx and Ilia of the Earth Federation starship Calnus, and learn the disease traces back to Asmodeus, a demon king who died 300 years earlier, so they travel back in time through a Time Gate. The view is from above, and random battles shift to an isometric 3D view and run in real time: the player controls one character and the AI the others, with special Symbology techniques costing MP. Eight of ten possible recruits can join in one playthrough, Special Points from battle buy skills such as cooking and item creation, and optional "Private Actions" in towns change how characters feel about each other and which endings appear.
trivia: Its voice clips during battle were rare on the Super Famicom.
Enix America had stopped publishing by the end of 1995, so the game never officially left Japan; fans made an English patch.
It was one of only two games to use the S-DD1 compression chip.
Criticism of its weak bosses led to harder battles in The Second Story.
Motoi Sakuraba composed its progressive-rock-style score.
devStory: Its staff had left Wolf Team after disputes with Namco over Tales of Phantasia and formed tri-Ace, whose first game this was, aiming for deeper skill and item systems; space was chosen as the setting for a larger story. Its 48 megabits of data used the S-DD1 compression chip, at a cost in audio quality, and a "Flexible Voice Driver" allowed compressed voice clips that changed with how strong the enemies were. Enix released it in Japan on 19 July 1996, and it sold about 235,000 copies there. Enix had closed its American branch and Nintendo was focused on the Nintendo 64, so it stayed in Japan until Tose's PSP remake, First Departure, in 2008.

title: Phoenix
description: Phoenix (1980) is an arcade shooter of birds, hatching eggs and a mothership, and one of the first shooters to end with a boss battle.
longDescription: The player's ship slides left and right, dodging missiles and diving enemies, and can raise a force field that blocks attacks for a few seconds before it needs about five seconds to recover. The first two stages bring formations of small phoenixes, some of which swoop at the ship. The next two bring eggs that drift side to side and hatch into large phoenixes, which must be hit in the body, since a wing shot off grows back. The fifth is a fortress: the player has to shoot through its hull and a rotating shield band to hit the pilot inside while small phoenixes attack. Then the cycle starts again, harder. That fifth stage makes it one of the first shooters with a boss battle.
trivia: Its original developer is unknown because the credits were overwritten; Retro Gamer suggested Tehkan.
The arcade version plays "Romance de Amor" at the start and "Für Elise" when a level is cleared.
Atari sued Imagic over Demon Attack, which it considered too close to Phoenix, and settled in 1983.
Bootleg versions appeared as Condor, Griffon, Vautour and Batman Part 2.
It was among the first shooters to end its cycle with a boss battle.
devStory: Its developer is unknown: Taito is credited in Japan, Germany's Nova Apparate credited a Tokyo company, G.G.I., and Amstar Electronics of Phoenix, Arizona, bought the North American rights. Taito released it in Japan in December 1980 and Centuri in the US in January 1981, and it was Centuri's best-selling title by 1982. General Computer Corporation's John Mraceck, an MIT student on an internship, and Michael Feinstein made the Atari 2600 version, cutting more than a third of the code to fit 8 KB; released in 1983, it sold over 600,000 copies. AllGame later said only Galaga beat it for enjoyment and replay value.

title: Jumpman
description: Jumpman (1983) is Randy Glover's platform game for Epyx, in which Jumpman climbs ladders and ropes to defuse bombs planted around a base on Jupiter.
longDescription:
Terrorists have sabotaged a base on Jupiter and planted bombs in its three buildings, and Jumpman defuses each one by touching it. He jumps and climbs ladders and two kinds of rope, each climbable in only one direction. Each level is one floor of a building, clearing all its bombs scrolls on to the next, and the buildings come in a random order. Smart darts speed up and fire straight at Jumpman when lined up with him, falling too far is dangerous, and each level has its own hazards.

When he is hit or falls, Jumpman tumbles to the bottom of the screen to an excerpt from Chopin's Funeral March, and since he is only defeated on reaching the bottom, grabbing the last bomb on the way down still completes the level. Points come from bombs and fast finishes, and the player picks the running speed: faster is riskier but scores more.
trivia: Compute! wrote that it "easily conquers that skepticism and establishes itself as a software classic".
Jumpman Junior, a 12-level cartridge version, was made for players without a disk drive.
Glover later worked on the swimming event of Summer Games.
Apogee's Jumpman Lives! (1991) was withdrawn at Epyx's request.
It was included on the THEC64 Mini in 2018.
devStory:
Randy Glover, living in Foster City, California, was inspired by seeing Donkey Kong at a local Pizza Hut to make a home computer version, and chose the Atari over the TI-99/4A. Albert Persinger wrote the first version on an Apple II and moved it to the Atari, a 13-level prototype that took four to five months. In early 1983 Broderbund wanted its own programmers involved, so Glover went to Automated Simulations, which let him finish it himself and hired him; the final game has 30 levels and was released on 26 February 1983. Glover ported it to the Commodore 64 with an improved sprite, and Mirror Images made the IBM PC version.

It was a best-seller for Epyx, selling about 40,000 copies on the Atari and C64 through 1987 and reaching about third to sixth on Billboard's games chart. It won a Certificate of Merit at the 1984 Arkie Awards.

title: Spelunker
description: Spelunker (1983) is Tim Martin's cave-exploring platform game, whose famously fragile hero gave Japanese baseball a word for injury-prone players.
longDescription:
The explorer sets off from the cave entrance at the top to reach the treasure at the bottom, collecting dynamite, flares and keys on the way. His air supply runs down and must be refilled at points in the cave, bats drop deadly guano, and a ghost can carry him off to the shadow world unless he blasts it with air, which leaves him unable to move for a few seconds. Six levels join seamlessly, each change of level bringing an extra life and bonus points, and after six levels the same layout begins again as a harder cave, six in all.

The NES and MSX versions have much smaller levels than the Atari and Commodore originals, and Irem's arcade version added shooting and scuba diving with its own level design. The Atari title screen plays an excerpt from Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition.
trivia: In Japan, "Speranker" is used for baseball players who are often injured, after the game's fragile hero.
The arcade version was the fourth most successful table arcade unit in Game Machine's February 1986 chart.
Irem made two Japan-only sequels, both called Spelunker II, in 1986 and 1987.
Spelunker HD (2009) on the PS3 expanded it to 10 caves of 10 levels.
Spelunker Party! came out on the Switch in 2017.
devStory:
Tim Martin developed it at MicroGraphicImage, a company founded with Robert Barber and Cash Foley by former staff of Games by Apollo, which went bust before Christmas 1983. Martin wrote the game logic, Foley built the graphics engine and level editor, and Barber designed the graphics and levels; it was too complex for the Atari 2600. Released on the Atari 8-bit computers in 1983, it passed to Broderbund in 1984, and Martin programmed the nearly identical Commodore 64 version. MicroGraphicImage ran out of money, but Martin paid off its debts through the NES and arcade versions.

Computer Gaming World called it "a thoroughly enjoyable game", and Ahoy! found the C64 graphics "amazingly intricate".

title: Renegade
description: Renegade (1986) is Yoshihisa Kishimoto's street-fighting game, called the first fully developed beat 'em up, which led directly to Double Dragon.
longDescription:
In the Western version an unnamed street brawler fights four gangs to rescue his girlfriend from a mob boss; in the Japanese original, Kunio, a high-school delinquent, defends his classmate Hiroshi from rival gangs. The isometric view allows movement up and down as well as across, so a jump button joined the two attack buttons, creating the standard three-button layout. The first hit briefly stuns an enemy, allowing combos: a stunned foe can be grabbed by the collar and kicked or thrown over the shoulder, double-tapping runs into punches and flying kicks, and the player can sit on a fallen enemy and pummel him.

The four stages, a subway platform, a harbour, a back alley and a parking lot leading into a building, are three screens wide, with the boss joining once three of his gang remain, from Jack on the subway to the gun-carrying Sabu. Players can also be knocked off the platform or into the sea. Both the player and the enemies have far more health than in Kung-Fu Master.
trivia: In Japan it is Nekketsu Kōha Kunio-kun.
Kishimoto drew partly on his own high-school fights and on Bruce Lee's Enter the Dragon.
Ocean's home computer version topped the UK all-formats chart in September 1987.
Ocean made its own sequels, Target: Renegade (1988) and Renegade III (1989), without Technōs.
Kunio later became Technōs's official mascot.
devStory:
Yoshihisa Kishimoto, who had made the laserdisc games Cobra Command and Road Blaster at Data East, pitched Technōs Japan a semi-autobiographical game drawn from his teenage fights and from Bruce Lee's Enter the Dragon. Technōs released it in Japan in May 1986 as Nekketsu Kōha Kunio-kun, the first Kunio-kun game, and it was Japan's top-grossing table arcade game that July. For the West, Taito published it with graphics restyled after the 1979 film The Warriors.

The Famicom version, Technōs's first home console game, sold about 400,000 copies, and Ocean's Spectrum version topped the UK all-formats chart in September 1987, Your Sinclair's readers voting it the second-best game of the year. It became the basis for Double Dragon.

title: Stunts
description: Stunts (1990), also known as 4D Sports Driving, is a 3D racing game of loops, jumps and corkscrews, with a track editor and replays that kept a fan community racing for decades.
longDescription: Players race one lap of a stunt track as fast as possible without crashing, over loops, jumps including over tall buildings, slalom roads and corkscrews, inside a square area fenced off at the edges. They race the clock or one of six computer opponents in 11 cars with automatic or manual gears. Pavement, gravel, ice and grass each grip differently, and the physics simulate oversteer and understeer, with grip depending on a curve's banking. Races can be saved and replayed from four camera views, and play can be resumed from any point of a replay, though the time then does not count. A built-in editor builds new tracks or changes existing ones.
trivia: In Europe it was sold as 4D Sports Driving because Broderbund held the Stunts name.
Programmer Chris Taylor played the opponent Skid Vicious.
PC Gamer US ranked it the 22nd best computer game ever in 1994.
Its copy protection makes the car crash about four seconds into the race after three wrong answers.
A yearly World Stunts Meeting was held in the mid-2000s.
devStory:
Distinctive Software in Burnaby, Canada, which had made Test Drive, began it as a demolition-derby arena game, which stalled because the cars mostly drove backwards. Don Mattrick acknowledged the influence of Hard Drivin', and since programmer Kevin Pickell could not match that arcade game's visuals, he added the track editor, which he used to build the default tracks. The physics were deliberately unrealistic so that jumps that would wreck a real car stayed fun, and glitches such as braking in mid-air were left in for lack of time. Replays store up to ten minutes by saving compressed control inputs.

Broderbund released it for MS-DOS in October 1990, and PC Gamer US ranked it the 22nd best computer game ever in 1994. A fan community racing and sharing replays lasted for decades.

title: Powermonger
description: Powermonger (1990) is Bullfrog's real-time strategy game on a 3D landscape, in which a captain conquers towns, feeds an army and sends orders that travel slowly to distant commanders.
longDescription:
Only the terrain is in 3D; people, trees and other objects are sprites, and the map can be rotated in steps and viewed at eight zoom levels. Villagers go about their lives fishing, farming, herding sheep, collecting wood or making things, and a query tool shows anyone's name, age, loyalty, home town and equipment. Victory comes from tipping the balance of power, shown on a scale under the minimap, by conquering most or all towns and killing rival captains.

Locals can be drafted, and neutral captains in some larger towns join after surviving a battle; each captain leads one army, which disbands if he dies. Orders to subordinate captains arrive by homing pigeon, with a delay that grows with distance. Food is the most important resource, from friendly towns, wild sheep, barter or plunder, and towns can "invent" equipment depending on nearby resources. Players cannot reshape the land as in Populous, but cutting down too many trees brings more rain or snow, slowing movement.
trivia: It won Computer Gaming World's Strategy Game of the Year for 1991.
Advertisements quoted Peter Molyneux calling it "Better than Populous".
Orders to distant captains are delivered by homing pigeon.
Amiga Power ranked it the 32nd best game of all time.
A 3DO version was planned but never released.
devStory: Peter Molyneux, Glenn Corpes and Kevin Donkin designed it at Bullfrog on an engine derived from Populous, with art by Gary Carr and Simon Hunter and music by Charles Callet, and Electronic Arts released it for the Amiga and Atari ST in October 1990 at £29.99. Computer Gaming World called it "simply superb ... a joy to play" and named it Strategy Game of the Year for 1991. The World War I Edition expansion followed in 1991, while fantasy, feudal Japan and American Civil War expansions were planned but never released.

title: Front Mission
description: Front Mission (1995) is the first game in Square's mech tactics series, set on Huffman Island in 2090, where wanzers take damage part by part.
longDescription:
Huffman Island, a Pacific island about the size of Oahu, has been split between the OCU and the USN since the first Huffman Conflict of 2070. In 2090 an OCU reconnaissance team led by Royd Clive is ambushed at a USN factory in Larcus, where the USN officer Driscoll destroys the wanzer of Royd's fiancée, Karen, and blows up the plant. The USN blames the OCU, starting the second Huffman Conflict, and Royd, discharged and listed as killed in action, joins the mercenary Canyon Crows a year later. The war leads him to the Nirvana Institute and its "B-device" wanzers, which wire soldiers' brains into their computers.

Wanzers, from the German Wanderpanzer, are built from four parts — a body, two arms and legs — each with its own health. Losing the body takes a wanzer out of the fight, losing an arm loses its weapons, and destroyed legs limit it to one space. Between missions the player customises parts, computers that improve accuracy and add special abilities, and backpacks for supplies, within a weight limit set by power output. Weapons are divided into melee, short-range, long-range and support fire, and an arena offers fights for money.
trivia: It was the first game Square had another developer make for it.
The original proposal was called "100 Mission".
It stayed in Japan until a Nintendo DS version reached North America in 2007.
Squaresoft's branding was left off at the developers' request.
A remake, Front Mission 1st: Remake, came out in 2022.
devStory:
Toshiro Tsuchida pitched it to Square as "100 Mission" through his company, and producer Shinji Hashimoto first found it "too radical"; Square had repeatedly said no to robots, but agreed in order to try a new genre, and Hashimoto insisted on lighter scenes to balance the dark tone. G-Craft developed it, Kow Yokoyama helped design the wanzers, and Yoko Shimomura, at Hironobu Sakaguchi's request, and Noriko Matsueda composed the music. Yoshitaka Amano's cover painting was judged too imposing, and only part of it was used.

Square released it in Japan on 24 February 1995, and it sold over 500,000 copies there; Famitsu gave it 31 out of 40. It began a series that ran to Front Mission 5 and spin-offs such as Gun Hazard.

title: Beyond Oasis
description: Beyond Oasis (1994), The Story of Thor in Japan and Europe, is Ancient's Mega Drive action-adventure, in which Prince Ali uses a gold armlet to summon four elemental spirits.
longDescription: Prince Ali finds a buried gold armlet that once belonged to a wizard who fought a long war against the wielder of a silver armlet, used to spread chaos and destruction. The gold armlet can summon four spirits — Dytto of water, Efreet of fire, Shade of shadow and Bow of plants — and Ali travels the land of Oasis winning each from its shrine, to stop whoever is using the silver armlet for evil again. As in The Legend of Zelda, he explores the map collecting items that restore health and mana. His knife has special attacks and never breaks, while swords, crossbows and bombs, some of which set targets alight, break after a set number of uses unless unlimited versions are found.
trivia: GameFan named it Action RPG of the Year in 1995.
A sequel, The Legend of Oasis, followed on the Saturn in 1996.
IGN compared its mechanics to Secret of Mana.
GamePro thought it a good entry point for newcomers to role-playing games.
It was preloaded on the Sega Genesis Mini.
devStory: Yuzo Koshiro produced and composed it at Ancient, with art by Ayano Koshiro and design by Kataru Uchimura, and Sega released it in Japan on 9 December 1994 as The Story of Thor, the name it also kept in Europe, and in North America in March 1995 as Beyond Oasis. EGM praised its large world and plot twists, Mean Machines Sega gave it 93% and GameFan named it Action RPG of the Year, while Next Generation, giving it 2 out of 5, found both its action and its role-playing average.

title: Dynamite Headdy
description: Dynamite Headdy (1994) is Treasure's Mega Drive platform game starring a puppet who fights by throwing his own head, which can be swapped for 17 different powered-up heads.
longDescription:
Headdy, a puppet, tries to stop the evil puppet king Dark Demon from turning the world's puppets into his minions; Dark Demon's army includes Trouble Bruin and the "key masters" who guard each stage. Headdy attacks by throwing his detachable head in any direction, and it can also grab hooks to pull him up to higher platforms. Seventeen power-up heads change his attacks and abilities, some only for a while, from spinning fireballs to invincibility, health and speed, and one opens a bonus stage of shooting basketballs into hoops.

His health is shown by a spotlight in the corner of the screen that changes colour, and falling off a platform does not kill him outright: he bounces back out and loses some health. Support characters appear in every stage.
trivia: Sega of America asked for a harder North American version, about twice as difficult, and much of the dialogue was removed.
A Master System version, based on the Game Gear port, was released only in Brazil.
Trouble Bruin is called Maruyama in Japan.
A 32X version was planned but cancelled.
It was included in Sega Ages 2500: Gunstar Heroes Treasure Box on the PS2.
devStory:
After Gunstar Heroes, Treasure split into four teams, and Koichi Kimura led this one from August 1993, wanting an original project that would also sell; Treasure's president Masato Maegawa was head programmer. The head-throwing attack was chosen to make the hero's attack distinctive, and the visuals drew on Western animation and Terry Gilliam. Sega released it in Japan on 5 August 1994 and in North America that September.

Critics praised its creativity, visuals and technical achievement; Computer and Video Games said it "breathes new life" into the platform genre, while GamesMaster found it patchy. A Game Gear version came out the same day in Japan.

title: Soul Edge
description: Soul Edge (1995), released abroad as Soul Blade, is Namco's weapon-based 3D fighting game and the first in the Soulcalibur series.
longDescription:
In 1583 the cursed sword Soul Edge, which feeds on the souls of its victims and of whoever wields it, surfaces at an auction and is taken by the pirate Cervantes de Leon. Nine warriors set out after it — Hwang, Li Long, Mitsurugi, Rock, Seong Mi-na, Siegfried, Sophitia, Taki and Voldo — some for power, some for revenge and some to destroy it.

Fighters can sidestep in and out of the screen and use three attack buttons for horizontal and vertical slashes and kicks, plus a block button. Every fighter carries a weapon, and a Weapon Gauge drains with each blocked blow; empty it, and the fighter is left unarmed. Critical Edge attacks use a third of the gauge, and Guard Impact deflects an attack for a free counter, which can itself be turned back. A ring out happens only when an opponent knocks a fighter out of the arena. The PlayStation version added the story mode Edge Master, more modes and costumes, and five unlockable characters.
trivia: It was the first game made with motion capture using passive optical markers.
The PlayStation version's opening won a SIGGRAPH '97 award for best game video of 1996.
The European release turned Li Long's nunchaku into a three-section staff to satisfy the BBFC.
Hwang began as a palette swap of Mitsurugi.
EGM gave it Best Intro in its 1998 Buyer's Guide.
devStory:
Project Soul made it as an experiment in weapon-based fighting games, with Teruaki Konishi directing, on Namco's System 11 board, the hardware behind Tekken. It reached Japanese arcades on 13 September 1995, and a Ver. II in 1996 made Hwang and Cervantes playable and added Guard Impacts and air combos. The PlayStation version, released in December 1996, was retitled Soul Blade abroad to avoid a trademark on the word "Edge".
