The PlayStation version averaged 91% on GameRankings and was a UK bestseller, and Next Generation said the arcade game had "enjoyed less success than it deserved". Soulcalibur followed in 1998.

title: Toki
description: Toki (1989) is TAD Corporation's arcade platform shooter, in which a tribesman turned into an ape spits energy balls to rescue Princess Miho from the witch doctor Vookimedlo.
longDescription: Toki, a muscular tribesman on a South Seas island, sees the witch doctor Vookimedlo kidnap Miho, the princess of his tribe, and turn the islanders into beasts. Toki becomes a Geeshergam, an ape-like minion, but keeps his mind and gains the power to spit projectiles. He crosses lakes, canyons, icy mountains and volcanoes towards Vookimedlo's golden palace on the island's summit. He is slow and dies to almost any attack, but his spit is powerful. Each stage has a timer and a boss. Power-ups strengthen the spit, lucky rabbit feet give bursts of agility and jumping, clocks add time, keys open bonus areas, magic coins add up to extra lives, and an American-football-style helmet protects against attacks from above.
trivia: In Japan it is JuJu Densetsu.
Ocean's home computer versions won Best Coin-Op Conversion at the 1991 Golden Joystick Awards.
Microids released a remake in 2018.
Some ports rename Toki as JuJu, Miho as Wanda and Vookimedlo as Dr. Stark.
Famitsu's reviewers called the NES version a "memorization game".
devStory:
TAD Corporation released it in Japanese arcades on 8 December 1989 as JuJu Densetsu, and Fabtek published it in North America in February 1990. RePlay listed it as the second most popular arcade game of December 1989, and critics were generally favourable; Hardcore Gaming 101's Kurt Kalata later called it "delightfully deranged".

Ocean's Amiga, Atari ST and Commodore 64 versions of 1991 won Best Coin-Op Conversion at the Golden Joystick Awards, though planned Spectrum and Amstrad versions never appeared. Taito published NES and Lynx versions, and Sega's Genesis version, Toki: Going Ape Spit, added levels but dropped the non-spit power-ups.

title: Snow Bros.
description: Snow Bros. (1990) is Toaplan's arcade platform game, in which the snowman twins Nick and Tom bury enemies in snow and roll them into giant snowballs.
longDescription: Nick and Tom, snowman twins in blue and red overalls, fight through 50 stages to rescue the princesses Puripuri and Puchipuchi, with a boss every tenth stage. Snow thrown at an enemy covers it until it becomes a snowball; partly covered enemies are frozen until they shake it off. A kicked snowball rolls, bounces off walls and eventually shatters, flattening enemies and setting other snowballs rolling, and wiping out every enemy with one kick makes bonus money rain down. Potions dropped by enemies add speed (red), more snow (blue) or range (yellow), and the green one inflates the player to fly and bowl enemies over for a while. If a stage drags on, an invincible pumpkin head appears and eventually releases ghosts that cannot be stopped.
trivia: It has been described as reminiscent of Bubble Bobble and Tumblepop.
The Mega Drive version added 20 levels and a section played as the princesses.
Ocean dropped co-op from its Amiga version to keep the frame rate stable; the unreleased version leaked in 2006.
The Game Boy version, Snow Bros. Jr., was published by Capcom in North America.
A Mexican hack, Snow Brothers 3: Magical Adventure, replaced the twins with footballers.
devStory:
Toaplan released it in Japanese arcades in April 1990, with music by Osamu Ōta, and Romstar distributed it in North America and Europe; it won an award from Gamest. Other companies made the console versions: Dual's Game Boy Snow Bros. Jr. added ten levels, Soft House's NES version added a story about the cursed princes, and Toaplan's own Mega Drive version of 1993 added 20 levels. Ocean France's home computer versions were never released.

Snow Bros. 2 (1994) was Toaplan's last arcade project, the company going bankrupt as it came out. The rights now belong to Tatsujin, which released Snow Bros. Wonderland in 2024.

title: Mega Man Legends
description: Mega Man Legends (1997) is Capcom's 3D action-adventure reinvention of Mega Man, in which Mega Man Volnutt explores ruins on a flooded Earth.
longDescription:
On a flooded Earth, Diggers explore ancient ruins guarded by Reaverbots, hunting refractors that power society; refractor shards serve as currency. Mega Man Volnutt, a Digger living aboard the airship Flutter with the Spotter Roll Caskett, her grandfather Barrell and Data, a monkey only Mega Man can understand, crash-lands on Kattelox Island. There the Bonne family of pirates — Teisel, Tron, who builds the robots and grows fond of Mega Man, and Bon, who only ever says "Babu!" — are after the legendary Mother Lode. Exploring the island's ruins awakens Juno, a unit from Eden who plans to wipe out its population.

Unlike the platforming of the original series, the game is set in 3D, with ledge climbing, diving, a manual camera and lock-on targeting. Shards become Zenny for upgrades, the Buster's attack, rate, range and energy depend on the parts equipped, and Roll builds new parts and special weapons from junk found in the ruins. Being rude to people raises prices and changes what they say.
trivia: It was shown at E3 1997 as Mega Man Neo.
Keiji Inafune said it did not sell well, arriving years before sandbox games became popular.
On the Nintendo 64 it was retitled Mega Man 64.
In Japan the hero is called Rock Volnutt.
A planned Mega Man Legends 3 was cancelled.
devStory:
Producer Keiji Inafune wanted a Mega Man unlike the earlier games, mixing action, role-playing and adventure; Yoshinori Kawano directed it, Shin Kurosawa wrote it and Makoto Tomozawa composed the music, and the humanoid characters were motion-captured. It was shown at E3 1997 as Mega Man Neo, briefly renamed Nova and settled as Mega Man Legends in March 1998. Capcom released it in Japan on 18 December 1997 and in North America that September; the localisation removed the option to kick a dog.

Reviewers praised its story, bosses and variety of weapons. Inafune later said it did not sell well, arriving years before sandbox games became popular.

title: Alundra
description: Alundra (1997) is Matrix Software's puzzle-heavy action-adventure, a spiritual sequel to Landstalker, in which a dream-walking elf enters the nightmares killing a village's people.
longDescription:
Alundra, a silent elf of the Elna clan of Dreamwalkers, follows a recurring dream in which a mysterious figure calls him "Releaser". His ship breaks apart in a storm, and he is washed ashore and taken to the village of Inoa by a man named Jess. The villagers are suffering nightmares, and some are being murdered in their dreams, which kills them in waking life too; some blame the newcomer. With the help of Meia, another Dreamwalker, Alundra learns that the demon Melzas, disguised as a god and aided by the village priest, is feeding on the villagers' prayers.

Played from above, it puts heavy emphasis on puzzles, alongside real-time combat and platforming. Sand slows Alundra and lava burns him, and the tools he finds open new areas. There are no experience points, so the player's own skill is what improves. Its main innovation is walking in dreams, with each dream level shaped by the dreamer's personality.
trivia: Its world contains more than 7,000 screens.
It was runner-up to Final Fantasy VII for RPG of the Year at Electronic Gaming Monthly and GamePro.
Working Designs sold over 100,000 copies in North America within a month.
In Europe it was released as The Adventures of Alundra.
It sold 143,114 copies in Japan by the end of 1997.
devStory:
It is considered a spiritual sequel to Climax Entertainment's Landstalker: producer Yasuhiro Ohori had worked on it, and map designer Kenji Orimo on Shining Force. Development at Matrix Software began as an action RPG before the PlayStation launched and took three years, and Kōhei Tanaka composed the music. Sony released it in Japan on 11 April 1997, and Working Designs brought it to North America in January 1998.

It scored 86 on Metacritic, the sixth-highest PlayStation game of 1997. Critics praised its story, characters, challenging puzzles and music, while finding its graphics closer to a 16-bit game. Alundra 2 followed in 1999.

title: Lady Bug
description: Lady Bug (1981) is Universal's maze game in the style of Pac-Man, with twenty turnstile gates that the player swings to reshape the maze and shut out pursuing insects.
longDescription: Like Pac-Man, it has the player clear a maze, here of flowers, hearts and letters, while avoiding enemies, here insects, steering a red, yellow and green ladybird. The twist is the twenty green turnstile gates, which swing as the player passes through them and change the layout of the maze, though never enough to seal part of it off completely. The maze border works as a timer: each time it goes round, another insect is released from the centre, up to four, and the timer speeds up on stages 2 and 5. A new type of insect arrives on each of the first eight levels, and from level 9 every level brings four different kinds.
trivia: Its ColecoVision version, a launch title for the console in 1982, was far more successful than the arcade original.
The ColecoVision version won its category at the 5th Arkie Awards.
Creative Computing said its turnstiles set it apart from Pac-Man clones.
In Japan it was re-released on the Casio PV-1000 as Fighting Bug.
Clones included Doodle Bug for the TRS-80 Color Computer and Bumble Bee for the BBC Micro.
devStory: Kazutoshi Ueda designed it, and Universal released it in Japan in October 1981 and worldwide that December. Electronic Games said it did "just all right in the arcades", and it won a Certificate of Merit as runner-up for Most Innovative Coin-Op Game at the January 1983 Arcade Awards. Coleco's version, a ColecoVision launch title in November 1982, became far more popular, adding a "Vegetable Harvest" bonus level for spelling SPECIAL; Electronic Games called it "proving to be one of the most successful home videogames ever" and "the most wonderful blend of strategy and maze-chase thrills ever concocted". An Intellivision version followed in June 1983.

title: Pooyan
description: Pooyan (1982) is Konami's arcade shooter, designed by Tokuro Fujiwara, in which a mother pig in a lift shoots down the balloons of the wolves that kidnapped her piglets.
longDescription: Mama, a pig whose piglets have been kidnapped by wolves, rides a lift up and down, controlled with a two-way joystick, and one button fires arrows and throws meat. In the first round wolves float down on balloons and the player shoots the balloons; any wolf that lands climbs the ladders behind the lift and eats Mama if she passes in front. In the second round the wolves start on the ground and float up to a cliff, trying to push a boulder over the edge, and the last "boss" wolf needs several hits. Airborne wolves throw rocks in both rounds. A slab of meat at the top of the lift's range, once thrown, makes wolves drop their balloons for bonus points, and bonus screens alternate between beating wolves with meat alone and shooting fruit. The music includes "The Other Day I Met a Bear" and part of "Oh! Susanna".
trivia: Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker includes "Pooyan Missions".
A world record of 1,609,250 points was set on 16 December 1983.
Its stage theme comes from Felix Arndt's "Desecration Rag".
A remake, Re:Pooyan, was commissioned through Konami's 2022 indie contest.
It was included in Konami Arcade Classics on the PlayStation.
devStory: Tokuro Fujiwara designed it at Konami, which released it in Japan in October 1982, with Stern Electronics distributing it in North America that November. Datasoft published Scott Spanburg's versions for the Atari 8-bit, Commodore 64 and Dragon 32 in 1983, and other versions followed for the Atari 2600, MSX, Apple II, TRS-80 and Famicom. Hamster re-released the arcade game in its Arcade Archives series in 2019.

title: Circus Charlie
description: Circus Charlie (1984) is Konami's arcade game in which Charlie the clown performs six circus acts, from jumping a lion through flaming hoops to swinging between trapezes.
longDescription: Charlie the clown works through six circus acts against the clock, collecting money bags and performing tricks for points, with leftover time paid as a bonus and running out costing a life. He rides a lion through flaming rings, walks a tightrope while jumping monkeys, bounces between trampolines past knife throwers and fire breathers (dolphins in a swimming pool on some sublevels), hops from ball to ball, rides a horse over trampolines and walls, and swings from trapeze to trapeze. After the sixth act the show starts again at a faster pace. A Level Select version lets each act be played only a limited number of times, after which the trapeze act repeats until the lives run out.
trivia: Its music is based on "American Patrol" and "The Blue Danube".
The Famicom and MSX versions drop the trampoline act.
In Konami's Mikie, head-butting the teacher's desk from below three times makes Circus Charlie appear for extra points.
The game has no ending.
Kouta Hirano drew a manga based on it, published from 1999.
devStory: Konami released it in arcades in 1984, with Centuri distributing it in North America in March and the Japanese release following in April, and Game Machine listed it as the third most successful table arcade unit in its 15 May 1984 issue. An MSX version came out the same year, Soft Pro's Famicom version in 1986, adding a harder "B" mode, and a Commodore 64 version in 1987. It was later included in Konami Arcade Classics on the PlayStation and Konami Classics Series: Arcade Hits on the DS.

title: Major Havoc
description: Major Havoc (1984) is Owen Rubin's vector arcade game for Atari, which runs a space shooter, a platform maze and a lunar-landing sequence back to back.
longDescription: Long ago the Vaxxian Empire enslaved most of humanity; it has since collapsed, but robot-controlled Vaxxian space stations remain, and scientists who escaped have cloned the hero Major Havoc to lead a clone army through a wormhole and destroy them. Each round runs three games back to back. First the Catastrofighter fights robot ships, each protected by a buckyball-like force field that must be shot away before the ship can be destroyed. Then it lands on a station by centring itself between moving lines, and Major Havoc goes in on foot, jumping obstacles on the way to the reactor, sabotaging it and escaping before the station explodes, guided by red arrows that read "OUT" on the way back. Each station is harder and gives less time. A game of Breakout in the corner powers the warp system for skipping levels and can earn extra lives.
trivia: Some games name the enemy Vaxxian homeworld "Maynard", after the Massachusetts town where Digital Equipment Corporation, maker of the VAX, was based.
It inspired the MSX game Theseus and served as the basis for Silpheed.
Atari Games' later Xybots was themed after it.
Its warp system is powered by a game of Breakout.
It was released on Microsoft's Game Room in 2010.
devStory: Owen Rubin developed it at Atari, with Mark Cerny designing and tuning some levels after joining about a year in. Atari released it as a dedicated vector cabinet with a roller controller in January 1984, followed in March by a conversion kit for older vector games such as Tempest, which used their own controls, such as Tempest's spinner. Play Meter's Gene Lewin scored it 2 out of 10 because of the cost of the dedicated cabinet. It was not a major commercial success in the West, but it had a significant influence on Japan's computer game industry.

title: Cadash
description: Cadash (1990) is Taito's arcade action-RPG platformer, in which up to four players — fighter, mage, priestess and ninja — on linked cabinets level up while rescuing a kidnapped princess.
longDescription:
Thousands of years ago the demons and monsters of the underground kingdom of Cadash shared the light with humans. Now the Balrog, a demonic wizard born of a human woman, has promised his followers the surface if he can mix his blood with a human king's. He kidnaps Princess Salassa from Deerzar, capital of Dirzir, the strongest human kingdom, and takes her to Castle Cadash for a ritual that would make him invincible, and her father, King Dilsarl, offers his whole kingdom to whoever saves her.

It mixes side-scrolling platforming with role-playing statistics, levels, money and magic. Players kill monsters, collect keys and gather gold and experience, buying items, weapons and armour in villages, against a timer that hourglasses can extend. The fighter has the strongest melee and defence but no magic; the mage has the strongest spells but is the weakest and slowest, and the only one who can easily beat the final boss; the priestess heals and shields; and the ninja is the only true long-range fighter. Two linked cabinets allow four players. The five stages, most with worlds above and below ground, end in Castle Cadash.
trivia: Game Machine named it the most successful table arcade unit in its 1 May 1990 issue.
The Genesis version keeps only the fighter and the mage.
In the arcade, the priestess's Recover Time spell adds 30 seconds in Japan and 60 elsewhere.
Inn prices in the Japanese and US arcade versions rise with every stay, up to 30,000 gold.
Hamster re-released it in its Arcade Archives series in 2023.
devStory:
Hiroshi Tsujino directed and designed it at Taito, with Keisuke Hasegawa producing and music by Pinch-Punch, and Taito released it in Japan in March 1990 and North America in April. Game Machine listed it as the most successful table arcade unit of May 1990, and RePlay gave the North American version a favourable review.

Working Designs translated the 1991 TurboGrafx-16 version, which rebalanced the characters, split levels into rooms and corridors and removed the time limit. The 1992 Genesis version kept only the fighter and mage and was the only one to sell extra lives in shops.

title: The Ninja Warriors
description: The Ninja Warriors (1988) is Taito's side-scrolling beat 'em up played across three screens side by side, in which two androids fight to overthrow a dictator.
longDescription: In a dystopian 1993, the US president Banglar has declared nationwide martial law, and a group of anarchist scientists led by Mulk, judging a direct fight with the military suicidal, build two androids, the red Kunoichi and the blue Ninja, to end his rule. Player one is Kunoichi and player two Ninja, and they fight waves of Banglar's forces across six side-scrolling levels. One button slashes with a kunai at close range, and the other throws a limited supply of shuriken. The cabinet joins three screens — one in the usual place and two lower ones reflected by mirrors on either side — into a single 4:1 picture, comparable to Abel Gance's Polyvision in Napoléon.
trivia: It was the eighth highest-grossing dedicated arcade game in Japan in 1988.
Natsume's 1994 Super NES game followed it, and new games in the series reached the Switch in 2019.
GamesRadar named Kunoichi the best assassin in video game history in 2008.
Taito reused its three-screen cabinet for Darius and Darius II.
Commodore User called it "gorgeous looking".
devStory:
Masaki Ogata directed it at Taito, with Hiroshi Tsujino and Yukiwo Ishikawa designing and music by Hisayoshi Ogura and the in-house band Zuntata. Taito released it in Europe in January 1988, Japan in February and North America in March through Romstar, and Game Machine ranked it third among upright arcade cabinets in April; it was Japan's eighth highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1988. Clare Edgeley of Computer and Video Games, who saw it at the January 1988 ATEI show, compared it to Shinobi and praised its huge screen.

Conversions followed for the Amiga, Atari ST, Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad, and Japan-only versions for the PC Engine and Mega-CD.

title: G-Police
description: G-Police (1997) is Psygnosis's combat flight game set in the domed cities of Jupiter's moon Callisto, where a pilot joins the police to investigate his sister's death.
longDescription:
Earth's resources ran out in 2057, a war over the solar system's resources ended in 2087 with Earth's governments stripped of military power, and corporations took control. In 2097, on the colonised moon Callisto, the war veteran Slater joins the G-Police, formed by Earth's last coalition government to keep order in the colonies, to investigate the apparent suicide of his sister Elaine, which he believes was murder. Gang warfare grows into a conflict between the corporations Krakov and Nanosoft, and Slater learns that pilots' gunships were sabotaged so that Nanosoft could harvest chips in their brains to power AI weapons.

The player flies a VTOL gunship — "a helicopter without the rotors" — through 35 missions, mostly inside urban domes, dogfighting, bombing, escorting ground units and defusing bombs, and scanning vehicles to tell criminals from civilians. The Havoc gunship gives way later to the Venom, and the views range from the cockpit to a bombing view from above.
trivia: Peter Chung, creator of Æon Flux, animated its television advertisement.
The clothing company Diesel designed the police uniforms and appears in the game as an evil corporation.
GamePro called its short draw distance "one of the worst cases of draw-in since 32-bit gaming began".
Its setting was inspired by Blade Runner.
It was runner-up for Computer Gaming World's 1997 Action Game of the Year, behind Quake II.
devStory:
A Psygnosis "microstudio" of about 70 people in Stroud made it, taking its setting from Blade Runner. It was backed by a reported $2.5 million advertising campaign, and Psygnosis released it for the PlayStation in October 1997 and Windows in November, with force feedback, 3D sound and Direct3D support on PC.

Critics praised its detailed cities, cut-scenes and varied missions but criticised the draw distance and controls; EGM scored it as high as 9 out of 10, and Edge called the PC version "a meeting of envelope-pushing code and solid gameplay". It won PC Zone's 1997 award for best use of innovative technology, and G-Police: Weapons of Justice followed in 1999.

title: Colony Wars
description: Colony Wars (1997) is Psygnosis's PlayStation space combat game, in which a pilot of the rebel League of Free Worlds fights the Earth Navy through a branching campaign with several endings.
longDescription:
By the fifth millennium the Solar System has been stripped bare, and colonies on distant worlds resent that most of what they mine goes to Earth. When the Tzar personally destroys a rebellious planet, the other colonies form the League of Free Worlds under "the Father". The game begins months after the League trapped and destroyed a Navy fleet in the asteroid belt near Bennay, with the player joining its combat duty.

The player flies one of seven League starfighters, chosen by High Command for each mission, carrying energy weapons, missiles or torpedoes, some with non-lethal EMP cannons, plus countermeasures and a grapple gun for capturing targets. Missions come in acts of three, and the campaign branches by performance across systems from Gallonigher to Alpha Centauri and Sol; failing a mission does not always lose the war, and the endings range from the Empire's victory to its surrender. A special scene appears only if the campaign is finished without failing a single mission.
trivia: The developers originally planned to let players choose between the League and the Earth Empire.
The mission tree was designed to hide mission failure.
Edge dismissed it as "little more than a 3D interpretation of Asteroids", while IGN gave it 9.3.
It was runner-up for EGM's Best PlayStation Game of 1997, behind Castlevania: Symphony of the Night.
Colony Wars: Vengeance followed in 1998 and Red Sun in 2000.
devStory:
Mike Ellis designed it and co-wrote it with Damon Fairclough, Mike Anthony programmed it and Tim Wright, also known for Wipeout, wrote the music. The team first planned to let players fight for either side but dropped this to build a larger campaign, and hid mission failure by moving the player straight on to the next branch. Psygnosis released it in November 1997, and it sold more than 150,000 copies in the US.

It averaged 91 on Metacritic. EGM made it Game of the Month, Crispin Boyer calling it "a breathtaking epic", and GamePro said it "easily ranks as the best space-combat game on the PlayStation", while Edge was unimpressed.

title: Um Jammer Lammy
description: Um Jammer Lammy (1999) is NanaOn-Sha's follow-up to PaRappa the Rapper, in which a shy guitarist plays her way through a day of mishaps to reach her band's first concert.
longDescription:
Lammy, a shy left-handed guitarist, leads the band MilkCan with Katy Kat on bass and vocals and Ma-san on drums, and must reach the band's first concert on time despite a run of mishaps. She feels confident only with a guitar in her hands, real or imagined, and along the way helps Chief Puddle put out a fire, delivers babies for Nurse Cathy Piller, rescues Captain Fussenpepper's plane and builds a new guitar from a tree with the beaver Paul Chuck, before facing Teriyaki Yoko's evil twin, Rammy.

As in PaRappa, Lammy trades turns with a teacher, hitting the symbols scrolling across the top of the screen or freestyling for extra points; ranks run from Good and Cool down to Bad and Awful, and playing well enough brings Fever mode and big bonuses. Sound morphers such as flanger, wah-wah and distortion unlock from the second stage, and the whammy bar is on the shoulder buttons. Co-op and versus modes unlock as stages are cleared, and finishing Lammy's story opens a PaRappa side story.
trivia: An arcade version with a guitar controller, Um Jammer Lammy NOW!, was released in Japan.
GameRevolution called its story "the most obtuse, disjointed, drug-induced mess of a story that has ever been conceived, period."
In Japan and Europe Lammy slips on a banana peel and goes to a Hell-like world; the North American version sends her to a volcanic island instead.
Fernandes Guitars sold a replica of Lammy's guitar in 2000.
The arcade version was thought lost until a cabinet owned by Jonathan Ross was documented in 2023.
devStory:
Masaya Matsuura designed it at NanaOn-Sha and composed the music with Yoshihisa Suzuki and Shigeyoshi Kawagoe, with art by Rodney Alan Greenblat. Matsuura chose a spin-off over a direct sequel and rock over rap, and Greenblat, who disagreed with both and whose idea of a goth theme was rejected, was outvoted; Lammy's look was influenced by Natalie Imbruglia. Matsuura made it deliberately hard after complaints that PaRappa was too easy.

Sony released it in Japan on 18 March 1999 and North America that August. Critics praised its sound and originality but found the story confusing and the difficulty high. It won Best Puzzle/Trivia/Parlor Game and Outstanding Achievement in Sound at the E3 1999 Game Critics Awards.

title: Brave Fencer Musashi
description: Brave Fencer Musashi (1998) is Square's 3D action RPG, in which a young swordsman summoned to another world must stay rested — or fall asleep on his feet — while defending the Allucaneet Kingdom.
longDescription:
Princess Fillet summons Musashi, reincarnated from a legendary hero, to the Allucaneet Kingdom to stop the Thirstquencher Empire, and gives him the sword Fusion; he must also recover Lumina, the Sword of Luminescence. Most of the townsfolk, Fillet included, are kidnapped, and his search takes him past half-vampire, half-zombie Vambees, a duel with his rival Kojiro, a false Fillet who turns out to be a disguised thief, and finally the empire's floating base, the Soda Fountain.

Fusion, a katana-like blade, chains combos and absorbs Bincho Energy or an enemy's skill, while the large Lumina gains elemental powers from five Scrolls. Rescued townsfolk teach new techniques, berries from Minku creatures raise maximum health, and pieces of Legendary Armor grant climbing and double jumps. A day-night cycle changes what townsfolk and creatures do, and Musashi tires over time: without sleep he fights worse and may nod off, and only inns restore him fully. A toy shop sells action figures, with new stock in each chapter.
trivia: In North America it came with a demo of Final Fantasy VIII.
Several reviewers compared it to The Legend of Zelda.
Its working title was Musashiden.
A playable demo was shown at the Spring 1998 Tokyo Game Show.
Musashi: Samurai Legend followed on the PS2 in 2005.
devStory:
Executive producer Hironobu Sakaguchi said the idea came up in February 1997. Yoichi Yoshimoto directed it, Yusuke Hirata produced, Koichi Ogawa wrote it, Tetsuya Nomura designed the characters and Tsuyoshi Sekito, in his first work for Square, composed the music. Kojiro is based on the swordsman Sasaki Kojirō. For the English release, names based on alcohol were changed to sodas.

Square released it in Japan on 16 July 1998, where it sold about 648,803 copies that year, and in North America on 12 November. It scored 81 on Metacritic, with praise for its graphics, action and soundtrack. Its team went on to help make Final Fantasy XI.

title: Breath of Fire III
description: Breath of Fire III (1997) is Capcom's PlayStation RPG and the first in the series with 3D environments, in which Ryu, the last of the dragon Brood, learns why his people were wiped out.
longDescription:
Miners find a preserved baby dragon, Ryu, the last of the Brood, who turns into a boy and is taken in by the thieves Rei and Teepo. After a job for Loki goes wrong, the horse-men brothers Balio and Sunder burn their home, and Ryu's journey brings him companions: Nina, a winged princess of Wyndia; Momo, an inventor's daughter who studies chrysm; Peco, an onion-like plant creature; and Garr, a warrior of the Guardians, who reveals that they wiped out the Brood on the orders of the goddess Myria. Years later, Garr asks Ryu's forgiveness and they seek the truth behind the genocide together, and Myria offers him a choice between peaceful seclusion and destruction.

Characters are 2D sprites in rotating 3D environments, each with a field ability for puzzles and hidden areas. Battles are turn-based with a party of three in formation. Ryu takes dragon forms by combining chrysms, party members train under Masters to learn skills and shift their stats, a Fairy Village can be built up for items and mini-games, and fishing tracks each catch's species and size.
trivia: It was the first Breath of Fire game with voice acting.
It sold at least 656,297 copies on the PlayStation.
A trailer was included on a Japanese Resident Evil 2 demo disc.
Garr is called Garland in Japanese, and Peco is Pecoros.
Sophia's song "Machi" was planned for an opening animation that was dropped.
devStory:
Makoto Ikehara directed and wrote it at Capcom's Development Studio 3, with Tatsuya Yoshikawa drawing the sprites and a jazz-influenced score by Yoshino Aoki and Akari Kaida, who also sang the ending song, "Pure Again". It was the first game in the series with 3D environments. Capcom released it in Japan on 11 September 1997, where it sold 425,497 copies that year, and in North America in May 1998.

Reviewers praised its craftsmanship, characters, sprites and dragon transformations, and criticised its familiar story, long loading times, frequent battles and soundtrack. It averaged 74% on GameRankings. A PSP version followed in 2005.

title: Blackthorne
description: Blackthorne (1994) is Blizzard's cinematic platformer in the style of Another World and Flashback, in which Kyle returns to his home planet with a shotgun to overthrow the tyrant Sarlac.
longDescription:
On the planet Tuul, the ruler Thoros, unable to choose between his two sons, killed himself in the desert, and his body became a light stone and a dark stone; the people of the darkstone, who rejected theirs, were turned into monsters by it, and their ruler Sarlac attacked the lightstone kingdom of Androth. King Vlaros sent his son Kyle to Earth with the lightstone. Twenty years later Kyle, a soldier and mercenary, is called back by the magician Galadril to kill Sarlac and reclaim his throne.

In large, maze-like levels Kyle runs, climbs and hunts for keys and items, and fights gunfights with a pump-action shotgun that his Androthi allies upgrade. Both he and the enemies can press themselves against the wall to let bullets pass, and he can fire behind himself without turning round. The 17 levels cross four areas, the Androth mines, the Karrellian forests and swamps, the Wasteland desert and Shadow Keep, and enemies grow stronger as he does.
trivia: Early sprites were rotoscoped, using more than 1,000 frames.
Kyle is named after Kyle Reese in The Terminator.
Electronic Gaming Monthly made the Super NES version its Game of the Month.
In some European countries it was released as Blackhawk.
It was included in the Blizzard Arcade Collection in 2021.
devStory:
Blizzard made it, inspired by Another World and Flashback, with Ronald Millar Sr. designing, Frank Pearce Jr. and Patrick Wyatt among the programmers and Glenn Stafford composing; Jim Lee drew the Super NES cover. Interplay released it for the Super NES in September 1994 and MS-DOS that December, and a 32X version by Paradox Development added a fifth area of snowy mountains in 1995.

EGM made the Super NES version its Game of the Month, praising its dark tone, animation and the option to kill prisoners after questioning them, and Next Generation called the PC version "one of the best arcade-style games the PC has ever seen". Blizzard later gave it away free on Battle.net.

title: Dead or Alive
description: Dead or Alive (1996) is Tecmo's 3D fighting game on Sega's Model 2 hardware, built around a hold button that catches attacking limbs, which helped the company back to profit.
longDescription:
DOATEC stages the Dead or Alive World Combat Championship, and the runaway kunoichi Kasumi enters to avenge her brother Hayate, crippled by their uncle Raidou; by leaving her village without permission she has made herself a fugitive under ninja law. The cast also includes Bayman, Gen Fu, Jann Lee, Leifang, Ryu Hayabusa, Tina Armstrong and Zack, with Raidou as the boss.

It borrows from Virtua Fighter but puts speed and counters first, favouring simple commands and reactions over long combos. In place of the usual guard, a hold button catches an attacking limb, with offensive and defensive holds; it was the first fighting game in which each attack type had its own counter. The edges of the arena are danger zones laced with explosives that launch fighters into juggles unless they roll clear. The Saturn version added tournament and training modes, and the PlayStation version added Ayane and Bass Armstrong.
trivia: Tecmo was near bankruptcy and wanted a hit to rival Virtua Fighter.
The Saturn version topped the Japanese charts.
Game Machine named it Japan's most popular arcade game in January 1997.
An enhanced version was included in Dead or Alive Ultimate for the Xbox in 2004.
Complex ranked it the seventh-best fighting game of all time in 2011.
devStory:
By 1995 Tecmo had lost money for three years running after heavy investment in sports games, and was near bankruptcy. Management asked Tomonobu Itagaki for a fighting or racing game like Virtua Fighter or Daytona USA, and he chose fighting, aiming for something fast and provocative; all its animation was motion-captured. It ran on Sega's Model 2 board, the hardware of Virtua Fighter 2, was shown in February 1996 and reached arcades in November.

Tecmo turned a loss of $5.2 million in 1995 into a profit of $9.2 million in 1996. The Saturn version of 1997 sold out its first 92,000 copies on release day, and the PlayStation version of 1998 was the first port of a Sega arcade game to Sony's console. Reviewers praised the hold system, while its exaggerated breast physics drew criticism.

title: Smash TV
description: Smash TV (1990) is Eugene Jarvis's twin-stick arcade shooter set on a violent 1999 game show, where contestants gun down waves of enemies for cash and prizes.
longDescription:
In a dystopian 1999, contestants on "the most violent game show of all time" fight through arenas as waves of enemies pour in through doors on all four walls. Between kills they grab money, weapons, temporary power-ups and gift-wrapped prizes such as toasters and VCRs. Exits open once an arena is cleared, and after the first arena of each level a map lets players choose their route, though they cannot go back. Each level ends with a boss, and the final boss is the sadistic host himself.

Like Jarvis's Robotron: 2084, it is played with two joysticks, one to move and one to shoot. Two players work together, though whoever collects the most cash and prizes earns an extra reward at the end of each level. Collecting enough keys opens the bonus Pleasure Dome, which was added after players complained that the first release could not be finished.
trivia: Its influences include RoboCop and The Running Man.
It won the AMOA's most innovative game award in 1990.
Total Carnage (1992), named after one of the host's catchphrases, shares much of its play but is not a sequel.
The ZX Spectrum version scored 97% in Crash and a Crash Smash award.
The Xbox Live Arcade version was the first to support online two-player play.
devStory:
Eugene Jarvis designed it at Williams and Mark Turmell programmed it; Turmell had left a cancelled Hasbro interactive-movie project to join Williams, and hired the artist John Tobias, with Tim Coman. Jon Hey composed the music, designed the sound and wrote the script, and Paul Heitsch voiced the announcer. Williams released it in April 1990, then sent a revised version with the Pleasure Dome.

It won the AMOA's 1990 award for most innovative game, and EGM later ranked it the sixth-best arcade game of all time. Beam Software and Probe made the console versions, titled Super Smash TV, and Ocean published the home computer versions.

title: Rampart
description: Rampart (1990) is Atari Games' arcade castle game, in which players rebuild their walls with Tetris-like pieces between cannon battles — a precursor of tower defence.
longDescription: Seen from above and played with a trackball, the game alternates between a timed building phase and a timed combat phase. It opens with the computer walling off one castle for the player, whose castles provide cannons to place inside the territory. In single-player games the cannons fire slow cannonballs at a fleet of ships shelling the walls, so targets must be led; in multiplayer, players fire at each other's walls across rivers. When combat ends, any area no longer fully enclosed is lost along with its cannons, and the building phase hands out Tetris-like pieces to patch the gaps or enclose more castles, each of which brings another cannon. Repairs are tricky because the pieces are usually bigger than the holes, and a player with no castle enclosed at the end of building loses. Defeated commanders walk the plank or are beheaded.
trivia: Computer and Video Games gave the arcade version 93%.
Konami's Famicom version added seven training levels and three difficulty settings.
Nintendo Power ranked the Game Boy version the fourth best Game Boy game of 1993.
The Super NES and MS-DOS versions let players trade cannons for power-ups.
A PlayStation 3 version with online multiplayer came out in 2007.
devStory:
John Salwitz and Dave Ralston created it at Atari Games, Salwitz programming and Ralston drawing the art, with music by Don Diekneite and Brad Fuller. It had a limited US release in October 1990 and a wide one in February 1991, with Namco distributing it in Japan. Julian Rignall of Computer and Video Games gave it 93%, and MegaTech gave the Mega Drive version 90% and a Hyper Game Award.

Versions followed on the NES, Super NES, Lynx, Game Boy, Master System, Mega Drive and home computers; the NES one, planned for Tengen, which lacked a Nintendo licence, went to Jaleco instead. Its defence of built structures, repaired between waves of attack, influenced the tower defence games of a decade later.

title: Thrust
description: Thrust (1986) is Jeremy Smith's gravity game for the BBC Micro, in which a ship tows a heavy pod out of a planet's caves on a swinging tractor beam.
longDescription:
The ship rotates and thrusts, and has to lift a pod out of the caves with its tractor beam and carry it into space, the two joined by a stiff rod. Gravity and inertia act on both, so the pair can swing and spin out of control, and touching the cave walls with either is fatal. Turrets fire shots that kill in one hit but can each be destroyed with one shot. Fuel, also collected with the tractor beam, runs down with every manoeuvre, and the shield uses fuel and stops the ship firing. Later levels add doors opened by shooting a panel.

Shooting the planet's reactor silences the turrets for a while, and enough hits send it critical, giving ten seconds to escape; leaving with the pod scores more than leaving without. After the six levels, the cycle repeats with reversed gravity, then with invisible planets and walls that show only when the shield is up, then with both, and hidden messages appear after levels 24, 48 and 72.
trivia: Its play was heavily inspired by Atari's Gravitar.
Firebird's budget Commodore 64 version, at £1.99, topped the Gallup all-formats chart.
Hidden messages on the BBC Micro version include "Support Hotol" and "Physics is fun".
Superior's launch competition offered a trophy, £250 and a book by Patrick Moore.
Bjørn Stabell cited it as an influence on XPilot.
devStory: Jeremy Smith wrote it for the BBC Micro, inspired heavily by Atari's Gravitar, and Superior Software published it in 1986; Rob Hubbard wrote the music for the Commodore 64 and Atari ST versions. Superior licensed conversions to Firebird, whose £1.99 Commodore 64 version came out first and topped the Gallup all-formats chart; nine weeks later Superior's full-price BBC version entered the BBC top ten at number one. Smith went on to co-write Exile with Peter Irvin in 1988, and died in an accident four years later. Thrust II followed in 1988.

title: Repton
description: Repton (1985) is Tim Tyler's BBC Micro puzzle game of diamonds and falling rocks, a calmer, more puzzle-minded cousin of Boulder Dash.
longDescription: Repton digs through an underground maze collecting every diamond before time runs out, including some locked in safes that open when he picks up a key. Falling rocks and monsters hatched from eggs can trap or kill him. There are 12 levels, and passwords let players skip ahead, though finishing with passwords brings a message daring the player to do it without them. Compared with Boulder Dash it is calmer and more ordered, with more emphasis on solving puzzles than on arcade improvisation. Its theme tune is George Botsford's "Black and White Rag", the Pot Black theme.
trivia: Tyler was inspired by a review of Boulder Dash but had never played it.
Its theme tune is "Black and White Rag" by George Botsford.
The first release of Repton 2 was impossible to complete because a diamond was hidden under a transporter.
Repton Infinity (1988) let players rewrite how every object behaves in a language called Reptol.
A lost 1988 Repton by a teenage programmer was rediscovered and released as Repton: The Lost Realms in 2010.
devStory: Tim Tyler wrote it for the BBC Micro and Acorn Electron, inspired by a review of Boulder Dash he had read without ever playing the game, and Superior Software released it in the summer of 1985; he took about a month over each of the first two games. Repton 2 followed that November, with spirits, skulls and transporters and no passwords at all, and Retro Gamer later called it the hardest to complete; the first release could not be finished because a diamond was hidden under a transporter. Matthew Atkinson's Repton 3 (1986) took eight months and added a map editor, and the series sold about 125,000 copies by 1990.

title: Mercenary
description: Mercenary (1985) is Paul Woakes's open-ended 3D vector adventure, in which a stranded pilot plays two warring factions against each other to earn a way off the planet Targ.
longDescription: On the way to the Gamma System of Damocles, the player crash-lands on the planet Targ, where the native Palyars are fighting a civil war against the invading Mechanoids, and has to find a way off. The world is explored in real-time 3D vector graphics, vast and sparse, and the tasks can be done in any order. As a "hired gun", the player can work for either faction, each wanting the other's installations destroyed and resources captured, or play them against each other to earn money for an escape. There are several ways to leave, and strategies can be combined to escape with the wealth intact. Benson, a "9th generation PC", gives advice on a scrolling ticker, and his sarcastic remarks supply much of the humour.
trivia: Zzap!64 gave it 97% and a Gold Medal.
It was also released as Mercenary: Escape from Targ.
Benson's sarcastic messages provide much of the humour.
The Second City expansion changed the sky colour on every system, from pink on the Amiga to yellow on the Spectrum.
A freeware Windows remake, MDDClone, was made with the original Novagen team's agreement.
devStory:
Paul Woakes and Bruce Jordan designed it, with art by Peter Gudynas, and Novagen released it for the Atari 8-bit computers in 1985, followed by Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, Atari ST and Amiga versions. Zzap!64 gave it 97% and a Gold Medal and Crash 96%, and Antic called the Atari graphics "awesome".

The Second City expansion of 1986 moved the action to the planet's other side, with red ground, a new city layout and new puzzles. Damocles (1990) and Mercenary III (1992) followed on the ST and Amiga, and Edge ranked the original 67th in its 2000 top 100.

title: Driller
description: Driller (1987) is Incentive Software's first-person 3D puzzle game, the first built on the Freescape engine, in which a probe must place eighteen drilling rigs to stop a moon from exploding.
longDescription:
Humanity left a ruined Earth for Evath, a habitable planet with two moons, Mitral and Tricuspid. The Ketars, outcasts banished from Evath, have abandoned Mitral in an unstable state, and it will explode within four hours, destroying the planet below. The trainee Lesleigh Skerrit, whose grandfather was wrongly banished as a Ketar, is offered promotion to the Driller Federation's elite for saving it, by guiding the probe "Last Hope" to place eighteen drilling rigs that let the gas escape.

Each of the eighteen regions of Mitral, which is shaped like a rhombicuboctahedron, needs a rig placed where at least half its gas can escape, found through clues in the landscape — an X marks the spot in the first — and by trial and error. Security systems left behind by the Ketars attack on sight; some can be shot, others must be switched off. The regions are platforms above the moon's true surface, and the probe can only rise and lower slightly on its hydraulics, so driving off an edge strands it. One area holds a garage with a hovering vehicle that can explore and fight but cannot place rigs.
trivia: In the US it was called Space Station Oblivion.
Orson Scott Card called its story a "thinly veiled excuse" for the 3D graphics, but still praised the game.
Mitral, the moon it is set on, is shaped like a rhombicuboctahedron.
Amstrad Action gave it 96%.
devStory:
Chris and Ian Andrew of Major Developments designed it as the first game on the Freescape engine, which drew filled-polygon 3D worlds the player could move through freely, looking up and down and turning, rare for 3D games of the time; a Your Sinclair reviewer said it took a year to build. Incentive Software released it in 1987.

CRASH gave it 97% and its readers voted it the best game of 1987, Zzap!64 gave it a Gold Medal, and Amstrad Action named it a Mastergame and later ranked it the fourth-best game of all time. The engine went on to power Dark Side, Total Eclipse and Castle Master.

title: Carrier Command
description: Carrier Command (1988) is Realtime Games' filled-polygon strategy game, in which a robotic aircraft carrier and its aircraft and amphibious tanks race an enemy carrier to claim 64 islands.
longDescription:
Scientists build two robotic aircraft carriers to colonise an archipelago of sixty-four islands, and terrorists seize the more advanced one to conquer it. From the ACC Epsilon, which has its own weapons and an automatic repair system, the player commands up to eight Manta aircraft and eight Walrus amphibious vehicles, four of each at once, flying or driving them directly. Neutral, tree-covered islands are claimed by dropping a command centre builder from a Walrus, and enemy islands captured by firing a virus pod into the front of their command centre. Vehicles that stray too far from the carrier lose contact and are destroyed. Every system can be repaired except the superstructure and the repair system itself, and if the superstructure is wrecked the game is lost.

It mixes real-time strategy with vehicle simulation, drawn in filled-polygon 3D with full 360-degree views on every version except the Commodore 64, which is top-down.
trivia: The Games Machine ranked it the number one game of 1988 and gave the Atari ST version 98%.
The team wrote it in 68000 assembly because C was too slow for 3D on 8 MHz machines; Ian Oliver recalled they "slept under our desks".
Bohemia Interactive remade it in 2012 as Carrier Command: Gaea Mission.
Andy Onions made the Spectrum and Amstrad versions single-handedly.
Carrier Command 2 came out in 2021.
devStory:
Realtime Games of Leeds, which had converted Starglider to 8-bit computers for Rainbird, was invited to pitch an original 16-bit game; a brainstorm at Rainbird's London office produced a half-page outline about a carrier attacking an archipelago, which programmers Ian Oliver and Graeme Baird expanded. They built it first on the Atari ST, writing terrain, flight dynamics and AI in 68000 assembly because C was too slow, and generated the islands from seed values so 64 bases would fit in memory; the work ran far over schedule. Dave Lowe and David Whittaker wrote the music. Rainbird released it for the ST and Amiga in 1988.

The Games Machine gave the ST version 98% and ranked it the best game of 1988, and Crash gave the Spectrum version 97%. Battle Command followed, and Hostile Waters (2001) was inspired by it.

title: Laser Squad
description: Laser Squad (1988) is Julian Gollop's turn-based tactics game for the ZX Spectrum, with action points, line of sight and hidden enemies — the direct ancestor of X-COM.
longDescription: Before each mission players spend a limited budget on weapons and armour, then deploy their squad on a grid and take turns moving, shooting and picking up objects with action points. Aimed shots cost the most and hit most often, snap and auto shots cost less and miss more, and line of sight decides who can see whom, with spotting an enemy giving a chance to fire. In one-player games the computer's movements stay hidden. Heavily loaded soldiers tire, and a unit that sees teammates die can panic and slip out of control. Each mission has a turn limit, and victory needs 100 victory points from objectives, kills or both. The scenarios include assassinating the arms maker Sterner Regnix in "The Assassins", destroying the Omni Corporation's computers in "Moonbase Assault" and rescuing captured squad members from the Metallix mines.
trivia: A demo of Laser Squad 2 became the starting point for UFO: Enemy Unknown, published by MicroProse.
Computer and Video Games gave it 97%.
Its hidden movement and line-of-sight rules were inspired by board games.
Commodore Force ranked it second among the top 100 Commodore 64 games in 1993.
Laser Squad Nemesis revived the name in 2002 as a play-by-email game.
devStory:
Julian Gollop began it after Rebelstar and founded Target Games with his brother Nick to make it; hidden movement and line of sight came from board games, and difficulty levels were added because he felt his earlier games were too easy. Julian programmed the Spectrum version and Nick converted it to the Commodore 64. The 8-bit release of 1988 had three scenarios, with more sold by mail order, and Blade Software took over publishing; Krisalis made the Amiga, Atari ST and PC versions.

Computer and Video Games gave it 97%, and Your Sinclair called it "a sophisticated strategy wargame... on a par with Elite for thinking warmongers". It is described as one of Gollop's most influential games and was instrumental to the X-COM series.

title: Zarch
description: Zarch (1987) is David Braben's solid-3D shooter for the Acorn Archimedes, in which a mouse-controlled lander stops alien Seeders spreading a virus across the landscape.
longDescription: The lander has a single downward thruster that lifts it, stopping above a flight ceiling, and it pitches and yaws but cannot roll, so it must tilt to move, and tilting too far flips it over into a crash. It has to be level to land and must return to the launchpad to refuel, where it is vulnerable, and a single shot destroys it. Alien Seeders spread a red virus that turns green land brown and red and mutates trees; later waves add fighters that attack the player, and a fast high-altitude bomber. Every shot costs a point, smart missiles and bombs are limited, and the end of each wave pays a bonus for uninfected land. A radar shows the whole landscape, though destroyed scanning towers leave blind spots. The controls are notoriously sensitive: moving the mouse during takeoff can wreck the lander on the pad.
trivia: It began as Lander, a demo bundled with Archimedes computers.
ACE gave it 979, its highest score at the time, under the headline "SOLID 3D - the future of games?"
Amiga Power ranked its port, Virus, fifth on its 1991 list of the best games of all time.
A wave's bonus depends on how much land is still uninfected.
Its landscape engine was reused for the tank game Conqueror.
devStory:
David Braben had an Acorn development machine for two weeks in January 1987 and wrote a demo, Lander, in ARM code in under three months; bundled with new Archimedes computers, it had no enemies, scoring for destroyed trees and buildings. Zarch grew from it, using the 256-colour mode, filled light-sourced polygons, shadows projected onto the ground and particle effects for thrust, explosions and the spreading virus, with hills generated from pseudo-random sine waves. Superior Software released it in 1987, and ACE gave it 979, its highest score at the time.

The 1988 ports, called Virus, came to the Atari ST and Amiga, coded by Braben, the PC, coded by Chris Sawyer, and the Spectrum.

title: Midwinter
description: Midwinter (1989) is Mike Singleton's frozen-world strategy RPG, in which the player recruits 32 islanders, each with their own history, to resist an invading general across a vast 3D island.
longDescription:
Around 2040 a meteorite strikes Burma and plunges the world into an impact winter. By 2099 the island of Midwinter — 160,000 square miles of snow, formed by volcanic activity in the Azores — is home to the Free Villages, and General Masters is trying to take it by force. John Stark, commander of the Free Villages Peace Force, survives an ambush with a few grenades, a sniper rifle and skis, and must alert the islanders, recruit allies and wage a guerrilla war, destroying Masters's headquarters at Shining Hollow before he takes the main settlements.

The island is drawn in shaded 3D polygons. Each of the 32 recruits gets two hours of game time in turn, and their histories decide who can recruit whom: Stark can win over his fiancée, Nurse Maddocks, but not the jealous Grazzini, and the saboteur Professor Kristiansen, the only one who can break the enemy's radio jamming, will only join for his grandson or his grandson's girlfriend. Recruits travel by ski, snowmobile, cable car and hang glider. They can be injured but not killed: a wounded arm spoils sniping and a wounded leg slows skiing, and the badly hurt must fire a flare and be carried to the nearest building, which may be in enemy hands.
trivia: Recruits can be injured but not killed.
Eurogamer called it "a priceless transitional specimen in the fossil record of gaming".
Harder settings add mortar fire guided by spotter planes, and attack aircraft.
Enemy units can be routed by killing their commander.
A fan remaster in Unreal Engine 5 entered early access in 2026.
devStory:
Mike Singleton designed it at Maelstrom Games, with George Williamson, Dave Gautrey and David Ollman programming the Amiga, Atari ST and DOS versions and art by Andrew Elkerton. MicroProse published it on its Rainbird label, with a novella in the manual telling the backstory.

It was very well received: Zzap gave the Amiga version 97% and a Gold Medal, and Amiga Format a Gold award. Edge later called it an "enormous accomplishment". Midwinter II: Flames of Freedom followed in 1991.

title: The Legend of the Mystical Ninja
description: The Legend of the Mystical Ninja (1991) is Konami's Super Famicom adventure, the first Ganbare Goemon game released in the West, mixing town exploration, side-scrolling action and minigames.
longDescription:
A ghost woman haunting a temple in Oedo turns out to be Kurobei, a ninja cat, and leads Goemon and Ebisumaru — Kid Ying and Dr. Yang in the West — into a hunt for Princess Yuki, the Emperor's daughter. The trail runs past the Otafu Army's anachronistic amusement park on Awaji Island, a palace in Iga guarded by clockwork ninjas and the Dragon Pond in Izumo.

Each stage, called a Warlock Zone, begins with a town for shopping, gathering information, learning techniques and playing minigames — air hockey, trivia, dice, a lottery and a recreation of the first level of Gradius — and ends with a side-scrolling section and a boss. Short-range weapons have three levels, extended by grey cats dropped by enemies, thrown weapons cost money and bombs can be bought or won. Each hero learns four Judo abilities, from an animal companion that rams enemies to temporary flight. Two players can play together, and can ride piggyback, one moving and jumping while the other attacks.
trivia: Electronic Gaming Monthly said it "didn't catch on too much in the U.S." but was popular in Japan, where it sold 521,205 copies.
IGN ranked it 32nd among the top 100 SNES games.
It is in the book 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die.
A Japan-only Game Boy Advance version came out in 2005.
It was on the Japanese Super Famicom Mini.
devStory:
Shigeharu Umezaki designed it at Konami, with music by Kazuhiko Uehara and Harumi Ueko. Konami released it in Japan on 19 July 1991 as Ganbare Goemon: Yuki-hime Kyūshutsu Emaki, in North America in February 1992 and in Europe in 1994. It was the first Ganbare Goemon game released in the West.

It sold 51,680 copies in its first week in Japan and 521,205 in all. Western critics rated it highly — Computer and Video Games gave it 93 and Super Play 90% — though EGM said it did not catch on in the US. Three more Super Famicom sequels followed.

sources.title: The Legend of the Mystical Ninja

title: Super Cobra
description: Super Cobra (1981) is Konami's follow-up to Scramble, a scrolling shooter in which a fuel-hungry helicopter fights through caverns to a base and carries off its loot.
longDescription: The player flies a helicopter through scrolling caverns, using a laser and bombs against defences, tanks and UFOs, with the goal of breaking through ten Super Cobra defence systems. Fuel drains steadily and is topped up by destroying fuel tanks. After the ten levels comes a base, which the helicopter must get through to carry off the loot.
trivia: It runs on the same arcade hardware as Scramble.
Stern built 12,337 cabinets in the US by October 1981, its third best-selling arcade game after Berzerk and Scramble.
Entex made a standalone tabletop handheld version.
It was paired with Scramble on Konami Arcade Classics for the PlayStation in 1999.
Hamster re-released it in its Arcade Archives series in 2020.
devStory:
Konami made it as a spiritual successor to Scramble, on the same arcade hardware, and released it in August 1981, licensing it to three foreign companies; Stern distributed it in North America and built 12,337 cabinets for the US by early October, about four months, making it Stern's third best-selling arcade game after Berzerk and Scramble.

Parker Brothers converted it to the Atari 2600, Atari 5200, ColecoVision, Intellivision, Odyssey² and Atari 8-bit computers, and Entex made an Adventure Vision version and a tabletop handheld. Arcade Express gave the Adventure Vision version 9/10, saying it "represents the state-of-the-art of scrolling shoot-outs", and the 2600 version won a Certificate of Merit at the 1983 Arkie Awards.

title: Tutankham
description: Tutankham (1982) is Konami's scrolling maze shooter set in the tomb of Tutankhamun, where the explorer's laser fires only left and right.
longDescription: An explorer loots the horizontally scrolling, maze-like tomb of Tutankhamun, guarded by asps, vultures, parrots, bats, dragons and curses, any of which kills on contact. The laser fires only left and right, and each level or life brings one screen-clearing flash bomb. Warp zones teleport the explorer around the level, which enemies cannot use. Keys open locked doors, but only one can be carried at a time, so getting a second means backtracking. Treasures are worth bonus points, the laser stops working when the timer runs out, and the big exit door ends the level, converting remaining time into points.
trivia: It appeared in a January 1983 LIFE photograph of six video game record holders.
Gauntlet and Time Bandit drew on its maze-shooter design.
Konami's King's Valley (1985) is considered its spiritual successor in Japan and shares its end-of-level music.
The DS compilation Konami Classics Series: Arcade Hits renames it Horror Maze.
Time Bandit's working title was Pharaoh.
devStory:
Konami showed it at Europe's ATE and IMA amusement shows in January 1982 and released it in Japan and North America that July, with Stern distributing it in the US. H. Tanigaki is credited as its designer. It topped the Play Meter charts in October 1982 and stayed in the top ten until January 1983, and that month LIFE photographed its record holder, Mark Robichek, among six game champions. Computer and Video Games later praised it as the first game to combine adventure with "frenetic" shooting.

Parker Brothers' home versions, released in June 1983, sold well, and Video's Kunkel and Katz called the Atari 2600 one "a superb translation".

title: Moon Cresta
description: Moon Cresta (1980) is a fixed shooter in which the player docks the three stages of a rocket together in mid-game, gaining firepower but becoming a bigger target.
longDescription: The player starts with a small ship carrying a single laser. After the first four waves it docks with a second stage, adding two lasers, and two waves later with a third, adding two more for five in all, but the combined ship is a bigger target. Each stage counts as a life, and misaligning a docking destroys the stage being docked. After eight waves the player returns to the first stage and the cycle repeats; if a stage has been lost, the next docking comes after only four waves. The game ends when all three stages are destroyed.
trivia: Centuri released it in North America as Eagle, adding an eagle-shaped enemy, with the slogan "The Eagle has landed".
It was the fourth highest-earning arcade game of 1980 in Japan.
Gremlin's Super Moon Cresta kit let enemies fire back.
Eurogamer gave it 9/10 in 2007.
PlatinumGames released a new entry, Sol Cresta, in 2022.
devStory:
Jorudan developed it, with Shigeki Fujiwara as designer, on hardware listed as Namco's Galaxian board, and Nichibutsu released it in Japan on 15 February 1980. It was the fourth highest-earning arcade game of 1980 in Japan, behind Pac-Man, Galaxian and Crazy Climber, and helped establish Nichibutsu in video games. In North America, Gremlin/Sega distributed it, and Centuri sold it as Eagle.

Incentive Software published versions for the Spectrum, Commodore 64, Amstrad and Dragon 32, and Crash gave its Spectrum version 90%. Retro Gamer noted that its multiple-ship mechanic came before Galaga's. The series continued with Terra Cresta in 1985.

title: Atic Atac
description: Atic Atac (1983) is Ultimate Play the Game's castle maze for the ZX Spectrum, in which a wizard, knight or serf hunts for the three pieces of the Golden Key of ACG.
longDescription: Trapped in a castle of several floors, linked by staircases, timed trapdoors and secret passages, the player must find the three pieces of the Golden Key of ACG to escape. The view is from above, with the action shown side-on. There are three characters to choose from — Wizard, Knight or Serf — each with a different weapon, a different grip on the floor and a secret passage only they can use. Up to three items can be carried at once, some always in the same place and others placed at random, from coloured keys for matching doors to items that deal with particular enemies and red herrings. Common enemies appear when a room is entered and are destroyed by touching them, at a cost in health, while some can only be repelled with the right item. Health drains as the player moves and returns with food, and each death leaves a gravestone for the rest of the game.
trivia: Computer and Video Games called it "the best yet from Ultimate".
It was a major inspiration for the TV show Knightmare, whose producer saw that a Spectrum could run a compelling adventure.
It was included in Rare Replay in 2015.
Retro Gamer readers voted it the eighth best game of all time.
Rare's Gregg Mayles said Grabbed by the Ghoulies was not inspired by it, despite its haunted-house theme.
devStory: Tim and Chris Stamper, with Tim's wife Carol, founded Ultimate Play the Game in Ashby-de-la-Zouch in 1982; Tim wrote Atic Atac and Chris designed the graphics, with the company keeping graphics and gameplay teams separate and working seven days a week. Ultimate's second game to need 48K, it came out for the ZX Spectrum in 1983, entered the chart at number five in November and replaced Valhalla at number one a fortnight later. Crash gave it 92%, praising its "marvellous" detail, and Computer and Video Games called it "the best yet from Ultimate". A BBC Micro version followed in 1985.

title: Hyper Sports
description: Hyper Sports (1984) is Konami's sequel to Track & Field, with seven new events from swimming and skeet shooting to weightlifting and pole vault.
longDescription: Like Track & Field, the game uses two run buttons and an action button for each player, and every event has to beat a qualifying time, distance or score to go on; after all seven, the cycle repeats faster and harder. In swimming the run buttons set speed while the action button times breaths, and in skeet shooting they fire left or right at clay birds, a perfect score unlocking a harder pattern. The long horse and pole vault leave the run-up to the computer: the player times the jump, push-off and twists. Archery sets the angle by holding the action button, triple jump fouls if the first leap passes the white line, and weightlifting builds power with the run buttons before the press.
trivia: In Japan it was Hyper Olympic '84, officially licensed for the 1984 Summer Olympics.
It became the number-one arcade game in the UK.
The home versions topped the UK all-formats chart in July and August 1985.
The Spectrum, Amstrad and Commodore 64 versions dropped the pole vault.
Konami announced a Switch reimagining, Hyper Sports R, in 2018 and cancelled it two years later.
devStory: Konami released it in Japan on 12 May 1984 as Hyper Olympic '84, officially licensed for that year's Summer Olympics, with Centuri publishing it in North America. It was less successful there than Track & Field, though Play Meter's Roger C. Sharpe called it an "exceptional follow-up", but it became the number-one arcade game in the UK. The ZX Spectrum version was the biggest-selling Spectrum game on the monthly Gallup charts, and Zzap!64 called the Commodore 64 one "a first rate conversion".

title: Zero Wing
description: Zero Wing (1989) is Toaplan's side-scrolling shooter, whose badly translated Mega Drive intro gave the internet "All your base are belong to us".
longDescription: In 2101 the space pirates CATS break a peace treaty and seize Earth's colonies, and Trent, who escaped the destruction of his mothership, flies the ZIG fighter through eight levels, each ending in a boss, to take revenge. The Seizer Beam grabs certain enemies to use as shields or throw at others. Three weapons — Red Cannon, Blue Laser and Green Homing missiles — are switched by collecting coloured items from destroyed carriers, and collecting the same colour upgrades the weapon. A hit costs a life and some firepower and speed, and after the last stage the game loops with harder enemies and bullets that burst from destroyed foes.
trivia: The Mega Drive version's English translation was done in-house; its intro was rediscovered in 1999 and became the "All your base are belong to us" meme.
The project began as a training exercise for new Toaplan staff and reused the Hellfire engine.
It was Toaplan's last side-scrolling shooter.
The Japan-only PC Engine CD version has a different story and two extra levels.
The Mega Drive version was never released in North America until Retro-Bit published it in 2020.
devStory:
Zero Wing began as a non-commercial project to train new Toaplan recruits on the engine from Hellfire, and was released when the team decided it was worth it; programmer Tatsuya Uemura said its stages and characters were "cobbled together" by staff from Hellfire and Truxton. Toshiaki Ōta led development. Namco published it in Japanese arcades in October 1989, and it was Game Machine's fourth most successful table arcade unit that November.

The Mega Drive version of 1991 added an introduction whose English, translated in-house by a Toaplan export employee rather than a professional, became one of the most cited examples of bad translation. Reviewers at the time praised its intro, graphics, sound and bosses; Computer and Video Games gave it 93%.

title: Batsugun
description: Batsugun (1993) is Toaplan's vertical shooter, regarded by many as the first "manic" or bullet hell shooter, in which ships level up their guns with experience.
longDescription: On a distant Earth-like planet, King Gladebaran VII has seized power through a string of coups, and the Skull Hornets, led by his exiled son Prince Olisis, fight back in the planet's most powerful jets. Players choose one of six pilots across three ships — the Sky Mirage, with rapid spreading beams; the Dragon's Whisper, with a continuous lightning beam; and the Judgement Flasher, with straight waves or a spread — and fly five levels with a main gun that reaches the top of the screen and three bombs. Destroying enemies earns experience, separate from the score, that levels the gun up twice; once it is maxed, experience adds bombs. "P" icons raise firepower and "B" icons add bombs up to seven. Extra lives come at a million points, gold medals and hidden bonus spots raise the score, and a hit costs a life, firepower and medals.
trivia: A Special Version, with a smaller hitbox, a shield and extra loops, was shown at the 1994 AOU Show but never officially released.
Toaplan closed in March 1994, before a planned sequel came out.
It influenced Cho Ren Sha 68K and Eschatos.
One pilot, Schneider, is the hero of Flying Shark.
Inoue said the cancelled sequel's idea of pairing firepower by gender was later used in Progear.
devStory:
It was Toaplan's last shoot 'em up, made by a small team that had mostly worked on Grind Stormer, with members holding several roles: Yuko Tataka, designer of Fire Shark, produced and co-designed it, Junya Inoue and Takeshi Kawamoto were the artists, Tsuneki Ikeda, later a Cave co-founder, was among the programmers, and Yoshitatsu Sakai composed the music. Toaplan released it in 1993, and Gamest placed it sixth for Best Shooting. A Special Version shown at the 1994 AOU Show was never released in arcades, and Toaplan went bankrupt in 1994.

Gazelle ported it to the Saturn for Banpresto in 1996, including both versions, and multiple publications consider it the first "manic" shooter.

title: Tiger-Heli
description: Tiger-Heli (1985) is Toaplan's first shoot 'em up, a vertical helicopter shooter whose screen-clearing bomb became a staple of the genre.
longDescription: The Tiger attack helicopter flies up a vertically scrolling screen against tanks, gunboats, artillery and aircraft, past buildings, level crossings, fuel depots and mine carts. Its short-range missiles hit both air and ground targets, while bombs destroy enemies and their bullets within range; enemy fire that hits a carried bomb sets it off. Cross-shaped bunkers that change colour release items when shot: green ones give up to two bombs, and red and grey ones up to two small helper helicopters, the red firing to the sides and the grey forwards. Reaching the helipad at the end of each of the four stages pays out for bombs and helpers carried, and after the fourth the game loops to the second at higher difficulty.
trivia: Game Machine listed it as the most popular arcade game in its 1 October 1985 issue.
The NES version reportedly sold more than a million copies in North America.
Its bomb concept became Toaplan's hallmark and a staple of the genre.
Nintendo had planned to release the NES version in North America as Helifighter.
An Atari 7800 version came out in 2025.
devStory:
Masahiro Yuge, Tatsuya Uemura and Yuichirō Nozawa, who had come to Toaplan from the bankrupt studios Orca and Crux, made it as Toaplan's first shoot 'em up, under the working title Cobra. A helicopter, inspired by Nozawa's Gyrodine, could hover, made bullets easier to see and suited a cocktail cabinet viewed from above, and the bomb was added to give players an aggressive weapon. Uemura said the team funded it themselves; Taito only distributed it, and Toaplan's name could not appear in the game.

Taito released it in October 1985, and Game Machine named it the most popular arcade game in its 1 October issue. Micronics ported it to the NES, which Acclaim published in North America in 1987. It helped establish Toaplan as a leading shooter developer, and the bomb became its hallmark.

title: Bump 'n' Jump
description: Bump 'n' Jump (1982) is Data East's vehicular combat game, in which the player's car bumps rivals off the road and leaps over water and obstacles.
longDescription: The player drives to the end of each course, knocking enemy cars into the sides of the road or jumping on top of them, and leaping over obstacles such as water; a flashing exclamation mark warns of a big obstacle ahead. Trucks cannot be bumped, only jumped on, and sometimes drop debris. A jump needs at least 100 mph. A car is lost by hitting either side of the road, an obstacle or the water. Each wrecked rival scores more on later levels, which are marked by changing seasons, and finishing a level without wrecking anything earns a 50,000-point bonus. Past 999,999 points the game switches to a "survival of the fittest" mode with no more extra cars.
trivia: In Japan it is Burnin' Rubber.
Next Generation ranked it 65th in its 1996 top 100 games, praising its jumping, bumping and sense of speed.
Two Commodore 64 clones appeared, one also called Burnin' Rubber.
John McNeill's 2013 score of 5,869,264 was not recognised by Twin Galaxies until 2015.
It appears on the Data East Arcade Classics compilation.
devStory:
Data East released it in Japan in November 1982 as Burnin' Rubber, on a dedicated board and on its DECO Cassette System, with music by Hiroaki Yoshida, and it was Japan's ninth highest-grossing arcade game of the year. Bally Midway released it in North America in March 1983, where it was among the thirteen highest-grossing arcade games of 1983.

Mattel licensed it for the Intellivision and Atari 2600 in 1983, and Coleco released a ColecoVision version in 1984. The Famicom version, Buggy Popper, reached the NES as Bump 'n' Jump in 1988, adding fuel cans that had to be collected because the car burns fuel when driven too fast.

title: Front Line
description: Front Line (1982) is Taito's overhead war game, one of the first run-and-guns, in which a lone soldier fights through infantry and tanks to lob a grenade into the enemy fort.
longDescription: A lone soldier, armed with a pistol and unlimited grenades, advances on foot against enemy infantry, then commandeers tanks to fight enemy armour, and must finish by throwing a grenade over the brick barricade of the enemy fort. A joystick moves him, a rotary dial, which can also be pressed, aims and fires the gun, and a button throws grenades and gets in and out of tanks. The light tank has a machine gun and is nimble but fragile, while the heavy tank's cannon is slower and survives one hit from a light tank; a single heavy-tank shot destroys either. A damaged tank must be abandoned within seconds. When the fort falls, a soldier waves a white flag, and the stage repeats with faster, deadlier troops.
trivia: It was runner-up for Coin-Op Game of the Year at the 1983 Arcade Awards, behind Pole Position.
It was the basis for SNK's TNK III, which in turn fed into Ikari Warriors.
An SNK programmer discovered it in an arcade before SNK made TNK III.
Nintendo's Sheriff (1979) uses the same rotary dial controller.
Extra lives come at 10,000 and 15,000 points, and never again.
devStory:
Tetsuya Sasaki designed it on Taito's SJ System board, and Taito released it on 10 November 1982. It was the seventh highest-grossing arcade game of 1982 in Japan, though its high initial difficulty limited its success in Britain, and Video Games listed its firing mechanism among the "misses" at that November's AMOA show. Versions followed for the ColecoVision, which needed the Super Action Controller, the Atari 2600, MSX, Famicom and Japanese computers.

It was one of the first games with ground combat and grenades, and one of the earliest overhead run-and-guns, years before Capcom's Commando (1985).

title: Xybots
description: Xybots (1987) is Ed Logg's split-screen 3D maze shooter for Atari Games, which began life as a sequel to Gauntlet.
longDescription: Major Rock Hardy and Captain Ace Gunn fight their way through a 3D maze of robots called Xybots, which aim to destroy humanity, alone or together, firing laser guns, using objects for cover and heading for each level's exit. The lower half of the screen shows the action and the upper half each player's status and a map of the level. The joystick moves the character, and rotating it turns him. Energy pods restore energy, and coins dropped by defeated Xybots buy energy, armour, speed, strength, firepower and maps of the maze and enemies in shops between levels. Some levels end with a large boss Xybot.
trivia: It was first conceived as Gauntlet III: Catacombs, until Atari's marketing department wanted a different name.
Its joystick rotated the player, which the article cites as one reason for its limited sales.
GamesTM called it "ahead of its time".
Commodore User called its two-player mode a "team game".
A Tengen Genesis version was announced in 1990 but never released.
