devStory: It grew from an attempt by Ed Logg and engineer Doug Snyder to make a first-person game without special hardware, and Logg first planned it as a second Gauntlet sequel, Gauntlet III: Catacombs, until Atari's marketing department wanted a different name; he and Bob Flanagan settled on a theme drawn from Major Havoc. Atari Games released it in November 1987. Reviewers compared it favourably to Berzerk and Gauntlet and praised its co-operative play, but in 2005 Logg recalled that players struggled to realise they could turn by rotating the joystick, and the game was not a financial success. Home versions followed in 1989 and a Lynx version in 1991.

title: Pit-Fighter
description: Pit-Fighter (1990) is Atari Games' street-fighting game built from digitised footage of live actors, in which up to three players brawl through 15 matches in front of a rowdy crowd.
longDescription: Three fighters — Buzz, an ex-wrestler, Ty, a kickboxing champion, and Kato, a third-degree black belt — take on opponents such as the Executioner, Southside Jim, Angel, Heavy Metal and Mad Miles across 15 matches, with up to three players at once, punching and kicking until an opponent's energy runs out. Every third fight is a Grudge Match against a clone of the player's fighter, or against the other players, where three knockdowns eliminate a fighter. The last is the Championship against the Masked Warrior, and players who reach it together must first fight each other to the death. The crowd joins in, attacking fighters, dropping weapons and shoving players back into the fight, and a power pill briefly raises strength and reduces damage. Pressing all three buttons triggers a super move.
trivia: Its fighters were digitised from live actors filmed against a bluescreen, making it the second fighting game with digitised sprites.
It topped the RePlay chart for upright cabinets in October 1990.
Pit Fighter II was over 75% finished for the Genesis when it was cancelled; its new fighters reappeared in Guardians of the 'Hood.
Several opponents are named after the actors who played them.
Computer Gaming World said the Amiga version "is the arcade game teleported".
devStory: Gary Stark and Mark Stephen Pierce designed it at Atari Games, with Stark and Paul Kwinn programming, on the Atari G1 board, using digitised footage of live actors filmed against a bluescreen. It came out in August 1990, topped RePlay's upright cabinet chart that October and sold 5,500 arcade units in the US. Julian Rignall of Computer and Video Games called it a "thoroughly enjoyable beat 'em up which really packs a punch", though Zzap!64 found it anticlimactic. Tengen and Domark published home versions from 1991, and the Super NES version dropped the crowd, the weapons and three opponents.

title: Kula World
description: Kula World (1998), released as Roll Away in North America, is a PlayStation puzzle-platformer in which a beach ball rolls over floating structures where gravity follows it round every edge.
longDescription: The player rolls a beach ball across floating structures, collecting keys to open each level's exit along with coins and jewels. Gravity turns with the ball as it rolls over edges, so walls become floors. Levels add moving platforms, transporters, bouncing platforms and jumping pills, growing more complex as the game goes on. Each stage holds one piece of fruit, and collecting five unlocks a bonus level in which every cube on every platform must be rolled over. Being spiked, captured, melted or burnt by a laser, falling off or running out of time costs points and restarts the level, and the game ends if the score falls below zero. Two players can race through stages in turn or play "copycat", repeating each other's moves and adding two more.
trivia: It was Game Design Sweden's only video game; the company became better known for Netbabyworld.
Playable demos came on the Demo One disc packed with European PlayStations in 1998.
Academic studies later used it to examine gamification in corporate training.
In Japan it was released as KulaQuest.
It lost the 1998 OPM award for Best Puzzle Game to Devil Dice.
devStory: Game Design Sweden AB — Stefan Persson, Jens and Jesper Rudberg and Johannes Söderqvist — developed it, with music by Twice a Man, and Sony released it in Europe on 10 July 1998, with Psygnosis publishing it in North America that November as Roll Away. It averaged 81% on GameRankings, with IGN giving it 8.9 out of 10. Edge compared its gradual introduction of challenges to "a good Nintendo title" but found little replay value, and it was nominated for Best Puzzle Game at the 1998 OPM Editors' Awards.

title: Uniracers
description: Uniracers (1994) is DMA Design's Super NES racing game for riderless unicycles, in which stunts mid-race give a burst of speed.
longDescription: Players race riderless unicycles around 2D tracks. Stunts, mostly jumps with rotations through 3D space, speed the unicycle up on race and circuit tracks and score points on stunt tracks, and landing on the wheel avoids a wipeout, which loses all the speed built up. Track markings warn of shortcuts and hazards, among speed boosts, corkscrews, loops and twists. There are nine tours of five tracks, 45 in all, and the first eight require beating computer opponents for bronze, silver and gold; the last ends in a race against the Anti-Uni, whose collisions turn the track invisible, reverse the controls and throw the background out of sync. Two players can race split-screen, a league mode takes up to eight, and each of the 16 unicycles has its own save file.
trivia: Mike Dailly says Pixar sued over the unicycle's resemblance to Red's Dream, limiting it to an initial run of 300,000; court records show the suit was against Nintendo of America and settled out of court.
The developers practised riding real unicycles in their offices.
In Europe it was called Unirally.
It has never been re-released.
Complex said in 2018: "Loops, flips, tricks, Uniracers had it all."
devStory:
DMA Design developed it under the working title "1x1", with Mike Dailly and Robbie Graham designing and Andrew Innes programming, and Nintendo released it in North America on 5 December 1994 and in Europe in 1995 as Unirally. Reviewers praised its pace and originality, Official Nintendo Magazine giving it 92 and Total! 90, while EGM's editors found it lacking charm. Nintendo Power ranked it the eighth best Super NES game of 1994.

Dailly later said Pixar sued over the unicycle's resemblance to its short Red's Dream and that Nintendo stopped making cartridges after the initial run; court records show Pixar sued Nintendo of America, and the case settled five months later.

title: Cool Spot
description: Cool Spot (1993) is Virgin Games' platformer starring Spot, the 7 Up mascot, who rescues his caged friends by collecting spots. It sold a million copies.
longDescription:
Spot jumps, throws soda bubbles in any direction at enemies and climbs by jumping up against surfaces. In each level he has to collect a set number of spots, a number that grows as the game goes on, to free a caged Spot, and each level has a time limit. His health is shown by a Spot face that sags as he takes damage from enemies, their shots and obstacles. There is no save feature, and flagpoles act as checkpoints.

Collecting enough spots opens a bonus stage, where hidden letters spelling 7 Up's slogan "UNCOLA" earn continues; a continue restarts the level where the last life was lost, but resets the score.
trivia: It came out at a time when other brand mascots, such as Chester Cheetah and the Noid, were also getting their own games.
The sequel, Spot Goes to Hollywood, followed in 1995.
It was preceded by Spot: The Video Game (1990) and Spot: The Cool Adventure (1992).
GamesMaster ranked the Genesis version 92nd among its top 100 games in 1996.
devStory:
David Bishop and Bill Anderson designed it at Virgin Games, with Cathie A. Bartz-Todd producing, David Perry programming and Tommy Tallarico composing; Mike Dietz was among the artists. Virgin released it for the Genesis in North America in April 1993, followed by Super NES, Master System, Game Gear, Amiga, MS-DOS and Game Boy versions. It sold a million copies.

Mega and Sega Pro gave the Genesis version 93%, and Pelit called it "one of the most enjoyable platform games in a long time".

title: Tobal No. 1
description: Tobal No. 1 (1996) is DreamFactory's 60-frames-per-second fighting game for Square, with characters by Akira Toriyama and a dungeon-crawling Quest Mode — and a demo of Final Fantasy VII in every box.
longDescription:
In 2048 the planet Tobal holds its 98th tournament to decide who gets the rights to its Molmoran ore, an energy source. The eight starting fighters, among them Chuji Wu, Oliems, Epon, Hom and Mary Ivonskaya, all get the same ending, and the plot is told only in the manual. Fighters move freely around the ring while facing each other, dash and jump, and attack with high, middle and low buttons, alongside a grappling system and blocks with throws and counters. The game runs at up to 60 frames a second, skipping textured polygons in favour of Gouraud shading.

Quest Mode puts the fighting system into a 3D dungeon of several floors with traps and enemies, including fighters from the main roster. Items found, dropped or bought with crystals can be eaten or thrown, and potions may raise maximum health or cut it to 1. There is no saving: dying sends the player back to the start. Beating certain characters there unlocks them, and clearing the 30-floor Udan's Dungeon unlocks Toriyama Robo.
trivia: Every copy included a playable demo of Final Fantasy VII and previews of Final Fantasy Tactics, Bushido Blade and SaGa Frontier.
It sold 752,000 copies in Japan in 1996, the ninth best-selling home game there that year.
The boss Nork was left unplayable because his size unbalanced the game.
Hom's robotic movements were motion-captured from a member of the team.
Tobal 2 followed in 1997 but stayed in Japan.
devStory:
Square founded DreamFactory as a subsidiary in November 1995 with 17 staff, all experienced in 3D fighting games, and Tobal was Square's first fighting game and first PlayStation release. Seiichi Ishii, who had worked on Virtua Fighter and the first two Tekken games, directed it, Toru Ikebuchi was lead programmer and Hironobu Sakaguchi supervised. Akira Toriyama designed the characters after a single meeting and supplied a basic story and world. Blood was left out to suit foreign markets, and the music came from a team including Yasunori Mitsuda and Masashi Hamauzu.

It came out in Japan on 2 August 1996 as the first game on Square's DigiCube label for convenience stores, topped the charts, and sold 752,000 copies there that year, much of that credited to its Final Fantasy VII demo. It averaged 83% on GameRankings.

title: The Tower of Druaga
description: The Tower of Druaga (1984) is Masanobu Endō's arcade maze game, in which the knight Gilgamesh climbs 60 floors to rescue Ki, uncovering treasures hidden behind deliberately obscure conditions.
longDescription: The knight Gilgamesh climbs 60 floors of a tower to rescue the maiden Ki from Druaga, an eight-armed, four-legged demon who means to enslave mankind with the Blue Crystal Rod. Each floor holds a key that opens the door to the next, guarded by slimes, knights, wizards, ghosts that pass through walls and dragons. Every floor also hides a treasure, such as a pickaxe, speed boots or a candle, revealed by a secret task like defeating certain enemies or entering a joystick code — and some are needed to finish the game. A time limit releases indestructible Will-o-Wisps.
trivia: Endō described it as a "fantasy Pac-Man"; the 60 floors were inspired by Sunshine 60, then Asia's tallest building.
It is credited with influencing Ys, Hydlide, Dragon Slayer and The Legend of Zelda, and with getting players to share tips and guidebooks.
Eurogamer called the 2009 Wii release "diabolically obtuse".
devStory: Masanobu Endō, creator of Xevious, designed the game after buying Dungeons & Dragons on a trip to North America, and Junko Ozawa composed the music. Namco released it in Japan in June 1984 on Mappy hardware, and it began the Babylonian Castle Saga, continued by The Return of Ishtar (1986).

title: Dragon Buster
description: Dragon Buster (1985) is Namco's side-scrolling action RPG, in which the swordsman Clovis fights his way to a dragon — the earliest game with a double jump, and one of the first with a health meter.
longDescription:
Clovis, son of the royal family's chief bodyguard, was disowned for his mischief as a boy and sent to train with a monk in the forest. When a dragon raids the land and carries off King Lawrence's 16-year-old daughter, Princess Celia, he learns he is the hero of the kingdom's legend and sets out for Dragon Mountain. On an overworld map the player picks among several routes to the castle, more in later rounds, through five kinds of level: caves full of bats and snakes, towers of many floors, the hard Boneyard, mountains to descend and mixed ruins.

Each level has several bosses, and the player must find the one guarding the exit. Clovis's vitality is shown on screen and recovers by 25% after each level, ending the game when it runs out, and every few mountains Celia is rescued, wearing a new outfit each time, before the game begins again.
trivia: It is described as the earliest game with a double jump.
Dragon Valor on the PlayStation was both a remake and a sequel.
It is also described as one of the first games with a visual health meter.
It appears as a hidden minigame in Tales of the Abyss.
Dragon Mountain, at the end of every round, is always the same.
devStory: Namco released it in Japan in January 1985, with music by Yuriko Keino, and it was a hit there, placing third in Game Machine's chart of table arcade units in its 1 March 1985 issue; Computer + Video Games praised its colourful graphics and ease for newcomers. Tose made the Famicom version, which reviewers praised for its larger scale of 138 levels, and Enix's PC-8801 version added an introduction and a new ending. Dragon Buster II followed in Japan on the Famicom.

title: Baraduke
description: Baraduke (1985) is Namco's run-and-gun through 48 floors, whose ending revealed its space-suited hero as a woman a year before Metroid.
longDescription: A space-suited fighter — Kissy for player one, Takky for player two — works through eight worlds of increasing difficulty, each with five floors and a boss floor, 48 in all, armed with a wave gun. Destroying every Octy on a floor, which drop power-up capsules, opens a pipe at the bottom that must be found to go on. Rescuing the one-eyed Paccets earns points and a chance at an extra shield in bonus games between floors. The bosses are the Blue Worm in worlds 1, 3, 5 and 7, the Turning Eye in worlds 2, 4 and 6, and the Octy King in the last. Kissy, actually Toby Masuyo, is a woman, though the player is led to believe otherwise until the ending shows her face.
trivia: In North America it was released as Alien Sector.
Kissy later appeared in Mr. Driller as Toby Masuyo, the mother of driller Susumu Hori, and in Namco × Capcom.
It was included in the fifth volume of Namco Museum on the PlayStation in 1995.
A Paccet appears in Pac-Man's "Namco Roulette" taunt in Super Smash Bros. for 3DS and Wii U.
Hamster re-released it in its Arcade Archives series in 2022.
devStory: Yukio Takahashi designed it, and Namco released it in Japan in May 1985 and in Europe that October; it was the 15th most successful table arcade unit in Game Machine's 1 September listing. Clare Edgeley of Computer and Video Games found "not much in the way of graphics" but plenty of shooting. In 2016 Hardcore Gaming 101 compared it with Metroid, a year later, for its faceless space soldier exploring alien caves and its female hero revealed at the end, and with Section Z for the way gravity and gun recoil affect the characters. Baraduke II followed in Japan in 1988.

title: Metro-Cross
description: Metro-Cross (1985) is Namco's obstacle-course race against the clock, in which a runner dodges pitfalls and tyres, rides skateboards and kicks drink cans across 32 rounds.
longDescription: Runner sprints automatically through 32 timed rounds while the player steers him and controls his speed. Slip zones slow him, pitfalls break beneath him and crackers flip him onto his back, and later rounds add giant tyres, moving walls, cubes, mice and bouncing chess knights and kings. Springboards launch him forward, sometimes straight onto a second springboard, and skateboards speed him up and make him immune to slip zones. Drink cans can be kicked for 100 to 5,000 points or a burst of speed, or jumped on to stop the timer for a few seconds. Time left over becomes bonus points, every fourth round adds the time saved from the three before it, and running out of time electrocutes him and ends the game.
trivia: Its European and Australian Xbox 360 release was renamed Retro-Cross.
A Metro-Cross theme appeared as downloadable content in Pac-Man 99.
Kicking a drink can can be worth up to 5,000 points.
It was included in Namco Museum Vol. 5 on the PlayStation.
Hamster re-released it in its Arcade Archives series in 2022.
devStory: Tatsuro Okamoto designed it and Nobuyuki Ohnogi composed the music, and Namco released it in Japan in May 1985, with Kitkorp handling North America that November; Game Machine ranked it Japan's ninth most popular arcade game in June. Home versions followed for the Famicom, Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC and Atari ST. A high-definition sequel, Aero-Cross, with simultaneous multiplayer, was in development for Xbox Live Arcade and PlayStation Network but was cancelled with the Namco Generations line.

title: Gaplus
description: Gaplus (1984) is Namco's sequel to Galaga and the third Galaxian game, in which the player's ship can also move up the screen and capture enemies with a tractor beam.
longDescription: Enemies called Galaga fly in rows, form up near the top of the screen and dive at the player's ship, the Ogre Header, through levels called Parsecs. Unlike in Galaga, the ship can move up and down as well as sideways. Some enemies drop upgrades: a tractor beam that captures enemies, a large drill that destroys many at once, and effects that slow enemies or cancel their shots. Extra lives come from score milestones, from completing a new ship out of dropped parts and from Rally-X flags released by shooting stars. Some stages open with the starfield reversing, followed by faster, harder waves. In the Challenging Stages the player juggles enemies by hitting them as many times as possible, each hit adding a dot to a word or phrase that earns a related bonus when completed.
trivia: North American operators could convert it with a kit that renamed it Galaga 3.
It was the most successful table arcade unit in Japan in May 1984, according to Game Machine.
Rally-X flags appear as bonus items.
An NES-style demake by M2 was included in Namco Museum Archives Vol. 2 in 2020.
Hamster released it as a standalone Arcade Archives title in 2022.
devStory: Namco released it in Japan in April 1984, with Bally Midway distributing it in North America that September, and Game Machine listed it as the most successful table arcade unit in Japan that May. It was the only game besides Phozon to run on Namco's Phozon hardware, and the third Galaxian game after Galaxian and Galaga. Galaga '88 followed in 1987.

title: The Legend of Valkyrie
description: The Legend of Valkyrie (1989) is Namco's top-down action-adventure for one or two players, in which the warrior Valkyrie helps defeat the warlord Kamooz. Gamest readers voted it the best arcade game of all time.
longDescription: After peace returns to Marvel Land, the fields of Xandra Land dry up, and Kurino Xandra sets out to find the Golden Seed, which is said to grant the wish of whoever drops it into the Northern Spring. He is joined by Sabina of the Koakuman tribe and Zuul, a former bandit with a map. When the warlord Kamooz attacks, wanting the seed to enslave the kingdom, the mythical warrior Valkyrie descends from the heavens, drives off his soldiers and joins them. Player one controls the sword-wielding Valkyrie and player two can join as Xandra, both with a projectile weapon. Health is lost to enemies, projectiles and falls, an hourglass timer ends the game when it runs out, and gold from enemies buys spells, weapons and items in shops whose prices rise. The eight areas, from grassy plateaus to icefields and dungeons, each end with a boss.
trivia: Development began as a four-player, Gauntlet-style game with several Valkyries, before those ideas were dropped.
One designer used the pseudonym "Koakuman" ("little devil"), which North American versions mistranslated as "Quarkman".
Its first fully English release came in Namco Museum Vol. 5 in 1997.
Gamest named it the best game of 1991, and its readers voted it the best arcade game of all time.
IGN called it the standout game on Namco Museum Vol. 5.
devStory: Namco character artist Hiroshi Fujii, who had worked on the Famicom's Valkyrie no Bōken, conceived it with a designer known only as "Koakuman", who designed the characters and enemies with inspiration from The Wizard of Oz. The team first imagined a vast open world with changing seasons, which the vertical arcade monitor forced them to cut, and a four-player Gauntlet-style game with several Valkyries was also abandoned. Koakuman described a female protagonist as "taboo" at the time. Namco released it in Japanese arcades in April 1989 on its System 2 board, with music by Hiroyuki Kawada, and it was widely successful. A PC Engine version with new stages and a password system followed in 1990.

title: The Hobbit
description: The Hobbit (1982) is Beam Software's illustrated text adventure based on Tolkien's novel, whose characters acted on their own in real time — "Thorin sits down and starts singing about gold."
longDescription:
The game follows Tolkien's 1937 novel, with illustrations based on originals by Kent Rees for many locations; on tape they were drawn as outlines and filled in on screen, which could take several seconds. Its "Inglish" parser understood complex sentences with pronouns, adverbs, punctuation and prepositions. Veronika Megler gave objects size, weight and solidity, so they could be put inside one another, tied with rope, damaged or broken.

The game runs in real time: leave it idle and it waits on the player's behalf, so events carry on. Other characters follow the same rules as the player, with their own loyalties, strengths and personalities — Gandalf wanders some fifty locations, picks things up, fights and can be captured — which makes each game unpredictable, sometimes to the point of an important character dying early. Megler found that animals were killing each other before the player arrived. One of its lines, "Thorin sits down and starts singing about gold", has entered popular culture.
trivia: Every copy came with a copy of Tolkien's novel.
It won the 1983 Golden Joystick Award for best strategy game.
CRL released a parody, The Boggit, in 1986.
Discworld Noir references its text in a scene with a wine barrel.
A strategy book, A Guide to Playing The Hobbit, was published in 1984.
devStory:
Beam Software acquired the computer rights in 1980, and Philip Mitchell and Veronika Megler developed it over eighteen months with Alfred Milgrom and Stuart Richie, with graphics by Russell Comte, Greg Holland and Paul Mitchell. Melbourne House released it for the ZX Spectrum in December 1982, with a copy of the novel in every box, and versions for the Commodore 64, BBC Micro, Oric and others followed. The manual warned that it could not be guaranteed free of errors, and version 1.1 introduced a bug that made it unwinnable.

It was a bestseller on the Spectrum in 1983 and sold more than 100,000 copies in its first two years at £14.95, and more than 500,000 in Europe. Its parser was reused in Sherlock, and its sequels began with Lord of the Rings: Game One (1985).

title: Saboteur!
description: Saboteur! (1985) is Clive Townsend's stealth action game, in which a ninja breaks into a warehouse, steals a disk listing rebel leaders and escapes by helicopter.
longDescription: An anonymous ninja infiltrates a warehouse to steal a floppy disk listing the names of rebel leaders, then escapes through the building, dark tunnels and a secret command centre to a helicopter. He can crouch, climb ladders, run, punch and drop-kick, starts with a single shuriken and can find bricks and lengths of pipe in rubbish piles and boxes to use as weapons. Guards stand still until they see him or hear too much noise, then give chase with fists and guns, alongside guard dogs and automatic guns. His energy falls from long drops, from crouching under water and from attacks, and returns when he rests somewhere safe, but the game ends if it runs out or the time limit expires. The difficulty level sets the number of guards, the time limit and how many security doors are locked on the way.
trivia: It reused routines and ideas from Townsend's cancelled game Death Pit.
Crash called it "one of the better releases on the Spectrum this year".
Your Sinclair ranked it 55th in its Official Top 100 Games of All Time.
A prototype of Death Pit was recovered and is available at World of Spectrum.
An enhanced version came to the Switch in 2018.
devStory: Clive Townsend designed and programmed it, building on routines and ideas from Death Pit, a game of his cancelled before Saboteur began, and Durell released it in 1985 for the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, Commodore 16 and Plus/4. Crash gave it 93% and a Smash, Your Sinclair a Megagame, and Sinclair User five out of five, while Computer and Video Games called it "a winner". Saboteur II: Avenging Angel followed in 1987, and Townsend made an official remake in 2015 and an enhanced version in 2017.

title: The Way of the Exploding Fist
description: The Way of the Exploding Fist (1985) is Beam Software's karate game for the Commodore 64, scored with yin-yang points instead of energy bars — the UK's best-selling computer game of 1985.
longDescription: Two karateka fight a series of one-on-one matches under the eye of a master, against backgrounds from a dojo to a field below snowy mountains, a Buddha statue and pagodas, each win bringing a harder opponent. Instead of energy bars, any blow that lands ends the round, scored with yin-yang symbols in the shobu nihon kumite system used by traditional karate: a loose or borderline hit earns a half symbol, waza-ari, and a clean one a full symbol, ippon, with two full symbols winning the bout. The fighter has 18 moves on the joystick or keys, from flying and roundhouse kicks to high and low punches. After several stages a bull charges in a bonus round and must be knocked out with a single blow, a nod to Mas Oyama.
trivia: It was one of the first games to borrow heavily from Data East's Karate Champ.
The Commodore 64 version uses more than 600 sprite images.
It won Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards.
Karate champion Jeoffrey Thompson was signed to promote it.
Its scoring follows the shobu nihon kumite system of traditional karate.
devStory:
Gregg Barnett, who had converted The Hobbit and Sherlock to the Commodore 64, made it at Beam Software with Bruce Bayley, Neil Brennan and David Johnston, and it was one of the first games to borrow heavily from Data East's Karate Champ. The C64 version uses over 600 sprite images, and Brennan's music draws on the 1952 orchestral piece Dance of the Yao People. Melbourne House released it in June 1985.

It topped the UK charts in September and October, was Britain's best-selling computer game of 1985 and sold 500,000 copies across Europe. Zzap!64 gave it 93% and Crash 92%, and it won Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards.

sources.title: The Way of the Exploding Fist

title: IK+
description: IK+ (1987), International Karate +, is Archer Maclean's three-way karate game on a beach, with bonus rounds of deflecting bouncing balls and a Rob Hubbard score.
longDescription: Three karateka fight at once on a beach, each trying to be first to six points, with one or two human players and the computer always controlling at least one fighter. Every two rounds a bonus game has players deflecting bouncing balls or, outside the Commodore 64 version, kicking away bombs. The single backdrop can be recoloured with keystrokes. The Amiga, Atari and C64 versions hide background antics — a Pac-Man, a descending spider, a U-boat periscope — and a key that makes all three fighters' trousers fall down, followed by a double-take. On the Amiga, typing a swear word earns a rebuke, and doing it again resets the game.
trivia: Rob Hubbard wrote the music for the 8-bit versions and David Lowe for the Atari ST and Amiga.
The Atari ST version took six months to make; the Amiga version took seven days.
Zzap!64 gave the Commodore 64 version 97%.
A finished International Karate Deluxe for the Atari ST and Amiga was never released.
Nintendo Power put the GBA version second on its 2005 list of the worst games ever.
devStory:
Archer Maclean designed it at System 3 as a successor to International Karate (1985), and wrote the Atari ST version entirely himself apart from the music, in assembly on a PC-based system that cross-compiled 800 KB of source in seven seconds. Rob Hubbard composed the music for the C64, Spectrum and Amstrad versions, and Dave Lowe arranged it for the 16-bit versions. It came out in October 1987 on the Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum, and on the Atari ST and Amiga in 1988; Activision published it in the US as Chop N' Drop.

Zzap!64 gave it 97% and a Gold Medal, and it won Best 16-Bit Soundtrack at the 1988 Golden Joystick Awards. A 2003 Game Boy Advance version was poorly received.

title: Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior
description: Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior (1987) is Palace Software's sword-fighting game, notorious for its decapitations and for a box cover photographed with Page 3 model Maria Whittaker.
longDescription: Two barbarians fight with swords in places such as a forest glade and a fighting pit, rolling, jumping low blows and using kicks, headbutts and sword attacks, each with 12 life points shown as six circles. A well-timed blow to the neck takes the opponent's head off instantly, and a goblin kicks the head away and drags the body off. Left idle, the fighters turn to the player, shrug and say "C'mon". In the story mode the player fights eight barbarians to reach the wizard Drax and rescue Princess Mariana; in head-to-head mode two players, or a player and the computer, fight timed bouts.
trivia: The box used photographs of Michael Van Wijk and Maria Whittaker rather than painted art, and UK complaints focused on the packaging more than the violence.
Germany banned the game for its violence; a version with green blood was later allowed.
In North America Epyx released it as Death Sword.
Each fight on the Amiga version opens with a sampled "Prepare to die!".
Barbarian II: The Dungeon of Drax followed in 1988 with the same models on the box.
devStory:
Steve Brown, who had made Cauldron, designed it at Palace Software, inspired by Frank Frazetta's paintings and Robert E. Howard's Conan stories and aiming for something "brutal and as realistic as possible". He worked out 16 moves with wooden swords and filmed them for the animators, copying the "Web of Death" from Conan the Destroyer, and the decapitation sound came from Red Sonja. Stanley Schembri programmed it and Richard Joseph wrote the music, and the subtitle was added to set it apart from a Psygnosis game also called Barbarian.

Palace released it in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum, and it topped the all-format charts, its first royalty cheque reaching £20,000. The British Board of Film Classification called its decapitations "storybook violence".

title: Nebulus
description: Nebulus (1987) is John M. Phillips's platform game, in which Pogo climbs rotating towers in the sea — the tower turns around him as he moves, giving a striking 3D effect.
longDescription: Pogo, a green creature, must destroy eight towers standing in the sea by climbing each from bottom to top and setting off a bomb at its peak. The towers are cylinders ringed with ledges joined by stairs and lifts, and as Pogo walks left or right the tower turns rather than Pogo moving across the screen, giving a sense of depth that reviewers praised. Most enemies are simple geometric shapes, some of which can be shot. Touching one knocks Pogo down to the ledge below, and with no ledge beneath he falls into the sea and drowns. At the top he goes through a door to bring the tower down, then boards a submarine, and in most versions a bonus stage follows in which he shoots fish.
trivia: In the US it was released as Tower Toppler.
It won Best Original Game at the Golden Joystick Awards.
The Commodore 64 version earned 97% and a Zzap!64 Gold Medal.
In Japan, as Kyoro Chan Land, the hero was replaced with Kyorochan and the jewels with Chocoballs.
Amiga Power ranked the Amiga version 14th among the best games of all time.
devStory: John M. Phillips designed it and wrote its music, and Hewson released it in 1987 for the ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and Acorn Archimedes. Zzap!64 gave the Commodore 64 version 97% and a Gold Medal, Crash a Smash, Your Sinclair a Megagame and Amstrad Action a Mastergame, and it won Best Original Game at the Golden Joystick Awards. U.S. Gold released it in America as Tower Toppler, and Bits Studios made Game Boy and NES versions as Castelian, with music by David Whittaker. Nebulus 2 followed on the Amiga.

title: Dizzy – The Ultimate Cartoon Adventure
description: Dizzy (1987) is the Oliver Twins' first Dizzy game for Codemasters, in which the somersaulting egg gathers four ingredients for a potion to defeat the wizard Zaks.
longDescription: Dizzy searches the fairy-tale land of Katmandu for four ingredients — a leprechaun's wig, a cloud's silver lining, a vampire dux feather and troll brew — to put in a cauldron and brew a potion that will defeat the evil wizard Zaks. He can carry only one item at a time, and some are needed to survive hazards, such as a raincoat against damaging rain. A great many hazards kill on contact, and he starts with just three lives, which makes the game hard. It relies less on inventory puzzles than the later games in the series.
trivia: His name comes from the somersaults he does when he jumps.
He was first conceived as a face with hands and feet; the egg came about after fans assumed he was one.
Eurogamer included it in its 2017 list of 10 games that defined the ZX Spectrum.
It was included in The Dizzy Collection.
devStory: The Oliver Twins wrote the game, planning its levels on the backs of spare rolls of wallpaper. The jumping animation came from their Panda Sprites software, which rotated images easily but distorted complex sprites, so the character had to be simple. Codemasters released it in 1987 for the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC, starting the Dizzy series, which continued with Treasure Island Dizzy and Fantasy World Dizzy. Sinclair User gave it 9/10.

title: Spellbound
description: Spellbound (1985) is David Jones's Magic Knight adventure for Mastertronic, played through a pull-down "Windimation" menu, in which the knight rescues a wizard trapped by his own spell.
longDescription: Magic Knight is transported to a castle full of trapped characters and must rescue his friend Gimbal, a wizard caught by his own "white-out" spell, cast while trying to make a better-tasting rice pudding, then return him and everyone else to their proper time and place. Less action-based than Finders Keepers, it is a graphic adventure with some platforming, played through drop-down menus called "Windimation" with commands such as "take object" and "talk to character". Most puzzles involve using objects in the right place or giving them to characters so they help, and spells, most needing particular objects, solve others. The other characters wander about, grow hungry and fall asleep, and Magic Knight must look after them and himself; his energy drains as he moves between rooms and when hit, and restoring it is one of the first puzzles. The castle runs from a basement to a roof garden, linked by a lift, and everything must be done within 48 in-game hours.
trivia: Rob Hubbard wrote the music.
Crime Busters (1986) was withdrawn after a dispute over its reported use of Spellbound's code.
Gimbal got himself trapped trying to make a better-tasting rice pudding.
An authorised MSX version finally appeared in 2023.
Its Windimation menus have been compared to later graphic adventures such as The Secret of Monkey Island.
devStory: David Jones designed and programmed it as the second Magic Knight game, with music by Rob Hubbard, and Mastertronic released it on its M.A.D. label in 1985 for the ZX Spectrum and Amstrad CPC. Commodore 64 and Atari 8-bit versions followed in 1986, along with an enhanced 128K Spectrum version. It won a Crash Smash, a Sinclair User Classic and a Your Sinclair Megagame. Knight Tyme followed in 1986 and Stormbringer in 1987.

title: Vulgus
description: Vulgus (1984) is Capcom's first arcade game, a vertical shooter designed by Tokuro Fujiwara, which introduced the Yashichi later used as a power-up across Capcom's games.
longDescription: The player's spaceship shoots down incoming enemies with an unlimited main gun and a limited supply of bombs, and "Pow" icons appear now and then to restock them. There are no separate levels: the background alternates between a planet's surface and open space, as in Xevious, and the game repeats with rising difficulty until the last life is lost. One enemy, the Yashichi, became one of Capcom's recurring symbols.
trivia: Capcom later gave the game away as freeware.
An NES follow-up, Titan Warriors, originally called Neo Vulgus, was never released.
Its Pow icon returned in 1941, Bionic Commando and Savage Bees.
The Yashichi reappears in many later Capcom games, usually as a helpful power-up.
In Marvel vs. Capcom 3, Deadpool says he is petitioning Capcom to make Vulgus 2.
devStory: It was Capcom's first arcade game. Tokuro Fujiwara designed it and Ayako Mori composed the music, and Capcom released it in Japan in May 1984, with SNK releasing it abroad that July. Game Machine listed it among Japan's most popular arcade games that June, and Play Meter's Roger C. Sharpe gave it a generally favourable review. Capcom later released it as freeware for PCs and PDAs, and it has appeared in Capcom Generation 3, Capcom Classics Collection and Capcom Arcade Cabinet.

title: SonSon
description: SonSon (1984) is Capcom's auto-scrolling arcade game loosely based on Journey to the West, starring a monkey boy patterned after Sun Wukong, with a pig partner for a second player.
longDescription:
Loosely based on Journey to the West, it stars a monkey boy modelled on Sun Wukong, fighting his way towards a statue of Buddha past bats, rats and mad bombers. The screen scrolls by itself, stopping only for major enemies, across six continuous rows of platforms, some with gaps. The hero walks automatically: up and down jump between rows, while left and right slow down or speed up against the scroll. His only attack is energy blasts from his staff, and touching an enemy or its shot costs a life, after which he returns on a cloud that makes him briefly invincible.

Fruit is worth points, and enough points earn an extra life. Certain fruit turns every enemy on screen into more fruit, and walking over some platforms can sprout a valuable bamboo shoot. A second player can join as TonTon, based on Zhu Bajie.
trivia: Marvel vs. Capcom 2 includes a character called SonSon, the original hero's granddaughter.
Its PC Engine sequel, SonSon II, was heavily based on Black Tiger.
A shop called SonSon appears in Ryu's and Guy's stages in Street Fighter Alpha.
The second player's TonTon is based on Zhu Bajie from Journey to the West.
Capcom made SonSon II itself, one of its few PC Engine games, according to composer Manami Matsumae.
devStory: Yoshiki Okamoto directed it and drew its art at Capcom, with Hirokazu Fujinaka programming and Ayako Mori and Tamayo Kawamoto composing. Capcom released it in Japan in July 1984, and Game Machine ranked it the fifth most successful table arcade unit of the month in its 1 August issue. Micronics made the Famicom version, released on 8 February 1986. It has since appeared in Capcom Generation 3, Capcom Classics Collection and on the Wii Virtual Console, and was the first free game in Capcom Arcade 2nd Stadium.

title: Exed Exes
description: Exed Exes (1985), Savage Bees in North America, is Capcom's insect-themed vertical shooter for one or two players, in which destroyed enemies can be turned into collectable fruit.
longDescription: One or two players fly up a vertically scrolling screen against insect- and skull-themed enemies over inorganic, mechanical backgrounds. Destroyed enemies can be turned into fruit to collect, which a Gamest Mook reviewer called the game's "greatest attraction"; the same reviewer said the enemies, backgrounds and music gave it a unique and exciting atmosphere.
trivia: Its full Japanese title is Super Floating Fortress Exed Exes; in North America it was Savage Bees.
The Famicom version was published by Tokuma Shoten, not Capcom.
It is one of the rotating arcade games in Street Fighter 6's Game Center.
Nintendo Life gave the Virtual Console release 4/10 in 2011.
Its character Colonel Issue cameos in Project X Zone 2.
devStory:
Yoshiki Okamoto directed it and worked on its art, Takashi Aoki programmed it and Tamayo Kawamoto composed the music. Capcom released it in Japan in February 1985 as Super Floating Fortress Exed Exes, and Memetron, its original North American licensee, released it there in April as Savage Bees. Game Machine ranked it the 15th most popular arcade game of March 1985. Micronics ported it to the Famicom, which Tokuma Shoten released on 21 December 1985.

It has since appeared in Capcom Generations 3, Capcom Classics Collection and its Reloaded follow-up, the Wii Virtual Console, Capcom Arcade Cabinet and Capcom Arcade 2nd Stadium.

title: Gun.Smoke
description: Gun.Smoke (1985) is Yoshiki Okamoto's Wild West shooter, in which bounty hunter Billie Bob walks up the screen firing left, right and centre with three buttons.
longDescription: Instead of a spaceship, the player controls Billie Bob, a bounty hunter in the Wild West, walking up a screen that scrolls automatically. Three buttons fire left, right and straight ahead, and pressing them in combination changes how he shoots. He dies to gunfire, to touching an enemy or to being trapped between an obstacle and the bottom of the screen. Power-ups include a horse for extra protection, boots for speed, bullets for faster shots, a rifle for longer range and a Yashichi for an extra life, while stars, bottles, bags and dragonflies are worth bonus points.
trivia: The NES version has a new story, set in Hicksville in 1849 against the Wingates gang, and different music.
The Amstrad CPC version was called Desperado – Gun.Smoke.
Its soundtrack was released by Alfa Records in 1986 with two unused tracks.
It was Japan's sixth highest-grossing table arcade game in the first half of 1986.
Capcom Arcade 2nd Stadium lists it as Gan Sumoku.
devStory:
Yoshiki Okamoto directed and designed it, also working on the art with Noritaka Funamizu, while Takashi Aoki programmed it and Ayako Mori composed the music. Capcom released it in Japan on 23 October 1985, with Romstar publishing it in North America. It was the second most successful table arcade unit in Game Machine's January 1986 chart and among the top five US arcade games in Play Meter that month, whose columnist Frank Seninsky called it "a number-one kit with great graphics". Computer and Video Games called it an "excellent" fast-paced shooter.

The NES and Famicom Disk System version followed in 1988 with a new story and music, and Topo Soft made a sequel for home computers, Desperado 2, in 1991.

title: Trojan
description: Trojan (1986) is Takashi Nishiyama's post-apocalyptic sword-and-shield game for Capcom, whose NES version added Capcom's first attempt at a one-on-one fighting mode.
longDescription: After a nuclear war worsened by demonic forces, warlord spirits from past eras return, possessing the strongest survivors and ruling the peaceful tribes under a supreme leader, Achilles. A young warrior who resists possession, and who once served Achilles until he learned of his massacres, takes the name Trojan and fights through pirates and gladiators to exorcise them. One button swings his sword and the other raises his shield, which can be held low, high or at an angle to block knives and arrows, and he jumps by pushing up. Some enemies throw magic balls that knock the sword and shield away when blocked, leaving him to punch and kick until they reappear. Each of the six stages has a sub-boss and an end boss, players can start from any stage, and, as in Ghosts 'n Goblins, the true ending comes only after a second playthrough.
trivia: It is considered a spiritual successor to Kung-Fu Master.
Computer and Video Games called it a worthy successor to Ghosts 'n Goblins.
In Japan it is Tatakai no Banka.
Its NES versus mode was Capcom's first one-on-one fighting mode.
Nintendo released the arcade version on its PlayChoice-10 system.
devStory:
Takashi Nishiyama, who had designed Kung-Fu Master at Irem before moving to Capcom, directed and designed it, and Capcom released it in North America through Romstar in March 1986 and in Japan in April as Tatakai no Banka. Clare Edgeley of Computer and Video Games praised its graphics and play.

The NES version, released in Japan that December, added power-ups, hidden rooms, an extra final boss, King Shriek, and a two-player versus mode in which the second player controls an enemy with identical moves. That mode was Capcom's first attempt at a one-on-one fighting game, and it is seen as a precursor to Nishiyama's Street Fighter (1987). A Spectrum version was programmed for Elite but never released.

title: Legendary Wings
description: Legendary Wings (1986) is Capcom's two-player shooter, in which winged warriors fly overhead stages and then fight on foot in side-scrolling sections to destroy the supercomputer Dark.
longDescription: In the distant future, the alien supercomputer Dark, which had guided humanity since ancient times, rebels, and Ares, the god of war, gives two young warriors the Wings of Love and Courage to destroy it. Each of the five areas begins as an overhead flying section in which the player shoots air enemies and bombs ground ones on the way to a palace, then becomes a side-scrolling section on foot, walking, crouching, climbing ladders and jumping to the boss, who is fought in the air. Optional "Danger" areas, around the middle of each level, have the player escape a giant mechanical face that inhales them, and hidden "Lucky" areas hold treasure chests. "P" items raise the gun through five levels up to the Psycho Flame, and a hit costs a life and the power-ups.
trivia: Its heroine, Michelle Heart, later appeared in Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes.
Hardcore Gaming 101 called the arcade version "remarkably average" but rated the NES version one of the better shooters on the console.
Its Japanese title is Aresu no Tsubasa.
A 1987 record of 612,500 points stood for 33 years, until Sam Griffith scored 694,000 in 2020.
Kalata called its stone faces "awesome and creepy".
devStory:
Takashi Nishiyama directed it at Capcom, with Hiroyuki Kawano, Hiroshi Matsumoto and Akira Kitamura designing and Tamayo Kawamoto composing. Capcom released it in arcades in November 1986, in versions with the heroes Michelle Heart and Kevin Walker or, in one overseas version, two nameless men.

The NES version of July 1988 added longer levels, flight in the side-scrolling stages, different bosses and a Turtle Dove form, and Hardcore Gaming 101's Kurt Kalata called it "one of the better shoot-em-ups for the console". IGN ranked it 70th among the greatest NES games.

title: Side Arms
description: Side Arms (1986) is Capcom's horizontal shooter, in which two Mobilsuit pilots fire left and right with separate buttons and can merge their suits into one eight-way-firing machine.
longDescription: The evil alien Bozon empire launches a full-scale attack on Earth, and Lt. Henry and Sgt. Sanders fight back in giant Mobilsuits, alone or together. An eight-way joystick moves the suit, two buttons fire left and right, as in Capcom's earlier Section Z, and a third cycles through collected weapons. Power-up icons change as they are shot, giving a speed upgrade, an orbiting bit, a fan-shaped shotgun, a three-way shot or a mega bazooka laser, though one is a speed downgrade. Two automatic power-ups look like enemies from Vulgus: the Yashichi gives continuous fire, and the Sakichi fires up, down and forward at once. The α and β power-ups merge a suit with its ally into one machine that also fires in eight directions; in two-player games one player steers and the other aims the extra gun.
trivia: Its full title is Hyper Dyne Side Arms.
Capcom made the PC Engine version, but NEC Avenue published it to avoid offending Nintendo, according to composer Takashi Tateishi.
Its Yashichi and Sakichi power-ups resemble enemies from Vulgus.
Being hit while merged splits the two suits apart again.
It was included in Capcom Arcade 2nd Stadium in 2022.
devStory:
Yoshiki Okamoto and Noritaka Funamizu designed it at Capcom, with Takashi Aoki programming, Akira Yasuda drawing and Ayako Mori composing. Romstar released it in North America in November 1986 and Capcom in Japan that December, and it was the ninth most successful table arcade unit in Game Machine's 1 February 1987 issue.

The 1989 PC Engine version, which Computer and Video Games scored 90%, let players change weapons from a pause menu but dropped two-player play, and a CD-ROM² version, Side Arms Special, added a "Before Christ" mode. Probe Software made the European home computer versions.

title: 1943: The Battle of Midway
description: 1943: The Battle of Midway (1987) is Capcom's follow-up to 1942, in which a P-38 Lightning flies 16 stages to sink the battleship Yamato, with a fuel meter in place of lives.
longDescription:
An unnamed US Navy ace flies a P-38 Lightning off Midway Atoll through 16 stages against Japanese air and sea forces, ending with the battleship Yamato. Eleven stages are air-to-sea battles against a battleship or carrier, and five are aerial fights against bomber squadrons or a single heavy bomber, brought down by shooting its engines. Instead of several lives there is one fuel meter that drains constantly and is refilled by power-ups, and in two-player games the planes can share fuel by overlapping.

Destroying a whole formation of red planes drops a power-up. The six weapons range from the starting machine gun to a shotgun that destroys enemy fire, a three-way gun, the bursting Auto, the continuous Shell and a rare laser obtained from a beckoning cat. The second button spends fuel on one of three special attacks — Lightning, a Tsunami that damages ships and halts the scrolling, and a Cyclone that wipes out enemy fire — or loops the plane when pressed with the first.
trivia: Okamoto said it drew protests from Japanese right-wing groups, who saw it as an insult to the war dead at Yasukuni Shrine.
The NES version renamed its warships and battlefields with fictional names.
An alternate arcade version, 1943 Kai, was released in Japan.
A fully destroyed battleship can release Mobi-chan from Side Arms, worth 100,000 points.
The rare laser is obtained by collecting a beckoning cat.
devStory:
Yoshiki Okamoto produced it, Noritaka Funamizu designed it and Kumi Yamaga composed the music, and it was Capcom's first follow-up to 1942 and one of its first games aimed at Western markets. Capcom released it in Japan in June 1987, where Game Machine listed it as the most popular arcade game in July, and it was Japan's second highest-grossing table arcade game of the year. Capcom's own NES version, released exactly a year later, added permanent upgrades bought with statistic points.

Okamoto said the setting was chosen to put the player on the winning side and the content was fantastical, with Yamato appearing at Midway, where it was not present.

title: Black Tiger
description: Black Tiger (1987) is Capcom's platform game, in which a barbarian hunts three demonic dragons, freeing wise men and spending Zenny coins on better weapons and armour.
longDescription: Three demonic dragons seize a kingdom and bring darkness and destruction, and a barbarian rises from the ruins to slay them across eight levels that scroll in eight directions, as Bionic Commando's also do, fighting enemies and bosses. Wise men rescued along the way give rewards, mostly Zenny coins, which buy weapon and armour upgrades, keys for treasure chests and anti-poison potions. Striking certain walls reveals coins, armour, full vitality, extra lives, extra time or points, hidden dungeons hold more, and the vitality bar can grow up to four times at score milestones. The Japanese version, Black Dragon, is harder, with extra falling rocks, higher prices and bosses that can no longer be dodged by crouching beneath them.
trivia: It was one of ten games in a $2,000,000 deal between U.S. Gold and Japanese coin-op makers.
Its planned release around October 1986 slipped because of "programming placement difficulties".
In Japan it was called Black Dragon.
SonSon II on the PC Engine was heavily based on it, aimed at a younger audience.
It was the first free game in Capcom Arcade Cabinet in 2013.
devStory:
Yoshiki Okamoto produced it, Masayuki Akahori programmed it and Tamayo Kawamoto composed the music. Its planned release around October 1986 slipped because of "programming placement difficulties", and Capcom released it in 1987; Game Machine ranked it sixth among Japan's table arcade units that October.

It was one of ten games in a $2,000,000 deal between U.S. Gold and Japanese coin-op makers, and U.S. Gold released Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum versions in 1989, with Softworx's Commodore 64 version in 1990. Computer and Video Games gave U.S. Gold's release 86%, and IGN gave the 2011 Wii Virtual Console release 7.5 out of 10.

title: Forgotten Worlds
description: Forgotten Worlds (1988) is the first game on Capcom's CP System board, a two-player shooter in which supersoldiers aim in sixteen directions with a rotating roll switch.
longDescription: In the 29th century the evil god Bios has destroyed most of Earth, leaving a wasteland called the Dust World, and two nameless supersoldiers are created to defeat him and the eight evil gods who serve him across nine stages. Up to two players fly with unlimited rifles, player one's long-range and player two's a short-range wide shot. A rotating "roll switch" aims in sixteen directions and fires when pressed; pressed rapidly, it unleashes a "megacrush" that wipes out every enemy on screen at the cost of vitality. A satellite module orbits each soldier and fires with them. Enemies drop blue Zenny coins, spent in shops at set points on satellite weapons, health kits, armour and tips for beating the bosses.
trivia: Its working title was Lost Worlds.
It took two years to make, on a budget cited as about $5,000,000.
It won Best Graphics at the 1988 Gamest Awards.
U.S. Gold's artists digitised its graphics from the arcade screen for the home versions.
The PlayStation 2 and Xbox compilation versions let players aim with the right analogue stick.
devStory:
Originally titled Lost Worlds, it took two years and was the first game on Capcom's CP System board, which the team tried to push to its limits with four megabytes of sprite data. Yoshiki Okamoto wanted something more imaginative than a regular side-scroller, and Capcom tried to make it easier after complaints that earlier games' bullets were too hard to dodge. It came out in Japan on 13 May 1988 and won Best Graphics at the Gamest Awards, but earnings were low amid many competing shooters and a shortage of chips for the board.

U.S. Gold's home computer versions of 1989, made by Arc Developments in four months, earned 97% from Zzap!64, and Sega's Genesis version kept seven of the nine stages.

title: U.N. Squadron
description: U.N. Squadron (1989), Area 88 in Japan, is Capcom's mercenary jet shooter based on the manga, in which pilots buy weapons between missions and fly on an energy bar instead of lives.
longDescription: Three mercenary pilots — Shin Kazama, Mickey Simon and Greg Gates — fight a terrorist group called Project 4, each flying a specific plane with slightly different abilities. Unlike Capcom's 1942 and 1943, the game scrolls sideways. As in Capcom's other shooters of the time, each pilot has an energy bar that drains with damage over a single life, rather than a stock of lives. Money from destroyed planes and vehicles buys special weapons and extra defences in a shop before each mission, and any weapons left unused at the end of a level are turned back into cash.
trivia: The North American release dropped all references to the Area 88 manga.
Entertainment Weekly gave the Super NES version an A and ranked it 12th among the greatest games of 1991.
Its spiritual successor is Carrier Air Wing.
Marc Ericksen, who drew the covers of Mega Man 2 and Strider, painted its poster art.
Home computer versions were published by U.S. Gold.
devStory:
Yoshiki Okamoto directed it, with music by Manami Matsumae. He said it was part of a Capcom strategy of using established characters from other media to reach wider audiences, as with its Willow and Dynasty Wars games, and in Japan it was released as Area 88, after Kaoru Shintani's manga. Capcom released it in August 1989, and it became a major hit in North America, topping RePlay's chart for software conversion kits in February 1990.

The Super NES version followed in 1991, letting every pilot buy from a range of aircraft starting with $3,000 and an F8 Crusader. It averaged 87% on GameRankings, Mean Machines gave it 94%, and IGN later ranked it 37th among its top 100 Super NES games, the highest-placed side-scrolling shooter on the list.

title: Captain Commando
description: Captain Commando (1991) is Capcom's four-player beat 'em up starring its former American mascot, with a mummy-like alien, a ninja and a baby in a robot as his companions.
longDescription:
In the Metro City of 2026, the setting of Final Fight, Captain Commando and his three Commando Companions fight super-criminals led by the alien tyrant Scumocide. The captain fires bolts of fire and electricity from his Energy Gloves; Mack the Knife is a mummy-like alien whose sub-sonic knives melt enemies; Ginzu, 41st successor of the Bushin-ryu ninja school, is the only one who throws shuriken; and Baby Head is a genius infant who fights inside a robot.

Following Final Fight's formula, two to four players each choose a different commando and fight through nine stages, each ending in a boss. Pressing attack and jump together unleashes a special attack at the cost of some health. Food is hidden in barrels, three kinds of firearm can be picked up and, unlike in Final Fight, carried between areas, and the heroes can climb into robots that punch, burn or freeze enemies.
trivia: The character began as a fictional spokesman in Capcom USA's console games before Akira Yasuda redesigned him.
Captain Commando became a playable character in Marvel vs. Capcom (1998).
The Super NES version cut the robots and the four-player mode.
Scumocide is called Genocide in Japan.
Street Fighter 6 links Ginzu's family to the Street Fighter universe through his father, Gou.
devStory:
Captain Commando had appeared on the packaging and manuals of Capcom's North American NES and Commodore 64 games from 1986 to 1989, in the "Captain Commando Challenge Series". For the arcade game Akira Yasuda, who found the original design "uncool", redrew him; Yoshiki Okamoto produced, Yasuda and Junichi Ohno designed it and Masaki Izutani composed the music. Capcom released it in North America in September 1991 as its 17th CP System game, and it sold about 15,000 arcade units.

Game Machine named it Japan's most popular arcade game in its December 1991 issue. The 1995 Super NES version was limited to two players and dropped the robots.

title: Knights of the Round
description: Knights of the Round (1991) is Capcom's Arthurian beat 'em up, in which Arthur, Lancelot and Perceval level up as they fight to overthrow the evil king Garibaldi.
longDescription:
Arthur pulls Excalibur from the stone, learning he is destined to be the first King of the Britons, and Merlin sends him with Lancelot and Perceval to overthrow the evil king Garibaldi and unite Britain. Like Final Fight and Capcom's The King of Dragons, it is a scrolling brawler, but with role-playing levels: the heroes are upgraded automatically with new weapons and armour. Blocking means pressing attack and pushing away just as an enemy strikes, which grants a few seconds of invincibility, though holding a guard too long tires the hero out, and some bosses can be hurt only after their attack is blocked. Attack and jump together unleash a desperation attack at the cost of some health, and horseback sections let riders trample enemies.

Arthur is balanced and strongest on horseback, Lancelot with his sabre the fastest but weakest, and Perceval, a blacksmith's son with a battle-axe, the strongest but slowest, and the only one who can dash.
trivia: Game Machine listed it as the most popular arcade game in Japan for two weeks in early 1992.
The Super NES version sold only 5,225 copies in Japan, according to Famitsu.
Perceval goes from blond to bald and bearded as he levels up.
Some bosses can only be damaged after their attack has been blocked.
It was included in Capcom Beat 'Em Up Bundle in 2018.
devStory: Capcom released it in North America on 27 November 1991 and Japan in January 1992, with music by Isao Abe, and Game Machine listed it as the most popular table arcade game over two weeks in its 1 March 1992 issue. Sinclair User gave it 78, saying fans of Golden Axe would like it. The Super NES version of 1994 got mixed reviews; GamePro praised its sprites but found its play slow and repetitive.

title: Cadillacs and Dinosaurs
description: Cadillacs and Dinosaurs (1993) is Capcom's three-player beat 'em up based on the comic Xenozoic Tales, in which four heroes fight poachers hunting dinosaurs in the 26th century.
longDescription: In the 26th century the Black Marketeers hunt dinosaurs, driving them to attack villages and people, and four heroes set out to stop them: Jack Tenrec, a mechanic and shaman; Hannah Dundee, a diplomat and explorer; Mustapha Cairo, Jack's friend and an engineer; and the enigmatic Mess O'Bradovich. Jack is the balanced fighter, Hannah the skilled one, Mustapha the fastest and Mess the strongest. Up to three players fight through eight stages, from the City in the Sea and a swamp forest to a desert and Jack's own garage, using guns, rocks, explosives and clubs, while dinosaurs roam as neutral creatures that attack anyone. Each hero has two special moves, and two or more players can launch a team attack. The trail leads to Dr. Simon Fessenden, who turns into a monster, twice. A defeated player gets a 20-second countdown to continue, with a villain holding a gun to their face.
trivia: It was made to tie in with the animated series Cadillacs and Dinosaurs, which aired the same year.
A version for the Capcom Power System Changer was previewed but never released.
Go Play listed it among the best CPS1 games "you're unlikely to ever play on a Capcom compilation".
In Japan it is Cadillacs Kyouryuu Shinseiki.
Its dinosaurs attack heroes and villains alike.
devStory: Based on Mark Schultz's comic Xenozoic Tales and made to tie in with the animated series that aired the same year, it came out in April 1993 on Capcom's CP System Dash board, with music by Isao Abe and Syun Nishigaki. Computer and Video Games gave it 89/100, and it was among Japan's most popular arcade games that June, ahead of Warriors of Fate, while RePlay listed it ninth in the US. It was never ported directly to home systems; the console game The Second Cataclysm is a different game.

title: Akalabeth: World of Doom
description: Akalabeth (1980) is the Apple II role-playing game Richard Garriott wrote as a Houston teenager, often counted as the first Ultima and nicknamed "Ultima 0".
longDescription: Lord British, Richard Garriott's alter ego, sends the player to kill ten monsters, each harder than the last, the final one a Balrog. Most of the game takes place in underground dungeons drawn in first-person wireframe, reportedly the first computer RPG with such graphics, with a simple overhead map of the world above and text descriptions. The Adventure Shop sells food, weapons, a shield and a magic amulet. Each world is generated from a "lucky number" the player types in at the start, so the same number gives the same world. Several things that became standard in Ultima appear here first: first-person dungeons, the need for food, a top-down overworld, hotkeys and Elizabethan English.
trivia: The name comes from Tolkien's Akallabêth, although the game does not follow Tolkien's story.
Garriott claims about 30,000 copies sold at $5 each to him; historian Jimmy Maher thinks the real figure was nearer 10,000.
The 1998 Ultima Collection included it, nicknamed Ultima 0.
Being written in Applesoft BASIC, its code could be edited by players.
Its home-made packaging warned "BEWARE FOOLISH MORTAL, YOU TRESPASS IN AKALABETH, WORLD OF DOOM!!"
devStory:
Garriott began it as a high-school project in his junior year on his school's PDP-11, under the working title DND, and friends who played Dungeons & Dragons tested it for two years. In summer 1979 he moved to an Apple II his father bought, switching from an ASCII overhead view to first-person dungeons after playing Escape. His boss at a ComputerLand store near Webster, Texas, suggested selling it, and Garriott spent $200 packaging copies in Ziploc bags with photocopied instructions and a cover drawn by his mother, at $20 each.

California Pacific then published it in 1980 at $35, paying him $5 a copy and crediting the author as "Lord British". Steve Jackson recommended it highly in The Space Gamer.

title: Freeway
description: Freeway (1981) is David Crane's Activision game about getting chickens across a ten-lane highway, alone or against a second player, in two minutes and sixteen seconds.
longDescription: One or two players guide chickens across a ten-lane highway full of traffic, scoring a point for each crossing, and after two minutes and sixteen seconds the higher score wins. With the difficulty switch on A, a chicken that is hit goes back to the kerb; on B it is only knocked back a lane. The select switch picks the road: Chicago's Lake Shore Drive or New York's Long Island Expressway at 3 a.m., or San Francisco's Bayshore Freeway at midnight, and eight modes vary the speed and amount of traffic.
trivia: Reviewers compared it with Frogger, but Crane said the two were made "in secure laboratories 6,000 miles apart".
It received an Honorable Mention for Most Innovative Game at the 1982 Arcade Awards, shared with Asteroids.
Its three highways are real: Lake Shore Drive, the Long Island Expressway and the Bayshore Freeway.
AllGame called the chicken "a bit sickly" but praised the engine and horn sounds.
It shipped the same month as Activision's Kaboom!.
devStory:
David Crane, one of the programmers who left Atari over pay to found Activision, linked the idea to a Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago, where he saw someone cross Lake Shore Drive. He based the play on the 1973 arcade game Space Race, and his first version had two men moving up the screen. Three days before the next CES, Activision CEO Jim Levy suggested a chicken instead, for the old joke; the plan to have the San Diego Chicken mascot promote it fell through. Activision released it in July 1981, alongside Kaboom!.

Electronic Games called it "wonderfully, joyously original", and in 1983 Videogaming and Computer Gaming Illustrated listed it among the five best 2600 games, "far more exciting and involving than Frogger".

title: Gridrunner
description: Gridrunner (1982) is Jeff Minter's fast Centipede-style shooter, written in about a week for the unexpanded VIC-20, which topped the US computer game chart in April 1983.
longDescription: Enemies snake down the screen in long, segmented, zig-zagging chains that can be broken apart, as in Atari's Centipede, with pods taking the place of Centipede's mushrooms. The player's small ship fires upwards and moves freely around the grid, while X-Y zappers patrolling the edges send out pulses that must be dodged. There are twenty waves, and the game plays faster than Centipede. The Commodore 64 Home Companion advised players to "forget the plot; fast action is the name of this game".
trivia: The name came from posters for Blade Runner.
Its sequel, Matrix: Gridrunner 2, was sold in the US as Attack of the Mutant Camels, a title Minter had already used for a different game.
It topped the US computer game sales chart in April 1983.
Minter wrote it in about a week.
A new version is included in Digital Eclipse's Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story.
devStory:
Jeff Minter wrote it in about a week for the unexpanded VIC-20, taking its name from posters for Blade Runner, and Llamasoft released it in 1982. HESware, Quicksilva and Salamander published versions for the Commodore 64, Atari 8-bit, ZX Spectrum, PET and Dragon 32, and in April 1983 it topped the US computer game sales chart.

Matrix: Gridrunner 2 (1983) added new enemies and a scrolling background, followed by Voidrunner (1987) and Super Gridrunner (1991). After a decade's gap came Gridrunner++ (2002), Gridrunner Revolution (2009), the only one with a full musical soundtrack, and a 2012 iOS version that Eurogamer called "the best shooter on iOS".

title: Raiders of the Lost Ark
description: Raiders of the Lost Ark (1982) is Howard Scott Warshaw's Atari 2600 adventure based on the film, played with two joysticks: one moves Indiana Jones and the other manages his inventory.
longDescription: Indiana Jones searches for the Ark of the Covenant, starting in Cairo in 1936, represented by an entrance room and a marketplace. A grenade blasts through the entrance room wall into the Temple of the Ancients, whose two dangerous paths lead to a treasure room with gold and artifacts for later. Crossing a mesa leads to the Map Room, which shows where the Ark lies, and to the south are a Thieves Den and a Black Market with sheikhs, a tsetse fly, a lunatic and essential items such as a shovel. Finally Indy parachutes off the mesa, slips in through a small hole and digs up the Ark while dodging thieves. Two controllers are needed: the second moves Jones and uses items, the first selects and drops them, so he can carry more than one at a time.
trivia: Warshaw opposed Atari's decision to print hints in the manual.
Bruce Chadwick wrote that it sold under a million copies by February 1983, below Atari's hopes.
Its second joystick manages the inventory, getting round Adventure's one-item limit.
Spielberg asked Warshaw to adapt E.T. next.
Electronic Games said it "doesn't quite live up to" the film.
devStory:
Howard Scott Warshaw volunteered when Atari offered the licence, seeing a film as a middle ground between arcade ports, which he thought an "exercise in futility", and original games. He met Steven Spielberg and began in mid-1981, cutting the film to its key points, adding a treasure room and a map room, and using the second joystick to escape Adventure's one-item limit. It fitted on an 8 KB cartridge, Warshaw drew most of the graphics and Jerome Domurat animated Indy.

Atari released it in November 1982. The Space Gamer called it "the adventure cartridge of the year", and Spielberg then asked Warshaw to adapt E.T.

sources.title: Raiders of the Lost Ark (video game)

title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
description: E.T. (1982) is Howard Scott Warshaw's Atari 2600 film tie-in, made in just over five weeks, whose returned and buried cartridges became a symbol of the 1983 video game crash.
longDescription:
E.T. must collect three pieces of an interplanetary telephone hidden in pits across six areas, while an energy bar drains with every step, teleport and fall. Reese's Pieces restore energy, and collecting nine lets him call Elliott, who brings a phone piece; a geranium found in a pit grants an extra life. An icon at the top of the screen shows what can be done in each area. A scientist takes E.T. away for observation, and an FBI agent steals phone pieces or candy.

Once the phone is complete, E.T. calls home and has to reach the landing zone before a clock runs out; his ship then takes him home, and the game restarts with the pieces moved and the score carried over. Critics attacked the gameplay, the visuals and how often E.T. falls into pits, and it is regularly listed among the worst games ever made.
trivia: Unsold cartridges were reportedly buried in a landfill at Alamogordo, New Mexico; diggers found E.T. cartridges there in April 2014.
It sold about 2.6 million copies by the end of 1982, but Atari's Ray Kassar later said about 3.5 million of the 4 million made came back.
Only about 10% of the roughly 1,300 cartridges recovered at Alamogordo were E.T.
The Smithsonian added an excavated cartridge to its collection in December 2014.
Electronic Gaming Monthly ranked it the worst game of all time.
devStory:
After the film's success in June 1982, Warner Communications' Steve Ross negotiated the licence with Steven Spielberg and Universal, reportedly for $20–25 million; Atari's CEO, Ray Kassar, called an E.T. game "a dumb idea". On 27 July Kassar gave Howard Scott Warshaw, who had spent seven months on Yars' Revenge and six on Raiders of the Lost Ark, a deadline of 1 September, reportedly for $200,000 and a trip to Hawaii. Warshaw met Spielberg, who suggested something like Pac-Man, but kept his own design. Jerome Domurat helped with the graphics, and there was no time for audience testing.

It came out in December 1982 and reached the top four of Billboard's video game chart, selling over 2.6 million copies by the end of the year. Retailers said the buyers were "mostly grandmothers", returns piled up, and the game became linked with the 1983 crash. Warshaw does not regret his work.

title: Attack of the Mutant Camels
description: Attack of the Mutant Camels (1983) is Jeff Minter's Commodore 64 shooter in which a small jet must bring down giant yellow camels before they reach its base.
longDescription: The player flies a small jet over a scrolling landscape, trying to bring down giant yellow camels before they reach the home base. Each camel takes several dozen shots to destroy and spits fireballs from its mouth, and if one reaches the base the game is lost. Destroying every camel in a wave leads to a "hyperspace" sequence of dodging high-speed missiles, followed by a new, slightly tougher herd. The set-up follows Atari's 1982 The Empire Strikes Back for the 2600, with camels standing in for the AT-AT walkers, in what has been called a surrealist style.
trivia: It was shown in the Smithsonian's "The Art of Video Games" exhibition in 2011.
Its sequel was Revenge of the Mutant Camels (1984).
Each camel takes several dozen hits to bring down.
Confusingly, Minter's Matrix: Gridrunner 2 was also sold in the US as Attack of the Mutant Camels.
It is modelled on Atari's The Empire Strikes Back, with camels in place of AT-ATs.
devStory: Jeff Minter designed and wrote it for Llamasoft, which released it in 1983 for the Commodore 64 and Atari 8-bit computers. Commodore User called it "skilfully-designed" and "excellent for camel/llama freaks and arcade action enthusiasts", and Home Computing Weekly praised its sound, graphics and documentation, its only criticism being that it was "perhaps a little too difficult!" In 2012 the assembly source code of an unreleased Konix version was published on GitHub.

title: F-15 Strike Eagle
description: F-15 Strike Eagle (1984) is Sid Meier's combat flight simulator for MicroProse, which sold more than 1.5 million copies across home computers, consoles and an arcade version.
longDescription: Based on the McDonnell Douglas F-15E Strike Eagle, it lets the player pick a theatre — Libya, much like Operation El Dorado Canyon, the Persian Gulf or Vietnam — and starts already airborne in an F-15 armed with missiles, bombs, drop tanks, flares and chaff. The task is to bomb a primary and a secondary target while fighting off enemy fighters, and the mission ends with a crash, a shoot-down or a return to base. MicroProse's Bill Stealey said its mechanics and manual drew only on non-classified information approved by the authorities.
trivia: It was MicroProse's best-selling Commodore game as of late 1987.
Computer Gaming World readers voted it Action Game of the Year in 1985.
The Soviet embassy in Washington reportedly bought four copies on launch day.
Its Libya scenario resembles Operation El Dorado Canyon.
Compute! listed it among its favourite games in 1988.
devStory:
Sid Meier designed it for MicroProse, and it appeared first on Atari 8-bit computers in 1984, followed by Apple II, Commodore 64, IBM PC and Atari ST versions in 1985; the first PC version was a self-booting disk with only CGA graphics, among MicroProse's first games for IBM compatibles. Computer Gaming World called it "an excellent simulation", and its readers voted it Action Game of the Year in 1985.

Sales passed 250,000 by March 1987 and a million by 1989, reaching more than 1.5 million in all. A 1991 arcade version ran on the TMS34010 processor, and NES, Game Boy and Game Gear versions followed, along with the sequels F-15 Strike Eagle II and III.

title: NARC
description: NARC (1988) is Eugene Jarvis's Williams run and gun about arresting or shooting drug dealers, the first arcade game on Texas Instruments' TMS34010 processor and one of the first "ultra-violent" games.
longDescription: Under "Project NARC", run from Washington by Spencer Williams, chairman of the Narcotics Opposition, the officers Max Force and Hit Man go after Mr. Big, head of the drug-trafficking and terrorist organisation K.R.A.K. One or two players shoot or arrest junkies, dealers and kingpins, each armed with an automatic weapon and a missile launcher whose kills end in gory explosions. Some enemies surrender and can be arrested, and the arrests, along with the drugs and money dropped by dead enemies, are tallied at the end of each level; arrests score more than kills. Players can buy in repeatedly, except on the final stage.
trivia: The NES version, made by Rare and sold as anti-drug, removed the blood and renamed K.R.A.K. to K.W.A.K.
The Pixies recorded Brian L. Schmidt's main theme as a B-side in 1990.
Actors in costume played its enemies, filmed on a treadmill.
Its digitising technology was later used for Mortal Kombat and NBA Jam.
A reimagined Narc came out in 2005, with Michael Madsen voicing the lead.
devStory:
Eugene Jarvis designed it, partly drawing on people he knew with drug problems, and programmed it with George Petro and Todd Allen, with music by Brian L. Schmidt.
