It was the first game of Williams' restarted coin-op division and the first arcade game on Texas Instruments' 32-bit TMS34010; that chip was too slow for Jarvis's design, so Williams engineer Mark Loffredo built a custom blitter. Enemies were played by actors in baggy costumes, their walks and runs recorded on a treadmill and digitised.

Unveiled at the 1988 AMOA Expo, where trade papers called it a "breakthrough game", it reached arcades in December 1988 and sold over 3,700 units. Parents criticised it as one of the first games with blood, and Crash later gave the Spectrum version 94% and 95%, calling it the best coin-op conversion of 1990.

title: The Colonel's Bequest
description: The Colonel's Bequest (1989) is Roberta Williams's Sierra murder mystery, in which student Laura Bow investigates on a decaying sugar plantation island off Louisiana in 1925.
longDescription:
In 1925 Laura Bow, a Tulane student, aspiring journalist and daughter of a detective, is invited by her flapper friend Lillian to the decaying plantation of the reclusive Colonel Dijon, who has gathered his relatives for the reading of his will. Murder follows, and Laura is stranded on the island with a household of suspects — among them the snobbish widow Gertie, the would-be actress Gloria Swansong, the gambler Rudy, the lawyer Clarence Sparrow and the physician Dr. Feels, many named after stars of the era. There is also an optional hunt for hidden treasure.

Characters keep their own schedules, so Laura can follow and eavesdrop on them. The clock advances a quarter-hour whenever she witnesses something new, with a new act each hour. There is no visible score, and the game can be finished without solving a single puzzle or naming the murderer; at the end a screen hints at everything that was missed. Most deaths are accidents, though in later acts the murderer can come for Laura, once in a shower scene borrowed from Psycho. The ending depends on what she does in the attic.
trivia: It was one of Sierra's last games with a text parser, along with King's Quest IV.
Its sequel, The Dagger of Amon Ra (1992), takes Laura to New York as a reporter.
Laura Bow is named after the silent film star Clara Bow.
The Colonel's surname is a nod to Cluedo's Colonel Mustard.
Adventure Gamers ranked it 84th among the best adventure games in 2011.
devStory:
Roberta Williams wrote it and directed it with Chris Iden, drawing on Agatha Christie and on the mansion murder of her own Mystery House; Jacqueline Austin designed it, Ken Williams produced and Ken Allen composed the music. It ran on Sierra's SCI0 engine in 16-colour EGA, and came out for MS-DOS in October 1989, with Amiga and Atari ST versions in 1990.

Reviews were positive. Computer Gaming World's Johnny L. Wilson warned that puzzle-solvers might find it too easy but praised its story and humour.

title: Railroad Tycoon
description: Sid Meier's Railroad Tycoon (1990) is the MicroProse business simulation, designed by Meier and Bruce Shelley, in which the player builds and runs a railway company for a century.
longDescription:
The player starts with $1 million, half equity and half loan, in one of four regions — the western or northeastern United States, Great Britain or continental Europe — and builds a railway over a century, closing the books every two years. Track, stations and trains are bought and scheduled by hand. Stations come in four sizes, from signal towers that act as passing loops to terminals that serve the widest area, and can add stores and hotels; trains carry mail, passengers and nine kinds of freight, and are built at engine shops. Up to 32 stations and 32 trains are allowed.

Supply and demand govern goods and passengers, and a stock market lets the player buy shares in their own company and in rivals, who use stock dealings and rate wars to try to force the player out. In the Simple economy large cities buy anything; in the Complex one, each city buys only certain goods. More capital can be raised by issuing bonds.
trivia: It was based on Avalon Hill's 1986 board game 1830: The Game of Railroads and Robber Barons.
Computer Gaming World named it Game of the Year for 1990 and added it to its Hall of Fame in 1992.
A Super NES port was shown in Nintendo Power in 1993 but never released.
The DOS version became freeware in 2006.
PC Gamer US called it "groundbreaking in every sense" in 1998.
devStory:
Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley designed it at MicroProse, with music by Jeff Briggs, drawing on Avalon Hill's 1986 board game 1830: The Game of Railroads and Robber Barons. Avalon Hill's president objected that MicroProse was making his board game into a computer game, then said, "Well, don't let it happen again." It came out in 1990 for MS-DOS and later the Amiga, Mac, Atari ST, FM Towns and PC-98.

Computer Gaming World named it Game of the Year in 1990 and added it to its Hall of Fame in 1992, and it won the Software Publishers Association's award for Best Strategy Program. PC Gamer US ranked it the fourth-best computer game ever in 1994. A Deluxe version followed in 1993, and the series continued with Railroad Tycoon II.

title: SimCity 2000
description: SimCity 2000 (1993) is Maxis's sequel to SimCity, designed by Will Wright and Fred Haslam, which moved the city into a near-isometric view with hills, underground pipes and subways.
longDescription:
Land now has height, and a separate underground layer holds water pipes, subways and road tunnels. New buildings include prisons, schools, libraries, museums, marinas, hospitals and futuristic arcologies, and transport runs from roads and highways to buses, railways, seaports and airports. There are nine kinds of power plant, from coal and nuclear to wind, solar, fusion and satellite microwave, and most wear out and must be rebuilt. Residential, commercial and industrial taxes are set separately, and city ordinances and highway connections to neighbouring cities shape growth; extreme debt ends the game.

News arrives in pre-written newspapers with random titles, a price that rises with the simulated year and sometimes an advice column. Querying a library and choosing "Ruminate" shows an essay by Neil Gaiman. There is no victory condition, though from 2051 a city with 300 Launch Arcologies sees them leave for space. Scenarios ask the player to rebuild after disasters, some based on real events such as the 1991 Oakland firestorm and Hurricane Hugo in Charleston, others fanciful, like a monster attacking Hollywood.
trivia: Build 300 or more Launch Arcologies in 2051 or later and they leave the city for space.
The Museum of Modern Art acquired it in December 2012.
The SimCity Urban Renewal Kit let players redraw its buildings, and its cities could be flown over in SimCopter.
The Japanese Saturn version puts up a Sonic statue when the city reaches 30,000 people.
It was the only main SimCity with a newspaper; later games used a news ticker.
devStory:
Fred Haslam was asked to make the sequel in December 1990, after he and Will Wright finished SimEarth; Wright, who had spent five years on the original, at first declined. Haslam spent most of 1991 on a top-down version before Maxis chose a near-isometric style like A-Train's, and when he struggled with it, Wright joined. Wright contributed arcologies, small-scale simulations and the underground view; Haslam the newspaper, which replaced the score, free-size zoning, bonds and neighbour connections. Mining, farming and one-way streets were cut.

It came out for the Mac and DOS in 1993, won the 1994 Codie for Best Simulation, and was named the best computer game of all time by PC Gamer UK in 1994. It sold about 4.23 million copies.

title: D
description: D (1995) is Kenji Eno's full-motion video horror game for the 3DO, played in a single two-hour sitting with no saves and no pause, which sold about a million copies in Japan.
longDescription:
In 1997, Los Angeles police tell Laura Harris that her father, Dr. Richter Harris, director of the LA National Hospital, has committed mass murder and barricaded himself inside. When she goes in, the hospital becomes a medieval castle; she has flashbacks of her mother being stabbed, and her father's apparitions warn her to leave before he turns into a monster and attacks her. The family, it emerges, is a bloodline of cannibalistic vampires linked to Dracula, and Laura killed and ate her mother as a child, a memory her father erased.

Laura moves through pre-rendered video between static screens with objects and paths to interact with. There is no saving and no pausing, and after two hours of real time she is pulled back to the real world and the game ends. What the player does decides the ending: approaching her transforming father gets Laura eaten, while shooting him with a revolver found earlier stops the change.
trivia: Eno reportedly submitted a clean version, then swapped in the disturbing one on the flight to the US.
GameFan named it 3DO Game of the Year for 1995.
In Japan it is known as D no Shokutaku, "D's Diner".
Its digital actress, Laura, returned in Enemy Zero and D2.
Nightdive Studios re-released the MS-DOS version in 2016.
devStory:
It was Warp's first major title, and Kenji Eno, who directed and wrote it, said he would quit making games if it failed. Inspired by Polarware's Transylvania games, it took about a year, with the video made on Amiga 4000 computers; finding his Dracula-based plot dull, Eno added violence and cannibalism and hid those scenes from the rest of Warp. It came out on the 3DO in Japan on 1 April 1995, followed by Saturn and PlayStation versions, and sold about a million copies in Japan, one of the few real 3DO hits there.

Sony made only about 28,000 PlayStation copies against some 100,000 orders, and Eno announced that his next games would be on the Saturn. GameFan called it "the best FMV game likely ever to be made".

title: Phantasmagoria
description: Phantasmagoria (1995) is Roberta Williams's seven-disc horror adventure, filmed with 25 actors and Sierra's first game to sell a million copies.
longDescription:
Adrienne Delaney, a mystery novelist, moves with her husband Don and their cat Spaz into a remote New England island mansion once owned by the magician Zoltan "Carno" Carnovasch, whose five wives all died mysteriously. Exploring the house, Adrienne releases the demon that possessed Carno and drove him to murder, and it takes hold of Don, who grows abusive and violent. Carno's old apprentice, Malcolm Wyrmshadow, explains the ritual that can trap the demon again.

Adrienne is always on screen, and the player directs her with a simple point-and-click interface: one cursor, eight inventory slots, a gauge showing progress through each chapter, a button to skip cinematics and a red skull that gives hints. Roberta Williams kept the puzzles relatively easy. The actors were filmed in front of a blue screen and set into more than 1,000 rendered backgrounds, and a password-protected option blurs the violence.
trivia: Australia refused to classify it, effectively banning it, and the retailer CompUSA would not stock it.
The script ran to about 550 pages, around four times a typical Hollywood screenplay.
A 135-voice choir sings the opening chant.
Williams later called it the game that best represented her career.
A sequel, Phantasmagoria: A Puzzle of Flesh (1996), was written by Lorelei Shannon without Williams.
devStory:
It was Roberta Williams's first horror game, inspired by Stephen King and Edgar Allan Poe; she said she had waited about eight years for CD-ROM technology to make a game with real actors possible. She spent six months on horror films and books before writing a script of about 550 pages, plus 100 pages of storyboards. Peter Maris directed the 25 actors in a $1.5 million studio Sierra built in Oakhurst, California, shooting about 600 scenes over four months, and art director Andy Hoyos conceived most of the death scenes. The budget grew from $800,000 to $4.5 million, and the game filled seven discs.

Released on 24 August 1995, it grossed $12 million in its first weekend and became Sierra's first million-seller. Reviews were mixed, praising its production values and suspense and criticising its pacing, easy puzzles and plot. A rape scene drew the most criticism, and parents' and religious groups called for a boycott.

title: Enemy Zero
description: Enemy Zero (1996) is Kenji Eno's Sega Saturn horror game set on a space station full of invisible creatures, which the player can only track by sound.
longDescription:
Laura Lewis, a "digital actress" first seen in Warp's D, wakes from cryogenic sleep aboard the biological research station AKI to an explosion and a creature trying to break out of a door marked E0, and finds the crew being killed one by one. The ship's log reveals that the mission, for Vexx Industries, is to capture the aliens as biological weapons, and that the crew is expendable.

Exploration alternates between video-based node sections with puzzles and an inventory, as in D, and real-time first-person corridors in which the enemies are invisible; the pitch of a tone tells the player how near they are and from which direction. Every gun must be charged before each shot, overcharging resets it, and the range is so short that charging too early or too late lets the enemy reach Laura, which ends the game at once. Early on she has no weapon at all and must avoid detection.
trivia: Michael Nyman composed the music after Eno persuaded him at a meeting in Kobe.
Fumito Ueda worked on it as an animator.
Twenty limited-edition copies were sold for about $2,000 each and delivered by Eno himself.
Laura is voiced in English by Jill Cunniff of Luscious Jackson.
GameFan named it its Best Import Game of 1996.
devStory:
Kenji Eno, who said the game explored why humans exist, first showed it at the 1996 PlayStation Expo in Tokyo. Angered by Sony's handling of D, he ended his presentation with the PlayStation logo morphing into the Saturn's, making it a Saturn exclusive. Yūji Sakamoto wrote it, Fumito Ueda worked on it as an animator, and development took nine months. Michael Nyman composed the score, recorded in London in 1996, after Eno met him in Kobe following the 1995 earthquake.

Warp released it in Japan on 13 December 1996, and Sega published it in the West in 1997 after Acclaim withdrew. Critics praised its video quality and the tension of invisible enemies but criticised the slow movement, and some called it an Alien rip-off. A Windows version followed in 1998.

title: Speed Race
description: Speed Race (1974) is Tomohiro Nishikado's Taito driving game on a vertically scrolling road, sold in America by Midway as Wheels and Racer.
longDescription: One or two players steer a car up a vertically scrolling road with a steering wheel and accelerator, scoring by passing other cars, with more points at higher speeds. A run lasts 90 seconds, shown with the score on an LED display above the screen, and enough points extend the timer. Hitting another car resets the player's speed and sends them back to the start of the track, and two difficulty settings add speed and traffic.
trivia: Wheels and Wheels II together sold 10,000 cabinets in the US, which Ralph Baer's figures make the best-selling arcade game of 1975.
Its success in Japan helped make 100 yen per play the standard arcade price.
Atari's Hi-way (1975) was influenced by it.
Speed Race V was Japan's second highest-earning arcade game of 1978, behind Space Invaders.
It was a major hit in Australia too.
devStory:
Tomohiro Nishikado developed it in 1974 after Atari's Gran Trak 10, which he disliked for its twisting tracks and complex controls, adapting the idea from Kasco's Mini Drive and Taito's Super Road 7. To simulate scrolling, he animated a background road image and tied the speed of oncoming cars to the player's. Taito released it in Japan in November 1974, charging 100 yen a play instead of the usual 50 because of its complex hardware; it was a major hit, and 100 yen became the standard Japanese arcade price for decades.

Midway brought it to North America in 1975 as Racer, which introduced a sit-down cabinet, and as Wheels. Speed Race DX became Japan's highest-grossing arcade game of 1977, and the series ran into the 1980s.

title: Gee Bee
description: Gee Bee (1978) is Toru Iwatani's cross between Breakout and pinball for Namco, described as the first video game Namco designed in-house.
longDescription: A rotary dial moves a set of paddles that knock the ball into walls of bricks, pop bumpers worth 10 points and spinners that slow it down. Lighting every letter of the NAMCO rollover targets (Gremlin's logo in North America) raises the score multiplier. The board is laid out to resemble a human face, and because of hardware limits, colour came from strips of cellophane on the monitor. The name comes from the Japanese word for the carpenter bee.
trivia: Iwatani had wanted to make pinball machines, and a video game with pinball elements was the compromise.
It was followed in 1979 by Bomb Bee and Cutie Q, whose cute characters later influenced Pac-Man.
It uses the font of Atari's unreleased 1976 arcade game Cannonball.
Its board is designed to look like a face.
It was re-released in Hamster's Arcade Archives in October 2025.
devStory:
In July 1976 Shigeichi Ishimura proposed a CPU-based arcade game, and Namco bought surplus PDA-08 microcomputers from NEC for the project. Toru Iwatani, who joined Namco in 1977 straight from college, wanted to make pinball machines, but his superiors refused, so he designed a video game mixing pinball with Breakout, with Ishimura helping on the programming. It became Namco's first in-house video game.

Namco released it in Japan in October 1978 and Gremlin in North America in January 1979. It sold about 10,000 units and was Japan's eighth highest-earning arcade game of 1978, but fell short of Namco's hopes because of low earnings per machine and competition from Space Invaders. It still helped establish Namco as a major developer in Japan.

title: The Portopia Serial Murder Case
description: The Portopia Serial Murder Case (1983) is Yuji Horii's detective adventure for Enix, a game Hideo Kojima named among his biggest influences, whose menu interface Horii reused in Dragon Quest.
longDescription:
Kouzou Yamakawa, president of a bank company, is found dead by his secretary in a locked room of his Kobe mansion, apparently stabbed by his own hand. The police send an unnamed, silent detective known as "Boss" to investigate with his assistant Yasuhiko "Yasu" Mano, who carries out most of his orders, and the case leads to Kyoto and Sumoto and to suspects including Yamakawa's nephew and heir. Only one character is the true culprit; the rest are red herrings, and naming the wrong one earns a rebuke from the police chief and reopens the case.

The original uses a verb-noun parser, so finding the right words is part of the puzzle, and has no save function. Paths to each objective vary, a telephone can dial any number and is needed to reach some characters, and items collected become evidence. The Japanese press called it "a game without game over". The Famicom version replaced typing with fourteen commands, added a cursor that serves as a magnifying glass or, in interrogations, a fist, and a 3D underground maze.
trivia: The 1985 Famicom version, the console's first adventure game, swapped the typed parser for a menu of fourteen commands and sold 700,000 copies.
Nintendo's Famicom Detective Club series was inspired by it.
Hideo Kojima counts it among his three most influential games, and hid the PC-6001 version in Metal Gear Solid V.
Square Enix's 2023 AI Tech Preview remake was poorly received.
Eiji Aonuma, later director of Ocarina of Time, was among its early players.
devStory:
Yuji Horii conceived it around 1981, aged 27, after buying his first computer and reading a magazine article about American text adventures, which he noticed were rare in Japan. He cited the manga artists Tetsuya Chiba, Mitsuru Adachi and Katsuhiro Otomo as influences, wrote it in BASIC, and wanted branching, nonlinear storytelling, though memory limited him to short branches. Enix released it on the PC-6001 in June 1983. The 1985 Famicom version was programmed by 19-year-old Koichi Nakamura of Chunsoft, Horii's first collaboration with him before Dragon Quest; Horii added the maze after playing Wizardry.

The Famicom version, the console's first adventure game, sold 700,000 copies. Its mature themes, among them murder, suicide, fraud and drugs, are cited as the reason it never came out in the West.

title: Libble Rabble
description: Libble Rabble (1983) is the Namco twin-stick puzzle game begun by Toru Iwatani, in which two arrows joined by a line wrap it round poles to fence in creatures.
longDescription:
The player steers two arrows at once, the red Libble and the blue Rabble, joined by a line that wraps around poles to enclose Mushlins and enemies; closing a loop scores more than simply meeting at the screen edge. A season ends when all the Mushlins are harvested. Killers, Changers and Demons are destroyed by looping them, while Shears cut the line, which is instantly replaced between the arrows. A life is lost if an enemy touches an arrow or the timer, which runs around the screen border, runs out; looping Mushlins and plants adds time.

Closing a loop sometimes sets off a detector showing a buried treasure chest, which opens when enclosed on its own. It releases six Topcups to round up for bonus letters, and completing the bonus word clears the season and leads to a timed bonus stage.
trivia: The 1994 Super Famicom version came with a D-pad cover to mimic the twin-stick controls.
Retro Gamer later called it an underappreciated puzzle classic, comparing it favourably with Qix.
Its working title was "Potato".
Video Games called the Super Famicom version a "politically-correct Super Bomberman".
A medley of its music plays on the Pac-Land stage in Super Smash Bros. for Wii U.
devStory:
Tōru Iwatani, creator of Pac-Man, got the idea in a crowded early-1980s disco, imagining tying people up with ropes, and from a childhood game with ropes and short metal poles. Its working title, "Potato", came from a planned tie-in with a crisp maker that fell through, and Toru Ogawa designed a new board for it. Midway through, Iwatani, overwhelmed by other projects, handed it to Seiichi Sato, who thought the prototype too simple and added the treasure chests, inspired by Wizardry; programmer Kazuo Kurosu felt the additions made it less appealing.

Namco released it in Japan in October 1983, and Game Machine ranked it second among new table arcade units in January 1984. Midway declined to release it in the US.

title: Snatcher
description: Snatcher (1988) is Hideo Kojima's cyberpunk adventure for Konami, in which an amnesiac agent hunts the robots replacing people in Neo Kobe City.
longDescription:
In 2047, after the Lucifer-Alpha bioweapon has killed half the world's population, the artificial island of Neo Kobe City is under quarantine: humanoid robots called Snatchers are killing people and taking their places. Gillian Seed, an American with amnesia, joins JUNKER, the task force hunting them, hoping to learn about his past and his wife Jamie. His chief gives him a robot navigator, Metal Gear Mk. II, and the investigation draws in the Snatcher-hunting bounty hunter Random Hajile and leads towards the origins of the Snatcher programme.

Play runs through text menus with commands such as move, look and investigate, over mostly still images with some animation, with simple puzzles and dialogue trees and an emphasis on linear storytelling. A few action scenes have the player shoot enemies across a 3×3 grid; the Sega CD version supports the Justifier light gun.
trivia: Kojima planned five acts but had to cut the story to two because of memory limits, so the original ends on a cliffhanger.
Its first working title was Junker.
The Sega CD translation changed a character's age from 14 to 18 and censored some content.
EGM ranked the Sega CD version 69th among the best console games of all time in 1997.
Kojima and Goichi Suda made a radio drama prequel, Sdatcher, in 2011.
devStory:
Hideo Kojima wrote and designed it at Konami, drawing on Blade Runner, Akira, The Terminator and Invasion of the Body Snatchers. It was first called Junker, renamed partly because Metal Gear already had a similarly named enemy. Development took about 18 months, two to three times longer than usual, with a team about half the size of a typical Famicom project, and the planned five acts were cut to two because of memory limits, ending the story on a cliffhanger. It came out on the PC-8801 in November 1988 and the MSX2 that December.

The Japanese computer versions were well reviewed but not commercially successful. The PC Engine CD version of 1992 added a third act, and the English Sega CD version, praised for its story and mature themes, sold only a couple of thousand copies in the US.

title: Sweet Home
description: Sweet Home (1989) is Tokuro Fujiwara's Famicom horror role-playing game, loosely based on the film of the same name, and the main inspiration for Resident Evil.
longDescription:
In 1959 the artist Ichirō Mamiya hid several frescos in his mansion and disappeared. In the present day five documentary filmmakers enter the abandoned house to recover them, and the ghost of a woman traps them inside, threatening death to all trespassers, as the mansion crumbles around them and fills with monsters. The ghost turns out to be Lady Mamiya, whose two-year-old son died in the house's incinerator thirty years earlier.

The five can explore alone or in groups of two or three, switching at any time, and each carries a tool the others need: a camera, a lighter, a medical kit, a lockpick or a vacuum cleaner. Other items can be dropped anywhere and picked up by anyone. Enemies, from zombies to ghosts and dolls, appear at random and are fought in first-person menu battles, health returns only with tonics found in the rooms, and notes and diaries carry both story and puzzle clues. Traps demand split-second decisions. A character who dies stays dead, with items matching their role left by the body, and the number who survive decides which of five endings plays.
trivia: Capcom no longer held the Sweet Home licence when it made Resident Evil, so it created a new setting.
It was released only in Japan, on 15 December 1989.
Its traps that demand a quick decision are seen as a forerunner of Resident Evil 4's quick time events.
In 2024 Shinji Mikami said he would be interested in remaking it.
The director of the visual novel Otogirisō said it was "so scary that you didn't want to continue playing".
devStory:
Tokuro Fujiwara directed it at Capcom, one of his first console projects after years of arcade games, and was sometimes frustrated by the Famicom's limits. Juzo Itami, the film's executive producer, produced the game, and the film's director Kiyoshi Kurosawa supervised it and told Fujiwara not to follow the movie exactly. Junko Tamiya composed the music. It came out in Japan on 15 December 1989, promoted with a trailer on the film's video release, and won a critics' choice award at Famitsu's Best Hit Game Awards; many critics thought it better than the film.

It was never released outside Japan, though a fan translation appeared in 2000. It became the main inspiration for Resident Evil, directed by Shinji Mikami with Fujiwara producing.

title: Monkey Island 2: LeChuck's Revenge
description: Monkey Island 2 (1991) is Ron Gilbert's sequel to The Secret of Monkey Island, the first LucasArts game with the iMUSE adaptive music system, remembered for its divisive ending.
longDescription:
Months after The Secret of Monkey Island, Guybrush Threepwood is on Scabb Island looking for the legendary treasure of Big Whoop. Largo LaGrande robs him and puts the island under embargo, and when Guybrush shows Largo the living beard of LeChuck, Largo uses it to raise the pirate as a zombie. The treasure map has been split into four pieces, and the search runs across Scabb, Phatt and Booty islands — through a Mardi Gras party, a spitting contest, a drinking contest, rigged gambling and a library catalogue — to Dinky Island, where the ending at the Big Whoop amusement park reveals LeChuck to be Guybrush's brother Chuckie.

It keeps the SCUMM interface of verbs and inventory icons beneath the picture. Guybrush cannot die; when a choice would be fatal, Elaine interrupts and the player can try again. Players could choose the full game or "Monkey 2 Lite", which skips many puzzles and was jokingly said to be meant for reviewers.
trivia: Gilbert said five scenes were cut to fit the game on floppy disks.
iMUSE was co-designed by Michael Land and Peter McConnell.
Gilbert called the "monkey wrench" puzzle his least accomplished, and apologised for it.
It was shown at the June 1991 Summer CES as The Secret of Monkey Island II.
The story finally continued in Return to Monkey Island (2022).
devStory:
Ron Gilbert directed it, with Tim Schafer and Dave Grossman co-designing, writing and programming, Steve Purcell as lead artist and newly hired artists Peter Chan and Larry Ahern. Work began shortly after the first game's release in October 1990, and it was the first adventure released under the LucasArts name. It was the first game to use iMUSE, with a score by Michael Land, Peter McConnell and Clint Bajakian. Gilbert said the ending, inspired by a tester's suggestion modelled on St. Elsewhere and by Blazing Saddles, was meant to be divisive.

It came out in December 1991 on six floppy disks for DOS and the Mac, and on eleven for the Amiga in 1992. It was a critical success but a commercial disappointment, and Gilbert left LucasArts in 1992 to co-found Humongous Entertainment. A Special Edition with new graphics and audio followed in 2010.

title: Policenauts
description: Policenauts (1994) is Hideo Kojima's Japan-only adventure game, written and directed by him over about four years, with occasional shooting sections.
longDescription:
In 2013 Jonathan Ingram, a Los Angeles police officer and one of five astronaut "Policenauts", drifts into space when a new suit fails during testing, and is revived 25 years later, preserved by its cryogenic system. Now a private investigator in Old Los Angeles, he is asked by his former wife Lorraine to find her missing husband, and when she is murdered outside his office, the trail leads him to Beyond Coast, humanity's first self-sufficient space colony. There he reunites with his old partner Ed Brown, now head of the colony police's vice squad, and uncovers a drug and organ-trafficking ring behind the Tokugawa pharmaceutical company.

Play is point-and-click: the player chooses actions from text menus, examines the scene with a cursor and picks dialogue options, and occasional first-person scenes call for shooting enemies; the Saturn version supports a light gun. The original PC-98 release used pixel art, while the 3DO, PlayStation and Saturn versions added cel animation and full-motion video.
trivia: It was first called Beyond, and Konami renamed it after a trademark problem.
An English Saturn version was advertised in North America in 1996 but cancelled; fans translated it in 2009 and 2016.
Meryl Silverburgh and the Tokugawa company reappear in the Metal Gear series.
Kojima added subtitles to later versions after a complaint from a hearing-impaired player.
In 2023 Kojima described an idea for a sequel.
devStory:
Hideo Kojima wrote and directed it at Konami. The idea dated from Snatcher, and he wrote the text in 1990, building a scripting engine to time its animation and music; the project stalled until 1992 and took four years in all. Its influences included debates on organ transplants, Toyohiro Akiyama's 1990 spaceflight, NASA research on the effects of spaceflight and buddy shows such as Starsky & Hutch, and the cylindrical colony drew on Gundam. Yoji Shinkawa was among the artists. It came out on the PC-9821 on 29 July 1994, followed by the 3DO in 1995 and PlayStation and Saturn in 1996.

Japanese critics praised its presentation, animation, voice acting and setting, and GameFan called it "a masterful achievement", while others found it slow.

title: Tokimeki Memorial
description: Tokimeki Memorial (1994) is Konami's high-school dating sim, which sold over a million copies and popularised the genre in Japan; Koji Igarashi wrote its scenario.
longDescription: The player is a freshman at Kirameki High School, planning each period from twelve commands: humanities, science or arts study, exercise, clubs (eleven of them), play, fashion, rest, phone calls, dates on holidays, an information magazine and settings. Each raises different parameters, such as appearance or trivia, and phoning his friend Yoshio Saotome reveals girls' reputations, information and good date spots. Girls who feel neglected turn into "bombs" and gossip, lowering every love meter, so players learn to date in rotation; later games in the series played the bombs down. The game avoids the sexual content found elsewhere in the genre.
trivia: Igarashi had help with the writing from his then-girlfriend, later his wife, while he was playing Castlevania: Rondo of Blood.
The series grew to more than fifty games, counting remakes and spin-offs.
Famitsu readers voted it the 23rd favourite video game of all time in 2006.
The Game Boy Color version was split into Sports and Culture editions, dividing the girls between them.
A Switch remaster, Forever With You Emotional, came out in 2025.
devStory:
Yoshiaki Nagata directed it at Konami and Koji Igarashi wrote the scenario, with advice from his girlfriend, later his wife, who was working on Castlevania: Rondo of Blood; Igarashi asked to move on to Castlevania rather than make a sequel. It came out on the PC Engine Super CD-ROM² on 27 May 1994, to surprise from players who thought dating games low-grade and knew Konami for Gradius. Three of Dengeki PC-Engine's four reviewers named it the best release of the month.

The PlayStation version of October 1995, Forever With You, made it far more popular, and Super Famicom, Saturn, Windows and Game Boy Color versions followed. It sold 1.1 million copies by 1996 and popularised dating sims in Japan.

title: The Last Express
description: The Last Express (1997) is Jordan Mechner's real-time adventure aboard the Orient Express in July 1914, drawn in rotoscoped Art Nouveau style.
longDescription:
On 24 July 1914, days before the First World War, Robert Cath, an American doctor fleeing the police over a murder in Ireland, boards the Orient Express in Paris to join his friend Tyler Whitney, only to find him dead. Cath hides the body and takes Tyler's place. Among the passengers are August Schmidt, Anna Wolff, Vassili Obolensky, Tatiana Obolenskaya, Alexei Dolnikov, Miloš Jovanović and the mysterious Kronos, and the plot turns on the Firebird, a Serbian mechanical music box that Tyler meant to trade for weapons.

The player explores the train in first person, entering compartments, knocking on doors, eavesdropping and talking to people, while the clock runs at six times real speed. About thirty passengers follow their own scripted plans, changing them only when the player interferes. The pause menu can rewind to any earlier point or fast-forward to the furthest one reached. There are about thirty ways to be killed or arrested, four alternate endings and one true ending, and the script runs to about 800 pages.
trivia: It went out of print within a year of release.
Producer Mark Netter later called it "a total commercial failure".
A nearly finished PlayStation port was cancelled when SoftBank left the games business.
The ending shows a map of Europe's borders from 1914 to 1994.
Paul Verhoeven said in 2011 he was developing a film adaptation with Mechner, which was never made.
devStory:
Jordan Mechner founded Smoking Car Productions in San Francisco in 1993; at its peak it had 60 full-time staff. Inspired by Myst and Infocom's Deadline, Mechner used rotoscoping, which he had used on Prince of Persia: the cast were filmed on 16mm against bluescreen over a 22-day shoot, and the frames were turned into black-and-white line drawings and coloured by hand, 40,000 in all. Elia Cmiral wrote the score. It took five years and cost $5–6 million.

Broderbund released it on 16 April 1997, but its marketing team had quit before launch, and when The Learning Company bought Broderbund it showed no interest; the game was out of print within months. Critics praised its period atmosphere, story, music, visuals and acting, and GameSpot named it 1997's Best Story, but by 2000 it had sold only about 100,000 copies.

title: Tomba!
description: Tomba! (1997) is the PlayStation platform adventure from Whoopee Camp, the studio Tokuro Fujiwara founded after leaving Capcom, built around 130 optional quests called events.
longDescription:
Long ago the Seven Evil Pigs used magic to corrupt an uncharted archipelago, while their underlings, the Koma Pigs, terrorised its people. Tomba, a boy who guards his grandfather's grave, chases the Koma Pigs after they steal his heirloom gold bracelet. A 100-year-old Wise Man explains the Evil Pigs' history and their hoarding of gold, and the Dwarf Elder gives Tomba a blue Evil Pig Bag that reveals their hideouts.

Tomba attacks by leaping onto enemies' backs, biting them and throwing them, and also uses flails and boomerangs. Most of the game is side-scrolling, but he can climb walls to switch between the foreground and background, and some areas use an isometric view. Its 130 "events" are tasks such as finding items, rescuing characters or clearing blockades; they can be taken on at the same time and in almost any order, and completing them earns Adventure Points that unlock more events and marked chests. Tomba starts with four vitality points, lost to enemies, sharp objects and deep water and restored by eating fruit.
trivia: It was released in Europe as Tombi!, possibly because "tomba" means "grave" in Italian.
It did not sell well enough for Sony's Greatest Hits range, but was the third best-selling PSOne Classic in its 2012 North American launch month.
The European opening theme is "No Sweat" by North & South.
Limited Run Games released Tomba! Special Edition in 2024, with a new soundtrack by Harumi Fujita.
Its sequel, Tomba! 2: The Evil Swine Return, sold less, and Whoopee Camp disbanded after it.
devStory:
Tokuro Fujiwara left Capcom in December 1995, after 13 years there and just after Resident Evil came out, and founded Whoopee Camp, where he directed, produced and led the design of Tomba!. He chose side-scrolling for its straightforward thrill and designed the non-linear event system and Tomba's gradual growth to set it apart. Harumi Fujita, a longtime Capcom collaborator, joined to compose the music after hearing about the new studio.

Whoopee Camp released it in Japan on 25 December 1997 as Ore! Tomba, and Sony published it abroad in 1998 with shorter load times, more responsive controls and better visuals. It averaged 84% on GameRankings; reviewers praised the number and freedom of its events, its controls and its visuals, and GameRevolution's Mark Cooke called it the first platformer to offer such freedom.

title: Resident Evil 2
description: Resident Evil 2 (1998) is Capcom's two-disc sequel directed by Hideki Kamiya, in which rookie cop Leon Kennedy and student Claire Redfield escape a zombie-filled Raccoon City.
longDescription:
On 30 September 1998, two months after the first game, Raccoon City has been overrun by zombies created by Umbrella's T-virus. Leon S. Kennedy, a police officer on his first day, and Claire Redfield, a student looking for her brother Chris, meet as the city falls. Their paths cross with Ada Wong, who says she is searching for her boyfriend, and Sherry Birkin, the daughter of the scientist William Birkin, who has injected himself with the G-virus and keeps returning in more monstrous forms. Umbrella also drops a Tyrant, known as Mr. X, into the police station to hunt for the virus.

It plays like the original, with tank controls, fixed camera angles over pre-rendered backgrounds, herbs to heal, limited inventory and ink ribbons for saving at typewriters. Leon and Claire have separate scenarios, and finishing one's A scenario unlocks the other's B scenario, which reflects what happened in the first — the "Zapping System", for four playthroughs in all. High ranks unlock weapons, costumes and the bonus missions "The 4th Survivor" and "The To-fu Survivor".
trivia: The PlayStation version sold 4.96 million copies, the series' best-selling release on a single platform.
Next Generation called it "the must-own title of the year".
George A. Romero directed a Japanese TV advert for it starring Brad Renfro as Leon.
The Nintendo 64 version squeezed both CDs onto a 64 MB cartridge.
Gabe Newell cited it as an inspiration for taking horror seriously in Half-Life.
Capcom remade it in 2019 with over-the-shoulder controls.
devStory:
Work began in early 1996, a month after the first game was finished, with a team of about 45 under director Hideki Kamiya; producer Shinji Mikami moved to an overseeing role after creative disagreements. A first version, now called Resident Evil 1.5, starring a character named Elza Walker, was scrapped at 60–80% complete because Mikami found it dull, and supervisor Yoshiki Okamoto had Noboru Sugimura write a new scenario that left room for a continuing series; Elza was reworked into Claire. The Zapping System was partly inspired by Back to the Future Part II, and the police station was modelled on the Osaka City Central Public Hall.

It came out in North America on 21 January 1998 and sold over 380,000 copies in its first weekend, then the fastest-selling game in North America, and over 3 million worldwide in six weeks. It averaged 93% on GameRankings.

title: Super Smash Bros.
description: Super Smash Bros. (1999) is Masahiro Sakurai's Nintendo 64 crossover fighter, in which twelve Nintendo characters try to knock each other off the stage rather than drain a health bar.
longDescription:
Instead of draining a life bar, fighters try to knock each other off stages with open edges. Every hit raises a fighter's damage percentage, and the higher it climbs, the farther later attacks send them; a fighter knocked off can use jumping moves to recover. All characters share the same control inputs for their moves, and matches add blocking, dodging, grabbing and throws, plus items such as Koopa shells, hammers and Poké Balls. Up to four players fight in stock or timed matches, alone or in teams, across nine stages including Planet Zebes from Metroid and Sector Z from Star Fox. A tie goes to sudden death, with every fighter at 300% damage.

Twelve characters are playable, eight from the start and four unlocked later, each with their series' symbol behind the damage meter. In single player, the player faces a fixed run of computer opponents, later known as Classic Mode, and the minigames Break the Targets and Board the Platforms. The fighters are presented as toy dolls in a comic-book style.
trivia: Satoru Iwata suggested the "Bros." in the title.
Marth, King Dedede, Bowser and Mewtwo were planned but cut.
Clefairy was considered in place of Jigglypuff.
Its North American TV advert used "Happy Together" by The Turtles.
Sakurai showed footage of the Dragon King prototype in 2022.
devStory:
Masahiro Sakurai of HAL Laboratory wanted to make a four-player fighting game and began with a concept called Dragon King: The Fighting Game. In September 1997 he built a prototype with Mario, Donkey Kong, Samus and Fox without telling Nintendo, and showed it to the company late that year; the idea was approved. Satoru Iwata joined the project, and Hirokazu Ando composed the music. Sakurai said a session of The King of Fighters '95 in an arcade inspired him to make a fighter beginners could enjoy.

It came out in Japan on 21 January 1999 and in North America that April, where it was launched with a costumed wrestling match in Las Vegas. Critics praised its multiplayer, music, simple learning curve and original style, but found the single-player mode short. It sold over five million copies by 2001.

title: Omega Boost
description: Omega Boost (1999) is Polyphony Digital's first game and its only non-racing title, a PlayStation mecha shooter produced by Kazunori Yamauchi with mecha designs by Shoji Kawamori.
longDescription:
AlphaCore, an AI of unknown origin, turned on humanity after people tried to shut it down, and when scientists developed time travel to stop it, AlphaCore stole the technology. It built the Timeshaft on the depleted planet ETA, planning to infect ENIAC, the first general-purpose computer, with a virus hidden in a vacuum tube. Humanity's answer is Omega Boost, a giant robot fitted with a Direct Drive System for time travel, whose pilot Lester J. Hemming is sent to swap the tube.

Enemies arrive in fixed groups, formations and order, and the player chooses only which to fight first within each wave. Despite the rail-shooter structure, most stages allow free flight, though some, falling through the Timeshaft, limit speed. The booster pack that gives the game its name lets the robot move in any direction and circle-strafe, with a scanning and lock-on system. After levelling up, Omega Boost learns the Viper Boost, which makes it glow blue and damage enemies on screen; the game can be finished without it, but using it adds "Pixy" to the final ranking title.
trivia: The opening song differs by region: Feeder's "Shade" in Japan, Loudmouth's "Fly" in North America and Cast's "Dreamer" in Europe.
Its soundtrack album, released in June 1999, is rare in its limited print.
Blue Box Toys made action figures of Omega Boost and Beta Boost, but a third, Herbarcher, was never released.
Famitsu scored it higher than most Western outlets, at 28 out of 40.
It ends with Omega Boost crashing into a North American forest in 1946.
devStory:
It was Polyphony Digital's first game after Gran Turismo and its only non-racing title. Yasushi Taki and Zaika Tei directed it, Kazunori Yamauchi produced it, and Shoji Kawamori, known for Macross, designed the mecha. Its resemblance to Panzer Dragoon fuelled rumours that former members of Sega's Team Andromeda had joined Polyphony, and they were true: its lead designer and programmer, Yuji Yasuhara, had worked on Panzer Dragoon Zwei.

Sony released it in Japan on 22 April 1999 and worldwide on 14 September. It averaged 73% on GameRankings, and some reviewers found its nine levels, plus as many unlockable special missions, too short; Next Generation called it "competent, but totally uninspired".

title: Dragster
description: Dragster (1980) is David Crane's drag-racing game, one of Activision's first releases, and the subject of one of gaming's best-known disputed world records.
longDescription: Each race is a short drag against either a second player or the clock, and the lowest time wins; a game lasts about six seconds. A countdown of a few seconds starts each round, and shifting during it disqualifies the driver. After the start, the player accelerates and shifts up through four gears. Crane designed it to hold players' interest for hours despite its length, and Activision gave it a new six-digit score display drawn as graphics that could slide across the screen, replacing the 2600's standard blocky score.
trivia: Todd Rogers's 1982 time of 5.51 seconds stood until 2018, when an analysis of the game's code showed 5.57 was the best possible; Twin Galaxies and Guinness removed his records.
Video magazine called it the least of Activision's early releases and its controls clumsy.
Guinness had recognised Rogers's time as the longest-standing video game record.
The current record of 5.57 seconds has been reached by several players.
Each race lasts only about six seconds.
devStory:
David Crane, who grew up in the rural Midwest among people "somewhat obsessed" with souping up cars, made it a homage to Kee Games' 1977 arcade game Drag Race. That game had a steering wheel, accelerator and gear shift; the 2600 offered only a four-way joystick and one button, and Crane called mastering control with that scheme his "crowning achievement" on the project. It was among Activision's first four cartridges in summer 1980, sold over 500,000 copies and made more than half of Activision's first-year revenue.

In 1982 Todd Rogers claimed a time of 5.51 seconds, which Twin Galaxies and Guinness accepted for decades. The speedrunner Eric Koziel later analysed the code and showed that 5.57 seconds is the best possible, and in January 2018 both bodies removed Rogers's records.

title: Doomdark's Revenge
description: Doomdark's Revenge (1984) is Mike Singleton's sequel to The Lords of Midnight, a larger and busier war-and-adventure game in which the lords of the Icemark act on their own.
longDescription:
After Doomdark's fall in The Lords of Midnight, his daughter Shareth, Empress of Icemark, takes revenge on Luxor by bewitching and kidnapping his son Morkin. Luxor sets out with Rorthron the Wise and Tarithel the Fey, who loves Morkin. Luxor's Moonring lets the player see through the eyes of any allied or recruited character and move them in turn each day. Five peoples — Fey, Barbarians, Dwarfs, Giants and Icelords — can be won over or fought, and unlike in the first game, lords travel and react on their own while Shareth gathers armies and lords to her cause; some lords are vassals who will only follow their liege.

Fortresses and cities can be sacked and taken, terrain limits how far characters move each day, and features such as pits, temples and fountains may help or harm, some opening on an underground tunnel world. Magic crowns help in recruiting, and runes give protection, speed or travel. The computer needs only Luxor's death, while the player's victories range from rescuing Morkin to destroying Shareth and bringing everyone home.
trivia: Amstrad Action gave it 95% and a Mastergame award.
Your Sinclair readers voted it the 71st best game of all time in 1993.
Computer and Video Games serialised a gamebook version in three parts from December 1984.
The planned third part, The Eye of the Moon, was to have a map four times larger and two-player play.
Drew Wagar's novelisation came out in 2021.
devStory: Mike Singleton made it as the sequel to The Lords of Midnight, with the same mechanics but far more characters and places, and Beyond Software released it on the ZX Spectrum in 1984, with Amstrad CPC and Commodore 64 versions in 1986. It was a major critical and commercial success. Beyond offered models of the main characters to the first player to reveal the final inscription on Luxor's Moonring, and 15-year-old Richard Harris won in November 1984, though the models reached him only in January 1986, as the publisher had not expected anyone to finish so soon. A third game, The Eye of the Moon, was planned but never released.

title: Gribbly's Day Out
description: Gribbly's Day Out (1985) is Andrew Braybrook's Commodore 64 game for Hewson, in which Gribbly Grobbly hops and floats about rescuing the little gribblets.
longDescription:
On the planet Blabgor, Gribbly Grobbly hops and levitates around each level, blowing bubbles to defend himself, and carries stranded gribblets to safety. Blabgorians are psychic, with no hands, a single foot and an oversized head for storing psychic energy, and gribblets are their armoured infants, who wander from home and, once flipped onto their backs, cannot right themselves.

The beasts that hunt them pass through several forms. Seed pods fly about and, on landing, become worm-like Topsies, which flip gribblets over before forming a chrysalis. Left alone, a chrysalis hatches into a Stomper, which is armoured against bubbles but drowns easily, and which absorbs an overturned gribblet to become a Flier. Killing a Flier releases the gribblet, which survives only if it lands on flat ground or is caught in the air. An energy web, some sections of which can be switched off, hurts on contact; it imprisons Seon, a Blabgorian corrupted by evil psi-energy, and when only one gribblet is left the web fails and Seon is set free.
trivia: Braybrook wrote it in about three months.
Stompers are immune to bubbles but drown easily in water.
A level ends when every gribblet has been saved or killed.
An Acorn Archimedes version, Gribbly's Day Out on the Arc, followed in 1992.
devStory: Andrew Braybrook designed and programmed it for the Commodore 64 over about three months, and Hewson Consultants published it in 1985. Hewson later reissued a revised version on its Rack-It budget label, and Coin-Age ported it to the Acorn Archimedes in 1992 as Gribbly's Day Out on the Arc.

title: Heart of Africa
description: Heart of Africa (1985) is Danielle Bunten Berry's follow-up to The Seven Cities of Gold, an exploration game set in 1890 in search of a lost pharaoh's tomb.
longDescription:
In January 1890 the player lands from a steamer north of Cairo and sets out across Africa to find the Lost Tomb of Pharaoh Ahnk Ahnk. Movement and menus are handled with the joystick. A small map sits in the centre of the screen, with the date above it and food, money, gifts and the held item to the right, and four icons on the left: a diary that records notes automatically, including dealings with native chiefs; a map showing how much has been explored; options for checking location or health, or leaving a cache of items marked with an X; and a hand for using items, which can change how natives behave, how terrain is crossed and whether buried treasure is found.

Items are bought or traded from natives in their huts, each city has one merchant dealing in valuable goods, and chiefs reveal where treasures lie if brought what they want. At times the explorer becomes delirious, scrambling the joystick until it passes. Games can be saved only in a pub in a port city, and finding the tomb, whose location changes every game, brings a splash screen and special music.
trivia: Unlike Seven Cities of Gold, it has only one map, as Compute! pointed out.
Ahoy! thought it too easy, since the tomb could be found by accident.
Up to ten saved games fit on one formatted disk.
The explorer sometimes becomes delirious, scrambling the controls.
devStory: Danielle Bunten Berry designed it at Ozark Softscape in the style of The Seven Cities of Gold, and Electronic Arts published it for the Commodore 64 in 1985. Computer Gaming World's Stewart McKames praised its graphics and side quests, calling it "something which none of the participants will soon forget", though a 1990 survey in the same magazine gave it two-plus stars as arcade-like and unhistorical. Compute!'s Neil Randall noted it had only one map but thought it would appeal to fans of Seven Cities of Gold.

title: Dragon Quest III
description: Dragon Quest III (1988) is Yuji Horii's Famicom role-playing game, released in North America as Dragon Warrior III, which sold about 1.1 million copies in Japan on its first day.
longDescription:
On their sixteenth birthday, the son or daughter of the warrior Ortega, who apparently died in a volcano fighting the archfiend Baramos, is sent by the King of Aliahan to finish the job. The world loosely follows Earth's geography, with towns echoing Rome, Portugal and Japan. The quest gathers keys, trades black pepper for a ship and collects six orbs to revive the giant bird Ramia, which flies the party to Baramos's castle. His defeat reveals the true villain, Zoma, who opens a way into the dark world of Alefgard, where the hero finally earns the title Erdrick, linking the game to the first two as their prequel.

The hero hires companions at a tavern from seven classes — Soldier, Fighter, Pilgrim, Wizard, Merchant, Goof-Off and Sage — which shape their stats and spells; at level 20 a character can change class at the Dhama temple, returning to level 1 with halved stats but keeping their spells. A day and night cycle controls when some people, items and quests can be found, an arena takes bets on monster fights, and save slots replaced the earlier games' long passwords.
trivia: About 300 students were arrested for truancy while skipping school to buy it; Enix later chose to release its games at weekends, though no law required it.
It was the best-selling game of 1988 in Japan, with 3.8 million copies.
Its 1996 Super Famicom remake sold 1.4 million copies in Japan.
Its hero is a guest fighter in Super Smash Bros. Ultimate.
An HD-2D remake came out in November 2024.
devStory:
Chunsoft developed it a year after Dragon Quest II, with Yuji Horii writing the scenario, Akira Toriyama drawing and Koichi Sugiyama composing; Chunsoft's president Koichi Nakamura said he did about 10% of the programming. Horii disliked long password codes, so the game saves to the cartridge, and wanted a silent hero, though one scene forced the hero to shout. Enix released it on 10 February 1988.

It sold over a million copies on its first day and 3 million in a week, grossed ¥20 billion within a month and topped the Japanese charts from February to May. Famitsu named it Game of the Year, its highest-rated game of 1988. The NES version, Dragon Warrior III, reached North America in March 1992, after 16-bit consoles had arrived, and sold about 95,000 copies.

title: War in Middle Earth
description: War in Middle Earth (1988) is a real-time Tolkien strategy game, designed by Mike Singleton with Alan Clark and Robert Clardy, that runs armies and individual characters at once.
longDescription: It mixes armies and individual characters in a single real-time game, with all the action happening at once. Armies move and fight across the map of Middle-earth while characters travel it too, and locations can be viewed from the map or at ground level. Individual characters take part in the larger battles, where they can live or die. Battles of about 100 units or fewer can be watched at ground level; bigger ones are shown only as numbers. At ground level characters can pick up objects and talk to figures such as Radagast and Tom Bombadil.
trivia: Computer Gaming World praised its faithfulness to the books but found little real strategy in it.
Compute! faulted only its "anticlimactic ending".
Spain's Microhobby rated its difficulty 100%.
It was released on eight different computer systems.
devStory: Mike Singleton designed it with Alan Clark and Robert Clardy, and Synergistic Software built it on its World Builders engine. Virgin Mastertronic released it in 1988 on the Melbourne House label for MS-DOS, the Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, MSX, Amiga, Atari ST and Apple IIGS. Computer Gaming World found it faithful to the book's events but short of genuine strategy, with replays feeling very similar, and Dragon gave it three stars out of five. Compute!'s Robert Gingher called it "an otherwise impressive game", faulting only its ending.

title: A Boy and His Blob: Trouble on Blobolonia
description: A Boy and His Blob (1989) is David Crane's NES puzzle-platformer, in which a boy who cannot jump feeds jelly beans to his blob friend Blobert to turn him into tools.
longDescription:
A boy befriends Blobert, a blob from the planet Blobolonia, whose emperor lets his subjects eat nothing but sweets. The boy can only walk left and right — he cannot jump or swim, and a long fall kills him — so progress depends on Blobert, who follows him and changes shape when fed jelly beans. Licorice makes a ladder, apple a jack, punch a hole, vanilla an umbrella, and ketchup calls Blobert over; a whistle turns him back. There are 14 flavours, mostly with punning or alliterative names.

The pair travel through caves and subways under Earth, screen by screen, past falling rocks, stalactites and snakes. Treasures and diamonds raise the score and buy vitamins at a drugstore, which are fired from a VitaBlaster once they reach Blobolonia. Extra jelly beans and peppermints add lives.
trivia: It won Best of Show at CES 1989 and a 1990 Parents' Choice Award.
Imagineering finished it in about six weeks, when NES games usually took six to eight months.
GamesRadar cited it as an early example of a computer-controlled partner.
The Japanese version redrew the hero as a younger boy.
A 2009 Wii reimagining by WayForward was made without Crane.
devStory:
David Crane designed and programmed it at Imagineering, Absolute Entertainment's in-house studio, with help from Garry Kitchen. He called the premise "an off-the-wall idea", based Blobert on Gloop and Gleep from The Herculoids, and wanted to push adventure games forward as he had with Pitfall!. Finding tool inventories "not very elegant", he made the blob the tools, choosing transformations that would look good on the NES. Licensed by Nintendo in summer 1989, it was finished in about six weeks, against the usual six to eight months; a grape bean that let the boy and blob be separated was treated by Nintendo as a bug and replaced with ketchup.

It was Absolute's first NES game, released in December 1989. Reviews were mixed — IGN faulted its controls and empty environments — but Retro Gamer called it one of the company's biggest hits.

sources.title: A Boy and His Blob: Trouble on Blobolonia

title: Welltris
description: Welltris (1989) is an official entry in the Tetris series, designed by Alexey Pajitnov and Andrei Snegov, in which flat pieces drop down the four walls of a well seen from above.
longDescription: Welltris keeps Tetris's falling blocks but turns the pit into a three-dimensional well seen from above. The pieces stay flat and slide down its four walls; they can be rotated and moved along a wall, and even from one wall to the next. On reaching the 8×8 floor a piece keeps sliding until an edge or another piece stops it. Completing a solid horizontal or vertical line clears it, and the remaining squares slide to fill the gap. A piece that comes to rest with any part on a wall freezes that wall for a while, so no pieces can be moved onto it, and the game ends when all four walls are frozen.
trivia: MacUser called it "highly addictive".
Pajitnov made it partly in reaction to Blockout, whose wireframe blocks he disliked.
Zzap!64 gave the Commodore 64 version 80%, noting its more colourful graphics.
Sinclair User gave the Spectrum version only 45%.
The MS-DOS version was added to Tetris Forever in December 2024.
devStory:
Alexey Pajitnov designed it with Andrei Snegov, his first Tetris sequel, at Doka, with Bullet-Proof Software as licensee and Sphere adapting it for Spectrum HoloByte. It was inspired by Blockout (1989), which Pajitnov disliked because its wireframe blocks showed only their edges: he wanted a 2D game with a strong sense of 3D, its flat pieces falling down the walls. The MS-DOS version came first in 1989, followed by Macintosh, Amiga, Amstrad CPC and Atari ST versions in 1990 and ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64 versions in 1991.

Dragon gave the Macintosh version five stars, MacUser called it "highly addictive", and Macworld praised its gameplay, music and graphics while complaining of its steep learning curve.

title: Ultima VI: The False Prophet
description: Ultima VI (1990) is Richard Garriott's role-playing game that put all of Britannia on one seamless map and turned a war against invading gargoyles into a search for peace.
longDescription:
Some years after Lord British regains his throne, gargoyles capture the Avatar and tie them to a sacrificial altar. Shamino, Dupre and Iolo rescue them, taking the sacred text the gargoyle priest was holding, and escape through a moongate to Castle Britannia, followed by three gargoyles. The gargoyles have seized the Shrines of Virtue, but it emerges that they have virtues of their own and face a prophecy threatening their race, and the quest turns from conquest to peace.

The whole world sits on one 1,024×1,024 tile map at a single scale, with towns and castles part of it rather than separate maps, and dungeons are seen from the same overhead view instead of first person. Characters show portraits when they speak, conversations have no length limit, objects can be moved and used and things crafted, and commands are reduced to ten icons for the mouse. The box included a cloth map of Britannia and a black glass moonstone.
trivia: It sold fewer than 100,000 copies in the United States in 1990.
Computer Gaming World added it to its Hall of Fame in 1992.
The FM Towns CD-ROM version is voiced, with Garriott as Lord British.
Garriott said he wished he had thought of the icon interface for the earlier games.
The Commodore 64 port cut the portraits, horses and some dialogue and quests.
devStory:
Richard Garriott designed it and produced it with Warren Spector at Origin, influenced by Times of Lore and Dungeon Master. It was the first Ultima not developed mainly on the Apple II, which never got a version. Herman Miller wrote the movement and combat routines and Cheryl Chen the conversation language. It was built for VGA graphics and a mouse, and supported sound cards for music, though sound effects still came through the PC speaker. It came out for MS-DOS in April 1990 and ended the "Age of Enlightenment" trilogy; its engine was reused for the Worlds of Ultima spin-offs.

Strategy Plus named it the best RPG of 1990, and Computer Gaming World's Scorpia, though unsure about the interface, called it a very good game.

title: Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake
description: Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake (1990) is Hideo Kojima's Japan-only MSX2 sequel, whose radar, hearing guards and crawling set the pattern for Metal Gear Solid.
longDescription:
In 1999, during an oil crisis, the Czech scientist Dr. Kio Marv creates OILIX, an algae that produces petroleum, and is kidnapped by Zanzibar Land, a Central Asian state that plans to hold the world hostage with it and old nuclear warheads. FOXHOUND's Roy Campbell calls Solid Snake out of retirement on Christmas Eve. Inside Zanzibar Land he works with the CIA agent Holly White and the bodyguard Gustava Heffner, faces bosses such as Running Man, Red Blaster and the stealth-suited Night Sight, defeats Gray Fox in the cockpit of Metal Gear D and hand to hand in a minefield, and finally beats Big Boss with a flamethrower improvised from a lighter and an aerosol can.

Guards now patrol across screens, have a 45-degree field of vision, turn their heads and investigate noises such as wall punches, gunshots and footsteps on certain floors. Snake can kneel, crawl into ducts and under desks, and pick up mines, while a 3×3 radar shows nearby enemies until an alert switches it off. Transceiver calls change with the situation, and Snake gains health and carrying capacity after each boss.
trivia: Kojima made it in response to Snake's Revenge, the NES sequel Konami was making for Western markets.
It had no official English release until Metal Gear Solid 3: Subsistence in 2006.
The original character portraits were modelled on Mel Gibson, Sean Connery, Tom Berenger and Richard Crenna.
Killing one of the children in the fortress costs Snake health.
Its "Theme of Solid Snake" appears in Super Smash Bros. Brawl.
devStory:
After the NES Metal Gear sold over a million copies in North America, Konami began Snake's Revenge for the West without Hideo Kojima. Kojima conceived his own sequel after a junior colleague on that project talked to him on a Tokyo train, and after winning approval despite the first game's poor Famicom sales, Kojima researched it by consulting a former Green Beret and playing survival games in a forest near the office. The ROM grew from 3 to 4 megabits, and the game used Konami's SCC sound chip. Kojima wanted to call it Solid Snake, after Indiana Jones; the sales department added "Metal Gear 2".

It came out on the MSX2 in Japan on 20 July 1990 and reached number one on MSX Magazine's sales chart that October. GameSpy later called it one of the best 8-bit games ever made, and IGN credits it with introducing noise attraction, crawling and enemy view cones.

title: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons
description: Commander Keen (1990) is the shareware platformer by the team that became id Software, whose smooth scrolling on the PC came from John Carmack's adaptive tile refresh.
longDescription:
Eight-year-old genius Billy Blaze builds a spaceship and becomes Commander Keen. While his parents are out he flies to Mars, where the Vorticons steal four parts of his ship and hide them in Martian cities. In The Earth Explodes he disables the Tantalus Ray cannons of a Vorticon mothership aimed at eight landmarks on Earth, and in Keen Must Die! he travels to the Vorticon homeworld to defeat the Grand Intellect — his school rival Mortimer McMire, whose IQ is a single point higher than his own.

Keen runs and jumps through side-scrolling levels reached from a top-down map, where he can also save. A pogo stick lets him bounce higher, and a raygun with limited ammunition deals with enemies, some of which cannot be killed. Yorps can be stunned by jumping on them, keycards open locked areas, food gives points, and an extra life comes every 20,000. Secret levels and messages in a Galactic Alphabet are hidden throughout.
trivia: It began after the team recreated the first level of Super Mario Bros. 3 on the PC; Nintendo turned down the demo.
Apogee had been taking about $7,000 a month; Keen brought in over $60,000 a month by June 1991.
Scott Miller sent the team a weekly $100 "pizza bonus".
It won Best Entertainment Software and Best Overall at the 1992 Shareware Industry Awards.
A planned trilogy, The Universe Is Toast!, was cancelled after Wolfenstein 3D's success.
devStory:
In September 1990 John Carmack, working at Softdisk in Shreveport, developed adaptive tile refresh, which allowed smooth scrolling on PCs. He and Tom Hall made a demo copying Super Mario Bros. 3, and the team pitched a PC Mario to Nintendo, which declined. Apogee's Scott Miller gave them a $2,000 advance — the whole budget — to make a game by Christmas, in three parts to suit Apogee's shareware model. Hall designed it, Carmack and John Romero programmed it, and they worked nights and weekends while still at Softdisk.

The first episode went up on bulletin boards on 14 December 1990, and the other two were sold together for $30. Apogee had been making about $7,000 a month; Keen brought in nearly $30,000 by Christmas and over $60,000 a month by June 1991. The royalties let the team leave Softdisk and found id Software.

sources.title: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons

title: Fire and Ice
description: Fire and Ice (1992) is Andrew Braybrook's Graftgold platformer starring Cool Coyote, who freezes monsters with his shots and defeats them to collect the pieces of each level's key.
longDescription: Cool Coyote has to find each level's exit door and unlock it with a key made of several pieces, which are carried by monsters. His shots do no damage on their own: enough hits freeze a monster for a short time, and touching it while it is frozen kills it and frees its piece of the key. The 1994 Amiga CD32 version added detailed background scenery, 256 on-screen colours and several layers of parallax scrolling.
trivia: A finished Mega Drive version was never released.
A Game Gear version was planned but also never released.
Amiga magazines scored it 90% and above, including 92% from Amiga Mania.
Spain's Super Juegos gave the CD32 version 90.
Its full title is Fire and Ice: The Daring Adventures of Cool Coyote.
devStory:
Andrew Braybrook designed it at Graftgold with Phillip Williams, with music by Jason Page, and Renegade published it on the Amiga and Atari ST in 1992 as Fire and Ice: The Daring Adventures of Cool Coyote. Amiga magazines rated it highly: The One and Amiga Mania gave it 92%, Amiga Mania making it game of the month, Amiga Action 91% and CU Amiga 90%, and critics called it an exceptionally well-made platformer.

An MS-DOS version followed in 1993, the CD32 one in 1994, a RISC OS version in 1995 and a Master System version for Virgin in 1996.

title: Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame
description: Prince of Persia 2 (1993) is Jordan Mechner's sequel, with bigger fights, richer scenery and a 75-minute limit, ending on a cliffhanger that was never resolved.
longDescription:
Eleven days after the first game, the Prince asks for the Princess's hand, but Jaffar, magically disguised as him, has him thrown out. The Prince flees by ship, is shipwrecked by Jaffar's lightning and wakes on an island of skeletons, while Jaffar seizes the throne and puts the Princess under a slow death spell. In the ruins of Basra the Prince finds his father's dagger and sword, and visions of his mother reveal that he is the royal survivor of a massacre. At a red temple of warrior monks he learns that his shadow can leave his body and claims a magic flame, which he uses to burn Jaffar.

The sequel is heavier on combat than the original, with up to four enemies at once, sometimes from both sides, and reinforcements replacing the fallen. Areas are larger and backdrops more varied, and the Prince escapes on a magic carpet and later rides a magical horse. A 75-minute limit starts partway in and runs in real time. Lives are unlimited, but lost time can only be recovered by loading a save.
trivia: Computer Gaming World named it Action Game of the Year in 1994.
Mechner said the planned sequel to resolve its cliffhanger never came.
The ending shows a witch watching the couple in a crystal ball.
A Genesis port by Microïds was cancelled and leaked in 2006.
The Xbox version of The Sands of Time hides the game in a secret area.
devStory:
Jordan Mechner designed it, but unlike the original did not program it himself; Broderbund developed it, with music by Jonelle Adkisson. It came out for MS-DOS in May 1993, followed by Mac, FM Towns and PC-98 versions, and a 1996 Super NES port by Titus.

Most reviewers considered it an improvement on the original. Computer Gaming World's Charles Ardai called it "in every dimension better" but criticised the save system, and the magazine named it Action Game of the Year in 1994. It had sold 750,000 copies by 2000. The trilogy closed with Prince of Persia 3D in 1999.

sources.title: Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame

title: Ultima Online
description: Ultima Online (1997) is Origin's online role-playing world, produced by Richard Garriott, with skills instead of levels, player housing and open player-versus-player combat.
longDescription: Characters improve by using skills rather than through levels or classes, keep houses that persist in the world, and craft goods for an economy run by players. At launch any player could attack any other. The original world, later called Felucca, kept those harsh rules, and the Renaissance expansion of 2000 added a mirrored world, Trammel, where fighting was only by consent and more land was open for housing. Richard Garriott's character Lord British was a major figure in the world. A planned artificial-life ecology was removed after players killed all the wildlife before it could spawn.
trivia: During the 1997 beta, a player called Rainz killed Lord British, Garriott's own character, with a fire field spell because his invulnerability had not been reset after a crash.
It reached about 100,000 subscribers within six months and peaked at around 250,000 in 2003.
Guinness listed it as the first MMORPG to reach 100,000 players.
Garriott left Origin in 2000 and took Lord British with him.
The Third Dawn expansion (2001) added a 3D client.
devStory:
Work began in 1995 on a $2.5 million budget, with Garriott, Starr Long, Rick Delashmit and Scott Phillips at the core and Raph Koster later joining as lead designer, writing public "designer letters" as Designer Dragon. It was shown at E3 in May 1996 as Shattered Legacy, and Origin said over 3,000 players took part in early alpha testing. An internal forecast put the ceiling at 15,000 subscribers.

It launched on 24 September 1997 at $65 and sold 65,000 copies by mid-November; in Japan, the first 5,000 sold out in 15 minutes, and EA called it its fastest-selling computer game. It reached 100,000 subscribers within six months, causing severe lag, and won Online Game of the Year at the first Interactive Achievement Awards, though reviewers were harsh: GameSpot gave it 4.9/10.

title: Roc'n Rope
description: Roc'n Rope (1983) is Tokuro Fujiwara's Konami arcade game, described as the first "wire action" game, in which an archaeologist fires a harpoon rope to climb towards a phoenix.
longDescription: An archaeologist armed with a flashlight and a harpoon gun must climb rocky platforms to reach a phoenix. He climbs by firing ropes up to the ledges above. He has no direct way to attack: man-sized dinosaurs and red-haired cavemen can be dazed with the flashlight, or left to get caught on a harpoon rope and fall. Fallen phoenix feathers and phoenix eggs make him invulnerable for a short time.
trivia: It became the basis for Capcom's Bionic Commando (1987), which Fujiwara intended as an expanded version of it.
Coleco made Atari 2600 and ColecoVision versions in 1984.
Its title is also written "Roc 'N Rope", as on the American flyer.
It is described as the first "wire action" game.
The hero cannot attack directly, only stun enemies or trip them on his ropes.
devStory: Tokuro Fujiwara, later known for his career at Capcom, designed it at Konami, which released it in Japan on 3 March 1983 and worldwide in April, with Interlogic publishing it in North America. It is counted among Konami's early arcade hits alongside Scramble, Frogger and Yie Ar Kung-Fu, and is called the first "wire action" game. Coleco released Atari 2600 and ColecoVision versions in 1984. Hamster later added it to its Arcade Archives series, and to Arcade Archives 2 for Switch 2, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series in December 2025.

title: Mikie
description: Mikie (1984) is Konami's school maze game, in which a student dodges staff while collecting hearts that spell out a letter from his girlfriend, to chiptune versions of Beatles songs.
longDescription:
Mikie runs through his school collecting hearts that spell out a letter from his girlfriend, while staff chase him; he can head-butt them or slam doors in their faces. In the classroom he bumps students out of their seats to find the hearts beneath them, then leaves through the corridor, where only the flashing "In" door is safe and others hide a boxing glove or hairy foot. The locker room has basketballs to throw and the cafeteria roasts to hurl at the cooks, while in the dance studio dancing girls stun him. In the last stage, the garden, footballers guard the hearts on his way to his girlfriend, Mandy.

A later revision, High School Graffiti Mikie, swapped the head-butt for a paralysing shout, made him sob instead of rolling on the floor when caught, and sped enemies up after each loop.
trivia: In Japan it was set in an office and titled Shinnyū Shain Tōru-kun, because of concerns about school violence.
Its music includes versions of "A Hard Day's Night" and "Twist and Shout", licensed through JASRAC.
One corridor door hides a girl worth 5,000 points.
The revised version changed the blackboard text from "E=MC2" to "Failure Teaches Success".
Crash gave the Spectrum version a Smash award.
devStory: Konami location-tested it in Japan with its high-school theme, but did not release it there as it was because its premise of sneaking out of school came during a period of school violence.
