Along the way Trevor can recruit one partner at a time: Sypha Belnades, a sorceress with weak physical attacks but powerful elemental magic; Grant Danasty, a pirate who clings to walls and can change direction in mid-jump; and Alucard, Dracula's son, who shoots fireballs and turns into a bat. Taking on a new partner means leaving the current one behind.

Its 16 stages, called blocks, split into two main routes partway through the third. The upper route crosses a lake to the castle's main bridge and front gate, while the lower route runs through tunnels and caverns and climbs the cliff beneath the castle; they meet in the main hall. Which partner Trevor has at the end, if any, decides the ending.
trivia: IGN ranked it fifth among the best NES games.
Entering the name "HELP ME" in the Western versions starts the game with 10 lives.
Koji Igarashi named it his favourite game in the series.
Its story was adapted into the first two seasons of Netflix's Castlevania series.
In Japan Grant throws daggers; in the West he stabs with one.
devStory:
Hitoshi Akamatsu directed it at Konami, with music by Hidenori Maezawa, Jun Funahashi, Yukie Morimoto and Yoshinori Sasaki. The Japanese cartridge, Akumajō Densetsu, carried Konami's VRC6 chip, which Maezawa helped create, adding two pulse channels and a sawtooth channel; much of the music layers them to imitate a synthesised string section. It came out in Japan on 22 December 1989 and in North America on 19 September 1990, on an MMC5 cartridge with the music reworked for the standard five channels.

Western releases also changed some enemy sprites, censored nudity and cut religious imagery. Famitsu praised its return to the first game's format, the new allies and the upgraded sound, though two reviewers found it too hard. AllGame called it "the greatest Castlevania game to ever grace the NES".

title: Crystalis
description: Crystalis (1990) is SNK's post-apocalyptic NES action RPG, set in 2097, a century after a nuclear war, where four elemental swords fight enemies and clear the way.
longDescription:
The year is 2097, a century after a global nuclear war that began on 1 October 1997. Civilisation has fallen back to a medieval state, mutated creatures roam the land, and the survivors have turned from science to magic, building a floating Tower meant to watch over the world. The hero wakes with no memory, a scientist frozen until the Tower activated, and is guided by four sages — Zebu, Tornel, Asina and Kensu — who teach him magic. He sets out to stop Emperor Draygon, who has revived forbidden science and wants to enter the Tower.

Played from above, it gives the hero swords of wind, fire, water and thunder, which slash at close range, fire elemental shots when powered up, and open the way past obstacles: the Sword of Water freezes narrow rivers into ice bridges. Some enemies are immune to certain elements, and bosses cannot be harmed until the hero reaches a required level, gained through experience. A fifth sword, Crystalis, waits in the final dungeon, and the last battle is against DYNA, a machine inside the Tower.
trivia: A Game Boy Color version in 2000, developed by Nintendo Software Technology, was criticised for its lower resolution and altered story and music.
The Game Boy Color version renames Draygon "Dragonia" and makes the Tower a weapon built by the villain.
Draygon's four generals are Kelbesque, Sabera, Mado and Karmine, each with an elemental weakness.
It was included in the SNK 40th Anniversary Collection in 2018.
devStory:
Kazuto Kohno directed and produced it at SNK, with music by Yoko Osaka. Two of the sages, Kensu and Asina, are based on Kensou Sie and Athena Asamiya from SNK's arcade game Psycho Soldier. SNK released it in Japan on 13 April 1990 and in North America that July.

Critics praised its graphics, music and story but found the combat repetitive, with many enemies falling to rapid button presses. IGN later ranked it 42nd among its top 100 NES games.

title: Dr. Mario
description: Dr. Mario (1990) is Nintendo's falling-capsule puzzle game, in which the player drops two-coloured capsules into a bottle to wipe out red, yellow and blue viruses.
longDescription:
Dr. Mario tosses two-coloured capsules into a bottle, and the player moves and rotates them as they fall. Lining up four of the same colour, horizontally or vertically, destroys capsules and viruses alike, and any unsupported pieces drop. A level ends when every red, yellow and blue virus is gone, and the game is lost if capsules block the bottle's narrow neck. Before play the player picks a starting level from 0 to 20, one of three speeds and the background music.

Scoring rewards both viruses destroyed and speed, with bonuses for clearing several viruses in one line. In two-player mode, chain reactions and multiple clears send extra capsule pieces into the opponent's bottle, and the first to win three rounds takes the match. The Game Boy version has a smaller bottle and plays a burst of Super Mario Bros.' invincibility music after a chain of four or more.
trivia: In North America it sold 2.5 million copies within six weeks.
ACE called it a "plagiarism" of Tetris, and some parents objected to the medicine theme.
Henk Rogers of The Tetris Company called it "a blatant attempt" at a Tetris replacement in 2018.
IGN ranked its soundtrack seventh among the top ten 8-bit soundtracks.
Sequels run from Dr. Mario 64 (2001) to the mobile Dr. Mario World (2019), and Dr. Luigi (2013) added L-shaped capsules.
devStory:
Gunpei Yokoi produced it at Nintendo R&D1, with Takahiro Harada programming, Hiroji Kiyotake on art and Hirokazu Tanaka composing. It came out on the NES and Game Boy together in Japan on 27 July 1990 and in North America that October, with an arcade version, Vs. Dr. Mario, in August.

In Japan it sold about 3.86 million copies across the Game Boy, Famicom and later Game Boy Advance releases, and worldwide it had sold 7 million cartridges within two months. Reviews were generally positive, though ACE gave it 510 out of 1,000 and called it a "plagiarism" of Tetris. Zero called it "easy to play and impossible to master".

title: Snake Rattle 'n' Roll
description: Snake Rattle 'n' Roll (1990) is Rare's isometric NES platformer, in which snakes Rattle and Roll eat Nibbley Pibbleys so they can ring a weigh-in bell.
longDescription:
Across 11 isometric levels, the snakes Rattle and Roll eat Nibbley Pibbleys until they are heavy enough to ring the bell on the weigh-in scale at the end, which opens the exit; a snake's tail flashes once it has eaten enough. Pibbleys of the snake's own colour make it grow faster, and yellow ones most of all. Dispensers spit out Pibbleys and bombs alike, and manhole lids hide Pibbleys, items, extra lives, bonus levels and sometimes enemies.

The snakes pick up food and fight with their tongues, or jump on enemies. A hit costs a tail segment, and falling too far, running out of time, touching sharp objects or being squashed costs a life; lingering in some water brings a shark. Items include a longer tongue, speed boosts, invisibility and, less helpfully, reversed controls, and hidden warps skip several levels. One or two players can play at once.
trivia: A Mega Drive version, released only in Europe, added a 12th level on a planetoid.
Game Players gave it its 1990 NES Excellence Award.
The landscape of level 7 spells "NINTENDO GAME BOY".
One sound effect quotes the two-note theme from Jaws.
The ending teases a sequel, Snakes in Space, which was never made; the Game Boy's Sneaky Snakes (1991) reused its play in 2D.
Its NES and Mega Drive soundtracks were released on vinyl in 2020.
devStory:
Tim Stamper worked on the graphics and concepts and Mark Betteridge programmed it, contributing most of the ideas and aiming for the smallest possible NES file size. Much of the design came from Marble Madness, which Rare had ported to the NES in 1989, including its fast scrolling. Howard Phillips was executive producer. David Wise wrote the music as twelve-bar, 1950s-style rock 'n' roll, after "Shake, Rattle and Roll" (1954), which the title parodies.

Nintendo released it in North America in July 1990 and in Europe in March 1991. Mean Machines gave it 94%, while Nintendo Power worried that its characters meant nothing to buyers; IGN later ranked it 32nd among its top 100 NES games.

title: StarTropics
description: StarTropics (1990) is Genyo Takeda's Western-only NES adventure, in which Mike Jones fights with a yo-yo — and a real letter in the box had to be dipped in water to progress.
longDescription:
Mike Jones, a 15-year-old baseball captain from Seattle, visits his uncle, the archaeologist Dr. Steven Jones, at his lab on C-Island in the South Seas, only to find he has disappeared. The chief of Coralcola gives Mike a yo-yo, and his uncle's robot, Nav-Com, lets him take a submarine out to search. The trail leads to aliens: Dr. Jones had found the wreck of an escape pod from the planet Argonia, whose three magic cubes are now held by the alien leader Zoda. Mike boards Zoda's ship, recovers the cubes and escapes as it self-destructs.

The game is split into chapters, each usually built around a local disturbance. Mike explores villages and talks to their people from a top-down view, then enters dungeons, seen up close, full of enemies and obstacles. Later weapons include baseball-inspired items. At one point the player has to dip a real letter packed with the game in water to reveal the code needed to continue.
trivia: It was never released in Japan.
Its sequel was Zoda's Revenge: StarTropics II (1994).
The hidden code is 747; Nintendo Power published it after fans asked.
The Virtual Console release renamed the yo-yo a "star" and put the letter in its electronic manual.
IGN ranked it 35th among the best NES games.
devStory:
Genyo Takeda, who also developed the Punch-Out!! series, produced, wrote and directed it at Nintendo R&D3, working with Locomotive Corporation. Masato Hatakeyama programmed it, Makoto Wada drew the art and Yoshio Hirai composed the music. Nintendo released it in North America on 26 December 1990 and in Europe in 1992.

Critics compared it to The Legend of Zelda, some unfavourably; IGN's Lucas M. Thomas called it "the natural evolution of the original Legend of Zelda". Nintendo Power ranked it 64th among the best games of all time in 1997.

title: Little Nemo: The Dream Master
description: Little Nemo: The Dream Master (1990) is Capcom's NES platformer based on the animated film of Winsor McCay's comic strip, in which Nemo feeds candy to animals to ride them.
longDescription:
Nemo, a young boy, travels through his surreal dreams to Slumberland, aiming to reach Nightmare Land and rescue Morpheus, Slumberland's king, from the Nightmare King. The side-scrolling levels run mostly left to right but also up and down, and each needs a set number of keys scattered across a large stage; how many is revealed only at the exit, which has a matching number of locks.

Nemo can feed candy to animals, such as a frog, a gorilla or a mole, and then ride them. Each has its own abilities, some needed to get past particular obstacles and others only making things easier, and some have more health than Nemo himself. The game is generally regarded as very hard.
trivia: Its composer, Junko Tamiya, is credited as "Gonzou".
In Japan it was called Pajama Hero Nemo.
Kirby's Adventure, three years later, had a similar mechanic of taking on other creatures' abilities.
Gaming Bus called it "punishingly difficult at times".
Anime News Network's Todd Ciolek said its rideable animals turned each stage into a puzzle.
devStory:
Capcom made it from the 1989 animated film Little Nemo: Adventures in Slumberland, itself based on Winsor McCay's comic strip, with Tokuro Fujiwara producing, Tatsuya Minami designing and Junko Tamiya composing. It came out in North America in September 1990, in Japan that December as Pajama Hero Nemo, and later in Europe through Nintendo.

GamePro scored it 23 out of 25, and EGM's reviewers, who called it "Rescue Rangers in a dream world", praised its pastel graphics and challenge; Mean Machines criticised sprite flicker and instant-death traps but liked the animal riding. AllGame called it "a wonderfully creative side-scrolling platformer", and IGN ranked it 68th among the best NES games in 2009.

title: Gimmick!
description: Gimmick! (1992) is Sunsoft's late Famicom platformer, in which the little green Yumetaro rides his own bouncing star, released only in Japan and Scandinavia.
longDescription: Yumetaro, a small green creature, is given to a young girl as a birthday present, and her other toys, feeling neglected, come to life one night and carry her off to another dimension. Yumetaro follows to rescue her. He can jump and conjure a star above the horn on his head, which defeats enemies and can be ridden as a platform to reach places he could not otherwise get to. The six stages each end with a boss and hide a magic item; after the sixth boss the girl is still missing and the game starts over, unless every item was collected without continuing, which opens a secret stage with an extra boss and the real rescue. The screen is laid out like an arcade game, with the action above and the score below.
trivia: The Japanese cartridge used Sunsoft's 5B chip, which adds a Yamaha sound chip with three extra channels.
The Japanese original has become a collector's item, listed at £320 in a 2014 UK guide.
At the Tokyo Toy Show, a dealer lost interest once he learned it was a Famicom game.
IGN included it in its 2018 list of the top ten NES games.
A sequel, Gimmick! 2, came out in 2024.
devStory:
Tomomi Sakai conceived it and directed, designed and programmed it, with staff including Yoshiaki Iwata and Hiroyuki Kagoya from Blaster Master. Masashi Kageyama composed the music over the telephone, Sakai in Nagoya and he in Tokyo, using every available channel in styles from pop and acid jazz to hard rock. Sakai left Sunsoft before release after the opening was rewritten and his name removed.

Sunsoft released it in Japan on 31 January 1992. A North American release was cancelled because management thought the characters too quirky beside Disney and Warner Bros. cartoons, and Bergsala imported small numbers to Scandinavia in 1993 as Mr. Gimmick, with eight lives instead of four and simpler music. Reviews were mixed, and Sakai blamed its difficulty and the industry's move to 16-bit consoles.

title: Mario Paint
description: Mario Paint (1992) is Nintendo's drawing, animation and music-making package for the Super NES, sold with the Super NES Mouse, and one of the console's best sellers.
longDescription:
Packaged with the Super NES Mouse, Mario Paint combines a drawing board, a colouring book, an animation program and a music composer, with sprites and sounds drawn from Super Mario World. The drawing board has 15 colours, 75 patterns, pens, an airbrush, fills, shapes and 120 stamps, plus a stamp editor for making more. Animation Land makes loops of four, six or nine frames and can move characters along recorded paths, and work can be recorded to a VCR.

The composer writes tunes in common or triple time with 15 instrument samples shown as icons — a piano as Mario's head, a trumpet as a Fire Flower, a Game Boy for a pulse wave — and sounds such as Yoshi, a dog's bark and a baby's hiccup. It is limited to quarter notes, three notes per beat and no sharps or flats. In the minigame Gnat Attack, the player swats 100 insects and then fights the boss King Watinga. Clicking on the title screen's letters triggers Easter eggs.
trivia: The first Homestar Runner episode, in 1996, was animated with it.
Super Mario Maker began as an idea for a Wii U Mario Paint, and keeps its Undodog undo button.
Masahito Hatakeyama cited its drawing and music tools as the inspiration for WarioWare D.I.Y.
Since the early 2010s, fans have made songs and covers with its composer and replica programs.
A Satellaview version in 1997 used a standard controller instead of the mouse.
devStory:
Hirofumi Matsuoka directed it and drew its art at Nintendo R&D1 with Intelligent Systems, under producer Gunpei Yokoi, and Hirokazu Tanaka, Ryoji Yoshitomi and Kazumi Totaka composed its music. It came out in Japan on 14 July 1992 and in North America in August. The bundle sold over a million units by March 1993 and over 2.3 million in all, one of the SNES's best sellers.

Nintendo Power gave it a Most Innovative award, and critics praised its accessibility and educational potential, though some found its limits too tight for serious work; Total! gave it 48%.

title: Axelay
description: Axelay (1992) is Konami's Super NES shooter, alternating side-on stages with top-down ones warped for a pseudo-3D effect.
longDescription:
Over six stages, each ending with a boss, it switches between vertical and horizontal scrolling like Konami's Life Force. The top-down stages warp scenery and enemies into view for a pseudo-3D effect, alongside parallax scrolling. Before each stage the player picks three weapons — a main gun, a special weapon and a bomb or missile — and can switch between them freely; one new weapon is added to the armoury after every stage, rather than from power-ups.

The weapons double as armour. A hit knocks out the weapon in use and drops the ship to a weak default gun, a second hit destroys it, and crashing into an enemy is instantly fatal. The player respawns where the ship was lost, and after the final stage the game loops back to the start with denser bullet patterns. The story sends the fighter D117B to recover lost weaponry and stop the Armada of Annihilation's invasion of the Illis system.
trivia: Electronic Gaming Monthly praised its Mode 7 effects.
Famitsu reported only 4,625 copies sold in Japan.
Finishing it twice in a row on the hardest setting shows a message promising Axelay 2, which was never made because of the first game's low sales.
Its D117B fighter is an unlockable aircraft in Konami's Airforce Delta Strike.
It is in the book 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die.
devStory:
It was designed by Konami staff who went on to found Treasure, the studio behind Gunstar Heroes. Kazumi Kitaue produced it, Kazuhiro Namba drew the pixel art and Taro Kudo composed the music. It was first planned as a Japan-only release but went international after letters from players and critics. Konami released it in Japan and North America in September 1992 and in Europe a year later.

It averaged about 81% on GameRankings, and EGM ranked it 91st among the best games of all time in 1997, citing its Mode 7 effects, bosses and weapon choices.

title: The Magical Quest Starring Mickey Mouse
description: The Magical Quest (1992) is Capcom's Super NES platformer, in which Mickey changes into magician, firefighter and climber outfits to rescue Pluto from Emperor Pete.
longDescription:
While playing catch, Pluto chases the ball and Goofy goes after him, leaving Mickey alone. Mickey falls into a magical land and learns that Emperor Pete has kidnapped Pluto. Across six levels he defeats enemies by jumping on them or by grabbing and spin-throwing blocks, collects hearts that extend his health and coins to spend in shops, and changes into four outfits.

The magician's outfit fires magic blasts that grow stronger when charged, lets Mickey breathe underwater and fly a magic carpet, and refills from magic lamps. The firefighter's uniform sprays water to put out fires, push blocks and form icicles, refilling from fire hydrants. Goofy gives him mountain-climbing gear with a grappling hook. Two players can take turns, and the whole adventure turns out to be a dream.
trivia: It sold 1.2 million copies.
A Game Boy Advance remake in 2002 added Minnie as a playable character, minigames and saving.
Its sequels were The Great Circus Mystery (1994) and the Japan-only Magical Quest 3 (1995).
IGN ranked it 23rd among its top 100 SNES games.
In Japan it was called Mickey's Magical Adventure.
devStory:
Capcom made it with Noah Dudley producing, Hisashi Yamamoto designing and Mari Yamaguchi composing, and released it in Japan on 20 November 1992 as Mickey's Magical Adventure, in North America that December and in Europe in March 1993. A Mega Drive version was planned but abandoned.

It averaged 86% on GameRankings, with EGM giving it 9 out of 10 and Super Play 89%. Critics praised its graphics, animation, bosses and outfit system but called it short and easy, largely because of its unlimited continues. It sold 1.2 million copies and led to two sequels.

sources.title: The Magical Quest Starring Mickey Mouse

title: Zombies Ate My Neighbors
description: Zombies Ate My Neighbors (1993) is LucasArts' two-player monster-movie run and gun, in which Zeke and Julie save their neighbours with bazookas, weed-whackers and soda cans.
longDescription:
Zeke and Julie, alone or together, have to rescue their neighbours — barbecue chefs, teachers, babies, tourists, cheerleaders, soldiers and dogs — from the monsters of the mad scientist Dr. Tongue. The 48 stages, seven of them optional bonus levels, run through suburbs, shopping malls, pyramids and haunted castles. The monsters come straight out of horror films: vampires, werewolves, giant demonic babies, squidmen, evil dolls, giant ants, blobs, mummies, pod people, chainsaw-wielding maniacs and zombies.

The exit opens once every neighbour on a level has been saved or killed. At least one must be saved, and losing them all ends the game, as does losing every life; some levels turn from day to night, when tourists become werewolves. The weapons are household oddities — an Uzi water gun, weed-whackers, exploding soda cans, ice pops, tomatoes, silverware, crucifixes, fire extinguishers and Martian bubble guns, along with bazookas — and some suit particular monsters: silverware kills a werewolf in one hit.
trivia: In Europe it was called Zombies, and chainsaw-wielding enemies became axe-wielding lumberjacks.
A secret level references another LucasArts game, Day of the Tentacle.
The flamethrower appears only in the Super NES version.
IGN compared it to Dead Rising (2006).
It was re-released with Ghoul Patrol in the Lucasfilm Classic Games collection in 2021.
devStory:
Mike Ebert designed it at LucasArts, with Dean Sharpe programming and music by Joe McDermott and George Sanger. It was built on the Super NES and ported to the Genesis about halfway through, and its monsters drew on 1950s horror films, Friday the 13th and The Texas Chain Saw Massacre. The team wanted a battery save but could not afford one. Konami published it in North America in September 1993 on the Super NES and that November on the Genesis.

Nintendo of America had the blood and gore removed or turned into purple ooze. Reviewers praised its humour, two-player mode, graphics and music, but it was not a great commercial success; it later became a cult classic. Its engine was reused for Ghoul Patrol (1994), Metal Warriors and Big Sky Trooper.

title: Plok!
description: Plok! (1993) is the Pickford brothers' Super NES platformer, in which a hooded hero throws his own arms and legs at enemies, with music by Tim and Geoff Follin.
longDescription:
Plok, king of Akrillic in the Polyesta archipelago, wakes to find his flag stolen from its pole. Chasing it to Cotton Island, he finds impostor flags such as underpants and a striped scarf, beats the Bobbins Brothers, and returns home to find Akrillic overrun by fleas: the theft was a ruse to lure him away. A dream sequence then sends the player back fifty years as Grandpappy Plok, in search of an amulet.

Plok fires his four detachable limbs at enemies; a limb flies back at once when it hits and more slowly when it misses, and with none left he can only bounce. Some puzzles need a limb left hanging on a coat hanger to hold a switch. In most levels every flea must be killed, and the last one drops a flag that floats up to its pole. Shells give extra lives and power the amulet's buzzsaw Speed Blade, and presents turn Plok into forms such as boxing-gloved Plocky or a flamethrowing Vigilante Plok, or, in the Fleapit, put him in vehicles from a unicycle to a flying saucer.
trivia: It began as a coin-op called Fleapit at Zippo Games, which was cancelled in 1990.
Comedian Chris Sievey, of Frank Sidebottom fame, was approached to voice Plok for Fleapit.
There are no passwords because of worries that magazines would print them, and no save battery because of cost.
Super Play ranked it 26th among the best SNES games in 1996.
A Mega Drive version was announced as finished in 1994 but never released.
devStory:
Ste Pickford sketched the hooded character at Zippo Games in 1988, naming him after letters on a cassette cover, and Zippo began a self-funded coin-op, Fleapit, on Rare's Razz Board hardware. It was cancelled half-finished in 1990. The Pickfords moved to Software Creations, and near the end of Equinox they pitched it again as Plok!; John Buckley programmed the Super NES version from VHS footage of Fleapit, whose code had been lost. Tim Follin wrote the title theme on a two-chord progression from "Tequila", and Geoff Follin did about three-quarters of the soundtrack. Late in development a dispute over difficulty moved the first eight stages into the Grandpappy dream and added eight easier ones.

Tradewest released it in North America in September 1993, Nintendo in Europe that December and Activision in Japan. Super Play gave it 90%, and critics praised its limbs, power-ups, humour and music while criticising the lack of saves or passwords.

title: Goof Troop
description: Goof Troop (1993) is Capcom's two-player puzzle adventure based on the Disney cartoon, an early design by Shinji Mikami before Resident Evil.
longDescription:
Goofy and Max are out fishing with their neighbours Pete and PJ when a pirate ship carries Pete and PJ off to the pirates' stronghold on Spoonerville Island. The pirates mistake Pete for their long-lost captain, Keelhaul Pete, swallowed by a whale years before, until the real one returns. Goofy and Max explore five areas — a beach, a village under siege, a haunted castle, a cavern and the pirate ship — alone or together, with Goofy slower but harder-hitting than Max.

Neither can attack directly. Enemies are beaten by throwing barrels and bombs, kicking blocks into them or knocking them off ledges. Puzzles revolve around items such as a grappling hook, a bell that lures enemies, candles, shovels, boards for bridge gaps and keys, and some doors open only once blocks are slid into place or every enemy is beaten. Each player can carry one item, or two when playing alone. Bosses are fought by throwing objects found in the room.
trivia: Reviewers liked it in co-op but found it easy and tedious alone.
It was included in The Disney Afternoon Collection.
Fruit protects the player from one hit, and red diamonds give extra lives.
Progress is kept with passwords.
devStory:
Satoshi Murata and Shinji Mikami designed it at Capcom — one of Mikami's first designs, before he became known for Resident Evil — with Patrick Gilmore producing and music by Yuki Iwai. Based on the Disney cartoon, it came out in North America in July 1993 and on the Super Famicom in Japan in July 1994.

Nintendo Power found the challenge "fairly low" but the game "still great fun". Scores ranged widely, from 88/100 in Super NES Force to 50/100 in Nintendo Game Zone.

title: Kirby's Dream Course
description: Kirby's Dream Course (1994) is HAL's isometric mini golf game in which Kirby is the ball, reworked from an unreleased game called Special Tee Shot.
longDescription:
King Dedede has stolen the stars from the night sky, and Kirby, rolled like a golf ball across isometric courses in the style of Marble Madness, has to win them back. The player sets the power, angle and spin of each shot to knock Kirby into enemies, each worth a star, and when one enemy is left it becomes the hole. Hitting certain enemies gives Kirby copy abilities — a tornado, a sparking ball that breaks obstacles, a UFO that floats briefly — which speed up a round.

There are eight courses of eight holes, and medals for each course unlock extras such as alternate versions. In two-player mode, players take turns on their own courses as Kirby and the yellow Keeby, competing for stars, which change colour when touched and can be stolen; copy abilities can make the opponent skip a turn, and the hole is worth two stars.
trivia: HAL designed it in 1992 as Special Tee Shot with its own characters, then shelved it after Kirby's success on the Game Boy.
In Japan it was called Kirby Ball.
Keeby's yellow comes from Miyamoto's early belief that Kirby was yellow.
A Nintendo 64 sequel, Kirby Ball 64, was demonstrated in 1995 but never released; some ideas went into Kirby Air Ride.
It was one of the 30 games on the Super NES Classic Edition.
devStory:
It began as Special Tee Shot, a 1992 HAL Laboratory golf game with its own characters, which was shelved after Kirby's success on the Game Boy and later reworked with Kirby and a power-up system. Takashi Saito directed it, Satoru Iwata and Shigeru Miyamoto produced it, and Hirokazu Ando composed the music. Nintendo released it in Japan as Kirby Ball on 21 September 1994 and in North America in February 1995.

Critics praised its oddness and invention, but some found it hard and its controls took getting used to. It averaged 77% on GameRankings, and IGN ranked it 38th among the best SNES games.

title: Live A Live
description: Live A Live (1994) is Square's Super Famicom role-playing game told in seven chapters across different eras, each lead designed by a different manga artist.
longDescription:
Seven scenarios, each with its own hero and each drawn by a different manga artist, can be played in any order: Pogo in prehistory (Yoshinori Kobayashi), the Shifu's student in imperial China (Yoshihide Fujiwara), the ninja Oboromaru in late Edo Japan (Gosho Aoyama), the Sundown Kid in the Wild West (Osamu Ishiwata), Masaru Takahara in the present day (Ryōji Minagawa), Akira Tadokoro in the near future (Kazuhiko Shimamoto) and the robot Cube in the distant future (Yumi Tamura). Finishing them opens the Middle Ages chapter of the knight Oersted, and then a final chapter, "Dominion of Hate", in which the player chooses the lead.

Battles are turn-based on a 7×7 grid, and skills can be used without limit, though some take turns to charge. Each chapter also plays differently: some have random encounters, others visible enemies or only scripted fights, and while some use experience levels, one has the hero learn techniques by watching opponents. Every chapter's villain carries the name Odio, or a version of it.
trivia: It stayed in Japan until an HD-2D remake reached the Switch worldwide in 2022.
It was Yoko Shimomura's first major score after joining Square.
Ted Woolsey said an overseas release was unlikely because its graphics fell short of other titles.
The 2022 remake sold 500,000 copies in its first three months.
devStory:
Takashi Tokita directed it, his first time directing, at Square's Development Division 5, and co-wrote it with designer Nobuyuki Inoue, who also designed the battle system. It was Yoko Shimomura's first job after joining Square. Active production began in December 1993 and took about a year and a half, on a 16-megabit cartridge, and Tokita dropped a rising difficulty curve so the chapters could be played in any order. It was meant to come out before Final Fantasy VI, but delays reversed the order.

Square released it in Japan on 2 September 1994. It sold only about 270,000 copies and was seen as a commercial failure; Tokita blamed competition from established series. Critics praised its storytelling and structure but found it short, and Retro Gamer called it "a one-of-a-kind experience".

title: Wild Guns
description: Wild Guns (1994) is Natsume's science-fiction western shooting gallery for the Super NES, in which Annie and bounty hunter Clint take revenge on the Kid family.
longDescription:
Annie, whose family was kidnapped and killed by the Kid gang, persuades the bounty hunter Clint to help her take revenge. The setting is the Wild West with science-fiction and steampunk touches. The player moves along the foreground, and holding the fire button turns the controller over to the crosshair, so moving and shooting cannot happen at once; with the gun holstered the character can jump, dive and roll. A "Look Out!" bubble warns when a bullet can be dodged.

Enemy bullets can be shot down, and doing so fills a gauge that unlocks the Vulcan gun, the strongest weapon, with temporary invincibility. A lasso stuns enemies, thrown dynamite can be tossed back, and dropped crates give points, bombs that clear the screen, and shotguns and machine guns. Six levels each have two stages and a mini-boss, then a third stage with a boss. Two can play together, or compete in target practice.
trivia: Original cartridges became rare collector's items.
The "Look Out!" warning was added because bullet distances were hard to judge in the game's false 3D depth.
Annie wears a dress partly to set her apart from Clint and partly to make her easier to animate.
A 32X version was reportedly planned for 1996 but never released.
Wild Guns Reloaded (2016), made by the original team as Tengo Project, added characters, stages and four-player support.
devStory:
A small Natsume team made it quickly and cheaply in about five months while waiting for its next big assignment. Shunichi Taniguchi led development, designed it and drew the graphics, with Toshiyasu Miyabe programming and Hiroyuki Iwatsuki on sound; the three had worked together on The Ninja Warriors (1994). Influences included Dynamite Duke, Blood Bros. and the space-western manga Cobra. No voice actors were hired, and Taniguchi recorded Clint's voice in the office bathroom.

Natsume released it in Japan on 12 August 1994; the North American release slipped to 1995. EGM gave it a unanimous 8 out of 10, praising its co-op play, and it is now called a cult classic.

title: Mega Man X2
description: Mega Man X2 (1994) is Capcom's sequel, in which X battles the three X-Hunters to win back the parts of Zero's body, using the Cx4 chip for wireframe 3D effects.
longDescription:
Six months after Sigma's defeat, X leads the Maverick Hunters and must take down eight Maverick leaders on a continent south of the North Pole, where three X-Hunters — Serges, Agile and Violen — have set up base. The X-Hunters taunt X with the remains of his fallen comrade Zero, and each can be fought in an optional battle for one of his parts. Collecting all three changes the ending; otherwise X has to fight a rebuilt Zero partway through the final stage. Sigma, revealed to be a computer virus, vows to return.

The eight stages can be played in any order, and each boss leaves a weapon that another boss is weak to. X starts with the dash, wall-climbing and a chargeable X-Buster, and finds Heart Tanks, Sub-Tanks and armour upgrades: leg parts for a mid-air dash and an arm part for two charged blasts in a row. There is an attack mech in Wheel Gator's stage and a hovercycle in Overdrive Ostrich's, and a hidden capsule late in the game grants a Shoryuken-like attack.
trivia: The Cx4 chip let the cartridge rotate and scale objects and draw simple 3D wireframes.
IGN ranked it 31st among the best SNES games.
Fans' designs for the Maverick bosses were considered and rejected.
The ending theme began as the final boss music, slightly altered.
Sho Tsuge wanted Flame Stag's theme cut, but it stayed.
devStory:
Keiji Inafune produced it and handled planning, story and art, with Sho Tsuge and Yoshihisa Tsuda designing and Yuki Iwai composing. Tsuda said Inafune brought Zero back because leaving him dead would be "a shame". The X-Hunters had been sketched before the first Mega Man X, and a fourth, female X-Hunter was cut for lack of resources. The team met weekly to get the most out of the Cx4 chip. Capcom released it in Japan as Rockman X2 on 16 December 1994 and in North America in January 1995.

GamePro called it "improved in almost every way" over the original, while Game Informer and Next Generation liked it but wanted bigger changes. It averaged 82% on GameRankings.

title: Mega Man 7
description: Mega Man 7 (1995) is the original series' Super NES entry, made in about three months, which introduced Bass and his robot wolf Treble.
longDescription:
Six months after Mega Man 6, Dr. Wily's four backup Robot Masters — Burst Man, Cloud Man, Junk Man and Freeze Man — activate and free him from prison. Only those four can be chosen at first; beating them opens Spring Man, Slash Man, Shade Man and Turbo Man. Each boss leaves a weapon that another is weak to. Along the way Mega Man meets Bass and his robot wolf Treble, who seem to be rivals and then allies, until Bass wrecks Dr. Light's lab and Wily reveals they are his creations.

Rush can dig up items, and collecting the letters R-U-S-H unlocks the Super Adaptor, combining a rocket arm with a short jetpack. At Eddie's shop, run by Auto, bolts buy items and power-ups, and Mega Man can also win the robot bird Beat and Proto Man's shield. A password shown in the ending opens a hidden two-player fighting mode, in the style of Street Fighter, with Mega Man and Bass.
trivia: Keiji Inafune handed his role to Hayato Kaji, who became head illustrator.
Ten people worked on the music.
Capcom first chose not to release the finished English translation, then relented after fans objected.
Capcom of America's president admitted too few copies were shipped at launch.
Mega Man spares Wily, saying "I am more than a robot!!"
devStory:
Development was rushed onto a three-month schedule. Yoshihisa Tsuda directed it under producer Tokuro Fujiwara, and Keiji Inafune handed his role to Hayato Kaji, though Inafune designed Auto; early sketches of Bass and Treble were named "Baroque" and "Crush". The Robot Masters came from Japanese fan contests that drew about 220,000 entries, and the fighting mode was added a week before beta and finished in two days. Capcom released it in Japan on 24 March 1995 and in North America that September.

Reviewers liked its colourful presentation, controls and challenge but felt it did little new and compared it unfavourably with Mega Man X; it averaged about 71% on GameRankings. It was the only numbered game of the original series on the Super NES, and its bolt shop became standard in the series.

title: Tetris Attack
description: Tetris Attack (1995) is Intelligent Systems' block-swapping puzzle game, Panel de Pon in Japan, given a Yoshi's Island look abroad and no connection to Tetris.
longDescription:
The player moves a cursor to swap pairs of side-by-side blocks, lining up three or more of a colour in a row or column. Cleared blocks let those above fall, which can set off chain reactions, and clearing more than three at once scores a combo. The stack keeps rising from the bottom, and the game ends when it reaches the top.

Modes include a Story Mode against a run of computer opponents, an Endless Mode that speeds up over time, a two-minute Timed Mode, Stage Clear, in which every block below a line must go, and Puzzle Mode, where a fixed arrangement must be cleared in a set number of moves with no rising stack. Several multiplayer modes have adjustable difficulty.
trivia: The Japanese version stars fairies; the Western one swapped in characters from Yoshi's Island.
Despite the name, it has nothing to do with the Tetris series.
Henk Rogers said in 2009 he regretted letting Nintendo use the Tetris name, which made the game "get lost in history".
Its sequels were mostly called Puzzle League in the West, among them Pokémon Puzzle League (2000).
Lip's Stick, from Panel de Pon, is an item in Super Smash Bros. from Melee onwards.
devStory:
Intelligent Systems developed it under producer Gunpei Yokoi. The Japanese original, Panel de Pon, stars fairies in a fantasy setting; for its international release that cast was replaced with characters and settings from Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island. It came out in Japan on 27 October 1995 and in North America in August 1996, alongside a Game Boy version.

Critics praised its graphics, addictive play, accessibility and two-player mode, and it averaged 90% on GameRankings. EGM named it SNES Game of the Year, Hand-Held Game of the Year and Puzzle Game of the Year for 1996.

title: Secret of Evermore
description: Secret of Evermore (1995) is the only Square game made by North American designers, an action RPG starring a boy and his shape-shifting dog, never released in Japan.
longDescription:
In 1965 a lab accident in the small town of Podunk, USA, sends a professor and three companions into Evermore, a world built from their own ideas of utopia. Thirty years later a teenage boy and his dog follow them in. The boy crosses four realms, each ruled by one of the castaways: Prehistoria, with cavemen and dinosaurs; Antiqua, with a colosseum and a pyramid; Gothica, with castles and dragons; and Omnitopia, a space station. The dog changes with each one, from wolf to greyhound to poodle to a laser-firing robot. The villain is Carltron, the professor's butler, an android made malevolent by an intelligence chip.

It borrows Secret of Mana's ring menu and real-time combat, in which a gauge sets the strength of each attack. The boy fights with swords, spears, axes and eventually a bazooka. There are no magic points: alchemists teach formulas that each need a pair of ingredients such as wax, limestone, clay or ash, and the dog can sniff out hidden ones. Each realm has its own currency, and two of them have markets where goods can be bartered.
trivia: It was Jeremy Soule's first video game score; he says he suggested the name "Evermore".
A Japanese release was planned for a few months after North America but cancelled.
The soundtrack CD was at first available only to customers who pre-ordered.
Some PAL copies came in large boxes with a strategy guide.
It is not a sequel to Secret of Mana, and it did not replace Trials of Mana.
devStory:
Work began in early 1994 at Square's office in Redmond, Washington, where a newly assembled team was asked for an American-flavoured game in the style of Secret of Mana; the story deliberately leans on B movies and American pop culture. Alan Weiss produced it, and George Sinfield was associate producer and writer. Its working title was Vexx and the Mezmers, and the game grew from a planned 12-megabit cartridge to 24 megabits late in development. A world called Romancia was cut.

It came out in North America on 17 October 1995 and in Europe in 1996. Reviewers praised its graphics, alchemy and ring menu but judged it below Square's earlier RPGs, and it averaged 81% on GameRankings. Many of its staff later joined studios such as Humongous Entertainment, Electronic Arts and Gas Powered Games.

title: Bahamut Lagoon
description: Bahamut Lagoon (1996) is Square's Japan-only tactical RPG, in which each squad's dragon grows by being fed weapons, armour and items.
longDescription:
On Orelus, a world of lands floating in the sky, the kingdom of Kahna is overrun by the Granbelos Empire. Byuu, captain of Kahna's Dragon Squad and a silent protagonist, leads the fight back. Battles combine grid-based tactics with turn-based combat, with squads of four characters under six selectable leaders.

Each squad leader has a dragon that is never controlled directly: the player gives general orders such as "Go!" or "Wait!". Dragons grow by being fed weapons, armour, accessories and items. Foods a dragon likes raise its loyalty, and foods it dislikes lower it but can still make it stronger.
trivia: It was originally titled Final Fantasy Tactics.
Fans translated it into English in 2002 and again in 2021.
An abandoned idea had the dragons fighting and eating each other.
It was never released outside Japan.
devStory:
Hitoshi Sasaki, known for his graphic design on Final Fantasy VI, conceived it and was lead designer and lead artist, after programmer Hiroshi Ono pitched the project to Hironobu Sakaguchi. It began in 1994 as a conventional RPG with random battles before turning tactical, and took two years. Kazushige Nojima, newly arrived from Data East, directed it, Motomu Toriyama wrote the scenario and Noriko Matsueda composed the music. The dragon breeding came in the later half of development, and the setting was inspired by Sasaki's flight over the Izu Peninsula.

Square released it in Japan on 9 February 1996, one of its last Super Famicom games before moving to the PlayStation. It sold over 474,600 copies that year, Square's third-best seller after Super Mario RPG and Tobal No. 1. Edge gave it 9/10 and called its sprite work among the system's best.

title: Alleyway
description: Alleyway (1989) is Gunpei Yokoi's Breakout-style Game Boy launch title, in which a paddle bounces a ball to clear walls of bricks.
longDescription:
The player's paddle, a spaceship, moves only from side to side at a fixed height, faster while A or B is held, and must keep the ball from falling into the pit while clearing every brick. The ball travels only at 15, 30 or 45 degrees. Grey and black bricks speed it up, and changing direction at the moment of contact sends it upwards faster. Hitting the body of the paddle returns the ball, but a corner knocks it into the pit.

The 24 regular stages are built from eight brick patterns in groups of three: every second one has bricks scrolling from side to side, and every third has them advancing downwards in bursts. After the fourth stage, hitting the ceiling halves the paddle's size, and indestructible bricks appear after the twelfth. A bonus stage follows every three regular ones, for 32 in all, with patterns based on Super Mario Bros. characters such as Blooper, Bullet Bill and Bowser and a shrinking timer. The player starts with five paddles and earns one more every 1,000 points up to 10,000, with no continues and no way to save.
trivia: The original box showed an unnamed pilot in a spacesuit; later international releases replaced that character with Mario.
Scores of 10,000 and above show Super Mario Bros. sprites: a fire flower, a mushroom and a starman.
The highest score it can display is 39,999.
The 3DS Virtual Console version added a save state.
Its name refers to the gateway in the game that the paddle must pass through.
devStory:
Gunpei Yokoi designed it, inspired by Breakout and Arkanoid, with Intelligent Systems also involved and Kenji Yamamoto composing. It was one of Nintendo R&D1's first Game Boy titles and launched with the system in Japan on 21 April 1989, alongside Super Mario Land, Baseball and Yakuman, two months before Tetris; North America got it that August. Nintendo's promotion was limited to a third of a page in its magazines.

Reviews were mostly poor: Mean Machines gave it 33%, calling it boring after a few screens, and EGM's reviewers said it added little to Breakout. AllGame, though, called it fun despite its simplicity, and the book Rules of Play praised its ball-collision sounds and varied levels. Yokoi later reused much of its code, including the paddle behaviour and physics, for Kirby's Block Ball.

title: Castlevania: The Adventure
description: Castlevania: The Adventure (1989) is the first handheld Castlevania, a four-stage Game Boy game starring Simon's ancestor Christopher Belmont, with no sub-weapons.
longDescription:
Christopher Belmont, an ancestor of Simon Belmont, sets out to defeat Dracula across four stages, each against a time limit and each ending with a boss. His whip can be upgraded to a chain whip and then a flame whip, but enemy hits knock it back down a level. There are no sub-weapons, and hearts restore health instead of powering them; crystals and gold crosses can also be collected.

The player has three lives, and losing them all restarts the level. Extra lives come at 10,000 points and every 20,000 after that.
trivia: Some EGM reviewers called it the best Game Boy game they had reviewed so far.
It was remade for WiiWare as Castlevania: The Adventure ReBirth.
A 2006 fan ROM hack, "Quick Fix", sped up Christopher's movement and stopped hits from downgrading the whip.
IDW's comic series Castlevania: The Belmont Legacy (2005) is based on it.
It was included in the Castlevania Anniversary Collection in 2019.
devStory:
Y. Yamada and Masato Maegawa programmed it, with art by N. Nakazato and K. Kimura. Maegawa had joined Konami straight from university and later left to found Treasure; in a 1997 interview he said the game "was not good". Konami released it in Japan as Dracula Densetsu (Legend of Dracula) on 27 October 1989 and in North America that December.

Contemporary reviews were warm — EGM praised its graphics, and Germany's Power Play called it the best Castlevania game — though Famitsu found it too slow. Later critics were harsher about its plodding pace and stiff controls: Nintendo Life gave it 3/10 and called it an "aching disappointment". Konami said it had grossed nearly $9 million at retail by 1991.

title: The Final Fantasy Legend
description: The Final Fantasy Legend (1989) is Square's first Game Boy game and the first SaGa game, renamed in the West to tie it to Final Fantasy, and Square's first million-seller.
longDescription:
A party of up to four climbs a tower linking four worlds — Continent, Ocean, Sky and Ruins — fighting the fiends that serve Ashura. Characters are humans, mutants or monsters, a choice that cannot be changed. Humans grow stronger by using items and can equip eight of them, mutants gain random stats and abilities after battles and can equip four, and monsters equip nothing but change form by eating meat dropped in battle, which can make them stronger or weaker. Weapons and spells break or run out after a limited number of uses.

Battles are turn-based, with turn order set by agility. A fallen member loses a heart and can be revived at a heart-marked building, until they have none left. At the top of the tower the party refuses Ashura's offer to rule the worlds, then meets the Creator, who reveals that the tower is part of a game he designed. A chainsaw kills instantly — even the Creator.
trivia: Satoshi Tajiri cited it as an influence on Pokémon.
It was the first SaGa game and Square's first Game Boy title.
Nintendo Power ranked it the third-best Game Boy game of 1990.
The one-eyed monster on its Japanese box art became the SaGa series mascot.
Its Game Boy games reached Europe officially for the first time in the 2020 Switch release Collection of SaGa: Final Fantasy Legend.
devStory:
Square's president Masafumi Miyamoto asked for a Game Boy game after seeing the success of Tetris, and Akitoshi Kawazu and Koichi Ishii chose to make an RPG. Kawazu directed and wrote it, adapting ideas from Final Fantasy III for the handheld and aiming for six to eight hours of play, the length of a flight from Narita to Honolulu; encounter rates were raised to suit short sessions. Nobuo Uematsu composed its 16-track score. Square released it in Japan as Makai Toushi SaGa on 15 December 1989 and in North America in September 1990, renamed to trade on Final Fantasy's success.

It was Square's first million-seller, shipping 1.37 million copies by 2003. Famitsu scored it 35 out of 40 and placed it in its Platinum Hall of Fame, while later Western critics praised its depth but found it hard and dated.

title: Balloon Kid
description: Balloon Kid (1990) is Nintendo's Game Boy sequel to Balloon Fight, in which Alice collects balloons left by her brother Jim, built on Balloon Fight's Balloon Trip mode.
longDescription:
Alice and her younger brother Jim live in Pencilvania, a city of pencil-shaped skyscrapers, and spend their days playing with balloons. When Jim ties his balloons into a rainbow, a strong wind carries him away, and he leaves a trail of balloons for Alice to follow. She floats on two balloons of her own, flapping upwards with the A button, while the screen scrolls automatically; she can also take her balloons off to walk and jump, and blows up two new ones if she lands safely after losing both.

The route runs through a forest, an ocean with a giant whale, an icy mountain and an industrial building. Balloon Birds and a giant fish that eats anyone flying too close to the water return from Balloon Fight, and the four bosses are beaten by bouncing on them. A two-player mode, loosely based on Balloon Fight's, has Alice race her rival Samm to collect the most balloons, and Balloon Fight's Balloon Trip mode returns with Alice as its star.
trivia: It appeared in Japan as the Famicom game Hello Kitty World in 1992, and later as Balloon Fight GB in 2000.
Balloon Fight GB added colour, saves and Super Game Boy frames.
Some of its music appears in the Game Boy Camera.
IGN's Lucas M. Thomas called it a "solid little adventure game".
It was re-released on Nintendo Classics in February 2026.
devStory:
Yoshio Sakamoto designed and directed it at Nintendo R&D1, with Gunpei Yokoi producing, Hirokazu Tanaka composing and help from Pax Softnica. Nintendo released it in North America in October 1990 and in Europe in January 1991, but not in Japan, making it one of few first-party Nintendo games not released there in its original form.

Mean Machines gave it 51%, finding it repetitive and easy, while Jeff Rovin's How to Win at Game Boy Games graded it B. It averaged 66.67% on GameRankings.

title: The G.G. Shinobi
description: The G.G. Shinobi (1991) is Sega's Game Gear ninja game, in which the Red Shinobi rescues four fellow ninjas and can then switch between them, with music by Yuzo Koshiro.
longDescription:
Terror has spread to Ninja Valley. The Master of the Oboro school sent his best pupils to investigate, and they traced a dark force to a base in Neo City; one by one the others went in, and contact with all of them was lost. Joe Musashi, the Red Shinobi and the oldest and strongest of the disciples, sets out to free them and destroy the "City of Fear".

The four kidnapped ninjas are each held in a different stage, and the four stages can be played in any order. Each one rescued joins as a playable character with their own weapon, ninjutsu technique and special ability, and the player can switch between them. After the four stages comes Neo City, a series of trap rooms, each needing a particular ninja's skills and most with two exits leading on, with more bosses before the last. The play is loosely based on The Revenge of Shinobi, with the character switching added.
trivia: Retro Gamer called it "unquestionably a classic slice of ninja heaven", if "notoriously difficult".
It was the first Shinobi game developed specifically for a portable system.
Its four main stages can be tackled in any order.
Its play has been compared to Mega Man's.
A sequel, The G.G. Shinobi II: The Silent Fury, followed in 1993.
devStory: Katsuhiro Hasegawa and Masahide Kobayashi designed it at Sega, with Kenji Shintani and Yūichi Matsuoka programming and Yuzo Koshiro composing the music. It was the first Shinobi game made for a handheld. Sega released it in Japan on 26 April 1991, in North America that June with cover art by Greg Winters, and in Europe in July. The Western box calls it simply Shinobi, while the title screen reads The G.G. Shinobi.

title: Final Fantasy Adventure
description: Final Fantasy Adventure (1991) is Square's Game Boy action RPG, a Final Fantasy spin-off that began the Mana series, followed by Secret of Mana.
longDescription:
The hero escapes imprisonment by the Dark Lord, who is hunting for the key to the Mana Sanctuary so he can control the Mana Tree. The key turns out to be the pendant of the heroine he rescues. The story runs through betrayals and sacrifices — Amanda, turned into a Medusa; the robot Marcie, who gives himself up at Dime Tower — to a final battle with Julius, the Dark Lord's advisor and the last survivor of the Vandole Empire. A rusty sword the hero is led to turns out to be Excalibur.

The world is seen from above on a square grid, much like The Legend of Zelda on the NES. Weapons clear obstacles such as trees and thorns, levelling up raises hit points, power and stamina, and spells cost MP. A power gauge fills over time and empties when the hero attacks; attacking with it full unleashes a special attack. A companion occasionally joins to help. The game can be saved at any point, and it let players attack townspeople, unusual for its time.
trivia: In Japan it was Seiken Densetsu, and in Europe Mystic Quest.
It was remade as Sword of Mana (2003) and Adventures of Mana (2016).
Its sequel, Secret of Mana (1993), turned it into the Mana series.
One track, "Chocobo Tanjou", is credited to Nobuo Uematsu.
GamesRadar ranked it 13th among the best Game Boy games.
devStory:
Square had trademarked the name Seiken Densetsu in 1987 for a Famicom Disk System game that was cancelled that October. After Final Fantasy III, Koichi Ishii was offered a spin-off, working title Gemma Knights. He conceived the story, designed all the characters and directed it, with Yoshinori Kitase helping on the script and Goro Ohashi building the game system; Kenji Ito composed most of the music. Ishii's influences included Moomin, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and The Lord of the Rings.

Square released it in Japan on 28 June 1991 and in North America that November, and claimed 700,000 copies sold worldwide, 500,000 of them in Japan. Famitsu gave it 33 out of 40, and IGN later praised puzzles that it compared to Link's Awakening.

title: Defenders of Oasis
description: Defenders of Oasis (1992) is Sega's Game Gear role-playing game drawn from the Thousand and One Nights, in which the Prince of Shadam fights an empire reviving the dark god Ahriman.
longDescription:
Long ago Jamshid sealed the dark god Ahriman away with three holy rings and founded the kingdom of Shadam. Now Ahriman is manipulating the Yufurat Empire, led by a descendant of his old servant Zahhak, into hunting for those rings. When Yufurat attacks, the King gives his son the second ring, and the Prince flees with Mariam, princess of Mahamoud and keeper of another. Along the way he finds a magic lamp whose Jinn declares him its master, and he is joined by Sindbad and by the thief Agmar, who breaks him out of prison.

The game is seen from above. Villages and castles hold people to talk to, shops that buy and sell weapons, armour and accessories, and a place to recover hit points and spell points. Outside them, battles start at random and at set story moments: the party's hit points sit at the top of the screen, up to three enemies in the centre and a text command menu at the bottom, and the two sides take turns until one is beaten. Knocked-out characters can be revived with an item or spell, or come back with a few hit points if the battle is won. Progress is saved automatically.
trivia: In Japan it was called Shadam Crusader: The Far Kingdom.
Its setting is drawn from One Thousand and One Nights, with Sindbad and Ali Baba's bandits appearing along the way.
Joe Hutsko of GamePro said its graphics approached Genesis quality.
Time Extension's Damien McFerran named it the Game Gear's best RPG.
It came to the Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console on 18 July 2012.
devStory:
Sega developed and published it for the Game Gear, one of the few original role-playing games made for the handheld. It came out in Japan on 18 September 1992 as Shadam Crusader: The Far Kingdom, and in North America that December with box art by Julie Bell. In its first month it was the seventh best-selling Game Gear title at Babbage's.

Sega Force gave it 90%, Paul Wooding praising the plot and the variety of items and characters, and Adrian Pitt calling its soundtrack among the best on the Game Gear. GamePro's Joe Hutsko scored it 15.5 out of 20; he was surprised by the detail given the game's size but found the combat tedious and the music repetitive. It was re-released on the 3DS Virtual Console in July 2012.

title: Sonic Chaos
description: Sonic Chaos (1993) is Aspect's Game Gear and Master System Sonic game, in which players can choose Sonic or Tails, who can fly and hover.
longDescription:
Dr. Robotnik has stolen the Chaos Emeralds, and Sonic or Tails must win them back across six zones of three acts each, the third act of every zone being a boss fight. It was the first Sonic game to make Tails a separate playable character with his own abilities: he can fly and hover over traps. Sonic gets the Super Peel-Out from Sonic CD, and Rocket Shoes let him fly briefly.

Collecting 100 rings in a level opens a special stage, and clearing it earns a Chaos Emerald. The ending depends on how many have been collected. The game is largely based on the Master System Sonic the Hedgehog 2 and is considered its follow-up.
trivia: In Japan it was called Sonic & Tails.
Its direct sequel, Sonic Triple Trouble, followed in 1994.
The Game Gear version is an unlockable in Sonic Adventure DX.
A fan remake with 16-bit-style graphics was announced in 2018.
devStory:
It was Aspect's second Sonic game, and the studio used what it had learned on the first to make it bigger, faster and better-looking. It came out in Japan as Sonic & Tails on 19 November 1993, and on the Game Gear and the PAL Master System on 23 November as part of Sega of America's "Sonic Three on One Day" launch.

It was the top-selling Game Gear game in the US in January 1994, and EGM named it the best Game Gear game of 1993. Later reviews were cooler about its level design, slow frame rate and soundtrack.

title: Mario's Picross
description: Mario's Picross (1995) is Nintendo's Game Boy picture-logic puzzle game, a hit in Japan whose poor Western sales kept its sequels there until Picross DS.
longDescription:
Number clues along the top and left of a 5×5, 10×10 or 15×15 grid tell the player how many squares to chisel in each row and column, with gaps of unstated length between groups. Squares can be marked with a cross to show they stay blank, and a completed line helps solve those that cross it, as in a crossword. Each puzzle has 30 minutes, and mistakes cost 2, then 4, then 8 minutes each; running out of time makes Mario fall over. A finished puzzle reveals its picture with a caption and a thumbs-up from Mario.

The 256 puzzles are split across four modes of 64: Easy Picross, Kinoko and Star from the start, and an untimed Time Trial, which shows no mistakes, once the others are done. A "With Hint" option uses a roulette to fill in a row and column before starting, and the menu records each puzzle's time and whether a hint was used.
trivia: Its sequels, Mario's Super Picross and Picross 2, stayed in Japan.
The next Picross released in English-speaking countries was Picross DS in 2007, which included downloadable puzzles taken from this game.
Mario's explorer outfit from the game is an unlockable costume in Super Mario Odyssey.
It came to the 3DS Virtual Console in 2011.
It was added to Nintendo Classics on 7 March 2025.
devStory: Jupiter and Ape developed it to capitalise on the popularity of puzzle games in Japan, and Jupiter went on to make most later Picross games. Nintendo released it in Japan on 14 March 1995, promoting it with TV commercials, and abroad later that year. It sold well in Japan but poorly in America and Europe despite a large advertising campaign, and it became a cult classic. Electronic Gaming Monthly's reviewers found its logic boring after the first few puzzles, while the main criticism elsewhere was the 15×15 limit on grid size. Game Informer later ranked it fifth among its favourite Game Boy games.

title: Donkey Kong Land
description: Donkey Kong Land (1995) is Rare's Game Boy version of the Donkey Kong Country formula, sold on banana-yellow cartridges, and the best-selling Donkey Kong game on the system.
longDescription:
Cranky Kong challenges Donkey Kong and Diddy Kong to repeat the success of Donkey Kong Country on the Game Boy, and King K. Rool and the Kremlings duly steal the banana hoard again. The Kongs cross 30 levels in four worlds, each ending with a boss. Donkey is stronger and Diddy faster, and the player can switch between them at any time. Rambi the rhino and Expresso the ostrich lend their abilities in some levels.

The levels run through jungles, coral reefs, cliffs and clouds, with barrel cannons, vines and hidden bonus stages. Collecting the letters K-O-N-G saves the game, and extra lives come from balloons or from collecting 100 bananas.
trivia: It sold about 3.91 million copies, the best-selling Donkey Kong game on a Game Boy system.
GamePro named it the best Game Boy game of 1995.
It started the yellow-cartridge tradition carried on by its sequels and Donkey Kong 64.
On a Super Game Boy it adds colour palettes and a jungle border.
Donkey Kong Land 2 (1996) and Donkey Kong Land III (1997) followed.
devStory:
Rare began work in 1994, alongside Donkey Kong Country. Tim Stamper asked programmer Paul Machacek to port Country, and Machacek proposed an original game in the same style instead, spending about three weeks adapting the engine from Rare's Game Boy Battletoads. Country's pre-rendered graphics were converted to sprites with Rare's ACM compression, and levels were designed fresh rather than copied. Hardware limits allowed only one Kong on screen at once, and fewer bonus stages and animal buddies. The team grew from Machacek alone to over 15 people, and David Wise and Graeme Norgate adapted the music, with Norgate also writing new tracks.

Nintendo released it in North America on 26 June 1995, in Japan as Super Donkey Kong GB and in Europe that August. Critics praised how well it carried Country's play, visuals and music to the Game Boy, though some found the monochrome screen hard to read.

title: Wario Land II
description: Wario Land II (1998) is Nintendo's Game Boy platformer in which Wario cannot die: enemy hits cost him coins or transform him, and some transformations open new paths.
longDescription:
Picking up after Wario Land: Super Mario Land 3, Captain Syrup and the Black Sugar Gang break into Wario's castle while he sleeps, steal his treasure, set off his giant alarm clock and leave a tap running to flood the place. Wario chases them to Syrup Castle. He cannot die: enemies make him drop coins or transform him, and touching fire, for instance, turns him into Hot Wario, who burns through obstacles and enemies. Some transformations are the only way to reach certain areas.

There are no timers, health or lives, unlike its predecessor, and the aim is to finish each level with as many coins as possible. Hidden exits change the story, unlock stages and lead to different endings. Finding every treasure unlocks five alternate endings and a "Really Final Chapter" in which Wario raids Syrup's secret pirate cave, and collecting all the picture tiles opens a minigame based on Flagman.
trivia: Electronic Gaming Monthly made it Game of the Month in May 1998.
A Game Boy Color version followed later in 1998.
PC Magazine included it among the ten best Game Boy games in 2019.
It was re-released on the 3DS Virtual Console in 2012.
devStory:
Takehiko Hosokawa directed it at Nintendo R&D1, with Takehiro Izushi producing, Masani Ueda designing, Hiroji Kiyotake on art and Kozue Ishikawa composing. It came out in North America on 9 March 1998, and a colour version followed as a Japanese launch title for the Game Boy Color that October.

EGM made it Game of the Month in May 1998, and the colour version averaged 88% on GameRankings. Its approach without time limits carried over to later games in the series.

title: Dragon Warrior Monsters
description: Dragon Warrior Monsters (1998) is the Game Boy Dragon Quest spin-off in which Terry recruits monsters with meat and breeds them into stronger ones.
longDescription:
Before the events of Dragon Quest VI, a monster kidnaps Milly from her brother Terry's home at night. A monster called Watabou tells Terry that the evil Warubou has taken her and brings him to the Kingdom of GreatTree, whose King gives him a slime, Slib, as his first monster. Winning the Starry Night Tournament grants a wish, so Terry sets out to win it and rescue his sister.

Instead of fighting alone, Terry recruits monsters: setting out meat in a battle may persuade one to join afterwards. Spare monsters live on the Farm, where those kept awake grow wilder and less willing to fight, and those put to sleep stop growing. Gates beneath the throne room lead to other worlds, each with a boss in its last area, and are opened by climbing the arena's ranks from G to S, three wins each. From Class F onwards, Terry can breed a male and a female monster at the Shrine of Starry Night into an egg that inherits traits, skills and stats from both, though the parents leave the party. Some monsters can only be bred.
trivia: Terry and Milly appear as children; both come from Dragon Quest VI.
A hidden gate opens after befriending over 100 monsters.
It was the first Dragon Quest game released in Europe.
A 3DS remake, Terry no Wonderland 3D, sold 513,000 copies in its first week in Japan in 2012.
It sold about 2.35 million copies in Japan, but only about 60,000 in North America by April 2000.
devStory:
Tose developed it, with Yuji Horii designing and writing, Akira Toriyama drawing the monsters and Koichi Sugiyama composing, and Enix released it in Japan on 25 September 1998 as Dragon Quest Monsters: Terry no Wonderland. It sold 1.22 million copies that year, the fourth best-selling game of 1998 in Japan, and 2.35 million in all. Eidos co-published it in North America and Europe in January 2000, where it was the first Dragon Quest game released in Europe; it sold 60,000 copies in North America by April.

It averaged about 80% on GameRankings. IGN said it had many of Pokémon's mechanics "but better", though it preferred Pokémon's capture system, and GameSpot said its "rock-solid gameplay makes it a worthwhile endeavor".

title: Pokémon Pinball
description: Pokémon Pinball (1999) is the Game Boy Color pinball game in which the ball is a Poké Ball and players catch all 151 Pokémon across two tables.
longDescription:
The ball is a Poké Ball, and the Red and Blue tables are covered in Pokémon. Each table has locations that decide which Pokémon can appear; a slot machine picks the first one at the start of a game, and each table has its own way of moving to the next, including locations not offered at first. The main goal is score, and the secondary one is to catch all 151 Pokémon, with the Pokédex saved between games.

In Catch Mode, which lasts two minutes, each of six hits on the pop bumpers reveals a sixth of a Pokémon's picture; then it appears and must be hit four times to be caught. Evolution Mode, also two minutes, is the only way to record evolved forms: of the evolution targets on the table, three hold evolution items, and collecting all three opens the centre hole, where sinking the ball evolves the Pokémon.
trivia: It sold 262,000 copies in 20 days, the fastest-selling Game Boy game at the time.
It was the fourth best-selling US video game of 1999.
GameSpot called its rumble "a waste [...] of an AAA battery".
CNET called it "more than a shameless cash-in on the Pokémon phenomenon".
Its sequel, Pokémon Pinball: Ruby & Sapphire, came out on the Game Boy Advance in 2003.
devStory:
Jupiter and HAL Laboratory developed it, with Tsunekazu Ishihara producing and Go Ichinose composing. Nintendo released it in Japan on 14 April 1999 and in North America that June, on a cartridge with a built-in rumble.

It sold 262,000 copies in its first 20 days and was the fourth best-selling game in the US in 1999, behind only Pokémon Red, Blue and Yellow. GameSpot gave it 8.7/10, praising its presentation but criticising its physics, and called the rumble "a nice novelty". It averaged about 82% on GameRankings.

title: SNK vs. Capcom: The Match of the Millennium
description: SNK vs. Capcom: The Match of the Millennium (1999) is SNK's Neo Geo Pocket Color crossover fighter, with 26 characters from both companies and the best seller on the system in Japan.
longDescription:
Fighters battle one-on-one, in tag teams of two or in teams of three that take turns. Players choose between three power gauges: an Average mode with a Capcom-style level gauge, a Counter mode with an SNK-style charge gauge, and a Rush mode whose meter boosts super attacks when full. Each character has a rival, fought between the fourth and fifth stages, and the last two stages bring a tag team of Geese and Bison, then Orochi Iori or Evil Ryu, depending on the player's side and whether the rival was beaten. Only clearing the final stage unlocks a character's ending; otherwise a bad ending plays.

The Olympic mode adds minigames, including a Martian-shooting game taken from Metal Slug 2's final boss and one in which Arthur from Ghosts 'n Goblins hops pits for treasure, along with time-attack, first-strike and survival events. Points earned there unlock a special attack for each character and, over a link cable, extras in Card Fighters' Clash, The King of Fighters: Dream Match 1999 and Capcom vs. SNK on the Dreamcast.
trivia: IGN gave it 10/10.
It sold 75,000 copies in Japan, the best seller there on the Neo Geo Pocket.
It lost a GamePro Readers' Choice Award for best handheld game to Pokémon Yellow.
Its Japanese title translates roughly as "Final Great Battle of the Strongest Fighters".
The 2021 Switch version added local multiplayer and TV play for the first time.
devStory:
It began after SNK's Takashi Nishiyama met Capcom's head of development Yoshiki Okamoto about working together, and the two won over their companies' presidents, Eikichi Kawasaki and Kenzo Tsujimoto. Art director Toyohisa Tanabe said the project was meant to help bring games to the struggling Neo Geo Pocket Color. The roster has 26 fighters, 13 from each company, from Terry Bogard and Kyo Kusanagi to Ryu and Morrigan.

SNK released it in December 1999 in Japan and North America, the first game in the SNK vs. Capcom series. IGN gave it 10/10 and called it "the finest fighting game ever to grace a portable screen". It sold about 75,000 copies in Japan, the most of any Neo Geo Pocket game there, and was re-released on Switch and Windows in 2021.
